House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi attended the inauguration wearing a navy blue button indicating support for the Affordable Care Act; she described it in a tweet as "a symbol of our solidarity and support for the ACA during today's inauguration." Other Democratic lawmakers wore similar buttons. Democrats said the buttons expressed support, not protest, though the repeal and replacement of the ACA is a top priority for the incoming Trump administration and congressional Republicans. Representative John Lewis of Georgia boycotted the event, stating that Trump "is not legitimate president," and more than 60 members of the Democratic caucus followed suit. George Washington University law professor Jonathan Turley criticized Pelosi's button, writing that she "snatched pettiness from the jaws of dignity" and called it a "regrettable departure from tradition." Celebrities largely stayed away from the inaugural festivities.

summary: Dr. Christine Blasey Ford testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Thursday, alleging that Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh sexually assaulted her in 1982 when both were high school students. Ford said she was "100 percent" certain that Kavanaugh and his friend Mark Judge were the perpetrators. Kavanaugh testified later the same day, denying the allegations. "I am innocent of this charge," he declared. "I have never done this to her or to anyone. That is not who I am. It is not who I was." Kavanaugh said he did not question that Ford "may have been sexually assaulted by some person, in some place, at some time." He added, "I intend no ill will to Dr. Ford and her family." During his testimony, Kavanaugh paused to fight back tears while recounting that his ten-year-old daughter Liza had suggested praying for Ford. "We should pray for the woman," he quoted his daughter saying. "That's a lot of wisdom from a ten-year-old." The committee declined to call additional witnesses, including Judge. Republicans moved to schedule a confirmation vote less than 24 hours after the hearing concluded. Demonstrators and onlookers gathered outside the hearing room, many becoming emotional while listening to the testimony.

summary: President Donald Trump prepared for a summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Singapore. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo told reporters the "only outcome the United States will accept" is the "complete and verifiable and irreversible denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula." Pompeo said Trump believes Kim has "an unprecedented opportunity to change the trajectory of our relationship and bring peace and prosperity to his country," and expressed hope the summit would set conditions for future talks. Trump said he is "very well prepared" and does not need to prepare very much, adding "It's about attitude." He also said, "I believe we're going to have a terrific success, or a modified success, but in one form or another." U.S. allies and some Republicans expressed concern that Trump may concede on issues they consider deal-breakers, including the definition of denuclearization and the U.S. military presence on the Korean Peninsula. National security hawks voiced skepticism about Kim's intentions and willingness to follow through on commitments.

summary: A special election to fill the U.S. Senate seat vacated by John Kerry when he became secretary of state is scheduled for June 25 in Massachusetts. The candidates are Democratic Representative Edward J. Markey and Republican Gabriel Gomez, a former U.S. Navy pilot and SEAL team member. Gomez called Markey "pond scum" during an interview with National Public Radio. Gomez was responding to a Markey campaign internet video that juxtaposed Gomez with Osama bin Laden, according to Politico. "For him (Markey) to be as dirty and low, pond scum, like, to put me up next to bin Laden, he's just got to be called what he is. It's that simple," Gomez told NPR. Those missed votes include one on legislation to approve the Keystone XL oil pipeline, a project Markey has said he strongly opposes. Markey has also not been highly visible with retail campaign events. President Obama endorsed Markey, calling him "a passionate and effective champion for middle class and working families" and citing his record on job creation, energy and the environment. summary: Democrat Terry McAuliffe, 56, a former Democratic National Committee chair and longtime Clinton confidant who had never held elective office, was elected governor of Virginia on Tuesday, defeating Republican Attorney General Kenneth T. McAuliffe benefited from a larger campaign war chest and portrayed Cuccinelli as a hardcore conservative tea party favorite whose social views were out of step with an increasingly suburban and diverse state. Cuccinelli appealed almost entirely to his party's conservative base. Turnout was low, and both candidates campaigned through Election Day. Planned Parenthood Votes spent over $1 million in October on ads depicting Cuccinelli as "extremely dangerous for women." A Washington Post exit poll found 30 percent of self-identified pro-life voters backed McAuliffe, including 13 percent of those who believe abortion should be illegal in all cases and 17 percent of those who believe it should be illegal in most cases.

Kim Chang Son, a close aide to Kim, had already arrived to prepare. Trump left the Group of Seven summit in Canada early Saturday morning for Singapore. The meeting would be the first between a sitting U.S. president and a North Korean leader. Beforehand, Trump said he would know within the "first minute" whether Kim was serious about abandoning his nuclear program and raised the possibility of further summits.

After the Tuesday meeting, Trump said Kim had made an "unwavering commitment" to the complete denuclearization of the Korean peninsula, though sanctions would remain. Trump said both leaders were "prepared to start a new history and write a new chapter between our nations." He said Kim had told him a North Korean missile testing site "is going to be destroyed very soon," and that he would be "stopping the war games," referring to unspecified military exercises. Trump added they had discussed human rights briefly.

summary:
Stormy Daniels' attorney Michael Avenatti appeared on CNN's "The Lead" on Friday and told anchor Jake Tapper that there are facts surrounding the case that occurred while Donald Trump was president. When asked to elaborate, Avenatti said he could not go into further detail. Asked about the argument that the alleged affair occurred when Trump was a private citizen, Avenatti responded, "It's all about the cover-up."

Separately, Bloomberg News reported that Daniels, whose legal name is Stephanie Clifford, did not receive a response to a settlement offer letter sent to Michael Cohen, Trump's longtime personal attorney. In the letter, Avenatti wrote that Daniels would wire the $130,000 she received into an account of Trump's choosing in exchange for voiding the nondisclosure agreement. Cohen had until noon Tuesday to respond. Avenatti posted on Twitter: "The president and Mr. Cohen have purposely ignored our settlement offer, thus doubling down on their efforts to muzzle Ms. Clifford and prevent her from telling the American people what happened. Time to buckle up."

Cohen has acknowledged paying Daniels $130,000 shortly before the 2016 presidential election but denied the payment violated campaign finance laws. Daniels has filed a lawsuit asserting the nondisclosure agreement is invalid because Trump never signed it.

Avenatti also stated that six additional women have come forward alleging sexual relationships with Trump, adding that some of them also claim to have signed nondisclosure agreements.

summary:
After finishing fourth in the Iowa caucuses Tuesday night, Newt Gingrich and his aides arrived in New Hampshire at 3 a.m. Wednesday. In Laconia, Gingrich met Republican lawmakers at the Barley House pub opposite the State Capitol, where a protester displayed an inflated cartoon depicting him in diapers as a "crybaby." The protester declined to identify herself. Gingrich vowed to aggressively challenge Mitt Romney and Ron Paul, whose ad campaigns he said had derailed his momentum in Iowa. On Friday morning, appearing on ABC's "Good Morning America," Gingrich said Romney should drop out of the race if he does not win the New Hampshire primary. "Look, this is one of his best states other than Utah and Massachusetts. If he doesn't win here, he couldn't stay in the race," Gingrich said.

Meanwhile, Rep. Michele Bachmann finished sixth in the Iowa caucuses with 5 percent of the vote. After the results, she cancelled a planned trip to South Carolina, where the primary is scheduled for January 21. On Wednesday morning, her campaign announced an 11 a.m. EST news conference. A senior Republican official with direct knowledge of her plans, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Bachmann would suspend her presidential campaign, effectively dropping out. The official said she realized after the Iowa results that "there was no viable way forward." Bachmann had insisted as recently as Tuesday night that she is the Republican "who can and who will" defeat President Obama.

President Trump announced Monday night that he would nominate Judge Brett Kavanaugh to the United States Supreme Court to replace retiring Justice Anthony Kennedy. In a statement, Trump said he did not ask about a nominee's personal opinions and that what matters is whether a judge can set aside those views to do what the law and Constitution require. "I am pleased to say that I have found, without doubt, such a person. Tonight, it is my honor and privilege to announce that I will nominate Judge Brett Kavanaugh to the United States Supreme Court," he said. Before the announcement, Trump had said Sunday he was "very close" to naming his nominee, and a quartet of federal judges was reportedly atop the shortlist. The nomination drew immediate partisan reaction. Democratic Rep. Lois Frankel brought a metal coat hanger to a briefing and said, "I'm alarmed that five men will take us back to these days, I call them days of coat hanger medicine," while describing a friend she found "nearly dead" at 15 after a "back alley abortion." Earlier in the month, abortion rights activists had sent wire coat hangers to Republican Sen. Susan Collins to press her to vote against any nominee who would overturn Roe v. Wade. The pick divided lawmakers along partisan lines, setting up what was expected to be a bitter confirmation battle in the Senate. Cartoonists also depicted the suspense surrounding the selection process.

summary: Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, speaking on a call organized by the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, called Iowa Republican Senate nominee Joni Ernst a disaster for progressive priorities such as protecting Social Security and raising the minimum wage. Reid said Ernst was so far to the right that many conservatives would dislike her positions, praised Democratic nominee Bruce Braley as a fine man with a good public-service record, and criticized Ernst for declining to meet with Iowa newspaper editorial boards and for relying on a campaign ad about castrating pigs. A Quinnipiac University poll released during the campaign showed the race tied at 47 percent each, with 4 percent undecided. Braley led 56-36 among those who had already voted. Independents split 44-44, Republicans backed Ernst 95-2, Democrats backed Braley 94-5, women supported Braley 51-42, and men supported Ernst 52-44. Ernst, a state senator from Red Oak, defeated Braley, a four-term congressman, for the seat held by Democrat Tom Harkin. After the election, President Obama called Ernst, a White House official said. Ernst's spokeswoman Caitlin Conant declined to comment on the conversation. During the campaign Ernst had been critical of Obama and sought to tie Braley to the president.

"I've been all over the place," Trump said. "You decided to stay home, and that's okay." Clinton responded, "I think Trump just criticized me for preparing for this debate. And yes I did. And you know what else I prepared for? I prepared to be president, and I think that's a good thing." The remark drew applause from an audience that had been instructed to remain silent. Trump did not reply and Holt moved to the next topic. Clinton also said of Trump, "He has a long record of engaging in racist behavior." After the debate, Mark Cuban said Trump was "cool and calm" when discussing trade deals and pressing Clinton on her past support for them, but criticized the rest of his performance. Cuban said Trump did not answer many of Holt's questions, failed to offer specifics, never took control of a question, appeared frazzled, and deflected or changed topics when Clinton offered specifics.

summary: President Donald Trump announced on Twitter early Friday that he and first lady Melania Trump had tested positive for COVID-19. "Tonight, @FLOTUS and I tested positive for COVID-19. We will begin our quarantine and recovery process immediately. We will get through this TOGETHER!" he wrote. A senior administration official said Stephen Miller, a senior adviser and architect of the administration's "America First" foreign policy and restrictive immigration measures, had also tested positive after previously testing negative. The official said White House officials had tried to contain an outbreak on the complex that had infected Trump, the first lady, and more than a dozen other aides and associates. Miller's wife, Katie Miller, who serves as communications director to Vice President Mike Pence, had previously had the virus and tested negative after the last time she saw her husband. She had been in Salt Lake City with Pence, where he was preparing to debate Democratic vice presidential nominee Kamala Harris, but left when she learned of her husband's diagnosis. Former Vice President Joe Biden tested negative on Friday, hours after Trump's announcement, and again on Sunday. Biden did not make a public appearance on Sunday. The president's positive test raised concerns that Biden may have been exposed during Tuesday's presidential debate, though the two candidates did not make contact and their podiums were roughly 12 feet apart. Trump was admitted to Walter Reed National Military Medical Center for treatment. He showed symptoms including fever and fatigue and required supplemental oxygen at points on Friday and Saturday. Biden continued campaigning, appearing in Michigan on Friday and delivering remarks there. His campaign paused negative advertisements while Trump was hospitalized; the Trump campaign did not reciprocate.

Separately, the White House did not publicly mark the first anniversary of the Fort Hood shooting on November 5. One account noted that Obama's remarks at the Fort Hood memorial a year earlier had led with what it described as a "shout out."

In 2008, both Barack Obama and John McCain added events on Election Day. Separately, Ohio voters will find five third-party candidates on the ballot besides Obama and Romney; if the race is tied, even 1% of votes for a third candidate could affect the outcome.

summary: Russian authorities detained Ryan Fogle, a third secretary at the U.S. Embassy in Moscow, on Tuesday, accusing him of working for the Central Intelligence Agency and attempting to recruit a Russian intelligence officer. The Federal Security Service said Fogle was carrying disguises — including two wigs and three pairs of sunglasses — a compass, special technical equipment, a large sum of cash, and written instructions for the recruit. The state-run outlet Russia Today released photos and video of the arrest showing Fogle wearing a blonde wig. The Federal Security Service said Fogle was handed over to U.S. embassy officials. Embassy spokesmen declined to comment. On Wednesday, U.S. Ambassador Michael McFaul was summoned to the Russian Foreign Ministry; he entered the building and left about 30 minutes later without speaking to journalists. No details of the meeting were disclosed. The Associated Press reported the public accusation against a U.S. diplomat was the first of its kind in more than a decade.

In the speech, Obama vowed to "destroy" the terrorist group. In a prior interview with NBC's "Meet the Press," he said the U.S. would "hunt down" ISIS "wherever they are" and emphasized that the effort "is not the equivalent of the Iraq war," adding he would not advocate deploying U.S. ground troops. CNN military analyst Lt. Gen. Mark Hertling, retired, described the operational challenges of expanding into a country with a civil war, an unfavored leader, sectarian conflict, and the need to coordinate a coalition while avoiding civilian casualties.

Santorum rejected the anti-Romney label, tweeting he was "the conservative alternative to Barack Obama" and telling CNN's Wolf Blitzer the results made it "very hard for the elite media to portray Gov. summary: U.N. Special Envoy for Syria Staffan de Mistura announced plans for peace talks in Geneva starting Friday, the first such negotiations in nearly two years. Vietnam's foreign minister Pham Binh Minh arrived in North Korea on Tuesday ahead of a planned second summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Hanoi on Feb. 27-28. Separately, South Korean officials agreed to increase payments for the presence of U.S. troops in South Korea following pressure from Trump. Senate Democrats on Tuesday blocked a Department of Homeland Security funding bill that included provisions reversing President Barack Obama's executive actions on immigration, which would provide deportation relief to millions of undocumented immigrants. The procedural vote to begin debate fell 51-48, nine votes short of the 60 needed to proceed. Democrats said they support funding the department but want immigration policy addressed separately. Alexis, who had a history of mental illness and multiple gun-related arrests, was shot and killed by law enforcement. He had been undergoing mental health treatment from the Department of Veterans Affairs but retained his security clearance, which allowed him to obtain an access card for the base.

In response, Pentagon leaders announced a review of the security clearance process at a news conference. Gen. Martin Dempsey, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said service members should not be stigmatized by questions about mental health on security clearance forms and expressed doubt that such questions would have revealed the problems Alexis was experiencing. The background investigation company USIS, formerly US Investigations Services, said it conducted a background check on Alexis in 2007 when he joined the Navy. The company also performed a periodic reinvestigation of former contractor Edward Snowden's clearance in 2011. USIS said it could not disclose the reason for the Alexis check or its results because of contractual prohibitions. The Office of Personnel Management has been investigating USIS since late 2011, according to Michelle B. Schmitz, assistant inspector general for investigations, who testified at a Senate hearing in June.

Spicer left his White House post in July 2017. Afterward, he told Entertainment Weekly that "everyone has been very gracious," adding, "it's not exactly a Republican crowd." On Thursday, Spicer said on ABC that the appearance was not part of an effort to "rehab" his image, stating, "I feel very good with my image. I'm very happy with myself." The cameo drew immediate criticism on social media. Journalist Mark Harris tweeted, "NO to Sean Spicer. It's so great that we can embrace someone who used a powerful position to abuse the press and lie to America." Kelly Dittmar, an assistant professor at Rutgers University, tweeted, "Do NOT cheer for Sean Spicer. This is how we normalize & excuse unethical, racist, sexist, etc. behavior." Author Roxane Gay argued the appearance reflected white privilege. Vanity Fair's Laura Bradley wrote that host Stephen Colbert "couldn't leave the stage without finding some special way to hit the president where it really hurts," calling Spicer a "secret weapon." Others speculated whether the appearance would anger Trump. On Monday, on ABC's "The View," co-host Joy Behar said Spicer's appearance was inappropriate because "he has to apologize for his lies." Behar said, "He's a liar. Trump lies, and he and Sarah Huckabee and the rest of them who have to go out there swear to the lies. I think that they all owe the American people an apology including him and then I'll have fun with you, Spicer."

summary: Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif issued a nuclear threat against Israel on Twitter late Friday after reading a false report on the website AWDNews.com. It claimed Ya'alon had threatened to destroy Pakistan with a nuclear attack if it sent ground troops to Syria to fight the Islamic State, also known as Daesh. The Israeli Defense Ministry responded on Twitter, stating the remark attributed to former Defense Minister Ya'alon was never made and that the reports cited by the Pakistani defense minister were entirely false. Both Pakistan and Israel possess nuclear arsenals. The episode followed a separate incident three weeks earlier in which a fake news story prompted gunfire at a Washington pizzeria.

summary: U.S. District Judge Frederick J. Scullin Jr. on Saturday struck down the District of Columbia's ban on carrying handguns outside the home, ruling in Palmer v. The case had been pending for five years. The court ordered the city to cease enforcement of the ban for residents and nonresidents alike. summary:
President Trump fired FBI Director James B. Comey on Tuesday. In a letter to Comey, Trump wrote: "While I greatly appreciate you informing me, on three separate occasions, that I am not under investigation, I nevertheless concur with the judgment of the Department of Justice that you are not able to effectively lead the Bureau." The FBI had been investigating whether Moscow coordinated with anyone in Trump's campaign to influence the 2016 presidential election in Trump's favor. The House and Senate intelligence committees were also conducting investigations.

The firing prompted immediate calls for an independent investigator or commission to examine Russia's election interference and any connections between Trump associates and the Russian government. Calls for an independent prosecutor had been made for months, primarily by Democrats. Following the dismissal, House Republican Justin Amash called for an independent commission. Senators Elizabeth Warren and Edward Markey, both Massachusetts Democrats, called for an independent prosecutor; Warren tweeted, "we need a real, independent prosecutor" and said Trump should not pick the person to conduct the investigation. Warren also said that while "there's no question that Comey made questionable decisions during the election," it was hard to believe Trump had fired the top official investigating his ties to Russia because Comey was unfair to Hillary Clinton. The letter, addressed to House Speaker John Boehner and the Senate, stated: "These personnel will support the operation of intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance aircraft for missions over northern Nigeria and the surrounding area." Obama wrote that the force will remain in Chad until its support is no longer necessary. Chad shares a border with northeastern Nigeria.

The girls were kidnapped last month. One account put the number at more than 200; another at almost 300. According to one report, they were taken from a remote town in predominantly Muslim northeastern Nigeria. Boko Haram seeks to turn Nigeria, a nation of about 170 million people, into an Islamic republic under sharia law; Christians make up roughly half the population.

The deployment is part of a widening commitment of U.S. resources. The military's Global Hawk drone, which can remain airborne for more than 28 hours, and the MC-12 Liberty reconnaissance plane are also part of the effort. The troops sent to Chad are part of a drone launch-and-recovery team.

summary: During the third and final presidential debate in Las Vegas, Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton and Republican candidate Donald Trump clashed over Russian President Vladimir Putin. The 90-minute debate occurred just under three weeks before Election Day, with early voting already underway in more than 30 states. Clinton accused Trump of favoring Putin over American military and intelligence experts, saying Putin would "rather have a puppet as president of the United States." Trump responded, "Nope. You're the puppet!" Clinton further accused Trump of being "willing to spout the Putin line" and "sign up for his wish list" after allegedly praising Putin in the past. Trump denied any relationship with Putin, stating he did not know him and that Putin had said nice things about him, adding that getting along would be good and that Putin had no respect for Clinton. Trump said he would condemn any foreign interference in the election but refused to accept allegations that Russia was behind the hacking of Democratic organizations. The Clinton campaign said the FBI was investigating Russia's involvement in the hacking of a top adviser's emails. Separately, Clinton adviser Jake Sullivan issued a statement linking to an NBC News translation of a Putin interview. Sullivan said Putin had confirmed Trump was "carrying Russia's water with his pro-Putin wish list of policies" and that Putin was trying to influence the election through cyber-attacks because he knew Clinton would stand up to him. In the interview, Putin reportedly expressed uncertainty about the U.S. election outcome, saying, "We don't know for sure how it will be after the elections... We don't know whether the presidential candidate Trump will be implementing his intentions, how far will he go in cooperating with us; or whether Mrs. Clinton, if she becomes president, will implement her threats and her harsh rhetoric about Russia."

summary:
The Senate Foreign Relations Committee approved a resolution authorizing the use of military force against Syria on Wednesday by a vote of 10-7, with one senator voting present. The amended resolution authorizes limited military intervention with a 90-day deadline and bars U.S. ground troops from combat operations. The committee's action clears the way for a full Senate debate.

To satisfy a procedural requirement that at least one day elapse between filing legislation and beginning debate, the Senate will convene a brief pro forma session on Friday — lasting approximately 30 seconds, according to a senior Senate aide — to formally file the resolution. This allows Senate Majority Leader Harry M. Reid (D-Nev.) to open debate on Monday evening when senators return from the five-week summer recess.

The administration has said it would not put U.S. boots on the ground in Syria. The resolution is considered more likely to pass in the Senate than in the House, where most Republicans have opposed it on grounds that it gives President Barack Obama too much discretion. Some Democrats also oppose the measure, citing reluctance to engage in another Middle East military mission as the United States draws down forces in Afghanistan.

Sen. Patrick Leahy (D-N.H.), who opposed the initial White House draft, welcomed the scheduled debate. "I remain skeptical of the United States going alone, and about what comes after. But this will be an important Senate debate, on deadly serious issues, about a resolution that may well see further changes," Leahy said. "It makes sense to have the debate and then decide, not to decide and then have the debate."

Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid said the Senate will not pass any continuing resolution that alters the health-care law. Meanwhile, the House and Senate have already approved a stand-alone bill ensuring troops receive paychecks during a shutdown; Reid brought it up by unanimous consent after Senate Republicans pressed for action, and it now awaits President Obama's signature. Earlier, Reid led Democrats in rejecting two other House proposals that would have kept agencies open while modifying the health law. Separately, House Appropriations Committee ranking member Nita Lowey, D-N.Y., questioned why legislation to reopen national parks would take priority over nutrition and service programs for seniors, poor mothers and children. Republican leaders plan to bring such "mini" appropriations bills to the floor under suspension of the rules, which requires a two-thirds vote and therefore Democratic support. Reid dismissed the approach as "just another wacky idea" the Senate will reject.

Gotta put people back to work and make it happen. So we're going to give it all we've got, absolute full-in 100 percent effort, because I worry we won't recognize our country if we don't do this." Asked on Monday at a campaign stop in Paducah, Ky., whether Mr. Clinton would hold a cabinet position, Mrs. Clinton shook her head and said, "No." Aides said Mr. Clinton's role would be narrowly defined to focus on hard-hit areas such as the Rust Belt, and they rejected any implication that Mrs. Clinton would outsource a central part of her administration to her spouse. Mrs. Clinton has not provided details about how a former president would fit into a policy-making role in her administration, a position without precedent in American politics.

summary: Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, 84, did not attend President Donald Trump's first State of the Union address on Tuesday. Instead, she delivered a previously scheduled talk at Roger Williams University in Rhode Island, which had been planned since August, according to the Providence Journal. Ginsburg also skipped Trump's 2017 address to a joint session of Congress after attending all eight of former President Barack Obama's congressional addresses. Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas were also absent from the 2018 State of the Union; historically, Justice Antonin Scalia had not attended a presidential address since 1997. Ginsburg stated she is not retiring and intends to continue at "full steam," noting she has hired law clerks through June 2020. Former Arkansas Governor Mike Huckabee posted a tweet about Ginsburg's absence that misspelled her surname and referenced her dozing during Obama's 2015 State of the Union, which she later attributed to wine consumed at a prior dinner. Representative Carlos Curbelo (R-Fla.) called Huckabee's remark "despicable" and "tasteless." In 2016, Ginsburg had called then-candidate Trump a "faker"; Trump responded on Twitter that her mind was "shot."

summary:
U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un met in Singapore on Tuesday for a historic summit. The two leaders signed a two-page document committing Kim to denuclearization, while Trump agreed to provide security guarantees for North Korea. Trump said he intended to invite Kim to visit the White House, and North Korean state media reported that Kim accepted the invitation.

Arriving back in the United States on Wednesday, Trump wrote on Twitter: "Everybody can now feel much safer than the day I took office. There is no longer a Nuclear Threat from North Korea. Meeting with Kim Jong Un was an interesting and very positive experience. North Korea has great potential for the future!" He added that North Korea was no longer the United States' "biggest and most dangerous problem."

Fred and Cindy Warmbier, parents of Otto Warmbier, thanked Trump for his comments about their son after the summit. "We appreciate President Trump's recent comments about our family," they said in a statement. "We are proud of Otto and miss him. Hopefully something positive can come from this." In Singapore, Trump had told reporters that Warmbier was a "very special person" and that his death had galvanized the administration's determination to deal with North Korea. "I think, without Otto, this would not have happened," Trump said. "Something happened, from that day. It was a terrible thing. It was brutal. But a lot of people started to focus on what was going on, including North Korea." "Otto did not die in vain," he said. "He had a lot to do with us being here today."

Warmbier, a University of Virginia student, was arrested by North Korean authorities in January 2016 for stealing a propaganda poster and sentenced to 15 years in prison with hard labor. After suffering still unexplained brain injuries, he was released on June 13, 2017, and died six days later.

summary:
During the second day of Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh's Senate confirmation hearings on Wednesday, Sen. Dianne Feinstein questioned him on abortion rights and the Second Amendment.

On abortion, Feinstein cited a Guttmacher Institute study, stating that deaths from illegal abortions in the 1950s and 1960s "ran between 200,000 and 1.2 million." The institute's 2003 report found that the number of illegal abortions performed annually during those decades was between 200,000 and 1.2 million, while the number of reported deaths was about 300 in 1950 and about 200 in 1965, with a caution that actual deaths were likely higher. Feinstein spokeswoman Ashley Schapitl said the statistic was written incorrectly in the senator's question and that Feinstein meant to cite the number of illegal procedures, not deaths.

On the Second Amendment, Feinstein asked Kavanaugh about a dissent he wrote when his colleagues on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit upheld a District of Columbia ban on semi-automatic rifles. Kavanaugh wrote in his dissent that semi-automatic rifles are in "common use" and protected by the Second Amendment.

On the third day of hearings, Sen. Cory Booker said he would release an email in which Kavanaugh reportedly expressed sympathy for racial profiling. Separately, the New York Times obtained an email in which Kavanaugh wrote that Roe v. Wade is "not established law and can be overturned."

summary:
Former national security adviser Michael Flynn pleaded guilty Friday in federal court to a single charge of lying to FBI agents about his conversations with Russian ambassador Sergey Kislyak during the presidential transition period in late December. The charge carries a maximum penalty of five years in prison. As part of the plea agreement, Flynn agreed to cooperate fully with special counsel Robert Mueller's investigation into Russian election interference and alleged coordination between Trump campaign officials and Moscow.

Court filings from the plea hearing indicate that Mueller's investigators are focused on the actions of President Donald Trump and his senior team. Investigators said Flynn was acting on the direction of at least one other senior Trump transition adviser, believed to be presidential son-in-law Jared Kushner.

The White House said late Friday morning that "nothing about the guilty plea or the charge implicates anyone other than Mr. Flynn." President Trump told reporters Saturday as he departed the White House for New York City: "What has been shown is no collusion. There's been absolutely no collusion, so we're very happy." Trump has previously called the investigation a "witch hunt" and a Democratic ploy, and said Saturday, "We'll see what happens."

The complaint against Flynn said he contacted Kislyak after the Obama administration imposed sanctions on Russia for meddling in the presidential election. Flynn reportedly discussed tensions between the U.S. and Russia regarding the sanctions. Russia agreed not to escalate the situation, a move Trump commended.

Flynn, a retired Army lieutenant general, served as White House national security adviser for less than one month before resigning under pressure. Vice President Mike Pence said Flynn misled him about the extent of his contacts with Russian officials during the transition.

summary: The father of the two Boston Marathon bombing suspects, Anzor Tsarnaev, said in an interview on Sunday that he planned to travel from Russia to the United States in several days to seek "justice and the truth," adding he had "lots of questions for the police" and wanted "to clear up many things." The suspects' mother, Zubeidat Tsarnaeva, told journalists on Monday that Tsarnaev planned to fly to the U.S. on Wednesday and that the family would try to bring the body of their elder son, Tamerlan Tsarnaev, back to Russia. Tamerlan Tsarnaev, 26, was killed in a gunfight with police early Friday. His 19-year-old brother, Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, was captured Friday night, alive but badly wounded, and hospitalized in serious condition. The FBI disputed Tsarnaeva's assertion that the bureau had tracked Tamerlan Tsarnaev for as long as five years. FBI chief spokesman Mike Kortan said he stood by an FBI statement issued Friday that the only communication the FBI had with Tamerlan Tsarnaev was a 2011 interview conducted at the urging of a foreign government, since identified as Russia. The FBI also stated on Sunday that agents did not know the identities of the alleged bombers until Friday. The U.S. Embassy in Moscow said it had sent a team of investigators to Dagestan, a province in southern Russia where the parents are staying, on Tuesday. An embassy official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the Russian government is cooperating with the FBI investigation into the April 15 Boston Marathon bombing. The Tsarnaev brothers are accused of setting off the bombs that killed three people and wounded more than 180 others.

summary:
On Friday, February 3, 2012, Republican presidential candidates campaigned ahead of weekend contests. Mitt Romney, Newt Gingrich, and Ron Paul appeared in Nevada, where caucuses were scheduled for February 4, while Rick Santorum campaigned in Missouri. Romney was slated to speak at 11 a.m. in Sparks, Nevada. Santorum was seen as poised to perform well in Minnesota caucuses on Tuesday, February 7, which could disrupt Romney's momentum following victories in Florida (January 31) and Nevada. On Monday, February 6, Romney's campaign began criticizing Santorum, who had previously avoided being a primary target.

Separately, campaign finance reports filed by a midnight Tuesday deadline showed Romney leading the Republican field with $57.1 million raised, followed by Ron Paul at $26.1 million, Newt Gingrich at $12.7 million, and Rick Santorum at $2.2 million.

Also on February 3, the Labor Department released January employment numbers. A Joint Economic Committee hearing on the report was set for 9:30 a.m. EST. President Obama was expected to announce a new jobs program at 11:30 a.m. in Arlington, Virginia. The House planned to take up an insider-trading ban already passed by the Senate. Defense Secretary Leon Panetta faced questions after an interview suggested he was concerned about a possible Israeli attack on Iran within months; Panetta had not denied the report. Forecasters predicted two feet of snow for the Denver area.

summary: Sen. Mark Udall (D-Colo.) became the first Democratic senator to call for Veterans Affairs Secretary Eric Shinseki's resignation, followed by Sens. John Walsh (D-Mont.), Kay Hagan (D-N.C.), Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) and Al Franken (D-Minn.), as well as a number of House Democrats. Calls for Shinseki's ouster came from both Republicans and Democrats in Congress amid widespread allegations of treatment delays at VA hospitals nationwide. President Barack Obama summoned Shinseki to the White House Friday morning for a meeting in which the secretary was expected to update the president on an internal review; Obama said in television interviews aired Thursday that he planned a "serious conversation" with Shinseki about whether he is prepared to fix the problems. The White House also said Obama is waiting for a full investigation before deciding who to hold responsible. Shinseki separately was scheduled to address the National Coalition for Homeless Veterans on Friday to provide an update on combating veterans homelessness. Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel, who previously expressed strong support for Shinseki, told reporters in Asia he would leave it to others to decide if Shinseki has to go. Shinseki wrote an op-ed calling the report's findings "reprehensible to me and to this department, and we are not waiting to set things straight," detailing steps taken and planned. Since Obama took office, the VA budget has increased 50 percent from $100 billion to $150 billion, while the number of those eligible for veterans' benefits more than doubled from 400,000 to 918,000.

summary: Julia Pierson resigned as director of the Secret Service on Wednesday amid bipartisan criticism over security breaches at the White House. White House press secretary Josh Earnest said Pierson's delay in informing President Obama about a September incident in Atlanta — in which an armed man rode an elevator with the president at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — was a crucial factor. Pierson had met with Obama the previous week but told him of the Atlanta lapse only minutes before it became public on Tuesday evening. Earnest said Obama concluded the agency needed new leadership and called Pierson on Wednesday to thank her for her service. The White House said Obama has full confidence in Joseph Clancy, a former special agent named acting director, and is awaiting a review to determine whether more personnel changes will follow. summary: French President Emmanuel Macron addressed the U.S. Congress on Wednesday, urging free and fair trade and warning that a commercial war between allies would be inconsistent with shared missions, history and current commitments for global security. The speech came as U.S. tariffs on European steel and aluminum were scheduled to take effect in coming weeks unless President Donald Trump signed a waiver, raising the prospect of a broader trade conflict. In a separate development, Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif wrote on Twitter that Macron was correct in stating there was no "Plan B" for the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, the 2015 nuclear agreement signed by the United States, Iran, France, Russia, China, Germany, the United Kingdom and the European Union. "It's either all or nothing," Zarif wrote, adding that European leaders should encourage Trump not only to remain in the deal but to implement the U.S. portion in good faith. Trump had set a May 12 deadline to either improve the accord or withdraw. In an interview broadcast Sunday on CBS's "Face the Nation," Zarif said withdrawal would isolate the United States, noting that advisors had told the administration the JCPOA was not a bilateral Iran-U.S. agreement and that leaving would signal the U.S. was not a reliable partner. "Iran has many options and those options are not pleasant," Zarif said. According to one report, Macron had previously stated that he persuaded Trump to order missile strikes in Syria despite the U.S. president's isolationist impulses. Macron was also scheduled to appear on Fox News Sunday for an interview with Chris Wallace at the Élysée Palace, ahead of an official visit to the United States later in the month.

summary: Egypt's military announced on Wednesday that it was ousting President Mohammed Morsi, the country's first freely elected leader, and replacing him with the chief justice of the Supreme Constitutional Court. Army chief Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi said in a televised address that the Islamist-backed constitution was suspended, early presidential elections would be called, and a government of technocrats would be appointed to run the country during an unspecified transition period. A new Cabinet would be formed, and el-Sissi warned that the armed forces and police would deal "decisively" with violence. A statement on the president's office Twitter account quoted Morsi as calling the measures "a full coup" that "represent a full coup categorically rejected by all the free men of our nation." An aide, Ayman Ali, said Morsi had been moved to an undisclosed location. Cheers erupted among millions of protesters nationwide who had demanded Morsi's ouster, and fireworks lit the Cairo night sky. Morsi supporters elsewhere in the city shouted "No to military rule." Despite the announcement, Morsi had insisted he would remain in power.

Senator Marco Rubio and former Florida Governor Jeb Bush, once political partners and neighbors in Florida, clashed during the third Republican presidential debate Wednesday night over Rubio's Senate voting attendance record. The Sun Sentinel had called for Rubio to resign before the debate. During the debate, Bush said: "What is it like a French work week? Do you have to show up for like three days? Just show up or resign." Rubio responded: "Someone has convinced you that attacking me is going to help you, but I'm not running against Jeb Bush or anyone else on this stage. I'm running for president because there's no way we can elect Hillary Clinton." Rubio also criticized the Sun Sentinel, calling it evidence of media bias. On Thursday, Bush defended his attack in a Fox News interview, telling host Jenna Lee it was not a mistake and saying it is a "mistake to run for an office and not serve." He dismissed an anonymous donor's suggestion that his campaign was "terminal" as "pretty funny." Rubio's team expressed confidence after the debate but urged donors to increase fundraising, which they described as the campaign's most serious obstacle to beating Bush. Some Bush supporters were described as despondent, privately questioning whether three debate performances had damaged his nomination prospects, while Rubio supporters were described as euphoric about his performance.

summary: U.S. and Iraqi intelligence officials said the Islamic State is assembling a team of scientists from Iraq and Syria, including some who formerly worked for Saddam Hussein's Military Industrialization Authority, to conduct research and develop chemical weapons, according to a published report. Separately, President Barack Obama spoke at a news conference in Antalya, Turkey, where he rejected the notion that the United States had underestimated the Islamic State group following the deadly attacks in Paris. Obama said the group's danger is the reason the United States is operating in Iraq and Syria and has mobilized 65 countries against it. He said reducing the territory the group controls in Iraq and Syria would reduce the flow of fighters and lessen the threat, and that disrupting the threat requires constant vigilance and communication. Obama called the Islamic State "the face of evil" and said the United States and its allies are shrinking its hold in Syria and Iraq. He said sending a major U.S. ground force would be a serious mistake, according to his military advisers, and would lead to an unsustainable strategy requiring long-term occupation. Obama said the U.S. military could easily march into Mosul, Raqqa, or Ramadi but that would only be a temporary solution, and asked what would happen if an attack originated in Yemen or Libya if 50,000 troops were sent to Syria.

Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell warned President Barack Obama that a State of the Union address devoted to rallying the Democratic base would diminish prospects for bipartisan legislation before the 2016 election. Speaking on the Senate floor, McConnell said the tone and issues Obama highlighted would reveal much about his presidency's final act. He said Republicans hoped the president would engage on free-trade legislation and tax reform, but expressed alarm that he was instead touting tax and fee increases on wealthy families and banks and free community college for lower- and middle-income students. "The American people aren't demanding talking point proposals designed to excite the base, but not designed to pass," McConnell said. "What they said they're hungry for is substance and accomplishment." He urged Obama to call for bipartisan jobs initiatives such as authorizing the Keystone XL pipeline, reforms to extend Medicare solvency, and a plan to balance the budget, advocating "realistic" reforms that could win GOP backing rather than programs that "spend more money we don't have." "We need to turn the page. The State of the Union offers that opportunity," he said. Earlier at a news conference, McConnell told reporters, "With all due respect to him, he doesn't set the agenda in the Senate," and added, "We're going to try to do the things that we think will make America a better place." Senate Finance Committee Chairman Orrin Hatch, speaking at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, characterized Obama's plan as class warfare. "This plan that we'll hear about tonight appears to be more about redistribution, with added complexity, and class warfare, directed at job-creating small businesses, than about tax reform which is unfortunate to me," Hatch said. He also remarked, "Sadly, it doesn't appear that President Obama gets it."

summary:
Fidel Castro, Cuba's revolutionary leader, died Friday at age 90. His brother Raul Castro, to whom he had handed power in 2006, announced the death. Castro's remains will be cremated per his wishes, with funeral details to be announced Saturday.

North Korea declared a three-day mourning period with flags at half-staff at official buildings. State media reported Kim Jong Un sent a wreath to the Cuban Embassy in Pyongyang, and a delegation of senior officials left for Havana for memorial services. A Japanese monitoring agency said Castro is the first foreign figure honored this way since Yasser Arafat in 2004.

President Barack Obama offered condolences to the Castro family, avoiding praise or criticism and addressing the Cuban people. "We know that this moment fills Cubans — in Cuba and in the United States — with powerful emotions, recalling the countless ways in which Fidel Castro altered the course of individual lives, families, and of the Cuban nation," he said. "History will record and judge the enormous impact of this singular figure on the people and world around him."

In Miami, large crowds of Cuban exiles celebrated late Friday, waving flags, cheering, dancing and banging pots and pans. Castro's government improved living conditions for the very poor, achieved health and literacy levels on par with rich countries and removed a powerful Mafia presence, but also tolerated little dissent, jailed opponents, seized private businesses and monopolized media. Opponents called him a dictator; hundreds of thousands fled, many settling in Florida and shaping U.S. policy toward Cuba.

summary: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un arrived in Singapore on Sunday for a historic summit with U.S. President Donald Trump scheduled for Tuesday, marking the first meeting between a sitting U.S. president and a North Korean leader. Singapore Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan tweeted a photograph of himself shaking hands with Kim at Changi Airport, writing: "Welcomed Chairman Kim Jong Un, who has just arrived in Singapore." Videos circulating on social media showed Kim's black limousine arriving Sunday afternoon at the St. Regis Hotel, where he is reportedly staying, surrounded by jogging bodyguards dressed in identical black suits. The temperature was about 90 degrees Fahrenheit with humidity at about 70 percent. The bodyguards, who run alongside the limousine, are part of what is known as the Central Party Office #6, or formally the Main Office of Adjutants, according to the BBC. The BBC reported the men are national service conscripts from the Korean People's Army selected for their skills, including marksmanship and martial arts prowess, as well as their appearance, and must be about the same height as Kim. Kim's close aide Kim Chang Son was already in Singapore preparing for the summit. Trump departed a Group of Seven summit in Canada ahead of schedule Saturday morning to travel to Singapore. At a news conference Saturday, Trump said he would know within the "first minute" of meeting Kim whether the North Korean leader was serious about abandoning his nuclear program. The 3,000-mile journey is the farthest Kim has traveled as leader, according to Time magazine, which reported he brought three airplanes and a convoy of armored vehicles from Pyongyang. Singapore said it has spent millions of dollars to secure the summit and its participants.

summary: On April 14, armed militants from Boko Haram abducted more than 300 girls from a secondary school in Borno state, Nigeria, driving them into the Sambisa forest. While some girls escaped, police said 276 remained missing. Boko Haram leader Abubakar Shekau claimed responsibility in a video message, stating: "I abducted your girls. I will sell them in the market, by Allah." Civic organizations reported that the girls were being forced to marry extremists for as little as $12 and had been trafficked across borders to Chad and Cameroon. The Obama administration announced it would send a team of military and law enforcement personnel to assist in the search. The U.S. Senate passed S.Res. 433 by voice vote condemning the kidnappings. Senator Reid called the situation "sickening" and described the Nigerian government's response as "very tepid." Representative Carolyn Maloney urged "decisive and swift" action including sanctions against Boko Haram, comparing the international response to that for the missing Malaysian aircraft. "Of course she's going to play the woman card. That's what she does. And the way to deal with the woman card is to attack her track record," Fiorina said.

Donald Trump said Clinton's remark that he has "demonstrated a penchant for sexism" makes Bill Clinton's past "fair game." Clinton's comment followed Trump's remark that she was "schlonged" by Barack Obama in the 2008 Democratic primary and his mocking of her for using the bathroom during a Democratic debate.

Blog posts from 2008 show Trump previously praised Hillary Clinton, writing "I know Hillary and I think she'd make a great president or vice-president," and calling her "smart, tough and a very nice person" and a "great trouper." He also called Bill Clinton a "great President." Trump has since stepped up attacks on Hillary Clinton, including criticism of Bill Clinton's past infidelities.

summary: The Trump campaign and Republican National Committee filed a lawsuit in Arizona alleging that poll workers in Maricopa County improperly instructed voters to press a green button on new voting machines to override errors, causing the machines to disregard votes cast in person on Election Day. Matt Morgan, general counsel for Trump 2020, said poll workers struggled to operate the machines. The campaign sought inspection of overvoted ballots. The Arizona filing was part of ongoing litigation in multiple battleground states as the president declined to concede the election. Separately, a lawsuit claiming that the use of county-issued Sharpie markers on Maricopa County ballots could have invalidated Election Day votes was voluntarily dropped by the plaintiffs without prejudice on Saturday, hours after news organizations projected Joe Biden's win. The Sharpie lawsuit had alleged that tabulation equipment was unable to record ballots marked with the markers. Arizona election officials said the claim was unfounded, and Attorney General Mark Brnovich stated after an investigation that there was nothing to the allegations. Maricopa County elections officials appeared in court on Thursday to explain to Judge Margaret Mahoney that the markers did not cause votes to go uncounted. The judge did not rule but asked both sides to discuss how quickly the case could move forward given the county was nearly finished processing ballots. Earlier, Trump campaign officials and legal advisers had reportedly been preparing to appoint their own slate of state electors in the event of a contested election, with Arizona noted as a battleground state with both a Republican governor and legislature.

summary:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and South Korean President Moon Jae-in met at the Demilitarized Zone on Friday for an inter-Korean summit in Panmunjom, South Korea. The two leaders shook hands and later declared their willingness to bring about an official end to the Korean War after 65 years and a commitment to denuclearization on the Korean Peninsula. According to one account, the leaders would attempt to negotiate a formal end to the war by the end of the year. Photographs from the meeting showed the two leaders smiling, exchanging friendly banter, attending a military ceremony, and holding private conversations over lunch.

Following the summit, U.S. President Donald Trump spoke by telephone with Moon Jae-in. Trump wrote on Twitter that he had "just had a long and very good talk with President Moon of South Korea" and that "things are going very well, time and location of meeting with North Korea is being set."

Later, during a meeting with German Chancellor Angela Merkel at the White House, Trump said peace negotiations on the Korean Peninsula had "never gone this far" and argued recent developments showed Kim was serious about eliminating nuclear weapons. Trump stated, "We're not going to be played, OK? We're going to hopefully make a deal, if not that's fine." He added that the United States "has been played beautifully like a fiddle" in the past by North Korea but said this time was different "because you had a different kind of leader."

Some national security experts expressed skepticism about the talks, saying they were concerned that Trump and Moon might give too much away to Kim in search of a deal. They said they worried Kim was not sincere about giving up his nuclear weapons and would only make partial concessions in an attempt to win relief from sanctions imposed by the United States, South Korea, and their allies, which they said had crippled North Korea's economy.

summary: An explosion occurred Monday night during a Marine Corps training exercise at the Hawthorne Army Depot in Nevada, near the desert community of Hawthorne about 140 miles southeast of Reno. The depot, which stores and disposes of ammunition, comprises hundreds of buildings across more than 230 square miles, an area also described as nearly 150,000 acres. Depot official Russ Collier told KRNV-TV the explosion was an accident unrelated to the ammunition stored at the facility. The Mineral County sheriff's office had no immediate details, and calls to the depot and U.S. Joint Munitions Command were not immediately answered. Army spokesman George Wright in Washington also had no details initially. NBC News reported Tuesday morning that six Marines were killed and eight wounded in what it described as an overnight live-fire exercise, then updated the toll to seven killed. The Marine Corps confirmed Tuesday in a statement that seven Marines from an expeditionary force based at Camp Lejeune, North Carolina, had died, saying "it is with heavy hearts we remember their courage and sacrifice." Sen. Dean Heller (R-Nev.) tweeted gratitude for their service.

summary:

Obama also urged Ukraine's military not to become involved in a conflict that must be resolved politically, expressing outrage about images of Ukrainian security forces firing automatic weapons on civilians. In a statement, Obama said Ukraine should respect the right to protest and that protesters must remain peaceful, calling for dialogue to reduce tensions and address grievances. The clashes began after parliament delayed a session scheduled for Tuesday to take up constitutional reform that would limit presidential powers; thousands of people marched toward the parliament building to pressure lawmakers, shouting "Shame!"

summary: On Christmas Eve, President Donald Trump spoke by phone with Collman Lloyd, a seven-year-old girl from South Carolina, as part of the NORAD Santa-tracking tradition. summary:
Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid formally introduced a resolution Friday authorizing President Barack Obama to use limited military force against Syria in response to alleged chemical weapons attacks. The measure was filed during a brief Senate session, setting up a procedural vote expected Wednesday on a motion to proceed to debate. Obama is scheduled to address the nation Tuesday on Syria.

Democrats anticipate some liberal opponents may vote to defeat the filibuster but oppose the measure on final passage, which would require a simple majority. The final vote could be close, potentially requiring Vice President Biden to cast a tie-breaking vote. If opponents exhaust procedural tactics, the earliest a final vote could occur is Sunday, though Friday is more likely. Senate Democrats are divided: Senator Joe Manchin (D-W.Va.) announced opposition Thursday, joining several Democrats who voted no in the Foreign Relations Committee. The larger uncertainty remains the House, where opposition is deeper; Speaker John Boehner (R-Ohio) has not outlined a formal timeline for consideration.

summary: A former student opened fire at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, on Wednesday, killing 17 people and injuring 14 others. The suspect, 19-year-old Nikolas Cruz, was charged Thursday with 17 counts of premeditated murder. Cruz had been expelled from the school last year for undisclosed disciplinary reasons and was a former Junior ROTC cadet. He legally purchased an AR-15 rifle less than a year before the shooting. In September, a YouTube user with the screen name "Nikolas Cruz" posted, "Im going to be a professional school shooter." Students and neighbors described Cruz as strange and hostile, saying he threatened others, talked about killing animals, and posted disturbing photos with guns on social media. The FBI acknowledged on Friday that it failed to act on a tip received January 5 from someone close to Cruz warning about his gun ownership, mental stability, desire to kill, and potential to carry out a school shooting. The bureau conceded the tip "should have been assessed as a potential threat to life." Florida Attorney General Pam Bondi said Friday that prosecutors will likely seek the death penalty, citing the cold, calculated, and premeditated nature of the attack, and noted Cruz's mental state and mental health history will be factors in the case.

summary:
President Barack Obama is expected to name Deputy National Security Adviser Denis McDonough as White House chief of staff, according to multiple reports. McDonough, 43, would succeed Jacob J. Lew, who was recently nominated to head the Treasury Department. A source familiar with the process told one outlet that McDonough is expected to be named to the post. Associates of McDonough said the announcement could come in the next several days, while another report said Obama is expected to announce the choice next week. Administration officials cautioned that Obama has not made a final decision.

McDonough has worked with Obama for years, serving in his Senate office and on the 2008 campaign. He was heavily involved in major foreign policy decisions including the end of the war in Iraq and the drawdown of troops in Afghanistan. Before joining Obama's team, McDonough worked for former Sen. Tom Daschle, D-S.D. Daschle told The New York Times that McDonough will face "a new set of challenges" and described his relationship with the president as "extraordinarily close." Daschle said the president wants "a fairly tightly knit, cohesive team that he trusts, rather than to bring in people who would have to learn anew his style and positions."

summary: The federal government entered its first partial shutdown in 17 years at midnight Monday after Congress failed to agree on a funding measure. The Republican-controlled House had voted early Sunday to attach a one-year delay of the 2010 health care law and a repeal of the medical device tax to a continuing resolution, passing the medical device repeal 248-174 and the delay 231-192. The delay included a provision allowing employers and health care providers to opt out of mandatory contraception coverage. The Democratic-led Senate rejected the House amendments twice on Monday. Minutes before midnight, the White House ordered the shutdown. About 800,000 federal workers faced furloughs; national parks and most federal offices closed. Critical functions — air traffic control, military operations, Social Security payments — continued. Separately, the Senate adopted by unanimous voice vote Monday a bill to ensure members of the armed forces receive paychecks on time during a shutdown; the measure had passed the House early Sunday and went to President Barack Obama for his signature. Civilian federal employees would face pay delays.

Secretary of State John Kerry, speaking at a press conference in London on Monday, described a potential U.S. military strike on Syria as an "unbelievably small, limited kind of effort." Kerry said the action would hold President Bashar al-Assad accountable without engaging troops on the ground or any prolonged effort, consisting of a "very limited, very targeted, short-term effort that degrades his capacity to deliver chemical weapons without assuming responsibility for Syria's civil war."

Senator John McCain, a prominent advocate for military response, said he would withdraw support for a strike if it was not extensive enough.

summary: The White House announced Monday the U.S. Digital Service, a team of digital experts to upgrade government technology infrastructure and make websites more consumer friendly, led by former Google engineer Mikey Dickerson, who took leave to supervise HealthCare.gov fixes after its troubled launch last fall. The move aims to institutionalize the approach that salvaged the health insurance website and apply it across federal agencies before problems arise. Senator Tom Carper said he hopes "the U.S. Digital Service will prevent future mishaps from occurring as it works to strengthen our agencies' digital systems and help agency leadership figure out what works and what they can do better when it comes to information technology." Carper noted that while "every organization, public or private, faces challenges successfully delivering results from large information technology investments ... the federal government continues to struggle more than the private sector," and called it "critical that we improve how federal agencies acquire, implement and manage information technology and provide a valuable return on the taxpayer dollars invested in these programs." The administration ultimately surpassed its HealthCare.gov enrollment targets, though the opening weeks of sign-ups were riddled with website troubles that raised questions about the administration's competence.

In October 2016, Trump had said at a Pennsylvania rally, "I love WikiLeaks," and "Boy, I love reading those WikiLeaks." Then-Attorney General Jeff Sessions said in April 2017 that arresting Assange would become a Justice Department priority.

summary: On the 50th anniversary of the March on Washington, multiple events marked the occasion. President Barack Obama, former presidents, and members of Martin Luther King Jr.'s family addressed thousands gathered on the National Mall to honor King's legacy. Separately, a coalition of Black faith leaders delivered a letter to Capitol Hill citing King's call to "dramatize a shameful condition" and urging Congress to pass a national law requiring background checks for all gun purchases, including private transfers. The letter stated that 60,000 Black children have been killed in gun violence since King's 1963 "I Have a Dream" speech. Meanwhile, a progressive movement organizing under the banner "The United Progressive Movement Against ALEC" held a gathering in Washington, framing the anniversary as a moment to protect working families, clean air and water, and justice for all Americans, and to counter corporate money in politics. The progressive group promoted a video titled "We Are All Connected."

A USC Dornsife/Los Angeles Times poll conducted May 21-28 among 1,511 registered voters with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points showed incumbent Democratic Governor Jerry Brown at 50 percent support ahead of the June 3 primary. summary:
The federal government partially shut down Tuesday after Congress and the White House failed to reach a spending deal for the new fiscal year, furloughing more than 800,000 federal workers. White House press secretary Jay Carney told MSNBC's "Morning Joe" that Congress's strategy "seems to be to do what they've done for the funding of government to the issue of whether or not the U.S. government will pay its bills" when the debt ceiling must be raised in a few weeks. The consequences, he said, "are unknowable, but they are catastrophic, without question."

President Obama issued a letter to federal employees the same day, thanking them for their service and promising to work with Congress to end the shutdown. He acknowledged that politicians in recent years have "treated you like a punching bag," citing frozen pay rates and sequester cuts that required furloughs, and said "none of this is fair to you." He urged workers not to lose heart: "Public service is noble. Public service is important. And by choosing public service, you carry on a proud tradition at the heart of some of this country's greatest and most lasting achievements."

Asked about the president's pay during the shutdown, Carney said individuals within the administration could "obviously" decide whether to donate their salaries but that the issue was more complicated than during sequestration, when Obama and other top officials cut their pay to match furlough days. Employees required to work should be paid eventually, Carney said; others "will not ever get paid unless Congress acts." The White House hoped Congress would vote for back pay. "It's the right thing to do," Carney said. The Washington Post reported that more than 70 lawmakers said they would forgo their pay during the shutdown.

summary: Presumptive Republican nominee Donald Trump appeared Sunday at the Rolling Thunder rally in Washington, D.C., an annual Memorial Day weekend event that draws tens of thousands of motorcyclists, many of them veterans, to pay homage to fallen heroes and raise awareness of prisoners of war, those missing in action, and veterans' issues. The "First Amendment Demonstration Run" began at noon from the Pentagon's north parking lot and proceeded through the Mall area. Trump told Bloomberg Politics beforehand, "I am doing it in honor of the great bikers who have been totally supportive of my campaign, and now I want to be supportive of them. I look forward to it!" Before thousands of bikers at the rally, Trump said, "Thousands of people are dying, waiting in line to see a doctor. That is not going to happen anymore." He pledged that, if elected, veterans could opt for private physicians "and we'll pay for it." Trump also promised to build "a real wall" along the Mexican border, saying Mexico would pay for it, and vowed better international trade deals, an end to Obamacare, victory over the Islamic State, and a rebuilt military. "We are going to beat ISIS. We are going to knock the hell out of them," he said. He provided few details on these proposals.

Former National Security Adviser Michael Flynn resigned after reports he discussed U.S. sanctions with Russian Ambassador Sergey Kislyak before President Trump's inauguration. The Washington Post reported that FBI agents interviewed Flynn on January 24 and he denied discussing sanctions, contradicting intercepted communications. Lying to the FBI is a felony, though prosecution would be a Justice Department decision; some officials said a case could be difficult because Flynn might parse the definition of sanctions. A Flynn spokesman had no response; the FBI declined to comment.

A video of Flynn leading "lock her up" chants at the July Republican National Convention resurfaced Tuesday. In his resignation statement, Flynn said the "fast pace of events" caused him to provide "incomplete information" to Vice President Pence and other senior officials about his communications with Russia. The Department of Justice, then led by acting Attorney General Sally Yates, had reportedly warned the White House one month earlier that Flynn posed risks including possible vulnerability to blackmail by Russia. summary:
At Thursday's Fox News Republican presidential debate in Detroit, Florida Sen. Marco Rubio defended Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder over the Flint water crisis. Asked by moderator Bret Baier why GOP candidates had not talked more about the issue, Rubio said he had discussed it, calling it a "terrible thing" and a "systemic breakdown." He added that "the politicizing of it, I think, is unfair." "I give the governor credit. He took responsibility for what happened, and he's talked about people being held accountable and the need to change this, Gov. Snyder," Rubio said. "This should not be a partisan issue." Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, seeking the Democratic nomination, has called for Snyder's resignation.

During Sunday night's Democratic presidential debate in Michigan, Snyder live-tweeted a defense of his administration. He tweeted that he is "taking responsibility" for the crisis and argued that the decision to use water from the Flint River was "never about money." "This was a failure of government at all levels that could be described as a massive error of bureaucracy," he tweeted.

The crisis began in 2013 when Flint left the Detroit water system as a cost-saving measure. Despite warnings, officials did not treat the corrosive Flint River water, causing lead to leach from pipes into drinking water. Independent tests in August showed high lead levels, and in September, Dr. Mona Hanna-Attisha found a spike in lead poisonings among Flint children.

summary: A plane presumed to be carrying North Korean leader Kim Jong Un landed at Singapore's airport on Sunday afternoon amid heavy security, ahead of a Tuesday summit with U.S. President Donald Trump. summary: An international aid group said Saturday that medical centers it supported near Damascus received more than 3,000 patients showing symptoms consistent with exposure to toxic nerve agents on Wednesday morning, and that 355 of them died. Doctors Without Borders said the statement was the first issued by an international organization working in Syria about the attack in suburbs northeast of the capital. Syrian opposition groups said at least 100 people were killed during a government offensive against rebel-held areas, and some activists said regime troops used "poisonous gas." The Britain-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights documented at least 100 deaths from Wednesday's attack, though it was not clear whether victims died from shelling or toxic gas. Other activist groups, including the Local Coordination Committees, claimed hundreds died in a "chemical weapons" attack in eastern Damascus suburbs, basing the estimate on symptoms suffered by victims. The Syrian government denied its troops used chemical weapons, dismissing the claims as baseless. Britain's foreign secretary, William Hague, said the country would ask the United Nations Security Council to discuss the claims and that U.N. chemical weapons inspectors already in Syria should be given access to the site. summary: A special Minnesota panel of three judges ruled Monday that Democrat Al Franken won the most votes in the 2008 Senate race against Republican incumbent Norm Coleman. The court determined that after a statewide recount and a seven-week trial, Franken leads by 312 votes. Coleman previously announced plans to appeal to the state Supreme Court and has 10 days to do so; the appeal could delay the seating of Minnesota's second senator by several more weeks. summary: The New York State Senate rejected a bill to legalize same-sex marriage on Wednesday after months of delays and what advocates described as arm-twisting of lawmakers sympathetic to the measure but representing conservative districts. The measure failed to pass during a floor debate that was streamed live on the Senate's website and accompanied by real-time updates on the chamber's official Twitter feed, including a remark from Senator Duane: "The time is never right for civil rights...(but) it's always the right time to be on the right side of history." Governor David Paterson, a Democrat who had made the issue a signature priority, said he would have signed the bill, which had already passed the Assembly. Paterson and advocacy groups said they at least wanted a floor debate and vote; advocates said they were not surprised by the outcome. The defeat followed a referendum in Maine earlier in November that struck down a gay-marriage law before it took effect. At the time, gay marriage was legal in Connecticut, Iowa, Massachusetts, and Vermont, with a New Hampshire law set to take effect January 1. New York recognized same-sex marriages performed in other states but did not allow them to be performed in-state. California had previously allowed gay marriage until voters approved Proposition 8 in 2008 banning the practice. On the same day, lawmakers also closed most of a $3.2 billion budget deficit, scaled back pension benefits for new government employees, and overhauled the public-authority system. Financial watchdogs said the concessions lawmakers made did little to change the state's fundamental fiscal problems, though the votes were seen as a rare sign of functionality from the narrowly divided Senate.

summary:
A shooting occurred Monday morning at the Naval Sea Systems Command headquarters at the Washington Navy Yard, where about 3,000 people work. The Navy said shots were fired around 8:20 a.m. Multiple law enforcement agencies responded, including police and federal agents. Ambulances were parked outside, streets in the area were closed, and flights at Reagan National Airport were temporarily halted. A U.S. Park Police helicopter hovered over the building and appeared to drop a basket or stretcher with a person onto the roof.

President Barack Obama received frequent briefings on the unfolding situation from senior aides and directed his team to stay in contact with the Navy, FBI, and local officials, the White House said.

Casualty figures varied across early accounts. A Defense Department official said several people were killed and as many as 10 wounded. The Navy initially reported multiple injuries but said the number and conditions of victims were not immediately known. Later, authorities said 14 people were wounded, including police officer Scott Williams, who was shot in the legs; Mayor Vincent Gray said Williams was "doing well." Twelve people were confirmed dead: officials revealed the names and ages of seven victims late Monday night and said they would release the identities of the remaining five after notifying families.

The suspected shooter was identified as 34-year-old Aaron Alexis, who died during a gun battle with police.

Naval Sea Systems Command is the largest of the Navy's five system commands, accounts for a quarter of the Navy's budget, and builds, buys, and maintains the Navy's ships and submarines and their combat systems.

Dan Greenhaus, chief strategist at BTIG, said the data supported the view that growth should accelerate in the second half of the year.
