A senior U.S. official said the meeting would mark Kiev's final attempt to engage with Russia before the West imposes further sanctions; another senior State Department official said the goal was for Russia to stop supporting separatists in eastern Ukraine and pull troops back from the border, adding that costs would increase if Russia did not de-escalate. It was not immediately clear how tough any new sanctions might be or whether they would target Russia's banking and energy sectors. Ukrainian diplomats planned to brief Russian Foreign Minister Sergey V. Lavrov on efforts to decentralize power and protect Russian-speaking minorities near the border, where unrest has surged in recent days. Secretary of State John Kerry, Ukraine's acting Foreign Minister Andrii Deshchytsia, and EU foreign policy chief Catherine Ashton were also expected to attend the meeting at a luxury hotel in Geneva. Obama administration officials played down expectations of a breakthrough or Russian concessions sufficient to avoid new U.S. penalties. Russia was seen as pursuing a strategy of pressing the West without triggering crippling sanctions or a military confrontation with NATO.

summary: President Barack Obama summoned Veterans Affairs Secretary Eric Shinseki to the White House on Friday morning amid mounting calls for Shinseki's resignation and widespread allegations of treatment delays at VA hospitals. Shinseki was expected to update the president on a review he had been conducting. In television interviews aired Thursday, Obama said he planned a "serious conversation" with Shinseki about whether he was prepared to fix the problems. Following the meeting, Obama announced he had accepted Shinseki's resignation and named Sloan Gibson as acting secretary. Obama called Shinseki a "very good man" but said the secretary "felt that new leadership would serve our veterans best, and I agree with him." An inspector general report released Wednesday had found that officials used inappropriate scheduling practices to conceal substantial treatment delays at veterans hospitals across the country. House Speaker John Boehner (R-Ohio) said the resignation "changes nothing" until the president outlines a vision and an effective plan, adding that "one personnel change cannot be used as an excuse to paper over a systemic problem." Boehner said he had not officially joined the bipartisan calls for Shinseki's resignation because doing so "takes people's eye off getting to the bottom of the problems." Fox News contributor and syndicated columnist George Will said on "Special Report with Bret Baier" that Shinseki was "obviously pushed" out, calling the resignation "rough justice" that would not cure the problems but would satisfy public desire for accountability. Will also referenced Obama's statement that Shinseki was "unhappy because bad news did not get to him" and suggested this could reflect a broad systemic problem in government.

President Barack Obama announced Thursday that the United States is prepared to take targeted military actions in Iraq if they would help fight a growing threat from extremist militants, and is ready to send as many as 300 military advisers to the country. The advisers would staff joint operations centers being established in Baghdad and northern Iraq. Obama emphasized that American combat troops would not be returning to Iraq. The U.S. has increased its intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance operations in Iraq to better understand threats to Baghdad. The announcement comes as violence has spread throughout Iraq, a situation that has drawn the president back into a conflict he had hoped to leave behind as a key accomplishment of his administration.

summary: Osama bin Laden was killed on Sunday in a U.S. special operations raid on a compound north of Islamabad, Pakistan. About two dozen Navy SEAL commandos carried out the mission, which President Obama ordered. No U.S. troops or civilians were injured in the firefight. Obama announced the death Sunday night, saying it "marks the most significant achievement to date in our nation's effort to defeat Al Qaeda" but warning "there's no doubt that Al Qaeda will continue to pursue attacks against us. We must and we will remain vigilant at home and abroad." He later said "this is a good day for America" and "the world is safer." Celebrations broke out near the White House and at Ground Zero in New York City. The White House was in a jubilant mood as details emerged Monday. One account identified bin Laden as the man behind the Sept. 11, 2011, terrorist attacks. In Iran, Foreign Ministry spokesman Ramin Mehmanparast said "We hope that this development will end war, conflict, unrest and the death of innocent people, and help to establish peace and tranquility in the region," adding "This development clearly shows that there is no need for a major military deployment to counter one individual." He also stated "Iran, as one of the main victims of terrorism, strongly condemns any act of terror in the world including organized terrorism in the Zionist regime [of Israel]." Iranian lawmaker Javad Jahangirzadeh said the United States killed bin Laden "to prevent possible leakage of the priceless intelligence that he had," asking "How could a terrorist hide himself from intelligence sources … and intelligence services cooperating with the West?" and arguing "Naturally the West was satisfied with bin Laden's performance over the past years, and today — as they believed their project had been completed and so to prevent the leaking of valuable information — they were forced to kill him."

Green Party candidate Jill Stein filed for a recount in Wisconsin on Friday and was raising funds for similar efforts in Michigan and Pennsylvania. On Saturday, Stein appeared on CNN's "Newsroom" to defend the effort, saying it "should be a non-partisan powered effort to ensure that we can rely on the integrity and security of our votes." She added: "The point to drive home here is that having a secure elections process benefits us all. I invite everyone. I invite Donald Trump's campaign, Hillary's campaign, we've had calls out to Gary Johnson's campaign — this should be a non-partisan people powered effort to ensure that we can rely on the integrity and security of our votes." President-elect Donald Trump called the recount a "scam" to fill Green Party coffers. Also on Saturday, Clinton campaign general counsel Marc Elias announced in a Medium post that the campaign would participate in the Wisconsin recount. summary: The House of Representatives voted Thursday to hold Attorney General Eric H. Holder Jr. in contempt of Congress, the first time a sitting attorney general has been so sanctioned. The vote was 255 to 67. The Republican-led House acted after Holder withheld documents requested for an investigation into Operation Fast and Furious, a Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives operation that ran from 2009 to 2011 in which guns were allowed to move from Arizona to Mexico in an effort to track them. House Speaker John A. Boehner told reporters Wednesday that last-minute talks with the White House about releasing documents had failed to avert the vote. At that time, more than 250,000 ballots remained uncounted out of about 2.4 million cast, and officials said counting might continue until Thursday. McSally later conceded. The victory flipped the seat from Republican to Democratic control. Sinema, a moderate Blue Dog Democrat, became the first openly bisexual person elected to the Senate and the first openly LGBTQ woman to win a Senate seat. She previously served as the first openly bisexual member of the House of Representatives, co-chaired the Equality Caucus, and co-sponsored the Equality Act. LGBTQ advocacy groups celebrated the win. Annise Parker, CEO and President of LGBTQ Victory Fund, called it a "game-changer" for the LGBTQ community and the Democratic Party. The Victory Fund had designated Sinema a "game changer" candidate, contributing $10,000 directly and raising more than $97,000 for her campaign. The Human Rights Campaign called the victory "historic" and reported deploying 18 staff members and thousands of volunteers in Arizona. Senator Tammy Baldwin congratulated Sinema, writing she was "very happy to say I'm no longer the *only* openly LGBTQ U.S. Senator" and praising Sinema's "steady leadership."

summary: The U.S. economy grew at a 2.5 percent annual rate in the second quarter, the Commerce Department reported Thursday, revising the figure sharply upward from an initial estimate of 1.7 percent. summary:
President Donald Trump announced Friday that he will nominate Deputy Secretary of State John Sullivan to be the next U.S. ambassador to Russia. Sullivan, the second-ranking official at the State Department under Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, would replace Jon Huntsman. Sullivan has served in senior positions at the Justice, Defense and Commerce departments during both Bush administrations, as well as at the U.S. mission to the European Union and in Ukraine, South Korea and Honduras. He was acting secretary of state after Rex Tillerson's departure in 2018 and has two decades of private law practice experience. He is a graduate of Columbia University Law School.

Huntsman's departure timing was described differently: two accounts said he resigned in August, with one noting speculation he would run for Utah governor, while a third said he left the post last week.

The nomination comes as Trump faces an impeachment inquiry. Former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Marie Yovanovitch testified in a deposition Friday that Sullivan told her in May that her tenure was being curtailed and that Trump had been pressing for her removal since summer 2018. Sullivan had also been considered for national security adviser, a post that went to Robert O'Brien.

If confirmed by the Senate, Sullivan would become the top U.S. diplomat in Russia at a time when U.S. intelligence agencies have concluded that Russia interfered in the 2016 presidential election, a finding Russia denies.

summary: Thailand's army chief, Gen. In a statement broadcast on national television, Prayuth said the Peace and Order Maintaining Command — comprising the army, navy, armed forces, and police — would take charge of governing. A deputy spokesman, Winthai Suvaree, later confirmed in a televised statement that Prayuth would head the military council now running the country, that the constitution was being suspended, and that the Senate and all courts would continue to function. The announcement followed two days of army-mediated talks between rival political leaders at a Bangkok military facility that failed to resolve the impasse; shortly before the declaration, armed soldiers in vehicles surrounded the building, preventing those inside from leaving. The unrest began in November when demonstrators demanded the resignation of Prime Minister Yingluck Shinawatra, accusing her of acting as a proxy for her brother, former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, who was ousted in a 2006 coup and lives in exile to avoid a corruption conviction. Thursday's action marked the twelfth coup since the absolute monarchy ended in 1932. The United States said there was no justification for the coup. Secretary of State John Kerry called it disappointing, warned of "negative implications" for the U.S.-Thai relationship, and said the U.S. was reviewing military assistance and other engagement. After the 2006 coup, the U.S. froze military aid for a year and a half until democracy was restored. Kerry urged the immediate restoration of civilian government and a return to democracy.

summary: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and South Korean President Moon Jae-in held an inter-Korean summit on Friday at Panmunjom in the Demilitarized Zone. Kim crossed the military demarcation line into South Korea, the first time a North Korean leader had done so since the Korean War ended in 1953. The two leaders shook hands, held hands, and together stepped over a cracked concrete slab into North Korean territory. An honor guard and red carpet ceremony marked the occasion. During closed-door talks, the leaders discussed denuclearization, which Seoul officials described as "sincere and candid." They issued a joint statement vowing to achieve "a nuclear-free Korean Peninsula through complete denuclearization" and declared their willingness to bring about an official end to the Korean War after 65 years. The statement did not include specific new measures on denuclearization, leaving the issue to a planned summit between Kim and U.S. President Donald Trump in coming weeks. It remained unclear whether the leaders made progress on the nuclear issue.

summary: During his confirmation hearing before the Senate Intelligence Committee on Thursday, CIA director nominee John Brennan defended the administration's drone strike program and faced questioning on interrogation techniques, classified leaks, and transparency. Brennan said the Obama administration has never killed terror suspects when capture was possible, and denied any link between the surge in drone attacks and the administration's reluctance to hold suspects in U.S. detention centers. Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine noted targeted killings have quadrupled under Obama; Brennan cited al-Qaida's growth in Yemen as the reason. Brennan denounced the CIA's harsh Bush-era interrogation techniques and vehemently denied involvement in classified leaks. Committee Chairwoman Dianne Feinstein, a California Democrat, said she wants to open more of the drone program to the public to correct what she called exaggerated reports of civilian casualties. Sen. Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, said the White House has not fulfilled its transparency promise on targeted killings. The White House has released an Office of Legal Counsel opinion justifying targeting U.S. citizens overseas, but Wyden said he wanted to see "any and all opinions" and that it was "not clear" that had been provided. Wyden asked whether Brennan would make public accidental deaths from drone strikes; the nominee said he would. Wyden also asked for a list of countries where the CIA has conducted lethal operations. "I would damn well make sure that this committee had that information" going forward, Brennan said. President Obama has pledged to close the Guantanamo Bay detention center, and no terror suspects have been sent there since 2009.

Russian officials said Saturday that the Federal Migration Service had not received an asylum request from Edward Snowden as of that day. Interfax quoted migration service head Konstantin Romodanovsky to that effect. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said the government had had no contact with Snowden. On Friday, Snowden met with lawyers and human rights advocates at Moscow's Sheremetyevo international airport, where he has been since arriving from Hong Kong on June 23. At the meeting, Snowden said he would request asylum in Russia, at least as a temporary measure before traveling to Venezuela, Bolivia, or Nicaragua, all of which have offered or expressed willingness to grant him asylum. The U.S. economy grew at a 2.2 percent annual rate in the fourth quarter of 2014, the Commerce Department said Friday in its second of three estimates, revising down from the initial 2.6 percent estimate issued last month. The revision marked a sharp deceleration from the third quarter's 5 percent annual growth rate, the strongest in 11 years. The downward adjustment stemmed largely from slower inventory accumulation by businesses, which subtracted 0.7 percentage point from the headline figure, while consumer demand remained healthy. Economists had expected a revision to 2 percent. The final estimate is due in late March.

U.S. stock indexes opened lower and remained mostly lower in midday trading. The Dow Jones industrial average fell 15 points, or 0.1 percent, to 18,199 in early trading and was down 27 points, or 0.2 percent, at 18,187 by 11:45 a.m. Eastern time. The Standard & Poor's 500 index was flat at 2,110. The Nasdaq composite slipped less than a point to 4,987 in early trading and was down six points, or 0.1 percent, at 4,981 by midday. J.C. Penney shares dropped 6 percent after the retailer reported a surprise loss.

Bond prices rose. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note fell to between 2.01 and 2.02 percent.

The assailant, dressed in an Afghan army uniform, opened fire on a group of international soldiers during a site visit at the Marshal Fahim National Defense University at Camp Qargha, a base west of Kabul, and was subsequently killed. Fifteen people were wounded, roughly half of them Americans, including a German brigadier general, two Afghan generals, and an Afghan officer. Greene was the highest-ranking U.S. Army officer killed in the Iraq or Afghanistan wars; CNN reported he was the first U.S. Army general assassinated in a combat zone in 141 years. President Barack Obama had not publicly addressed the killing as of Wednesday, and administration officials told CNN the president did not want to give special attention to a general when so many soldiers had lost their lives in Afghanistan. Greene, an engineer by training, was known for integrating smartphones, video conferences, and virtual worlds into military training and used such technology to communicate frequently with his family in the United States. The attack came as so-called insider attacks had largely declined: 16 coalition deaths in 10 attacks in 2013, compared with 53 deaths in 38 attacks in 2012.

summary:
Michael Brown, 18, was shot and killed by a Ferguson police officer near an apartment complex on Saturday afternoon. The St. Louis County Prosecuting Attorney's office confirmed Brown had no criminal record, including no prior misdemeanors or felonies. According to police, Brown pushed the officer into his car, a struggle ensued, and Brown reached for the officer's weapon before a shot was fired inside the vehicle followed by additional shots. Brown was unarmed. A preliminary autopsy showed he died from gunshot wounds; an official autopsy was pending. Brown's body was released to his family on Wednesday afternoon.

Around 1 a.m. Wednesday, a second police-involved shooting occurred near the intersection of Chambers Road and Sheffingdel Court. St. Louis County police responded to reports of shots fired and four or five armed suspects wearing ski masks. Officers saw multiple subjects running and gave chase. Police said one suspect pointed a handgun at an officer, who opened fire, critically wounding the suspect. The officer was not injured. The other suspects were not located. St. Louis County Police stated this shooting was separate from the "Ferguson detail" related to Brown's death.

Protests occurred nightly since Saturday. On Wednesday, police asked protesters to gather only during daylight hours. Wednesday evening, police used tear gas to disperse crowds. Wednesday night, St. Louis County Police clashed with protesters, deploying Long Range Acoustic Devices (LRAD), rubber bullets, smoke grenades, and tear gas canisters, causing protesters to scatter.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressed a joint session of Congress on Tuesday at 11 a.m., warning that current negotiations over Iran's nuclear program could pave "Iran's path to the bomb." He was welcomed with thunderous applause from Republicans and most Democrats. The speech had been arranged by congressional Republicans without prior consultation with the White House, which angered Obama officials. President Obama did not attend the address; instead, at 11:30 a.m. he participated from the Situation Room in a secure videoconference on Ukraine with the leaders of Great Britain, France, Germany, Italy, and the European Union. Obama said Monday the speech was a distraction but would not permanently damage U.S.-Israeli relations. After the address, Obama said it offered "nothing new" and that Netanyahu "didn't offer any viable alternatives" to diplomacy on preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons. Secretary of State John Kerry had previously said Netanyahu was "wrong" on the U.S.-led talks. A column by Fareed Zakaria noted that Netanyahu has argued for nearly 25 years that Iran is on the verge of producing a nuclear weapon. Netanyahu faces a parliamentary election in Israel on March 17.

The development complicated the position of 80 House Republicans who had signed a letter to Speaker John Boehner vowing not to support a continuing resolution without denying funds for the implementation of the Affordable Care Act.

summary: A person climbed a fence and entered the south grounds of the White House at about 11:38 p.m. Friday, the U.S. Secret Service reported. The individual, who was carrying a backpack, was arrested without further incident near the south entrance. President Donald Trump was at the White House at the time. The agency did not identify the individual or provide an update on the person's status; standard practice is to hand intruders over to the local police department. Homeland Security Secretary John Kelly was briefed on the incident and kept aware of the situation the entire time, White House press secretary Sean Spicer said. A Kasich victory in Ohio was seen as positioning him as the main establishment alternative to Trump as the contest moved toward more moderate Northern states, including Northeastern states voting in April.

Okrent worked in the paid media department and had been involved with Obama's political campaigns since 2004, including the 2004 Senate race and the 2008 presidential campaign, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. He collapsed Friday morning after working out at a gym, according to Fox Chicago, and was found unconscious and unresponsive. Chicago paramedics were called to the headquarters and provided emergency treatment before transporting Okrent to Northwestern Memorial Hospital, where he was pronounced dead a short time later, the Chicago Sun-Times reported.

President Obama was campaigning in southern Virginia when he learned of the death, according to USA Today and the White House pool report. He called Okrent's family to express condolences and later spoke to campaign staff in a conference call, the White House press office said. Okrent's mother, Lynn Pollack, told Fox Chicago that Obama said he could not know how horrible the family was feeling and that, as a father, he could not imagine the loss. Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney tweeted condolences Friday evening, and Obama senior adviser David Axelrod responded, according to the Chicago Sun-Times.

President Barack Obama declined a request to meet with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during Netanyahu's visit to the United States later this month. The White House cited scheduling conflicts as the reason. Netanyahu's office had contacted the White House expressing hope for a meeting, and Netanyahu said he would change his own schedule and travel to the U.S. capital for the purpose. This would mark the first time during Obama's presidency that Netanyahu travels to the United States as prime minister without meeting Obama. The decision comes amid tensions between Israel and the United States over Iran's nuclear program. Netanyahu publicly criticized the Obama administration for refusing to set clear "red lines" that would prompt a U.S. military strike on Iran's nuclear facilities. Following the White House's rejection, Obama and Netanyahu held a phone call Tuesday night. After the call, Netanyahu struck a more moderate tone, saying it was his duty to uphold Israel's vital interests and security, "not that it's easy, because leadership is tested in upholding them even if there are disagreements with friends, even the best of friends."

summary:
President Barack Obama flew to Orlando on Sunday evening ahead of a planned Monday campaign swing with former President Bill Clinton through Orlando, Youngstown, Ohio, and northern Virginia as Hurricane Sandy approached the Eastern seaboard, forecast to make landfall Monday. The White House announced Obama would return to Washington early Monday afternoon to monitor the storm; spokesman Jay Carney said the president continued to receive regular updates. The Virginia rally had been previously canceled. Republican nominee Mitt Romney also modified his schedule because of the storm.

Accounts differed on Monday's Orlando event. One account said Obama and Clinton would still appear together at the University of Central Florida in Orlando on Monday morning before Obama returned to Washington and Clinton continued to Ohio joined by Vice President Joe Biden. Another account said Obama cancelled the Orlando appearance and returned to Washington, with Clinton appearing alone. The Ohio and Virginia rallies were also described as cancelled. Obama's Tuesday trip to Green Bay, Wisconsin, was canceled to keep him in Washington.

The Obama campaign said it would withhold fundraising emails starting Monday in Virginia, Pennsylvania, North Carolina, New Jersey, and Washington, D.C. A separate report said the campaign had not stopped sending fundraising emails. The White House released photos Tuesday morning of Obama meeting with federal officials on storm response. Biden was reported headed to Florida, while Clinton was reported traveling to Minnesota and Colorado; another account placed Clinton in Ohio with Biden on Monday. Tuesday and Wednesday campaign events in Florida, Ohio, Colorado, and Wisconsin remained uncertain.

The Markey video highlighted Gomez's role as a spokesman for a conservative super PAC that criticized the Obama administration's handling of information about the bin Laden killing. Gomez responded with a television advertisement accusing "dirty Ed Markey" of running ads smearing Gomez by comparing him to bin Laden and blaming him for the Newtown shooting. summary: President Barack Obama attended the Group of 20 summit in St. Petersburg, Russia, on Thursday and Friday. On Thursday, Obama and Russian President Vladimir Putin exchanged handshakes and smiles during a welcoming ceremony after months of tension, including Obama's cancellation of a planned one-on-one summit last month after Russia granted temporary asylum to former National Security Agency contractor Edward Snowden. The two leaders did not have a formal meeting scheduled, but National Security Council spokesman Ben Rhodes said he anticipated informal interactions. Also on Thursday, the White House said Obama was making phone calls to skeptical U.S. lawmakers from the summit to build support for a proposed military strike against Syria, and Deputy National Security Adviser Benjamin Rhodes told reporters a list of calls would be released. Obama pressed fellow leaders to back intervention, while Putin said Obama had not proved the Syrian government was responsible for a recent chemical weapons attack. Obama had told reporters Wednesday he was confident Congress would authorize force to punish Syrian President Bashar al-Assad. On Friday, at a news conference, Obama said he had discussed reports of NSA spying with Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff and Mexican President Enrique Peña Nieto, telling them he took the allegations seriously and would work with their teams to resolve the tension.

The original tweet was deleted shortly afterward, though social media users captured and shared screenshots of both versions. Trump subsequently stated the star was "a basic star, often used by sheriffs who deal with criminals and criminal behavior," calling it a "Sheriff's Star" or "plain star," and accused the "dishonest media" of trying to depict it as the Star of David. Former campaign manager Corey Lewandowski, then a CNN commentator, also described it as a Sheriff's star. The incident drew widespread criticism on Twitter, including comparisons to Holocaust imagery.

summary: FBI Director James Comey announced Tuesday that the bureau would not recommend criminal charges against Hillary Clinton for her use of a private email server while secretary of state. Comey said Clinton and her aides were "extremely careless" with highly sensitive information and that foreign actors likely gained access to her messages. Republican nominee Donald Trump responded by calling the decision "very unfair" and accusing the FBI of "bad judgment." He tweeted a comparison to former CIA Director David Petraeus, who in April 2015 received two years' probation and a $100,000 fine for sharing classified material with his biographer, Paula Broadwell. Trump had said in May 2016 that Clinton "should suffer" for the email matter and should not be allowed to run for president. Later Tuesday, President Obama appeared with Clinton at their first joint campaign rally in Charlotte, North Carolina, after arriving on Air Force One. Obama defended Clinton, saying he had "had a front-row seat to her judgment and her toughness and her commitment to diplomacy." He criticized Trump as a "serial tweeter," saying, "Everybody can tweet, but nobody actually knows what it takes to do the job until you've sat behind the desk." Obama also rejected Trump's "Make America Great Again" slogan: "America is really great... The rest of the world thinks we're pretty darn great. You can look that up. That's a fact." Clinton campaign chairman John Podesta told reporters the FBI director's critique "hardly" overshadowed the event, calling it "a great day."

summary: President Donald Trump announced Monday via Twitter that he had made his decision on a nominee for the United States Supreme Court and would reveal the choice live from the White House on Tuesday at 8:00 P.M. The announcement had originally been scheduled for Thursday. The vacancy was created by the death of Justice Antonin Scalia in 2016; the court has operated with eight justices since then. Former president Barack Obama had nominated Merrick Garland, but Senate Republicans declined to act on the nomination. Trump said he would select from a list of 21 potential judges released during his campaign. Reports identified several federal appellate judges as leading candidates: Neil Gorsuch of the 10th Circuit in Denver, Thomas Hardiman of the 3rd Circuit in Philadelphia, William Pryor of the 11th Circuit in Atlanta, and Raymond Kethledge of the 6th Circuit in Cincinnati. Confirmation will require 60 votes in the Senate, meaning Republican leadership would need support from at least eight Democrats. Last week Trump met with Senate leaders, after which Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer and Senator Dianne Feinstein said they wanted a "mainstream" nominee. The accelerated timetable came as controversy continued over Trump's executive order temporarily halting entry of refugees and travelers from seven majority-Muslim countries.

summary: President Donald Trump nominated Judge Neil M. Gorsuch on Tuesday to fill the Supreme Court vacancy created by the death of Justice Antonin Scalia on February 13. The announcement was made at a White House ceremony. Senate Majority Whip John Cornyn (R-Texas) said the same day that he was thrilled to support the nominee, calling Gorsuch "eminently well-qualified" and likening him to Scalia as a leader who believed judges should not legislate from the bench. Cornyn noted that Republicans had blocked consideration of President Barack Obama's nominee during the final year of his term so voters could decide in the 2016 election. On Saturday, Vice President Mike Pence addressed the Federalist Society for Law & Public Policy Studies in Philadelphia, stating that he and Trump had full confidence Gorsuch would be confirmed and pledging to work with Senate leadership to secure an up-or-down vote "one way or the other." Pence described Gorsuch as "cut from the same cloth" as Scalia, an originalist and textualist with a long history of defending separation of powers, checks and balances, and constitutional federalism that restricts the national government to enumerated powers. Pence urged the Senate not to filibuster the nomination. CNN published a collection of opinion commentaries assessing the nomination, including pieces on Gorsuch's background, the Republican obstruction tactic, and House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi's characterization of the appointment as "very hostile."

summary: President Donald Trump sent a letter to House Speaker Nancy Pelosi on Thursday informing her that a planned congressional delegation trip to Brussels, Egypt and Afghanistan "has been postponed" while the partial government shutdown continues. Pelosi had sent Trump a letter a day earlier suggesting they reschedule his State of the Union address, slated for Jan. 29, due to the shutdown. Trump has not responded specifically to that demand. On Thursday, during a speech at the Pentagon on missile defense, Trump said Democrats should go around Pelosi and negotiate with him on border security. "While many Democrats in the House and Senate would like to make a deal, Speaker Pelosi will not let them negotiate. The party has been hijacked by the open-borders fringe," he said. "Hopefully, Democratic lawmakers will step forward to do what's right for our country." Trump said he tried to hold two meetings at the White House including Democrats this week; one drew no Democrats, but a second involving the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus did involve some Democrats. They agreed to the meeting but said in a statement there cannot be any negotiations until the government is fully opened. Pelosi told reporters Thursday, "I'm not for a wall," and said even after the government opens she will not agree to any money for a border fence. Also on Thursday, Trump revealed that Pelosi was planning to lead a congressional delegation to Afghanistan. He revoked her use of a military plane because of the shutdown but announced that she and the other lawmakers were free to fly commercial. Pelosi termed it "very irresponsible" for Trump to reveal the travel plans. On Friday, a senior White House official said Pelosi was lying when she accused Trump of endangering her and other lawmakers by revealing their travel plans. "When the speaker of the House and about 20 others from Capitol Hill decide to book their own commercial flights to Afghanistan, the world is going to find out," the official said. "The idea we would leak anything that would put the safety and security of any American at risk is a flat-out lie."

Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer ordered U.S. and Michigan flags lowered to half-staff on all state buildings, grounds and facilities until sunset Thursday to honor victims of weekend mass shootings in El Paso, Texas, and Dayton, Ohio. She encouraged local governments, businesses and residents to do the same. Whitmer called gun violence "a public health crisis" requiring "action to make sure firearms don't end up in the hands of someone who wants to hurt themselves or others." Two shootings occurred within hours of each other. One account put the toll at 29 killed and about 50 injured; another said 31 people were killed and dozens wounded. Civic groups mobilized to help cover medical, funeral and other costs. At a San Diego fundraiser Sunday night, former Vice President Joe Biden misstated the locations, referring to "the tragic events in Houston today and also in Michigan the day before." He later corrected himself, according to a pool report. The fundraiser, held at the home of businessman Mark Arabo, drew about 75 attendees who received a three-course meal. Biden said he does not hold President Trump personally responsible for the shooting but noted the president has influence on the country. He also said, "You know what, the president's words have meaning, no matter who he or she is. They are the face of America."

summary:
President Obama on Tuesday nominated three candidates to the National Labor Relations Board: Republicans Harry Johnson and Philip Miscimarra, and Democrat Mark Gaston Pearce, who is currently serving on the board and was renominated. In February, Obama had renominated Democrats Sharon Block and Richard Griffin to the five-member board. With these nominations, five nominees — two Republicans and three Democrats — await Senate confirmation. Obama urged the Senate to confirm them swiftly so the bipartisan board can continue its work.

The board's status has been uncertain since January, when a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit ruled unanimously that Obama exceeded his constitutional authority by making recess appointments of three board members in January 2012 while lawmakers were on break, bypassing Senate confirmation. The court found the Senate had remained in "pro forma" sessions, not a formal recess. The administration argues the appointments were constitutional because the Senate was on vacation. Republican senators who joined a lawsuit contended the pro forma sessions denied Obama recess-appointment power, and the court agreed. Currently, Pearce is the only undisputed board member.

Separately, House Republicans are expected to vote this week on a bill that would prevent the board from conducting business until the Senate confirms new members constituting a quorum or the Supreme Court rules the board has authority to act. The White House says Obama would veto the bill, which it argues would hurt the middle class and jeopardize workers' rights, and maintains the recess appointments were valid. The bill is not expected to advance in the Senate.

summary: The Senate voted 81-18 Wednesday night to end a 16-day partial government shutdown and avoid a federal default, sending the measure to the House where it was expected to pass before the end of the day. Democratic Majority Leader Harry Reid and Republican Minority Leader Mitch McConnell announced the bipartisan compromise several hours before the vote. The legislation would fund the government through January 15 and extend the Treasury's borrowing authority through February 7, with one account noting the borrowing extension could last a month longer. The Treasury had set a deadline of 11:59 p.m. Thursday, when Secretary Jacob Lew said the government would reach the $16.7 trillion debt limit and could no longer borrow to meet its obligations. President Barack Obama, through White House Press Secretary Jay Carney, applauded Reid and McConnell for forging the compromise and urged Congress to act swiftly to end the shutdown and protect the full faith and credit of the United States. Reid said the compromise would provide the economy with the stability it desperately needs. Regarding the possibility of another shutdown when the temporary funding expires on January 15, McConnell declared there would not be a government shutdown, while Senator Ted Cruz did not rule out that option, saying he would "do anything, and I will continue to do anything I can, to stop the train wreck that is Obamacare." McConnell also said the Affordable Care Act would not be repealed until he becomes Senate majority leader and a Republican occupies the White House. McConnell faces a Republican primary challenge from Matt Bevin. Radio host Mark Levin called for McConnell's defeat, and former Alaska Governor Sarah Palin suggested she may support Bevin.

summary: President Barack Obama dispatched Attorney General Eric Holder to Ferguson, Missouri, to meet with federal authorities investigating the August 9 shooting of Michael Brown, an unarmed 18-year-old Black teenager, by a white police officer identified as Darren Wilson. Holder was scheduled to travel to the St. Louis suburb on Wednesday after providing a formal briefing to Obama in Washington on Monday; both men returned Sunday from a week's vacation on Martha's Vineyard. Holder announced Sunday that a federal medical examiner would conduct an independent autopsy, citing "extraordinary circumstances" and a civil rights investigation by the FBI. An earlier independent autopsy determined Brown was shot at least six times, including twice in the head. The shooting sparked more than a week of nightly protests. Police used tear gas and sound projectors against demonstrators, some of whom threw Molotov cocktails and bottles. Missouri Governor Jay Nixon deployed the National Guard early Monday to control the unrest. Senior White House aides made repeated urgent calls to Nixon, state police officials, and civil rights leaders in recent days. Funeral services for Brown were planned for Monday, though the exact time and location had not been finalized, according to family attorney Benjamin Crump.

summary:
A YouGov poll of Republican primary voters found Donald Trump leading his rivals on several leadership qualities. Seventy-five percent of respondents described Trump as bold, 62 percent as strong, and 64 percent as a Washington outsider. By comparison, 23 percent said Marco Rubio was bold, 29 percent said he was strong, and 5 percent considered him a Washington outsider. Rubio led only in the categories "typical politician" and "establishment candidate." Ted Cruz received the highest rating for being a true conservative at 54 percent, and also led on being religious, partisan, and honest at 42 percent.

Separately, Heidi Cruz, wife of candidate Ted Cruz, praised Donald Trump's former television program "The Apprentice" in comments to The New York Times. "I'm not great at TV references, but I did like The Apprentice because it was a show that gave people a chance to have a start," she said. "There was a measurable result and decision. That's a thing I like about the private sector." The Times also cited a 2004 commencement address at Southern Adventist University in Tennessee where she said: "I love that show, because those people risked failure in front of 28 million viewers to go for something that they really wanted. This wasn't just any failure. This was banishment from the Park Avenue board room on television ... To me, that takes guts."

Former Senate Majority Leader Bob Dole said in an interview Wednesday that Ted Cruz would be worse for the Republican Party than Donald Trump if either won the presidential nomination. "Nobody likes him," Dole said, predicting "cataclysmic" and "wholesale losses" for the GOP if Cruz prevailed.

The Iowa caucuses, which begin the Republican nomination process, were scheduled for Feb. 1.

summary: A federal judge in Hawaii on Wednesday placed a nationwide hold on President Trump's revised travel ban order, hours before it was scheduled to take effect. U.S. District Judge Derrick Watson blocked the second executive order, which would have barred travelers from six predominantly Muslim countries from entering the United States and halted the U.S. refugee resettlement program. The entry restrictions had been set to take effect at 12:01 a.m. Thursday, according to one account, or 12 a.m. EST Thursday according to another. Watson, an Obama appointee, found that the plaintiffs, including the state of Hawaii, showed a "strong" likelihood of succeeding in their lawsuit arguing the policy violates the Establishment Clause and would cause "irreparable harm." The judge called the administration's argument that the ban did not discriminate against Muslims because it applied to all religions in the affected countries "fundamentally flawed," writing that "the illogic of the government's intentions is palpable. The notion that no one can demonstrate animus toward any group of people by targeting all of them at once is fundamentally flawed." The revised order had been issued March 6 in an attempt to address issues that prompted the first version to be struck down. summary:
Two mass shootings occurred within hours of each other over the weekend in El Paso, Texas, and Dayton, Ohio, leaving 31 people dead and dozens wounded. Former Housing and Urban Development Secretary Julián Castro, one of two Texans running for president, said President Donald Trump has propagated racism, bigotry and white nationalism and "often serves as their national spokesperson." Castro added, "Donald Trump is unfit to lead our nation. His words could not be more hollow." He noted Trump said "we must condemn racism, bigotry and white nationalism" but continues to serve as their spokesperson.

Former President Barack Obama tweeted on Monday calling for more gun control, writing before all details were known. Civic groups have mobilized to help victims cover medical, funeral and other costs. CNN's Impact Your World is updating a page with opportunities to assist.

Obama called on Congress to pass legislation protecting voting access.

He telephoned plaintiffs in the challenge to California's ban; the Court did not rule on the merits but effectively allowed same-sex marriages to resume in the state. He also applauded the ruling striking down the Defense of Marriage Act provision denying federal benefits to married gay couples. "This was discrimination enshrined in law. He directed Attorney General Eric Holder to work with the Cabinet to review all federal statutes to ensure benefits are made available under the ruling.

The Obama administration became directly involved: senior White House aides placed urgent calls to Nixon, state police, and civil rights leaders, and Attorney General Eric Holder was in frequent contact with the governor and the State Highway Patrol. Holder announced Sunday that a federal medical examiner would conduct an independent autopsy as part of an FBI civil rights investigation. On Monday, President Obama said Holder would travel to Ferguson on Wednesday; independent autopsy results released by then showed Brown had been shot at least six times, including twice in the head. Obama and Holder had both been vacationing on Martha's Vineyard and returned Sunday; Holder was scheduled to brief the president Monday. summary: President Barack Obama held a news conference Monday in Antalya, Turkey, at the conclusion of the G-20 summit, three days after the Islamic State attacks in Paris. He described the Islamic State as "this barbaric terrorist organization" and acknowledged the Paris attacks as "a terrible and sickening setback." Obama rejected the notion that the United States had underestimated the group, saying its danger was the reason the U.S. was operating in Iraq and Syria and had mobilized 65 countries against it. He said reducing the territory controlled by the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria would reduce the flow of fighters and lessen the threat, and that disrupting the threat required constant vigilance and communication. Obama called the Islamic State "the face of evil" and said the U.S. and its allies were shrinking its hold in Syria and Iraq even as the group demonstrated an ability to spread terror beyond the region. He said sending ground troops would be a mistake, citing the opinion of his military advisers, and noted the U.S. military could easily march into Mosul, Raqqa, or Ramadi but that would only be a temporary solution. "If the US sent 50,000 troops into Syria, what would happen if an attack originated in Yemen or Libya?" he asked. One account said Obama appeared angry at reporters' repeated questions about the minimal success of his strategy, Republican proposals for more active engagement, and critics of his decision to allow 10,000 Syrians into the United States. Another account noted former Florida Governor Jeb Bush had declared that the response to terrorism should be to declare war.

Turkish Foreign Minister Mevlut Cavusoglu said U.S. forces in Syria are intentionally stalling the fight against Islamic State militants as an excuse not to cut ties with the Syrian Kurdish People's Protection Units (YPG), leaving "pockets" with Islamic State militants intact to justify continued cooperation with the militia. Cavusoglu said ties with the United States are "at a critical stage" and Washington needs to take "concrete steps" to regain Turkey's trust. Turkey considers the YPG a terrorist group linked to the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), which has waged a decades-long insurgency in Turkey. The YPG is the main ground element of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), which the United States has armed, trained and aided with air support and special forces to fight Islamic State. Turkey launched Operation Olive Branch last month, an air and ground assault in Syria's northwest Afrin region to drive the YPG from the area south of its border. Ankara Mayor Mustafa Tuna announced plans to rename Nevzat Tandogan Street, where the U.S. Embassy is located, to Olive Branch Street. In November, Turkey renamed the street where the United Arab Emirates embassy is located after an Ottoman military commander, reacting to an Emirati minister's retweet of a claim that the Turkish president's "forefathers" pillaged Medina. U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson arrived in Ankara on Thursday for two days of talks. He and President Tayyip Erdogan held what was described as a "productive and open" meeting about improving ties strained over Syria policy, following weeks of escalating anti-American rhetoric from Ankara.

Kentucky Senator Rand Paul said Monday during an appearance in South Carolina that the only decision he has made about a potential 2012 presidential campaign is that he will not run against his father, Texas Representative Ron Paul, according to the South Carolina Post and Courier. Paul added that he is traveling to early primary states because he wants the Tea Party to have influence over the 2012 nominee. He also acknowledged making stops in Iowa and New Hampshire and would not rule out a run if his father does not seek the nomination. In a separate interview with the Associated Press on Thursday, Paul said he is considering a presidential bid if his father decides not to run, and that he is being urged by supporters in several states to enter the race. Ron Paul, who ran for the Republican nomination in 2008 and later as the Libertarian Party candidate, has not yet made up his mind about 2012, though party organizers in Iowa say he is working diligently to build support among caucus-goers. In an ABC News interview last month, Rand Paul said of a potential campaign, "Come back and ask me in a few months."

summary:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu intensified his public pressure on the Obama administration over Iran this week. In an interview on NBC's "Meet the Press" recorded for Sunday broadcast, Netanyahu said a policy of containment for Iran would not work because Tehran is guided by a "leadership with an unbelievable fanaticism," adding, "You want these fanatics to have nuclear weapons?" He also said he disagrees with the argument that war with Iran would be worse than a nuclear-armed Iran. Earlier in the week, Netanyahu criticized the U.S. containment policy directly, saying peaceful methods are not working, and declared Tuesday that Israel will not wait for the Obama administration to approve military action against Iran's nuclear program. 

Tensions were also reported over a possible meeting between Netanyahu and President Obama in New York later this month. The Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported Tuesday that the White House had declined a meeting. CNN later reported, citing Israeli sources, that the White House rejected a meeting even after Netanyahu offered to travel to Washington after his New York visit. The White House said scheduling conflicts prevented the meeting. 

On Wednesday, a day after Netanyahu publicly criticized the administration for refusing to set clear "red lines" that would trigger a U.S. military strike on Iran, he spoke by phone with Obama overnight and adopted a more moderate tone. "As prime minister of Israel, it is my duty to uphold the vital interests of the State of Israel, to ensure its security and its future," Netanyahu said in remarks relayed by his office. "I uphold these interests, not that it's easy, because leadership is tested in upholding them even if there are disagreements with friends, even the best of friends." In Israel, the public was generally sympathetic to Netanyahu's stance but concerned about possible damage to ties with the White House. The Washington position remains that diplomacy and sanctions should be given more time to pressure Tehran to abandon its suspect nuclear work.

summary:
President Barack Obama canceled a planned trip to California to remain in Washington and work on a congressional resolution authorizing military action in Syria, the White House said Thursday. The president had been scheduled to visit California next week. While traveling in Sweden and Russia earlier in the week, Obama pressed lawmakers by phone, and his top officials lobbied Congress for support. A Senate panel has approved a resolution, but a significant number of senators remain unconvinced and opposition is growing in the House.

Rep. Adam Kinzinger (R-Ill.), a supporter of military action, criticized the administration on ABC's "This Week" Sunday for failing to build relationships with Congress before seeking its support. Kinzinger said his office reached out to the White House a week and a half earlier offering to help round up votes for a strike, but had received no response and did not know who his White House liaison was. "You can't begin to build a relationship for the first time when you need their support on something like this," Kinzinger said. He added that the president had "made this decision correctly" in arguing that the Syrian government's alleged use of chemical weapons mandates a military response.

A Washington Post-University of Maryland poll released Monday showed former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton leading the Democratic presidential field among registered Maryland Democrats with 43 percent support, followed by Vice President Joe Biden at 26 percent, Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders at 20 percent, former Maryland Gov. Martin O'Malley at 4 percent, former Virginia Sen. Jim Webb at 1 percent, and former Rhode Island Gov. Lincoln Chafee at less than 1 percent. Biden had not declared his candidacy. Separately, an NBC News/SurveyMonkey poll conducted after the first Democratic debate in Las Vegas found Clinton the winner, the third such debate poll showing a Clinton victory and the second by a firm considered reputable. No scientific poll showed a Sanders victory, though Sanders performed strongly on social media and in focus groups. In the NBC poll, 25 percent of respondents rated Webb's performance as the worst, 22 percent rated Chafee's the worst, and views of O'Malley were mildly negative; 35 percent thought no candidate performed badly. Lawrence Lessig, Chafee, Webb, and O'Malley were not factors in the horse race. During the Las Vegas debate, a remark by Sanders became the most retweeted of the night with more than 12,000 shares and helped him dominate social media attention and online searches. Sanders edged Clinton in Twitter mentions, 41 percent to 39 percent, while Webb, O'Malley, and Chafee combined for 20 percent. Sanders gained the most Twitter followers during the debate, was the most searched candidate on Google, and was the top candidate discussed on Facebook. Sanders's campaign reported raising $26 million in the previous quarter, close to Clinton's $28 million, including $2 million in online donations on the final filing day.

summary: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration announced Wednesday it would allow the use of an experimental test to screen blood donations for the Zika virus. The test, manufactured by Roche Molecular Systems, a New Jersey-based unit of Swiss drugmaker Roche Holding AG, may be used in areas with active mosquito-borne transmission of Zika. The decision follows FDA guidance issued in February recommending that blood no longer be collected from regions where the virus is circulating; as a result, Puerto Rico halted local blood donations and imported nearly 6,000 units of red blood cells from the continental United States. The new screening test will allow Puerto Rico to resume collecting donations from residents. Dr. Peter Marks, director of the FDA's Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, said "the bottom line is we are going to work with blood centers in Puerto Rico to try to help as many as possible make use of the investigational test," and estimated the test would be ready "within the next week or so." In a separate statement, Marks called the test's availability "an important step forward in maintaining the safety of the nation's blood supply." Luciana Borio, the FDA's acting chief scientist, said "the close collaboration between the FDA and the product manufacturer was essential to expediting availability."

The Associated Press reported Monday night that Hillary Clinton had secured enough delegates to become the presumptive Democratic nominee, the first woman to win a major-party presidential nomination. According to the AP count, Clinton had 1,812 pledged delegates and the support of 571 superdelegates, reaching the 2,383 needed. summary: President Barack Obama called Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell early Wednesday after Republicans won control of the Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections, but accounts differ on whether the two spoke. A White House official said Obama called to congratulate McConnell, who had won re-election in Kentucky, and left a message because McConnell had already left for the day. In public remarks in Kentucky, McConnell said he spoke with Obama on Wednesday and looked forward to finding areas of agreement, specifically citing trade agreements and rewriting the tax code. McConnell said voters expect the newly empowered Republicans and the Democratic White House to find common ground for fast action, but he did not expect Obama to agree with everything the Republican-led Senate proposes and anticipated some Republican ideas would draw a veto. McConnell also said it would be a "mistake" for Obama to take unilateral action on immigration, warning such a move would antagonize Republicans, though he added the new Republican majority wants to act on immigration. summary: President Obama delivered a speech Thursday at the White House urging the Republican-controlled House to pass comprehensive immigration reform this year. summary:

summary:
The Department of Justice and the FBI have opened an investigation into Cambridge Analytica, the British-based data firm that worked for President Trump's 2016 campaign, according to a New York Times report published Tuesday citing an American official and others familiar with the matter. The probe is in its early stages; prosecutors have questioned former employees and banks that handled the company's business dealings. Christopher Wylie, who ran research for the firm and later disclosed its connection to Facebook, told the Times he had been questioned by the FBI.

The investigation follows reports that Cambridge Analytica obtained personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users under the pretense of academic research but used it for political purposes. Facebook suspended the firm in March over concerns it had violated platform policies. That same month, Chief Executive Alexander Nix was suspended after hidden-camera footage showed him saying the firm blackmailed political clients' rivals.

Cambridge Analytica announced in early May that it would cease operations and enter bankruptcy proceedings, stating that media coverage had driven away customers and suppliers and left the company no viable alternative. The firm maintained it never misused Facebook data and expressed "unwavering confidence that its employees have acted ethically and lawfully." The Justice Department, the FBI, and Cambridge Analytica all declined to comment to the Times.

On Wednesday, the ranking member of the House Oversight Committee called for a subpoena of Cambridge Analytica.

President Donald Trump said in an interview with NBC's Chuck Todd, set to air Sunday on "Meet the Press," that he believes he would win the 2020 election "easier" if Democrats launch impeachment proceedings against him. Asked why House Speaker Nancy Pelosi has held off her impeachment caucus, Trump responded, "Because I think she feels that I will win much easier." He added, "I think I win the election easier, but I'm not sure that I like having it." Todd had asked whether impeachment is "good politics" for Trump.

Pelosi, in an appearance last month on Jimmy Kimmel's late-night show, offered a different explanation for Trump's posture. She said the "silver lining for him is, then he believes that he would be exonerated by the [Republican-controlled] United States Senate." Pelosi added there is "a school of thought that says, 'If the Senate acquits you, why bring up charges against him in the private sector when he's no longer president?' So when we go through with our case, it's got to be ironclad."

Pelosi and other Democratic leaders have largely avoided calling for impeachment hearings, arguing the House should conduct oversight investigations and see where the facts lead, and that there should be bipartisan support for impeachment. As of Friday, 73 Democrats and one Republican supported launching an impeachment inquiry, a group comprising lawmakers in swing districts, safe seats, first-term representatives and long-serving members. Support for impeachment among voters has grown but remains limited; an NBC News/Wall Street Journal poll released Sunday found 27 percent of Americans believe there is enough evidence to begin impeachment hearings now, up 10 percentage points from the previous month.

summary:
President Donald Trump announced on Twitter early Friday that he and first lady Melania Trump had tested positive for COVID-19. "Tonight, @FLOTUS and I tested positive for COVID-19. We will begin our quarantine and recovery process immediately. We will get through this TOGETHER!" he tweeted. The White House physician said in a letter released by the press office that both were "well" and that he expected the president to continue carrying out his duties without disruption while recovering.

Later Friday, Trump posted a video filmed at the White House and shared on social media as he prepared to travel to Walter Reed National Military Medical Center. "I think I'm doing very well, but we're going to make sure that things work out," he said in the video. He added that the first lady continued to do "very well." "Thank you very much. I appreciate it. I will never forget it," he said.

The White House said the president would work from the presidential offices at Walter Reed for the next few days "out of an abundance of caution, and at the recommendation of his physician and medical experts," according to press secretary Kayleigh McEnany. McEnany said Trump "remains in good spirits, has mild symptoms, and has been working throughout the day." A White House official also confirmed the president was experiencing mild symptoms, and the first lady said she had "mild symptoms" but was "feeling good."

Trump, wearing a mask, gave a thumbs-up as he left the White House to board Marine One for Walter Reed. The New York Times reported that Trump appeared lethargic during a Thursday fundraiser and fell asleep while flying back from a Minnesota rally on Wednesday night. More than 208,000 people in the United States had died from the virus this year.

Chair Lynn Krogh criticized Scozzafava's endorsement of Owens, saying it was "driven by bitterness" and that she "would rather see a Pelosi-Democrat sitting in Congress than a member of her own party." The seat was vacant because Republican John McHugh had resigned to become Army secretary.

summary:
Florida Gov. Rick Scott signed an executive order Friday scheduling a special election to fill the U.S. House seat vacated by Rep. Trey Radel (R-Fla.). The order sets the primary for April 22 and the general election for June 24 in the 19th Congressional District, which includes the Gulf Coast cities of Fort Myers and Naples. Radel won the district with 62 percent of the vote in 2012; Mitt Romney carried it with a nearly equal share in the presidential election.

Radel resigned Monday, several weeks after returning to work following a stay at a rehabilitation center in Florida. On Nov. 20, he pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor charge of cocaine possession and was sentenced to a year of probation. Court records show he admitted purchasing 3.5 grams of cocaine from an undercover officer on Oct. 29 in Washington. After his arrest, several Republican leaders called for his resignation. Radel initially pledged to remain in office and rebuild trust after completing in-patient treatment for drug and alcohol abuse, but later said he could no longer effectively serve his constituents.

The House Ethics Committee announced Wednesday that it had formally ended its investigation into Radel, launched Dec. 12, because it no longer had jurisdiction after his resignation. The panel said it was "unable to complete its work" before he stepped down.

A crowded Republican primary field is expected; former state Rep. Paige Kreegel has already announced her candidacy. Meanwhile, a separate special election to replace the late Rep. Bill Young (R-Fla.) is already underway, with Republican David Jolly and Democrat Alex Sink nominated in their respective primaries earlier this month and a general election set for March 11.

summary: The Obama administration on Monday gave conditional approval for Royal Dutch Shell to drill for oil in the Chukchi Sea off Alaska's coast, a decision that could allow the company to become the first energy producer in the U.S. Arctic. The Interior Department's Bureau of Ocean Energy Management approved Shell's exploration plan after what Director Abigail Ross Hopper described as a thoughtful approach recognizing significant environmental, social, and ecological resources in the region and establishing high standards for protecting the ecosystem, Arctic communities, and the subsistence needs and cultural traditions of Alaska Natives. Federal scientists estimate the region could hold up to 15 billion barrels of oil. The decision was welcomed by the oil and gas industry, which had criticized the administration for moving too slowly on Arctic offshore drilling. Environmental groups called it a setback, citing concerns about climate change and the risk of spills in fragile Arctic waters, with some warning a drilling accident could have consequences more devastating than the 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill that killed 11 people and released millions of barrels of oil in the Gulf of Mexico. The approval came one day before senators, including Bill Cassidy, introduced bills to expand offshore drilling; Cassidy's office said 87 percent of the Outer Continental Shelf remains off-limits. Earlier this year, the Interior Department had proposed opening limited areas in the Atlantic and Arctic to drilling while maintaining a ban in the eastern Gulf of Mexico, a plan congressional Republicans called too restrictive.

The White House had informed members of Congress that intelligence reached this conclusion within the previous day. On Tuesday, White House spokesman Jay Carney said the administration remained unconvinced that the Assad regime had used chemical weapons, stating, "We have not come to the conclusion that there has been that use," and that the U.S. supported an investigation. President Barack Obama said Friday, April 26, that the deployment of chemical weapons by the Syrian government would be a "game changer" but noted that intelligence assessments proving such use were still preliminary. Obama said the use of potential weapons of mass destruction on civilian populations "crosses another line with respect to international norms and international law" and that the U.S. must "act prudently" and "make these assessments deliberately." The administration has previously called chemical weapons use a "red line" that would provoke U.S. military action. The conflict between rebel groups and the Assad regime had killed at least 60,000 people and displaced millions.

summary: Negotiators from Iran and six world powers met in Geneva over several days to seek an agreement that would temporarily halt Iran's nuclear program in exchange for sanctions relief. On Thursday, European Union foreign policy chief Catherine Ashton met with Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif to discuss arrangements. Zarif told reporters, "If everyone tries their best, we may have one [breakthrough]... We expect serious negotiations. It's possible." U.S. officials signaled the United States was prepared to offer limited sanctions relief if Iran halted its nuclear development program and reversed part of it. Secretary of State John Kerry flew to Geneva on Friday, interrupting a Middle East trip. On Friday, Kerry, Ashton, and Zarif met for five hours. A senior U.S. official said Kerry and Ashton planned to meet separately at their Geneva hotel on Saturday morning before inviting Zarif to join. On Saturday, the talks ended without a deal after France objected that the proposed agreement did not sufficiently curb Iran's nuclear capacities, particularly Iran's refusal to suspend work on a plutonium-producing reactor and to downgrade its stockpile of higher-enriched uranium. The French sought tougher conditions than those accepted by the other negotiating nations, including the United States, according to the Associated Press. Ashton and Zarif issued a joint statement: "A lot of concrete progress has been achieved but some differences remain." The negotiations faced fierce opposition from Israel and uncertainty in the U.S. Congress.

Louisiana Governor Bobby Jindal ended his Republican presidential campaign on Tuesday, telling Fox News, "I've come to the realization this is not my time." Jindal had trailed in polls, raised little money, and failed to qualify for prime-time debate stages. His campaign reported $261,000 cash on hand as of early October. He was the third Republican to withdraw, following former Texas Governor Rick Perry and Wisconsin Governor Scott Walker, leaving 14 candidates in the race. Jindal's campaign centered on detailed policy proposals, strong criticism of front-runner Donald Trump — including calling him a "narcissist" and "an egomaniac" in a September speech — and extensive outreach to Iowa conservatives. Trump responded to Jindal's departure on Saturday, saying Jindal had spent $1,000 to register in New Hampshire and "dropped out the next day. Such a waste." On "Fox and Friends," Trump also said Jindal had been "a little nasty" but added, "I think he's a nice guy. I think he's a good man." Trump also criticized New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio on Saturday, having recently referred to himself as the "Ernest Hemingway of 140 characters."

summary: Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg did not attend President Donald Trump's first State of the Union address on Tuesday. Instead, the 84-year-old justice spoke at Roger Williams University School of Law in Rhode Island, an engagement planned in August. Ginsburg also skipped Trump's address to a joint session of Congress in 2017, after attending all eight of former President Barack Obama's addresses to Congress. During her Rhode Island appearance, Ginsburg expressed concern that the federal judiciary could be perceived as a political branch of government and called for "great leaders on both sides of the aisle to say 'Let's stop this nonsense' and start working for our country the way we should." She praised Senators Elizabeth Warren, Amy Klobuchar, and Susan Collins for working across party lines. Ginsburg said she feels fine and credited her health to her personal trainer. She dismissed retirement speculation, stating she would continue at "full steam" and noting she had hired law clerks through June 2020. Other justices have previously declined to attend presidential addresses; Justice Antonin Scalia had not attended since 1997. Separately, former Arkansas Governor Mike Huckabee posted a tweet about Ginsburg's absence that misspelled her name and referenced her dozing during Obama's 2015 address, which she attributed to wine at a prior dinner. The tweet drew criticism, including from Representative Carlos Curbelo, Republican of Florida, who called it "despicable" and "tasteless."

summary: Alabama Democratic Sen. Doug Jones appeared Sunday on CNN's "State of the Union" and said he would make an independent judgment on President Donald Trump's nominee to replace Supreme Court Justice Anthony Kennedy. "I'm open to voting yes. I'm open to voting no. We don't know who the nominee is going to be yet," Jones told host Dana Bash. "I don't think my role is to rubber stamp for the President, but it's also not an automatic knee-jerk no, either." He added, "I am going to make an independent judgment and a view. I don't think anyone should expect me to simply vote yes for this nominee just simply because my state may be more conservative than others. I think even the people of Alabama like to make sure they have judges that adhere to the rule of law." Jones said the nominee would receive "a very, very good, hard and fair look to determine what I believe to be the best interest of my constituents, but also the country." Trump said last week he had narrowed a list of four potential nominees to three or two and planned to announce his choice Monday evening. As a Democrat representing a state Trump won by a wide margin, Jones faces pressure from both parties ahead of the November election.

Donald Trump fired campaign manager Corey Lewandowski on Monday. A day later, on Tuesday, the campaign announced a series of new hires: Jim Murphy as national political director focusing on battleground states, Lucia Castellano as director of human resources, Brad Parscale to head the digital team, and Kevin Kellems as director of surrogates. The campaign also added staff to the Communications Division to expand research and rapid response capabilities, with more hires expected before the July convention. Advisers said one reason for Lewandowski's dismissal was that he had blocked new hires for a campaign viewed as inadequately staffed for a general election. In an interview with CNN's Dana Bash on Monday afternoon, Lewandowski said he had no professional regrets about how he ran the campaign, adding that his biggest personal regret was not having his family more involved. He did not disclose a reason for his firing, describing himself as a "very straight shooter" and saying, "I'm not smart enough to lie." He said his duty was to give his best advice and opinion. Separately, the campaign has made payments for web advertising to a company called Draper Sterling, a reference to the "Mad Men" characters Don Draper and Roger Sterling, which has little footprint beyond a New Hampshire home. Parscale had already been tweeting Trump campaign statements for weeks before the announcement.

On a foggy Monday afternoon in Washington, Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, a Nevada Democrat, opened the week's session by paying tribute to retiring Senator Ben Nelson, a Nebraska Democrat who is leaving at the end of the Congress. Reid praised Nelson's thick gray hair, calling it "a mop of real hair" and noting that constituents have called Nelson's office to verify it is not a toupee. "It's his hair. He'll pull it for you any time just to show you that it's real," Reid said. Reid remarked that his wife has told him on many occasions that she thinks Leahy is handsome because he refuses to wear a comb-over.

The president returned to the White House late Wednesday afternoon. summary: On Thursday evening, August 8, a toddler squeezed through the White House fence on the North Lawn in front of the residence, prompting a Secret Service response. According to one account, the breach occurred just before President Barack Obama was scheduled to address the nation on Iraq, causing a temporary lockdown and delaying the briefing. Agents scrambled to intercept the child, who had maneuvered between the bars of the fence, and returned him to his parents. Secret Service spokesman Edwin Donovan issued a statement: "We were going to wait until he learned to talk to question him, but in lieu of that he got a timeout and was sent on way with parents." The incident was resolved quickly. The following morning, Friday, the U.S. Capitol visitor center was closed briefly after authorities found an unattended stroller outside; a Capitol Police spokesman said the stroller was "deemed non-hazardous." There was no word on whether the White House plans to modify the fence.

Caitlyn Jenner, formerly Bruce Jenner, debuted Monday on the cover of Vanity Fair and posted her first tweet at 12:17 p.m., a photo of the cover with the quote "Call me Caitlyn." The tweet was retweeted more than 180,000 times, and the name change generated 1.5 million tweets, peaking at 11,000 per minute. Jenner reached 1 million followers in four hours and three minutes, a Guinness World Record for fastest to that milestone, breaking the mark set by President Obama when he launched @POTUS in May. Obama had reached 1 million in just under five hours, surpassing Robert Downey Jr.'s 2014 record.

White House press secretary Josh Earnest said Obama believes Jenner showed "tremendous courage" for her public transition and that it is "worthy of our respect." Obama also asked followers to share their stories on the Organizing for Action website. Jenner had come out as transgender in a 20/20 interview with Diane Sawyer last month.

summary: Exxon Mobil Corp. and former Chairman and Chief Executive Rex Tillerson agreed to sever all ties to comply with conflict-of-interest requirements ahead of his confirmation hearings for Secretary of State under President-elect Donald Trump. Under the agreement, announced as Tillerson awaited Senate hearings scheduled to begin January 11, more than 2 million deferred Exxon shares he would have received over the next 10 years — valued at about $182 million at a recent closing price of $90.89 — will be transferred to an independently managed trust barred from investing in Exxon. The share awards will be canceled, and Tillerson will surrender entitlement to more than $4.1 million in cash bonuses payable over three years, along with retiree medical and dental benefits and administrative, financial and tax support. Tillerson also committed to sell the more than 600,000 Exxon shares he currently owns. The company said the net effect reduces compensation owed to Tillerson by approximately $7 million; Tillerson said he expects a loss of about $7 million from the arrangement. Tillerson stepped down as CEO on January 1, 2017, and Exxon President Darren Woods is set to become chairman and chief executive in January. Exxon shares have risen 6.5 percent since the November 8 election. Lawmakers from both parties have raised questions about Tillerson's business dealings and ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Former Democratic National Committee interim chair Donna Brazile, in excerpts from her forthcoming book, described a memorandum between Hillary Clinton's 2016 presidential campaign, the DNC, and the joint fundraising committee Hillary for America (HFA). The agreement gave the Clinton campaign control over the party's finances, strategy, and all money raised in exchange for helping the DNC retire lingering debt. Brazile wrote that the arrangement 'was not illegal, but it sure looked unethical' and 'compromised the party's integrity,' adding: 'If the fight had been fair, one campaign would not have control of the party before the voters had decided which one they wanted to lead. Brazile took over as interim chair after Representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz stepped down before the Democratic National Convention amid accusations that DNC staff favored Clinton.
