President Donald Trump, commenting on the book excerpts, tweeted that Brazile said she 'paid for and stole the Dem Primary' and called for Justice Department and FBI action. On Fox News' 'The Ingraham Angle,' Trump said the actions described were 'illegal' and 'really unfair to Bernie Sanders,' adding that he received many Sanders supporters' votes over trade policy.

President Donald Trump announced Tuesday morning via Twitter that he was removing Rex Tillerson as secretary of state and naming CIA Director Mike Pompeo as his replacement. Trump also announced that Gina Haspel, Pompeo's deputy at the CIA, would become the new CIA director, which would make her the first woman to lead the agency. A report late last year said Tillerson had referred to Trump as a "moron," prompting Trump to challenge him to an IQ test. Tillerson had recently stated the United States was considering lifting a travel ban on Chad. Haspel's appointment would require Senate confirmation.

summary:
The Senate on Tuesday rejected a proposal to create a bipartisan task force on the deficit, an amendment to a $1.9 trillion increase in the debt limit. The measure received 53 votes, short of the 60 required. President Obama had endorsed the plan after pressure from moderate Democrats. The panel would have been authorized to recommend changes to the tax code and entitlement programs including Social Security and Medicare, with its plan subject to a vote after the midterm elections. Republicans opposed to tax increases joined Democrats concerned about benefit cuts to defeat it. Key Republicans said they would refuse to participate in such a commission, which would have lacked legal authority to compel congressional action.

In his State of the Union address Wednesday night, Obama called for creation of a bipartisan budget task force and urged senators to restore the pay-as-you-go law, saying, "When the vote comes tomorrow, the Senate should restore the pay-as-you-go law that was a big reason for why we had record surpluses in the 1990s." He outlined a broader deficit-reduction effort including a three-year freeze on non-defense discretionary spending and a commission on deficit reduction to be established by executive order, a step he had previously pledged to take if Congress failed to act.

On Thursday, the Senate adopted statutory pay-go rules on a 60-40 party-line vote, with all Democrats in favor and all Republicans opposed. The House had approved a similar rule 265-166 in July. Republicans argued the rule would provide cover for tax increases. The Democratic National Committee identified five previous votes in which Republican senators who opposed the measure had supported pay-go restoration.

The United States conducted airstrikes against Islamic State targets in northern Iraq on Friday, the Pentagon confirmed. Rear Adm. John Kirby, the Defense Department's press secretary, announced the strikes. The operation marked the first direct U.S. combat role in Iraq since 2011. President Barack Obama had authorized the strikes Thursday night, citing threats to American military trainers and personnel in Erbil, the Kurdish regional capital, which hosts a U.S. consulate.

The strikes were carried out by Navy F/A-18 fighter jets flying from the aircraft carrier USS George H.W. Bush and by armed drones, including Predator drones. The jets dropped 500-pound laser-guided bombs.

The first strike, conducted by two F/A-18s, hit a mobile artillery piece near Erbil that had been shelling Kurdish forces defending the city near U.S. personnel. Later, four F/A-18s struck a stationary convoy of seven vehicles and a mortar position outside Erbil, dropping a total of eight laser-guided bombs. A drone struck a mortar position; when Islamic State fighters returned to the site moments later, they were attacked again and killed. Another drone strike hit a mortar position Friday afternoon.

summary: Acting White House chief of staff Mick Mulvaney held a press conference on Thursday in which he said the United States withheld nearly $400 million in military aid to Ukraine in part to pressure the Ukrainian government to investigate a theory that Democrats manipulated the 2016 election. "That's why we held up the money," Mulvaney said. When ABC News reporter Jon Karl asked whether that described a quid pro quo, Mulvaney responded, "We do that all the time with foreign policy," and added, "Get over it. There's going to be political influence in foreign policy.... Elections have consequences." Mulvaney later said his remarks had been "misconstrued" by the media. On Sunday, Mulvaney said he had not offered his resignation. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo appeared on ABC's "This Week" the same day and said he never saw a quid pro quo being pursued in the decision-making process regarding Ukraine aid. summary:
The Supreme Court issued two major rulings on same-sex marriage on the same day. In United States v. Windsor, the Court struck down Section 3 of the Defense of Marriage Act as unconstitutional because it denied legally married same-sex couples federal benefits available to other married couples. The vote was 5-to-4 along ideological lines. Justice Anthony Kennedy wrote the majority opinion, joined by Justices Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Breyer, Sonia Sotomayor, and Elena Kagan. Justice Antonin Scalia read a dissent from the bench accusing the majority of demonizing opponents of same-sex marriage as "enemies of human decency." Chief Justice John Roberts and Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas also dissented. In Hollingsworth v. In a separate ruling in Shelby County v. Holder, the Court struck down Section 4 of the Voting Rights Act, the formula determining which jurisdictions must obtain federal preclearance for voting changes. The vote was 5-to-4. Roberts authored the majority opinion, joined by Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, and Alito. At a conference of judges and lawyers in West Virginia, Roberts said the justices had become too aggressive in questioning attorneys during oral arguments, "overdo it a bit," and use the hour-long sessions to debate each other through the lawyers because they have not discussed the cases beforehand. Justice Thomas, who had not asked a question in seven years, had made the same criticism. Roberts suggested lawyers not attempt to respond when justices pose rapid-fire questions.

Republican strategist Steve Schmidt, appearing on Nicolle Wallace's MSNBC program, attributed the apology to Hogg's fearlessness, saying, "Maybe that's what happens after you've been down range of an AR-15 that kills your classmates and comes close to killing you. The Post reported that this animosity partially led to the firing.

summary:
Thousands gathered at a park near Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, for a "March for Our Lives" rally on Saturday, one month after a gunman killed 17 people at the school on Feb. 14. Organizers said 20,000 people attended the Parkland event. Participants wore maroon T-shirts in the school's color and carried signs reading "why do your guns matter more than our lives?" and "our ballots will stop bullets." They chanted "Enough is enough." After the rally, participants marched two miles toward the school and passed it in silence to honor the victims.

In Washington, D.C., a separate march drew an estimated 800,000 people, according to organizers. Nationwide, the rallies attracted hundreds of thousands of demonstrators across the country. Delaney Tarr, a student at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School, addressed the Washington crowd, saying, "If they continue to ignore us, to only pretend to listen, then we will take action where it counts. We will take action every day in every way until they simply cannot ignore us any more."

Voter registration was a focus of the demonstrations. By 8:30 p.m. Saturday, at least 4,000 people had registered to vote at protests across the United States, Reuters reported. Organizers of registration drives said they hoped to sign up at least 25,000 people that day. Sari Kaufman, another Marjory Stoneman Douglas student, spoke at the Parkland rally, saying, "With this movement, we will ensure record-breaking turnout not just in the next presidential election, not in the next midterm election, but in all elections. We're here today to give you the tools to make a change."

Thousands of protesters assembled in Cairo's central Tahrir Square, while a youth group leading the campaign said it had collected more than 22 million signatures calling for Morsi to step down; the claim could not be verified, and Morsi supporters questioned the authenticity of the signatures. In a separate part of the city, thousands of Morsi supporters had staged a sit-in since Friday in an eastern Cairo district near the presidential palace. CNN correspondent Ben Wedeman described the anti-Morsi demonstration as the largest public protest he had ever seen in Egypt. Many observers feared the rival demonstrations could turn violent.

summary: Following the June 2015 shooting at Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Charleston, South Carolina, multiple officials and organizations moved to remove the Confederate battle flag from official and public spaces. South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley called for the flag's removal from the state capitol grounds. In Alabama, Gov. Robert Bentley ordered the Confederate battle flag removed from the state Capitol grounds on Wednesday morning; two workers took down the flag that had been flying over a Confederate memorial near the Statehouse in Montgomery. Bentley told Al.com he ordered the removal "partially" because of Charleston, saying, "This is the right thing to do. We are facing some major issues in this state regarding the budget and other matters that we need to deal with. This had the potential to become a major distraction as we go forward. I have taxes to raise; we have work to do. And it was my decision that the flag needed to come down." The Associated Press reported Wednesday that U.S. Sen. Roger Wicker became Mississippi's second top-tier Republican to call for changing the state flag, which has incorporated the Confederate battle emblem in its canton since Reconstruction. Wicker said the flag "should be put in a museum and replaced by one that is more unifying." In South Carolina, lawmakers were reportedly considering a temporary removal ahead of a formal vote expected the following month. NASCAR Chairman Brian France told The Associated Press on Saturday that he personally found the Confederate flag an "insensitive symbol" and offensive. France said NASCAR would be aggressive in dissociating the flag from its events and was exploring how far it could go to eliminate the flag from races, where fans frequently display it in infield camping areas and tailgates. NASCAR had earlier stated it backed Haley's call and noted it bars the flag symbol in any official NASCAR capacity. France said, "We want to go as far as we can to eliminate the presence of that flag."

summary: Congress approved a temporary spending measure on Wednesday to avert a government shutdown at midnight on the last day of the fiscal year. The legislation funds federal agencies through Dec. 11. The Senate passed the bill earlier in the day by a 78-20 vote. The House then approved the measure. One account put the House vote at 257-151, with 186 Democrats and 91 Republicans in favor and all opposition votes cast by Republicans. Another account put the House vote at 277-151. Before the final vote, the House approved a procedural rule governing debate by a 239-187 margin, with three Republicans opposing. The House also adopted a separate resolution to cut off federal funding to Planned Parenthood, described as an "enrollment correction," which was expected to fail in the Senate. Debate on the spending bill was delayed by lawmakers who demanded the must-pass legislation be used to strip Planned Parenthood of federal money because of its practice of supplying tissue from aborted fetuses for scientific research. The stopgap measure provides 10 weeks to negotiate a broader budget deal that would extend past the 2016 presidential election.

summary: At the first presidential debate Monday night in Hempstead, N.Y., Hillary Clinton became the first woman to stand on stage for a general-election presidential debate. The debate was moderated by Lester Holt. During the event, Donald Trump said, "I have much better judgement than she has. There's no question about that. I also have a much better temperament than she does." When Clinton received the floor, she said, "Whoo! OK," prompting audience laughter. She then inhaled, exhaled, smiled, and moved her shoulders in a motion described as a shimmy before beginning a point about NATO. In response to a question from Holt about whether she believes police have "implicit bias" against black Americans, Clinton said, "I think implicit bias is a problem for everyone. Not just police. I think unfortunately too many of us in our great country, um, jump to conclusions about each other. And therefore I think we need all of us to be asking ourselves hard questions about, you know, why am I feeling this way."

summary: Congressional leaders reached a bipartisan agreement Sunday on a spending bill to fund federal agencies through September, averting a government shutdown. The measure, expected to be made public Monday and still requiring votes in both chambers, would provide more than $1 trillion for day-to-day operations of virtually every federal agency through the end of the fiscal year. The agreement denies funding for a southern border wall but includes increased funding for border security and a $15 billion down payment on military strengthening. It also increases funding for the National Institutes of Health by $2 billion to $34.1 billion, rejecting the Trump administration's proposal to cut the NIH budget by $1.2 billion for the remainder of the fiscal year. The package provides tens of millions of dollars to reimburse local law enforcement agencies for costs incurred protecting President Trump and his family, notably benefiting New York City for Trump Tower protection. The deal represents the first major bipartisan legislation to advance during Trump's presidency. House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi said the omnibus stands in sharp contrast to the administration's plans to reduce medical research funding.

summary: Former Denver Broncos quarterback John Elway endorsed Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney on Monday in Colorado, two days before the first presidential debate between Romney and President Barack Obama in Denver. Elway, a Hall of Famer and former Stanford quarterback, said he supported Romney because he was a "proven leader with the experience and background to turn around our struggling economy." He added: "In these tough economic times, we need a president who understands how to get America working again – by standing on the side of taxpayers and small-business owners who do the real job creating. America needs a comeback team -- Mitt Romney and Paul Ryan are that team." Romney responded in a statement: "leaders come in many forms, and John Elway has always exemplified leadership, first as a quarterback for the Super Bowl champion Broncos, and now as an executive vice president for the team. He's had to overcome challenges during his career, and he knows what it takes to turn things around when things get tough. I'm proud to have him on my team as we campaign to lead the comeback this nation desperately needs." The Romney campaign announced the endorsement ahead of a campaign appearance at the Wings Over the Rockies Air and Space Museum in Denver. The first presidential debate took place Wednesday at the University of Denver. During the debate, Obama said Romney favors cutting a fifth of the Education Department's budget, while Romney countered that Obama directed $90 billion to "green jobs," a sum he said would hire 2 million teachers. Obama pointed to running mate Paul Ryan's budget proposals as making sharp cuts across the board; Romney retorted that Washington invested in failed energy research. Obama is scheduled to hold a campaign rally Thursday at Sloan's Lake Park in Denver.

summary: President Obama visited the Key Bridge in Washington on Tuesday to promote his infrastructure agenda. The bridge, which links the Georgetown neighborhood to northern Virginia and is named after "Star-Spangled Banner" author Francis Scott Key, has undergone repairs financed by the Highway Trust Fund. In a mid-afternoon speech at Georgetown Waterfront Park overlooking the Potomac River, Obama called on Congress to renew the Highway Trust Fund, which is expected to exhaust its resources by August or expire at summer's end without congressional action. He also urged Congress to close tax loopholes and direct the revenue to infrastructure projects. The White House said that without renewal, states would have to delay or cancel road projects, placing as many as 700,000 jobs at risk. Obama criticized congressional Republicans for inaction, saying, "I haven't heard a good reason why they haven't acted... It's not like they've been busy with other stuff. No, seriously!" He said the Key Bridge is one of several bridges undergoing federally funded repairs after being deemed structurally deficient. Earlier, infrastructure was on the agenda at a mid-morning Cabinet meeting. Obama ordered Cabinet members to travel the country this summer to hear directly from Americans about their concerns and ideas for expanding opportunity and growing the economy. The White House said Obama wants his Cabinet secretaries to recommend new executive actions he can take without congressional approval.

Hillary Clinton campaigned in Ames, Iowa, on Saturday, January 30, 2016, alongside former U.S. Representative Gabby Giffords and her husband, Mark Kelly. Giffords, who was gravely wounded in a 2011 shooting in Tucson, Arizona, endorsed Clinton at the event, telling voters, "Come January [2017] I want to say these two words: 'Madam President.'" Kelly and Giffords founded Americans for Responsible Solutions to push for expanded background checks after the shooting; the gunman in that case had acquired his weapon via a background check. Clinton used the appearance to draw a contrast with rival Bernie Sanders on gun policy. She urged caucus-goers to make gun control a "voting issue" and asked them to "think of this" when they caucused on Monday night. Clinton cited Sanders' past votes against a waiting period for gun purchases and for granting gun manufacturers legal immunity from lawsuits. Sanders, who has highlighted his "D- rating from the NRA," now supports efforts to repeal that immunity and says he has been a tough opponent of the pro-gun lobby. Clinton also noted her endorsement by the Brady Campaign to Prevent Gun Violence. Separately, the New York Times editorial board endorsed Clinton for the Democratic nomination. One report cited internal campaign data showing Clinton leading Sanders in enthusiasm, 73 to 69, with her definite-voter percentage rising from 69 percent earlier in the month to 83 percent.

summary: Former President George H.W. Bush, 93, was admitted to Houston Methodist Hospital on Sunday, April 22, for treatment of an infection that had spread to his blood. The admission came one day after the funeral of his wife, former first lady Barbara Bush, who died April 17 at age 92; the couple had been married 73 years. On Wednesday, April 25, Bush posted a tweet thanking Houston Mayor Sylvester Turner, the city police and transit agency, Second Baptist Church, St. Martin's Episcopal Church, and "really all Houstonians" for their professionalism and care during the memorial services for his wife. The tweet did not mention his own health. A family spokesman, Jim McGrath, said Bush was "responding and recovering." According to one account, Bush was moved from intensive care to a regular patient room Wednesday afternoon. On Friday, April 27, McGrath said in a tweet that Bush would remain hospitalized through the weekend but was "in excellent spirits," focusing on "regaining strength" and looking forward to resuming his schedule and going to Maine next month. In an interview with The Associated Press, McGrath added that Bush was "responding to treatments and appears to be recovering" and called him "the most goal-oriented person on this planet." Bush also greeted well-wishers on Friday.

summary: Herman Cain is expected to withdraw from consideration for a seat on the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, ABC News reported Thursday citing an administration official and a source familiar with the matter. Cain's 2012 presidential campaign ended after four women accused him of sexual harassment; Cain denied the allegations. Republicans also expressed concern about Cain's support for cutting interest rates. summary: President Barack Obama on Monday addressed the mass shooting at the Washington Navy Yard in Southeast Washington, about 3 1/2 miles from the White House. The White House said Obama continued to receive briefings throughout the day from Lisa Monaco, assistant to the president for homeland security and counterterrorism, and Alyssa Mastromonaco, deputy chief of staff. The White House also postponed "Musica Latina," a performance celebrating Latin music during Hispanic Heritage Month scheduled for Monday evening, out of respect for the victims and their families. summary:
President Trump dismissed Veterans Affairs Secretary David J. Shulkin on Wednesday and nominated Dr. Ronny L. Jackson, the White House physician and a Navy doctor, to lead the department. Jackson has served as physician to the last three presidents. In January, he conducted Trump's first physical exam since taking office and held an hourlong press briefing on the results, describing the president's health as excellent and remarking, "It's just the way God made him." The White House said Trump has full confidence in Jackson's ability to lead the VA and pointed to his Navy experience as a valuable asset. The New York Times reported that some aides acknowledged Trump's personal relationship with Jackson carried more weight in the nomination than the doctor's professional experience.

The change has renewed debate over veterans' health care, specifically whether to expand the option for veterans to use their benefits to see private doctors rather than relying on the VA's network of 1,700 hospitals and clinics serving 20 million veterans. Major veterans groups, including the Veterans of Foreign Wars and the American Legion, oppose such a shift, arguing it would undermine the VA system. They are aligned against Concerned Veterans for America, an advocacy group funded by Charles G. and David H. Koch. Democrats and these veterans groups said they fear the administration will push for a major change they have bitterly opposed. The department has been described as bruised by scandal and months of intrigue.

summary: Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, 85, fell in her office at the Supreme Court building in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday night, fracturing three ribs. She initially returned home but experienced discomfort overnight and was taken to George Washington University Hospital early Thursday morning by Supreme Court police for treatment and observation. The hospitalization caused her to miss Thursday's formal investiture ceremony for Justice Brett Kavanaugh. Ginsburg performed some work from her hospital room Thursday night. The Supreme Court announced Friday morning that she had been discharged. Court spokeswoman Kathy Arberg said Ginsburg was "doing well and plans to work from home today." Ginsburg, appointed by President Bill Clinton in 1993, is the court's oldest member and a leading liberal voice. She has a history of health issues: colon cancer in 1999, pancreatic cancer in 2009, a heart procedure with a stent implanted in 2014, and a fall in 2012 that broke two ribs. In April, Justice Sonia Sotomayor underwent shoulder replacement surgery after a fall at home. Ginsburg has said she hopes to serve five more years, noting that former Justice John Paul Stevens served into his 90s.

summary: President Barack Obama authorized the provision of arms to Syrian rebels fighting President Bashar al-Assad, U.S. officials announced Thursday, June 13. According to The Wall Street Journal, the authorization came through a classified order directing the CIA to supply weapons to the rebels and their allies. The White House declined to elaborate on the order but stated Obama had decided to increase military support in both "scope and scale." Deputy National Security Advisor Ben Rhodes said the conclusion that the Syrian regime had used chemical weapons against rebels weighed heavily in the decision, referring to the chemical weapons use as a "red line." The White House disclosed it had conclusive evidence of such use by Assad's government. Administration officials said the arms provision would require a limited no-fly zone inside Syria to be enforced from Jordanian territory; Jordan has offered military bases to the United States and its allies to protect a safe zone inside the kingdom. Anonymous U.S. military officials estimated four weeks to establish the zone. The decision drew criticism. At the Faith and Freedom Coalition's annual meeting Saturday, former Alaska Gov. Sarah Palin said, "Until we have a commander in chief who knows what he is doing... let Allah sort it out!" On ABC's "This Week," former House Speaker Newt Gingrich called the plan ineffectual against Russian and Iranian military support for Assad, saying it would set the United States "up to be defeated" and that Russian President Vladimir Putin would be "quite happy on behalf of Russia to be part of defeating the United States." summary:
The U.S. economy added 288,000 jobs in June, and the unemployment rate fell to 6.1 percent from 6.3 percent, the Labor Department reported. It was the fifth consecutive month of job gains exceeding 200,000, a streak last matched during the 1999-2000 technology boom. Monthly job gains so far in 2014 averaged 230,833, up from 194,250 in 2013. The unemployment rate reached its lowest level since September 2008.

The June gains were distributed across multiple industries. Retail employment rose by 40,200, health care and social assistance by 33,700, and restaurants and bars by 32,800. Factories added 16,000 jobs, and local governments added 18,000 education workers, a figure economists attributed to an extended school year following a high number of winter snow days. Construction added 6,000 jobs. Temporary positions accounted for 3.5 percent of the jobs added, well below the roughly 10 percent monthly average during the five-year recovery.

The Labor Department revised May's gain upward to 217,000 from an earlier estimate and April's to 304,000.

President Barack Obama, speaking at 1776, a technology startup hub in Washington, D.C., on Independence Day, said the report showed the recovery was taking hold. "We're making progress," he said, citing the fastest job growth since 1999. He urged Congress to work with him to create more jobs and credited entrepreneurs for "trying to figure out how we do well by doing good." The White House said the venue illustrated the president's commitment to promoting entrepreneurship.

summary: Former Panamanian President Ricardo Martinelli, 66, was extradited from the United States to Panama on Monday to face charges of political espionage and embezzlement. Martinelli, who served as president from 2009 to 2014, had been jailed in Miami since his arrest at his home in June 2017. Panama's highest court issued an arrest warrant in December 2015, after which Martinelli fled to the United States. Panama requested extradition last year; Martinelli initially contested it but later dropped his appeals. U.S. officials turned him over at Panama City's international airport after a flight from Miami landed. The U.S. State Department said the extradition followed normal procedures under the bilateral treaty and that Panamanian courts would determine his guilt. The Justice Department said he is accused of illegally monitoring the communications of more than 150 people, including journalists and political opponents, and embezzling over $10 million in public funds. Martinelli has denied the charges. His wife, Marta de Martinelli, said he agreed to extradition because of a health problem. After arriving, Martinelli appeared handcuffed in photos released by Panama's security ministry and was taken to Renacer prison, where former strongman Manuel Noriega had been held. During a hearing with investigating judge Jeronimo Mejia on Monday, Martinelli said he had heart problems, prostate cancer, and glaucoma; the judge ordered medical experts to examine him. Martinelli was subsequently hospitalized for three days. Doctors evaluated him and said he was suffering from hypertension but was stable. On Thursday, he was returned to jail. His lawyer, Carlos Carrillo, complained that he had not been allowed to speak with his client.

The Senate passed a $15 billion jobs bill Wednesday on a 70-28 vote. On Monday, a procedural vote to advance the legislation passed 62-30, with five Republicans — including newly elected Sen. Scott Brown of Massachusetts — joining Democrats; Sen. Ben Nelson of Nebraska was the only Democrat to vote against cloture. The bill, a scaled-down version of an $85 billion draft set aside for Majority Leader Harry Reid's $15 billion plan, exempts employers from Social Security payroll taxes on new hires who were unemployed, funds highway and transit programs through 2010, and extends a tax break for business investments such as equipment purchases. It does not extend the deadline to apply for unemployment benefits or the COBRA health insurance subsidy. The House passed a $154 billion jobs bill last year that included $79 billion to extend unemployment benefits and the COBRA subsidy.

Brown voted for final passage, breaking with most Republicans. In a statement, he said: "This jobs bill is far from perfect, and ideally would include deeper and broader tax cuts. I supported this measure because it does contain some tax relief that will help Massachusetts businesses put people back to work." He added that he "reserves the right" to vote against the legislation if it changes dramatically during negotiations with the House: "Right now, this is a tax-cutting bill. But if it comes back to the Senate full of pork, waste, fraud and abuse, I reserve the right to vote against it."

Earlier, Brown told Fox News he would support cloture: "I came to Washington to be an independent voice, to put politics aside, and to do everything in my power to help create jobs for Massachusetts families. This Senate jobs bill is not perfect. I wish the tax cuts were deeper and broader, but I will vote for it because it contains measures that will help put people back to work." He said he "was disappointed with the continuation of politics-as-usual in the drafting of this bill, as it was crafted behind closed doors, without transparency and accountability. I hope for improvements in that process going forward. All of us, Republicans and Democrats, have to work together to get our economy back on track. I hope my vote today is a strong step toward restoring bipartisanship in Washington."

summary: The Senate on Wednesday unanimously approved the North Korea Sanctions and Policy Enhancement Act, legislation imposing strict sanctions intended to limit Pyongyang's ability to finance nuclear warheads and missiles. The bill targets those who knowingly do business with North Korea to benefit its nuclear weapons program, arms-related materials, luxury goods, human rights abuses, activities that negatively impact cybersecurity, and the use of coal or metals in those activities. The measure mandates sanctions rather than leaving them to presidential discretion and authorizes $50 million to broadcast messages directly to people in North Korea. It also imposes what Senator Cory Gardner, a first-term Republican from Colorado and co-sponsor, called the first punitive measures in response to a violation of U.S. cybersecurity infrastructure, which he said could set a precedent for sanctions against other cyber-perpetrators. summary: President-elect Donald Trump spoke by telephone with Taiwan's president, Tsai Ing-wen, on Friday. Trump's transition team confirmed the call late Friday, stating the two leaders "noted the close economic, political, and security ties exists between Taiwan and the United States." Tsai offered congratulations on Trump's election victory, and the two discussed the close economic, political, and security ties between the two countries. The conversation marked the first between a U.S. president or president-elect and a Taiwan leader since 1979, when the United States severed diplomatic ties with Taiwan. A senior White House administration official told the New York Times the outgoing administration was not informed of the communication until after it occurred. Trump posted on Twitter: "The President of Taiwan CALLED ME today to wish me congratulations on winning the Presidency. Thank you!" He said the action fulfilled campaign promises to protect voting rights, women's rights, and LGBT rights. McAuliffe cited a 4 percent unemployment rate, the largest budget surplus in state history, and $1 billion in education spending. Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton praised the order. summary: Initial claims for state unemployment benefits totaled 339,000 in the week ending April 20, the Labor Department reported Thursday. One analysis said the drop in initial claims indicates that expected job losses from federal spending sequestration have not yet materialized; another suggested the data signal hiring may be improving from March's sluggish pace.

summary: President Donald Trump and former Vice President Joe Biden met Tuesday in Cleveland for the first of three scheduled presidential debates in the 2020 election. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the audience was limited and the candidates were spaced apart on stage. The announced topics were the candidates' records, the coronavirus pandemic, the economy, racial injustice and protests, and the integrity of the 2020 election. A Hill-HarrisX poll conducted online from October 3 to 6 among 2,841 registered voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 1.84 percentage points, found former Vice President Joe Biden leading President Donald Trump by 45 percent to 40 percent nationally. Biden's lead had narrowed by 2 points from a September 30–October 1 poll when he led by 7 points. More than 6 million voters had already cast ballots. How can we trust him to protect this country?" The remarks came a week after Biden's campaign temporarily suspended negative ads following Trump's positive test. The House voted, with bipartisan support, to impeach Trump on a charge of inciting the violent mob, making him the only president impeached twice. The Senate was scheduled to reconvene the day before the inauguration and was expected to take up the trial during Biden's administration.

summary: U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson concluded his first major trip to Asia with a meeting in Beijing on Sunday with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Great Hall of the People. Tillerson said the United States looked forward to stronger ties with China. Both sides publicly sidestepped contentious issues including possible punitive trade measures and the South China Sea. He said the House would vote Thursday on his "Plan B" legislation, which would extend tax rates for individuals making less than $1 million per year. "Tomorrow, the House will pass legislation to make permanent tax relief for nearly every American, 99.8 percent of the American people," Boehner said. "Then the president will have a decision to make. He can call on the Senate Democrats to pass that bill or he can be responsible for the largest tax increase in American history." He also said, "I hope the president will get serious soon about providing and working with us on a balanced approach." On Monday, Republican leadership rejected an Obama proposal that the White House said included $1.2 trillion in additional revenues and $1.22 trillion in spending reductions; GOP aides said the plan actually contained $850 billion in spending cuts.

summary: A memorial service was held Tuesday in Prescott Valley, Arizona, for 19 members of the Granite Mountain Hotshots who died June 30 fighting a wildfire near Yarnell, about 80 miles northwest of Phoenix. The fire burned about 13 square miles and more than 100 structures before being controlled over the weekend; residents of Yarnell were allowed to return home on Sunday after nine days. One crew member serving as a lookout survived. Vice President Joe Biden, Arizona Gov. Jan Brewer, Sen. John McCain and Homeland Security Secretary Janet Napolitano spoke at the service, which drew thousands of firefighters and law enforcement officers from across the country along with the firefighters' families. Biden called the Hotshots men of "uncommon valor" and "the most disciplined, tenacious and physically fit men in the world," adding, "Firefighting is not what they did. It was who they were." He quoted Psalm 122:1 and recounted that his wife and one-year-old daughter were killed in a 1972 car accident weeks after his first Senate election, and that his two sons were rescued by firefighters. "I know them because they saved the life of my two sons," he said of the Hotshots. Biden praised the firefighters' families for supporting what he called ordinary Americans doing extraordinary things.

summary: The White House Correspondents' Association announced Friday that comedian Joel McHale will host its annual dinner on May 3 in Washington, D.C., marking the organization's centennial. McHale, host of E!'s "The Soup" and star of NBC's "Community," is known for satirizing politics and pop culture. WHCA President Steven Thomma said in a statement: "We're thrilled that Joel will headline the dinner when we celebrate our centennial. He's sharp, funny and just the type of comic who can navigate the unique challenge of our dinner, making fun of Democrats, Republicans and especially the news media. Washington can use a little good-natured ribbing." The dinner, the 100th in WHCA history, traditionally draws the president and first lady, senior government officials, and members of the press corps along with celebrity guests. The association, founded in 1914 to represent the White House press corps, works to maintain independent news media coverage, advocate for access, handle logistics for reporter pools, and provide scholarships to journalism students. Proceeds from the dinner fund scholarships and awards recognizing excellence in journalism. President Obama has attended every WHCA dinner since taking office and has delivered comedy routines at the event.

summary:
President Donald Trump visited Nashville, Tennessee, on Wednesday, the 250th anniversary of Andrew Jackson's birth, where he laid a wreath at Jackson's tomb at The Hermitage and delivered remarks comparing his own presidency to Jackson's. Earlier that day, Trump visited Detroit, Michigan, to discuss job creation and the automotive industry with auto executives and workers at the American Center for Mobility. White House Press Secretary Sean Spicer had announced the wreath-laying and the Nashville rally, which was Trump's second since taking office.

At The Hermitage, Trump referred to Jackson as "the people's president" and said the visit was "inspirational" and that he is "a fan." He recounted Jackson's capture by the British during the Revolutionary War: "Captured by the red coats and ordered to shine the shoes of a British officer, Jackson simply refused. From that day on Andrew Jackson rejected authority that looked down on the common people." Trump added, "It was during the revolution that Jackson first confronted and defied an arrogant elite. Does that sound familiar?" He told the audience, "People are proud again of our country and you're going to get prouder and prouder and prouder."

In Detroit, Trump said, "Today, I will be visiting the home of Andrew Jackson on the 250th anniversary of his birth. And they say my election was most similar to his –– 1828. That's a long time ago. That's a long way. That's a long time ago."

Trump has previously displayed admiration for Jackson, hanging his portrait in the Oval Office and criticizing the Treasury Department's decision to remove Jackson from the front of the $20 bill. Jackson's historical reputation has declined in recent decades, particularly among Democrats, who have moved to remove his name from places of honor because of his record on slavery and the forced relocation of American Indian nations.

summary: President Donald Trump delivered his first State of the Union address on Tuesday night, followed by the Democratic response from Representative Joseph Kennedy III of Massachusetts. Trump called for bipartisan unity and described his immigration proposal as a "down the middle" compromise; Democrats booed some of his proposals. summary: On Wednesday, Speaker Nancy Pelosi sent a letter to President Donald Trump suggesting they reschedule the State of the Union address planned for January 29, citing security concerns because the Secret Service, the lead agency for security, had not been funded due to the partial government shutdown. Pelosi wrote: "Sadly, given the security concerns and unless government re-opens this week, I suggest that we work together to determine another suitable date after government has re-opened for this address or for you to consider delivering your State of the Union address in writing to the Congress on January 29th." That same day, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen dismissed the concerns on Twitter, writing: "The Department of Homeland Security and the U.S. Secret Service are fully prepared to support and secure the State of the Union. We thank the Service for their mission focus and dedication and for all they do each day to secure our homeland." The Secret Service is part of DHS, where essential security employees were working without paychecks. On Thursday, Trump sent a letter to Pelosi informing her that a planned trip to Brussels, Egypt and Afghanistan "has been postponed" while the shutdown continues. The partial government shutdown began December 22 after Trump rejected a Senate bill that would have funded a number of agencies through the fiscal year while keeping DHS running through February 8. Trump opposed the bill because the DHS portion did not include money for his border wall. The House, then led by Republicans, approved a bill in December providing $5.7 billion for the wall and border security; Senate Democrats blocked that bill. The two sides had made little if any progress to end the 26-day shutdown, the longest in U.S. history. Roughly 800,000 federal workers were furloughed or working without pay as a result.

The New York Times reported Friday that Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein raised the idea of invoking the 25th Amendment to remove President Donald Trump from office. Rosenstein denied making the suggestion. The White House confirmed that Trump and Rosenstein held an extended conversation about the article. United States Ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley, who attends Cabinet meetings, said she had never heard any Cabinet member discuss using the 25th Amendment against Trump and called the notion "absurd." She added that no one had questioned the president's mental stability. The 25th Amendment, ratified in 1967, establishes procedures for presidential succession and temporary transfer of power if a president is disabled or unable to fulfill duties. It requires the vice president and a majority of the Cabinet to declare the president unable to discharge powers, and a two-thirds vote in both chambers of Congress to make the removal permanent. The amendment was previously used to guide Gerald Ford's succession after Richard Nixon's resignation.

summary: President Obama delivered an Oval Office address Tuesday evening marking the end of combat operations in Iraq. Earlier Tuesday, Obama visited Fort Bliss, Texas, where he thanked service members who he said had shouldered the burdens of the war. "At every turn, America's men and women in uniform have served with courage and resolve," Obama said at Fort Bliss. He added: "There were patriots who supported this war, and patriots who opposed it. And all of us are united in appreciation for our servicemen and women, and our hope for Iraq's future." Before the speech, Obama was expected to telephone former President George W. Bush, who launched the 2003 invasion of Iraq and authorized the 2007 troop surge. Obama also spoke with Bush before his February 2009 address that set a withdrawal date for combat troops, White House Press Secretary Robert Gibbs said. Gibbs said Obama would not use the phrase "mission accomplished," which Bush declared in 2003, and would emphasize that more work remains in Iraq despite the end of the combat phase. "You won't hear those words coming from us," Gibbs said. "That is not to say that violence is going to end tomorrow. We understand that those who would foment violence will still continue to try to do so." Gibbs added: "I do think it is important to remember, as you said, this is a commitment that the president made, and a commitment that he intends — and will keep." Gibbs reiterated that Obama would not have invaded Iraq in 2003 but declined to say whether the situation would be better or worse had the United States not invaded under Bush.

summary:
Republican leaders expressed growing alarm that mainstream presidential candidates were attacking each other too fiercely while Donald Trump and Senator Ted Cruz dominated the field ahead of the Iowa caucuses on Monday and the New Hampshire primary eight days later. Elected officials, lobbyists, and donors signaled that candidates such as former Florida Governor Jeb Bush should withdraw if they failed to show strength soon.

On Thursday night, the Republican debate in Iowa proceeded without Trump, who boycotted the Fox News event and instead held a rival fundraiser in Des Moines for veterans. Moderator Megyn Kelly opened by asking Cruz about the "elephant not in the room." Cruz began by praising Iowa — "Iowa in 2017 will not be flyover country, it will be fly-to country" — then mimicked Trump's style: "Let me say, I'm a maniac, and everyone on this stage is stupid, fat and ugly, and Ben, you're a terrible surgeon." He added, "Now that we've gotten the Donald Trump portion out of the way," drawing laughter. Turning serious, Cruz thanked the other candidates for showing Iowans respect by attending and said he had not insulted Trump personally, adding he was glad Trump was running. "There is a difference between personal insults and attacks," he said. Bush remarked sarcastically, "We always had such a loving relationship."

Days before the caucuses, Cruz had challenged Trump to a "mano-a-mano" debate. After Trump announced he would skip the Fox News debate, the Cruz campaign launched a website featuring a Donald Duck caricature with Trump's face and the text: "Ted Cruz is willing to stand up defend his record, anytime, any place. summary: Fox News host Bill O'Reilly apologized on Tuesday to U.S. Rep. Maxine Waters, a California Democrat, for comments he made about her hair during an appearance on "Fox & Friends." According to one account, the original comment was made on Tuesday morning; another placed it two days before a Wednesday interview. On his program "The O'Reilly Factor" later Tuesday, O'Reilly said Waters would not appear on his show because "she does not want to be challenged," and described her views as "extremism" while saying she deserves a hearing. summary:

Vice President Mike Pence and other officials had previously denied that Flynn talked about sanctions with the Russian envoy, and the vice president was reportedly angered that Flynn misled him about the conversations.

The resignation emboldened congressional Democrats to demand a broader investigation into President Trump's ties to Russia. Nearly a dozen Democratic senators sent a letter Tuesday to Attorney General Jeff Sessions stating that "an independent investigation is now necessary to determine what General Flynn did, who knew about it and when."

Senator John McCain, Republican of Arizona and chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, reacted to the resignation. On Tuesday, McCain said the situation was "dysfunctional as far as national security is concerned" and asked: "Who's in charge? Who's in charge? Who's making policy? Who's making decisions?" In response to a question about whether President Trump instructed Flynn to discuss sanctions with the Russian ambassador, McCain said: "I have no information, so I have no comment." Asked if the president should detail whether he had those discussions, McCain said: "I think the whole issue of Russia and our relations with Russia, and our approach to Russia, all those questions should be answered."

On Wednesday, McCain said he is sending a list of questions to the White House to try to uncover how and why Flynn misled Pence. "First we need to ask questions and get answers and then decide" what's next, McCain said. "We will be doing that." He said Congress should first try to get an explanation from the White House. "I'm worried about a situation where the Vice President of the United States is lied to by the national security adviser," McCain said. "We need to ask questions and get answers."

summary:
NBC News invited all three Democratic presidential candidates — Hillary Clinton, Bernie Sanders, and Martin O'Malley — to debate Sunday night in Charleston, South Carolina. The most engaged states were Vermont, New Hampshire, Oregon, Iowa, and Maryland. The top issues discussed were Wall Street, Medicare, Benghazi, crime and criminal justice, and climate change. During the debate, Sanders and O'Malley criticized Clinton over her Wall Street donations.

U.S. District Judge James Robart in Seattle issued a temporary nationwide injunction Friday afternoon blocking enforcement of significant parts of President Donald Trump's executive order on refugees and travel from seven majority-Muslim nations. The ruling came in a lawsuit brought by Washington Attorney General Bob Ferguson. Ferguson said the decision shuts down the executive order immediately, though a written copy of the order was not immediately available. Robart was appointed by former President George W. Bush.

Hours earlier on Friday, U.S. District Judge Nathaniel Gorton in Boston declined to extend a temporary restraining order that had been in place since the previous Sunday and was set to expire February 5. Gorton wrote in a 21-page ruling that the American Civil Liberties Union had not demonstrated the need for an extension, adding he was not deciding the case's merits. That case was brought by the ACLU on behalf of two state university professors, with Massachusetts Attorney General Maura Healey's office later joining. The Boston order had prohibited the removal of visa holders who had arrived in the United States and were detained or flown out.

The federal government suspended enforcement of the ban on Saturday pending appeal. It was unclear whether the Boston decision would be appealed. Religious groups, state attorneys general, residents and visitors had filed more than 50 lawsuits challenging the directive since its issuance a week earlier. ACLU Massachusetts director Carol Rose said Saturday the group applauded the reinstatement of visas for people from the seven nations but said thousands continue to have their constitutional rights violated.

summary: President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un held a historic summit in Singapore, the first between sitting leaders of the two countries. They reached a broad agreement that offered few specifics but included promises of U.S. security guarantees and a reiteration from Kim of his country's commitment to "complete denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula." After the summit, Trump announced that the United States would stop joint military exercises with South Korea, which he called "war games," unless and until negotiations with the North go poorly. The announcement caught allies off guard and sparked confusion among international allies and lawmakers on Capitol Hill. Schumer accused Trump of using the address to "manufacture a crisis, stoke fear, and divert attention from the turmoil in his administration." Their serious, side-by-side appearance prompted widespread reaction on social media, where users compared them to "disappointed parents," the "American Gothic" painting, a law-firm commercial, and a hostage video.

The National Federation of Independent Business released its Small Business Optimism Index for January 2013 on Tuesday, showing a 0.9-point increase to 88.9. The index remained at a level indicating continuing pessimism among small business owners, marking the fourth-lowest reading in the survey's 40-year history. The survey was based on responses from 2,033 randomly sampled small business owners in the NFIB's membership, collected throughout January. On employment, 11 percent of surveyed owners reported adding employees over recent months, 9 percent reported reducing employment — up from 4 percent in December — and 80 percent made no net change. Uncertainty about the economy has kept many owners from hiring, borrowing, and expanding. One account cited increasing regulations as a factor in the bleak outlook. The NFIB has frequently criticized the Obama administration's small business policies, and its financial contributions have largely supported Republicans and opposed Democrats, according to the Center for Responsive Politics.

The special counsel's office, led by Robert Mueller, announced charges of obstruction of justice, witness tampering, and making false statements. According to the indictment, the false statements concerned Stone's interactions related to WikiLeaks' release of hacked Democratic National Committee emails in 2016, and some were made to the House Intelligence Committee. The indictment marked the first criminal case in months from Mueller's investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election and any ties to the Trump campaign. A spokesman for Mueller, Peter Carr, said Stone would appear in court later that Friday.

President Trump criticized the FBI's handling of the arrest in an interview with the Daily Caller released on Thursday. He said he was upset by the manner of the arrest, particularly that it was televised, calling it "a very, very disappointing scene." Trump suggested the FBI had tipped off CNN to film the arrest. CNN denied receiving information from the special counsel's office and said its reporter had gone to the scene on a hunch. Asked whether he would ask the FBI to review its policies for such cases, Trump said he would consider it.

summary: President Donald Trump declared a national emergency at the U.S. southern border on Friday, invoking authority to redirect billions of dollars in federal funds for a border wall. On Monday, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton responded on Twitter, listing four issues she called "real national emergencies": "relentless gun violence," "children separated from their families at the border," "climate change," and "Americans dying for lack of health care." Clinton retweeted a post labeling the declaration a "#FAKENationalEmergency" and shared House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's statement that it would be "a gross abuse of the power of the presidency." Last week, Clinton said she did not believe there was a crisis at the border and warned against "breaking new ground and causing new precedents." She also mocked Trump for using her 2016 campaign slogan "Stronger Together" during a rally in El Paso, Texas, where a Trump supporter attacked a BBC cameraman. On Wednesday, El Paso County and the Border Network for Human Rights filed a 39-page lawsuit in federal court in El Paso seeking to have the declaration declared unconstitutional and to block any federal action taken under it. A similar suit was filed Tuesday by 16 states with Democratic attorneys general. Trump said he would prevail over the legal challenges.

summary: Democratic presidential candidate Andrew Yang appeared at a debate in Houston on Thursday and made two notable proposals. He reintroduced his "democracy dollars" plan, under which every American would receive $100 to donate to candidates or causes of their choice, a concept similar to one previously offered by Senator Kirsten Gillibrand. At the start of the same debate, Yang announced that his campaign would use supporter donations to fund a Freedom Dividend pilot program, providing $1,000 per month for one year to ten American families. Fellow candidate Pete Buttigieg responded, "It's original, I'll give you that." Yang's campaign had teased a "big" and "unprecedented" announcement the day before. The democracy-dollars proposal drew extensive reaction on Twitter. Separately, on Wednesday, footage of Yang shooting basketballs went viral. A Fox News producer suggested a game between Yang and Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas. Cruz initially declined, saying, "You gotta poll 5% or more to play on my court." Yang cited a Hill/HarrisX poll showing him at five percent. Cruz accepted late Wednesday night, proposing a four-on-four game Friday afternoon in Houston — Yang plus three paid staffers versus Cruz plus three paid staffers, with no outside ringers — and a $5,000 donation by the loser to a non-political charity of the winner's choice. Cruz previously defeated late-night host Jimmy Kimmel 11-9 in a 2018 game.

summary:
Rev. Al Sharpton and actor Martin Sheen visited anti-war activist Cindy Sheehan on Sunday at "Camp Casey," a protest site near President Bush's ranch in Crawford, Texas. Camp Casey is named for Sheehan's son, Army Spc. Casey Sheehan, 24, who was killed in Iraq last year. Sharpton, a former Democratic presidential candidate, said he felt a moral obligation to stand with Sheehan and other families who "have become the conscience of this nation." Sharpton and Sheehan laid roses at crosses near the camp. Sheen, who portrays a president on NBC's "The West Wing," told a crowd of more than 300 people, "At least you've got the acting president of the United States," and added, "I think you know what I do for a living, but this is what I do to stay alive."

Sheehan began her vigil on Aug. 6, vowing to remain through Bush's monthlong vacation unless he met with her. She left briefly last week to visit her 74-year-old mother, who had suffered a stroke in Los Angeles, and returned Wednesday. Bush has said he appreciates Sheehan's right to protest and sympathizes with her, but aides said there were no plans to change his schedule to meet with her. Sheehan and other grieving families met with Bush about two months after her son's death, before she became a vocal opponent of the war.

Several cars with pro-Bush signs drove slowly past the campsite. McLennan County sheriff's deputies arrested one man on a misdemeanor assault charge for allegedly shoving an anti-war demonstrator. Sheehan's protest has drawn anti-war activists to Crawford and prompted peace vigils nationwide, as well as harsh criticism from supporters of the U.S. effort in Iraq. After the protest ends Wednesday, organizers plan a bus tour, with the first stop probably in the southeast Texas district of U.S. House Majority Leader Tom DeLay, culminating in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 24.

summary:
Republican presidential front-runner Donald Trump boycotted the Fox News debate in Des Moines on Thursday night, holding a rival veterans' fundraiser instead. At a morning rally in Fairfield, Iowa, Texas Senator Ted Cruz reacted to Trump's absence, saying, "Apparently, Megyn Kelly is really, really scary," calling Trump a "fragile soul" and adding that if he faced tough questions his "hair might stand." Cruz told the crowd, "If someone did that – didn't show up at the interview – you know what you'd say? You're fired!" He also challenged Trump to a one-on-one debate during an interview with radio host Mark Levin, saying, "If Donald is afraid to defend his record, it speaks volumes."

At the debate that evening, moderator Megyn Kelly asked Cruz about the "elephant not in the room." Cruz opened by telling Iowans, "Iowa in 2017 will not be flyover country, it will be fly-to country." He then imitated Trump: "Let me say, I'm a maniac, and everyone on this stage is stupid, fat and ugly, and Ben, you're a terrible surgeon." After laughter, Cruz turned serious, thanking the candidates who appeared for showing Iowans "respect" and stating he had "not insulted Donald personally," adding he was glad Trump was running. "There is a difference between personal insults and attacks," he said. Former Florida Governor Jeb Bush sarcastically remarked on Trump's absence: "We always had such a loving relationship." Senator Rand Paul criticized Cruz's immigration statements, calling them "insulting," while Bush touted his family's political legacy.

summary: Sen. Bernie Sanders won the Wyoming Democratic caucuses on Saturday, his eighth victory in the last nine contests, capturing more than 55 percent of the vote. Despite the win, the state's 14 pledged delegates were split evenly between Sanders and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. The Clinton campaign said the result left Clinton with 1,287 pledged delegates to Sanders's 1,037 and a lead of nearly 2.4 million in the popular vote, adding that her advantage in pledged delegates was nearly insurmountable and would become harder to overcome after each contest. According to The Associated Press, Clinton also led in superdelegates, 469 to 31. Sanders learned of the Wyoming victory while speaking at a rally at LaGuardia Community College in Queens; his wife, Jane, went on stage to inform him. "Alright, news bulletin. We just won Wyoming," Sanders told the crowd, adding, "We appreciate and thank the people of Wyoming so much for their support." He was campaigning in New York City ahead of the state's April 19 primary, which offers 247 pledged delegates. The Sanders campaign said he was pulling closer to Clinton in New York, where she once represented the state in the Senate and where he was born and raised. Nationally, the campaign said Sanders led Clinton in two of the past three polls and fared better than she did in head-to-head matchups against Donald Trump and other Republican candidates. On CNN's "Inside Politics" Sunday, New York Times reporter Jonathan Martin said the Democratic primary rules favor the candidate who builds an early lead, noting that even when Sanders wins a state like Wyoming, splitting delegates makes it difficult to close the gap.

summary: Department of Homeland Security Deputy Secretary Elaine Duke announced Friday that she will retire in April, concluding a year of service that included several months as acting secretary. Duke was sworn in as the department's seventh deputy secretary on April 8, 2017, after President Donald Trump nominated her following a career that spanned the administrations of Presidents George W. Bush and Barack Obama and a period in the private sector running a consulting firm. She became acting secretary in July 2017 when John Kelly resigned to become White House chief of staff, and helped guide the administration's response to the 2017 hurricane season. Her tenure as acting secretary drew scrutiny after she described the recovery effort in Puerto Rico as a "good news story," and she reportedly felt pressured by Kelly to revoke a temporary immigration status for thousands of Hondurans. Duke remained in the deputy role after Kirstjen Nielsen, a Kelly confidant, was confirmed as secretary in December. Nielsen said in a statement that Duke had "selflessly served the federal government for three decades, and this Department for more than 10 years spanning multiple Secretaries," and wished her and her family the best. A successor was not immediately named; the position requires Senate confirmation.

Students at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, returned to classes on Wednesday for the first time since the February 14 shooting that killed 17 people, with the school operating on half days this week before resuming a normal schedule, according to Broward County Public Schools. Teachers had returned on Monday to prepare and were greeted by a small group of parents and local residents holding "Welcome back" signs, as well as a rainbow visible over the campus. Signs displayed messages including "Welcome back! We love you." The building where the shooting occurred remained closed. Superintendent Robert Runcie said officials would be accommodating, with measures including counselors and service dogs in classrooms, and were working with students who did not want to return to arrange transfers. The former student, 19-year-old Nikolas Cruz, has been charged with premeditated murder. About 100 students met with state legislators last week to advocate for stricter gun laws.

Separately, on February 20, police were called to Oberlin High School in Louisiana after a student commented that a square root symbol "looked like a gun," prompting speculation of a terroristic threat. The Allen Parish Sheriff's Office searched the student's home and found no guns or evidence of access to guns, and no evidence of intent to harm. The office stated the student "used extremely poor judgment in making the comment, but in light of the actual circumstances, there was clearly no evidence to support criminal charges."

summary:
President Donald Trump signed the Allow States and Victims to Fight Online Sex Trafficking Act (FOSTA) at a White House ceremony on Wednesday, April 11. The legislation amends the Communications Act of 1934 to create an exception for sex trafficking, removing the broad legal protections websites previously had from liability for user-posted content and making it easier for federal and state prosecutors to target sites that enable prostitution and sex trafficking. The law authorizes increased penalties — fines and up to 25 years in prison — for anyone who promotes or facilitates the prostitution of five or more people or who contributes to sex trafficking through reckless disregard, and it permits victims to pursue civil action against trafficking sites.

During the signing, a sex trafficking survivor identified to reporters only as "MA" dabbed and danced in the Oval Office as Trump delivered remarks. She was the first person to sue Backpage.com, a classified advertising website that has been criticized for failing to police sex trafficking and prostitution of minors on its platform; seven people associated with Backpage were recently indicted on charges of facilitating prostitution, conspiracy, and money laundering. After the remarks, MA was given a brief moment to speak with the president. Trump said during the ceremony, "Trafficking is probably worse today than at any time in our history. You are not alone."

The White House characterized the underground sex economy as a multi-million dollar industry and cited a 2014 Urban Institute report estimating the underground sex trade in eight cities — Atlanta, Dallas, Denver, Kansas City, Miami, Seattle, San Diego, and Washington, D.C. — at a combined $40 million to $290 million.

Trump responded by saying he hoped "nasty mouth" Warren would be Clinton's running mate and repeated his characterization of her as "Pocahontas," accusing her of claiming Native American heritage while a professor at Harvard.

summary: Texas Gov. Rick Perry campaigned in Iowa on Monday for the Republican presidential nomination after formally entering the race the previous weekend. Perry told the Associated Press that his economic record is unmatched in the GOP field, saying, "I respect all the other candidates in the field, but there is no one that can stand toe-to-toe with us." He pledged that if elected he would call for a six-month moratorium on federal business regulations he said were holding down job growth. A radio spot airing in Iowa last week stated the governor "has a proven record of controlling spending and creating jobs" and suggested he could replicate Texas' success nationally. In a budget speech several months earlier, Perry said Texas stood "in stark contrast to states that choose to burden their residents with higher taxes and onerous regulatory mandates." Texas has accounted for at least one-third of jobs created nationwide since the recession ended, its economy has grown about twice as fast as the national rate, and home prices have remained stable while much of the country saw sharp declines. Perry declined through a spokesman to be interviewed for one article. Rep. Louie Gohmert (R-Texas) downplayed the idea that Perry supports Texas secession, telling The Iowa Independent on Tuesday, "I think those comments were made tongue in cheek," adding, "I've talked to Rick. I've known him since Texas A&M. And I know he has no intention of ever seeing Texas secede." Gohmert said the Civil War "pretty well decided whether a state can secede or not" and that Perry understands "we're stronger as a country united." Perry was reported to have said in 2009 that Texas joined the U.S. voluntarily and can leave "anytime we want," and that Texas is "kind of thinking about that again." Perry entered the race too late to be formally listed in the Ames Straw Poll but received 718 write-in votes, placing sixth behind Rep. Michele Bachmann (R-Minn.), Rep. Ron Paul (R-Texas), former Minnesota Gov. Tim Pawlenty, former Sen. Rick Santorum, and Florida businessman Herman Cain.

summary:
During the final presidential debate between Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump, Clinton made a critical remark about Trump while discussing entitlement costs, prompting Trump to interject, "Such a nasty woman." The following day, Thursday, in Delaware, Ohio, Trump addressed controversy over his debate response regarding acceptance of the election results. He stated: "I will totally accept the results of this great and historic presidential election. If I win." Trump also declared the debate "amazing" and asserted that "everybody said I won," citing online polls showing 90 percent support. He raised the question of voter fraud mentioned during the debate, emphasizing the need for fairness in the election.

Separately, campaign advertising data showed a significant disparity in television spending. Since June, approximately 300,000 presidential campaign commercials had aired, concentrated in Florida, Ohio, and North Carolina, with a small number on national networks. According to Kantar Media/CMAG, 80 percent of ads were run by or on behalf of Clinton, while 18 percent were by or on behalf of Trump. Trump has relied instead on rallies, free media coverage, and Twitter posts, stating, "I don't even know why I need so much money. Why do I even need these commercials?" Most competitive areas saw Clinton running far more ads, a departure from typical campaigns where both sides advertise heavily.

summary: President Barack Obama announced Wednesday that he will return 5 percent of his $400,000 annual salary to the Treasury, retroactive to March 1 and continuing through the end of the fiscal year in September, in solidarity with federal workers facing furloughs due to the sequester. The 5 percent figure approximates the level of spending cuts to nondefense federal agencies that took effect that day. According to an administration official, the president will write a monthly check of $1,667.67 starting in April. It is unclear whether he will continue the practice beyond the fiscal year. Treasury Secretary Jacob Lew also plans to contribute a portion of his salary to nonprofit organizations assisting those affected by the cuts, though the amount and recipients have not been finalized. Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel said he will return 5 percent of his paycheck, and Secretary of State John Kerry will donate 5 percent of his salary to charity. The automatic government-wide spending cuts, known as the sequester, total $85 billion and began taking effect March 1.

summary: Associate Justice Antonin Scalia, 79, was found dead Saturday at the Cibolo Creek Ranch, a resort in the Big Bend region south of Marfa, Texas, federal officials said. Scalia had arrived at the ranch on Friday and attended a private party with about 40 people. When he did not appear for breakfast, a person associated with the ranch went to his room and found a body. The death was described as from apparent natural causes. Chief U.S. District Judge Orlando Garcia of the Western Judicial District of Texas was notified by the U.S. Marshals Service. Vice President Joe Biden issued a statement Saturday calling Scalia "one of our most influential justices." Biden, who as a senator voted unanimously to confirm Scalia in 1986 and later said he regretted that vote, said he and Scalia had fundamental disagreements about constitutional interpretation but shared a belief that sharp debates and deep respect for the adversarial process were essential to the judicial system and democracy. Biden and his wife offered condolences to Scalia's family. Scalia's death immediately prompted debate over a successor. Prominent Republicans called for the next president to make the nomination, while President Barack Obama said he would nominate a new justice despite objections. With the Court at eight members, a 4-4 tie in a case would leave the lower court's decision standing, binding on the immediate parties but setting no national precedent.

New Hampshire state representative Al Baldasaro, a delegate for Donald Trump and an adviser to the Republican presidential nominee on veterans issues, made two sets of public comments during the 2016 campaign. In an interview on "The Jeff Kuhner Show," first reported by BuzzFeed, Baldasaro said of Hillary Clinton: "The whole thing disgusts me. Hillary Clinton should be put in the firing line and shot for treason." He called Clinton a "disgrace" and the "Jane Fonda of the Vietnam," adding: "She is a disgrace for the lies that she told those mothers about their children that got killed over there in Benghazi. She dropped the ball on over 400 emails requesting backup security. Something's wrong there." Baldasaro identified himself as a veteran of Desert Shield and Desert Storm and the father of a son who served in Iraq as a Marine Corps helicopter avionics technician. Ryan told reporters the nation would be "living with Obamacare for the foreseeable future," adding that "Obamacare is the law of the land, it's going to remain the law of the land until it's replaced." summary: A respiratory illness outbreak at the Greenspring Retirement Community in Springfield, Virginia, has killed two residents and hospitalized either 18 or 20 others, according to differing accounts. Health department spokesman Benjamin Schwartz said the two residents who died had been hospitalized with pneumonia and were older individuals with complex medical problems, though the department also stated in a news release that it does not know the full medical history or the extent to which pneumonia contributed to the deaths. summary: The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear Alabama's appeal seeking to revive provisions of its 2011 immigration law, leaving in place a ruling by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit that blocked those provisions. The appeals court, acting at the request of the Obama administration, had ruled that federal immigration law "comprehensively addresses criminal penalties for these actions undertaken within the borders of the United States, and a state's attempt to intrude into this area is prohibited because Congress has adopted a calibrated framework." The 11th Circuit also said immigration law is primarily a federal responsibility and that Alabama lacked authority to enforce the challenged provisions. Justice Antonin Scalia dissented from the denial of certiorari, voting to hear the appeal, but offered no reasoning. The court's order in Alabama v. United States, No. 12-884, gave no reasons, consistent with custom. The appeals court had upheld other parts of the Alabama law, including a provision allowing police to check immigration documents during stops for other purposes; a similar provision in Arizona's law was upheld by the Supreme Court last year. Another Alabama provision targeting public school students in the country illegally had been thrown out by the appeals court. The law's stated purpose was to reduce the "number of illegal aliens" in Alabama. It takes four justices to place a case on the Supreme Court's docket.

summary: Merck chairman and CEO Kenneth Frazier announced Monday morning that he was resigning from President Donald Trump's American Manufacturing Council, citing the president's response to a white nationalist rally in Charlottesville, Virginia, over the weekend. The rally, which protested the planned removal of a statue of Confederate General Robert E. Lee, drew white supremacists and neo-Nazis and turned violent, leaving one woman and two police officers dead. Frazier, a Philadelphia native, said in a statement: "America's leaders must honor our fundamental values by clearly rejecting expressions of hatred, bigotry and group supremacy, which run counter to the American ideal that all people are created equal." He added: "As CEO of Merck and as a matter of personal conscience, I feel a responsibility to take a stand against intolerance and extremism." A longer version of the statement released by some outlets included the line: "Our country's strengths stems from its diversity and the contributions made by men and women of different faiths, races, sexual orientations and political beliefs." The council, comprising several business executives, was aimed at boosting job growth. Unbelievable! Each and every CEO on the President's American Manufacturing Council should be asked today where they stand. Are they going to stand with intolerance and racism or are they going to stand with their employees and customers?" Trump's initial response to the Charlottesville violence had been heavily criticized for condemning all sides without specifically naming white supremacists.

On Monday, a North Korean official told CNN that Pyongyang is not interested in diplomacy with the United States until it achieves a long-range intercontinental ballistic missile capable of reaching "all the way to the East coast of the mainland US." The official said North Korea views nuclear weapons as necessary to deter the United States from attempting to overthrow the regime of Kim Jong Un, citing the examples of Iraq and Libya. Many experts believe North Korea would not use the weapons first, assessing that Kim values his regime's survival above all else.

He warned that "the entire U.S. mainland is within our firing range" and that if the U.S. invades, "it will not escape our severe punishment in any part of the globe."

That evening Obama spoke at a Business Council dinner and took questions, with the sequester a main topic. Obama wanted a debt-reduction deal that included both budget cuts and higher taxes by ending loopholes and breaks benefiting the wealthy. Republicans opposed any tax increases, saying the emphasis should be on less spending. Obama warned of dire consequences from the cuts, including airport delays and unguarded border crossings.
