summary: U.S. District Judge Frederick J. Scullin Jr. on Saturday struck down the District of Columbia's ban on carrying handguns outside the home, ruling in Palmer v. District of Columbia that the prohibition violated the Second Amendment. "There is no longer any basis on which this court can conclude that the District of Columbia's total ban on the public carrying of ready-to-use handguns outside the home is constitutional under any level of scrutiny," Scullin wrote in his 19-page opinion. "Therefore, the court finds that the District of Columbia's complete ban on the carrying of handguns in public is unconstitutional." The lawsuit was brought by several individuals who had been denied permits to carry a weapon. The court ordered the city to allow residents and nonresidents to carry handguns outside their homes. On Tuesday, Scullin stayed his ruling until Oct. 22 to give city lawmakers time to respond with new legislation; the plaintiffs did not oppose the 90-day stay. The city has asked Scullin to stay the ruling pending appeal, but he said he would not rule on that request until at least August. The decision comes six years after the Supreme Court's 5-4 ruling in District of Columbia v. Heller, which struck down the city's total ban on handgun ownership. Second Amendment Foundation lawyer Alan Gura, who argued the case, wrote in a blog post: "Congratulations Americans, your capital is not a constitution-free zone."

summary: The Obama administration on Thursday expelled 35 Russian diplomats and closed Russian diplomatic facilities in response to what it said was Russian hacking of the Democratic National Committee and other political institutions to influence the 2016 presidential election. He said the United States and other countries were in the process of confirming reports of chemical weapons attacks against rebels, adding that knowing chemical weapons exist in Syria does not indicate when or how they were used, and that the United States would put significant resources into the investigation. Senator John McCain (R-Ariz.) called Obama's statement disappointing, saying the president had acknowledged a line was crossed but still required direct evidence. According to a report attributed to Debka, which the outlet noted sometimes gets things wrong, military intelligence sources said the meeting with King Abdullah II of Jordan was intended to finalize an agreement for a U.S. deployment of 20,000 troops to Jordan, building on 200 troops announced the previous week to prepare King Hussein Air Base Mafraq near the Iraqi and Syrian borders. The reported purpose of the surge was to protect Jordan's royal family from Syrian jihadists and a potential Arab Spring-style uprising, and would be coordinated with Israeli forces with buffer zones on Syria's borders.

summary: The United States and five Arab allies began airstrikes against the Islamic State and at least one other extremist group in Syria early Tuesday, the first such strikes in Syria since the crisis began more than three years ago, according to the U.S. military and Syrian activists. The air campaign targeted the groups' bases, training camps and checkpoints in at least four provinces. By Thursday the Pentagon said the United States had conducted more than 198 airstrikes against Islamic State targets in Iraq and 20 in Syria, using a mixture of fighter and attack aircraft, bombers and drones, and had launched more than 40 missiles from Navy ships in the Persian Gulf. The Pentagon estimated the cost of U.S. efforts against the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria at $7 million to $10 million per day, up from $7.5 million per day a month earlier. Overnight and early Friday, activists reported a second consecutive day of strikes on oil installations and other facilities in Islamic State-held territory in Deir el-Zour province in eastern Syria. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights said the strikes hit at least two oil-producing areas and that air raids also targeted the Islamic State group's headquarters in the town of Mayadeen. The Local Coordination Committees reported four strikes on Mayadeen. Officials said they would continue targeted strikes in Iraq and Syria but that it was too soon to know what effect the strikes were having on the terrorist network's capabilities.

summary: President Barack Obama traveled to Roseburg, Oregon, on Friday to meet privately with families of the victims of the October 1 mass shooting at Umpqua Community College that left eight students and one teacher dead. The White House said the purpose of the visit was to spend time with the families, and no public address was scheduled. Upon arrival at the airport, Obama was greeted by several hundred people, roughly half of whom were protesting his calls for gun-safety measures, holding signs reading "Gun free zones for sitting ducks," "Obama is wrong," and "Nothing trumps our liberty." The meeting with families was closed to the press. Afterward, Obama said he would continue pushing for new gun-safety measures, stating, "We're going to have to come together as a country, but today is about the families." Following the Oregon visit, Obama traveled to Seattle, Washington, for a Democratic National Committee roundtable fundraiser and an event for Senator Patty Murray and the Washington State Democratic Party, then to San Francisco for another DNC roundtable.

summary: ABC News suspended investigative reporter Brian Ross for four weeks without pay on Saturday after he filed an inaccurate report on Friday. Ross had reported that Michael Flynn would testify that Donald Trump, while running for president as a candidate, directed him to contact Russian officials. Later that day, ABC issued a correction. The network's statement said the reporting had not been fully vetted through editorial standards and that continued reporting determined the information was wrong. Accounts of the correction differ: one version states ABC clarified that Trump's direction to Flynn came during the presidential transition, after the election, not during the campaign; another version states the clarification said Trump asked Flynn during the campaign "to find ways to repair relations with Russia and other hot spots." Fox News host Sean Hannity criticized the error and the suspension, calling the latter "too little, too late." ABC's statement said, "We deeply regret and apologize for the serious error we made yesterday... It is vital we get the story right and retain the trust we have built with our audience — these are our core principles. We fell far short of that yesterday."

summary: A shooting occurred Wednesday afternoon at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School at 5901 Pine Island Road in Parkland, Florida. A 19-year-old male, identified as Nikolas Cruz, opened fire with an AR-15. Seventeen people were killed and 14 others wounded. Cruz, who had been expelled from the school, was taken into custody later and charged Thursday with 17 counts of premeditated murder. The FBI acknowledged on Friday that it had received a tip on January 5 from someone close to Cruz warning about his gun ownership, mental stability, desire to kill, and potential to carry out a school shooting. The FBI did not investigate the claims or notify its Miami field office, and conceded the tip "should have been assessed as a potential threat to life." President Trump on Thursday ordered U.S. flags flown at half-staff at all public buildings, military installations, and embassies until sunset Monday, stating in a proclamation that the nation "grieves with those who have lost loved ones in the shooting." The incident was described as the 18th school shooting of 2018; researchers and gun-control advocates have logged school shootings at a rate of about one per week since 2013. Former senior FBI official Katherine W. summary:
The United States embassy in Israel is scheduled to open in Jerusalem on Monday, coinciding with Israeli Independence Day, after President Donald Trump recognized Jerusalem as Israel's capital in December and ordered the relocation from Tel Aviv. The move fulfills a campaign promise and breaks with the international community, which has traditionally viewed Tel Aviv as Israel's capital. Israelis regard the ancient city as their capital, while Palestinians view East Jerusalem as the capital of a future Palestinian state.

On Friday, thousands of Indonesian Muslims rallied in Jakarta's National Monument park against the embassy move, waving Palestinian flags and carrying banners including one reading "Stop, Trump!". President Joko Widodo reiterated Indonesia's support for the Palestinian people, saying the country would continue to fight with the Palestinians and that Palestine would remain at the centre of Indonesia's diplomacy. Indonesia, the world's largest Muslim-majority country, does not have diplomatic ties with Israel.

In Jerusalem, banners reading "Trump Make Israel Great" were hung ahead of the opening. The city's soccer club, Beitar Jerusalem, celebrated the move and sought to change its name to "Beitar Trump Jerusalem." The Israeli government has celebrated the relocation. Fox News host Jeanine Pirro said Trump had fulfilled biblical prophecy, comparing him to King Cyrus and stating that Jerusalem is the eternal capital of the Jewish state. Protests sparked by the December announcement continued in the region, with more expected on Friday.

summary: The vice presidential debate between Republican nominee Mike Pence and Democratic nominee Tim Kaine took place Tuesday night in Farmville, Virginia. "We trust Hillary Clinton as president and commander in chief, but the thought of Donald Trump as commander in chief scares us to death." Kaine proceeded to recite a series of Trump's controversial remarks and episodes, including that Trump "trash talks the military" and "loves dictators" with a "Mount Rushmore of his favorites." Kaine repeatedly challenged Pence to defend these statements while expressing astonishment at the prospect. At one point during Kaine's recitation, Pence interjected, "Oh come on, come on." summary:
The House of Representatives passed a resolution condemning anti-Semitism, Islamophobia and other forms of hatred by a vote of 407 to 23 on Thursday. All 23 votes in opposition came from Republicans, including Representatives Liz Cheney, Peter King, Paul Gosar and Louie Gohmert; Representative Steve King voted "present." The resolution was drafted after controversy over remarks by Representative Ilhan Omar, Democrat of Minnesota, but did not name her; Omar voted for the measure. The resolution condemned anti-Semitic and anti-Muslim hate speech, noting recent acts of mass violence by white supremacists, the persistence of anti-Semitic tropes, and violence against American mosques. Gohmert delivered a speech before the vote denouncing the resolution as too broad.

The controversy followed Omar's remarks at a panel at Busboys & Poets in Washington, where she questioned why it was acceptable to criticize the oil and pharmaceutical industries but not "Israeli influence over U.S. Mideast policy" due to "a powerful lobby," and asked why she was not allowed to "talk about the political influence in this country that says it is OK for people to push for allegiance to a foreign country." She later tweeted that she would refuse to "have allegiance/pledge support" to Israel as a condition of serving in Congress. Fellow panelist Representative Rashida Tlaib, Democrat of Michigan, applauded.

Cheney said Sunday that the Democratic Party, which controls the House, has "a real problem" and that "the extent to which [Democrats] are now abiding by anti-Semitism, enabling anti-Semitism in their party is something we watch them struggle with, but something that's really dangerous for the country." Other Republican lawmakers said the resolution should have named Omar directly and called for her removal from the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

summary: Britain's ambassador to the United States, Kim Darroch, resigned on Wednesday after diplomatic cables critical of President Donald Trump were leaked and published in the Mail on Sunday. The cables, spanning two years, described the Trump administration as "inept," "incompetent," "dysfunctional," "unpredictable," "faction riven" and "diplomatically clumsy." In one memo, Darroch wrote: "We don't really believe this administration is going to become substantially more normal; less dysfunctional; less unpredictable; less faction riven; less diplomatically clumsy and inept." Darroch said in his resignation letter that his posting was due to end this year, but "in the current circumstances the responsible course is to allow the appointment of a new ambassador" and that "the current situation is making it impossible for me to carry out my role as I would like." He added he was "grateful to all those in the UK and the US, who have offered their support during this difficult few days." Prime Minister Theresa May called the resignation "a matter of regret." Her spokesman, James Slack, said contact had been made with the Trump administration setting out the view that the leak was unacceptable and that he had seen "nothing to suggest hostile state actors were involved." The British government said it was hunting for the source of the leaks. President Trump responded on Friday, saying "I wish the British ambassador well" and that "some people just told me ... he actually said very good things about me." Earlier, on Monday, Trump had tweeted he would "no longer deal with" Darroch, and on Tuesday called him "a pompous fool," "wacky" and "a very stupid guy." The British government stood by Darroch after the leak.

President Donald Trump, in a pre-Super Bowl interview with Fox News Channel's Bill O'Reilly aired Saturday, said he respects Russian President Vladimir Putin but that does not mean he will get along with him. "I do respect [Putin]," Trump said. "I respect a lot of people, but that doesn't mean I'm going to get along with them. He's a leader of his country. I say it's better to get along with Russia than not." Trump added he would like Russia's assistance in fighting ISIS and Islamic terrorism. When O'Reilly said, "Putin's a killer," Trump responded: "[There are] a lot of killers... We've got a lot of killers. What do you think? Our country's so innocent?" The next day, Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, in an interview on CNN's "State of the Union" with Jake Tapper, called Putin "a thug" and noted he is a former KGB agent. McConnell rejected any equivalency between the human rights records of the United States and Russia. "I don't think there's any equivalency," McConnell said. "America is exceptional... There's a clear distinction here." He added, "I obviously don't see this issue the same way as he does." McConnell also said, "I'm not going to critique every utterance of the President." Before President Obama left office, senior administration officials leaked a classified CIA assessment that Putin personally approved attempts by Russian intelligence to sway the 2016 U.S. presidential election in favor of Trump.

summary:
The Taliban announced in late January 2014 that they had captured a military working dog during an engagement in Afghanistan's Laghman province. Insurgent spokesman Zabiullah Mujahid said the capture occurred about a month earlier — approximately late December 2013 — during a battle in the eastern province. The Taliban distributed a video showing a brown dog, identified as "Colonel," on a leash held by an armed fighter; the animal wore a black harness that the Taliban said carried a video camera. Mujahid said the dog was being held in a "safe place" in Laghman and was uninjured and not mistreated.

The Taliban initially described the dog as American, stating on Twitter that "mujahideen seized US dog" during an "attempted nighttime raid" by U.S. forces on December 23. A U.S. military official said Thursday that the dog belonged to British forces, not U.S. forces, and declined to be named because NATO policy leaves national announcements to each country. The NATO-led International Security Assistance Force (ISAF) confirmed that one of its military working dogs went missing following a mission in December 2013, but said it was ISAF policy to defer identification to the appropriate national authorities. The coalition gave no further details.

Military working dogs — commonly German Shepherds, Labradors, and Spaniels — are used by ISAF forces for bomb detection and during special operations raids. The practice of bringing dogs into Afghan homes during raids is sensitive because many Muslims consider dogs unclean.

summary: President Trump arrived in France on Friday for an official visit coinciding with Bastille Day. During a tour of the Hôtel National des Invalides, a museum complex in central Paris housing Napoleon Bonaparte's tomb, Trump greeted French first lady Brigitte Macron, saying "You're in such good shape." He then turned to President Emmanuel Macron and said, "She's in such good physical shape," and added, "Beautiful," addressing Mrs. Macron. Mrs. Macron appeared to take hold of Melania Trump's arm and step backward; Mrs. Trump stood beside her, smiling. The exchange was broadcast live on Macron's official Facebook account and circulated widely online. At the Fairfield rally, Cruz said, "Apparently, Megyn Kelly is really, really scary," called Trump a "fragile soul" and said if he faced tough questions his "hair might stand." Cruz added, "I would ask that he at least show respect to the great men and women of Iowa," and, to applause, "If someone did that – didn't show up at the interview – you know what you'd say? You're fired!" In an interview with radio host Mark Levin, Cruz challenged Trump to a one-on-one debate, saying, "If Donald is afraid to defend his record, it speaks volumes."

At the Des Moines debate, moderators addressed Trump's absence first. Cruz opened by praising Iowa voters: "I am so grateful for the diligence, for the seriousness with which the men and women of Iowa approach this process." He then joked, "I'm a maniac, and everyone on this stage is stupid, fat and ugly... Now that we've gotten the Donald Trump portion out of the way," before pivoting to policy. Cruz also mocked the moderators: "Gosh, if you guys ask one more mean question, I may have to leave the stage." After Cruz spoke, Sen. Marco Rubio (R-Fla.) said, "Don't worry. I'm not leaving the stage, no matter what you ask me."

summary: Texas state Sen. Wendy Davis, a 50-year-old Democrat from Fort Worth, intends to run for governor in 2014, according to multiple reports. Davis gained national attention in June with a nearly 13-hour filibuster that temporarily blocked a strict abortion bill at the Texas Capitol. The bill, later signed by Gov. Rick Perry, requires doctors to have admitting privileges at nearby hospitals, limits abortions to surgical centers, restricts when and where women may take abortion-inducing pills, and bans abortions after 20 weeks. The filibuster drew hundreds of supporters to the Capitol and earned Davis a mention from President Obama's campaign Twitter account. Sources told Fox News that Davis plans to file candidacy paperwork Wednesday or Thursday of the following week. The Associated Press reported that her decision gives Democrats a potentially competitive candidate in a state where they have not won a statewide office in more than a decade or held the governor's mansion for nearly 20 years. Republican Attorney General Greg Abbott, the likely GOP nominee following Perry's decision not to seek re-election after 14 years, has already raised more than $20 million. Texas is among the most expensive states for campaigning due to its large media markets. Davis is expected to receive national fundraising support; EMILY's List, which backs Democratic women who support abortion rights, has been raising her national profile, and several U.S. senators have agreed to help her fundraise. Democratic strategists cite the state's growing Hispanic and African American populations and an influx of less conservative white voters as demographic shifts that could make the race competitive.

summary:

summary: Vice President Joe Biden and Republican vice presidential nominee Paul Ryan met Thursday in Danville, Kentucky, for the only vice presidential debate of the 2012 campaign. summary:
North Korea announced on February 12, 2013 that it had conducted a third nuclear test. The White House issued a statement the same day calling the test a highly provocative act that undermined regional stability, violated numerous United Nations Security Council resolutions, contravened commitments under the September 19, 2005 Joint Statement of the Six-Party Talks, and increased the risk of proliferation. The statement noted the test followed a December 12 ballistic missile launch and said North Korea's nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs constituted a threat to U.S. national security and international peace and security. The United States would remain vigilant and steadfast in defense commitments to allies in the region, strengthen close coordination with allies and partners, and work with Six-Party partners, the United Nations Security Council, and other UN member states to pursue firm action.

President Barack Obama spoke by telephone with Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe and South Korean President Lee Myung-bak. In the call with Abe, Obama reaffirmed that the United States remains steadfast in its defense commitments to Japan, including the extended deterrence offered by the U.S. nuclear umbrella. In the call with Lee, the two leaders condemned the test as a highly provocative violation of North Korea's international obligations and agreed to work closely together, including at the United Nations Security Council, to seek a range of measures aimed at impeding North Korea's nuclear and ballistic missile programs and reducing the risk of proliferation. Obama unequivocally reaffirmed that the United States remains steadfast in its defense commitments to the Republic of Korea, including the extended deterrence offered by the U.S. nuclear umbrella. Obama also thanked Lee for his leadership and friendship over the past four years and pledged to work closely with President-elect Park to further strengthen U.S.-ROK cooperation.

Trump also called Kim Jong Un a "madman." summary:
Democrat Doug Jones defeated Republican Roy Moore in Alabama's U.S. Senate election Tuesday. Moore faced allegations from women who said he pursued them when they were teenagers and he was in his 30s; he denied wrongdoing. Moore did not deliver a concession speech Tuesday and has not conceded, with his campaign awaiting the official vote count. On Thursday he released a statement thanking his wife and supporters and calling the race "very close."

Alabama Sen. Richard Shelby, who did not support Moore, told reporters he was "relieved" Moore lost and that "a lot of Republicans are relieved" Moore and "some of his people aren't the face of the Republican party." He said Moore's loss lets the state avoid a senator who would be "radioactive" and "controversial." Shelby declined to say whose name he wrote in on the ballot, adding he was "conflicted" because Republicans would lose a seat but also "proud" of his state.

Republican National Committee governing member Joyce Simmons of Nebraska resigned over the party's continued financial support for Moore. In her resignation letter she wrote that she wished she could serve the "national Republican Party that I used to know well" and criticized Moore's views on church and state, his stated desire to outlaw homosexuality, and a 2011 radio interview in which he said eliminating amendments after the 10th would "eliminate many problems."

President Donald Trump told reporters Moore should concede: "I think he should. He tried. I want to support the person running." Trump called Jones to congratulate him and welcomed him to the White House. On Wednesday Trump tweeted: "I said Roy Moore will not be able to win the General Election. I was right!" and "Roy worked hard but the deck was stacked against him!"

summary: German Chancellor Angela Merkel traveled to Sochi, Russia, on Tuesday for her first visit to the country since 2015, where she held discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin followed by a joint press conference. The leaders discussed the conflict in eastern Ukraine, the Minsk ceasefire accords, and European Union sanctions imposed after Russia's 2014 annexation of Crimea, which are up for renewal this summer. Merkel called on all sides in the Ukraine conflict to work toward the ceasefire envisaged by the Minsk accords, saying implementation could lead to the lifting of EU sanctions against Russia. "For me the aim is to reach the point in the implementation of the Minsk accords where we can lift the European Union's sanctions against Russia," Merkel said. Putin rejected accusations that Russia meddled in the 2016 United States presidential election, calling them "simply rumors" and stating, "We never interfere in the political life and the political processes of other countries and we don't want anybody interfering in our political life and foreign policy processes." He added that the claim was being used as part of the political fight in Washington. U.S. intelligence agencies have said they have definitive evidence linking Moscow to the hacking of Democratic Party email accounts with the aim of benefiting Donald Trump's campaign and harming Hillary Clinton's campaign. Former Democratic nominee Clinton, speaking at the Women for Women International annual luncheon in New York, said Putin "certainly interfered in our election" to hurt her and help Trump. Merkel said Germany would take "decisive measures" if it believed there was foreign meddling in its upcoming election. Relations between Germany and Russia remain strained over the unresolved conflict in eastern Ukraine and the Syrian civil war, where Putin supports President Bashar Assad while Merkel has said Assad must go. Merkel had traveled to the United States in March to meet with President Trump.

Former Republican members of Congress issued a statement calling on President Donald Trump to accept the results of the 2020 presidential election. The group said Trump's allegations of fraud are unfounded and threaten confidence in democracy. "As former Republican Members of Congress who swore an oath to the Constitution, we believe the statements by President Trump alleging fraud in the election are efforts to undermine the legitimacy of the election and are unacceptable," the statement said. "Every vote should be counted and the final outcome accepted by the participants because public confidence in the outcome of our elections is a bedrock of our democracy." The former lawmakers added it is their hope the nation will recognize that President-elect Joe Biden has won the election.

Meanwhile, Trump continued to challenge the results. On Twitter he wrote: "WE WILL WIN!" and "WE ARE MAKING BIG PROGRESS. RESULTS START TO COME IN NEXT WEEK. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN!" Tim Murtaugh, communications director for the Trump campaign, said on Fox Business the campaign has "high confidence that as the president pursues his lines of legal recourse – including the recounts in Georgia and Wisconsin, at least – we do feel like there is a runway for the president to win this and win reelection."

As of Monday afternoon, Biden had received 75.67 million votes nationally and Trump 71.07 million votes, with tighter margins in battleground states that decided the Electoral College. While some prominent Republican lawmakers and politicians congratulated Biden, a sizeable number of Republicans supported Trump's legal challenges and his right to pursue them.

summary: Albuquerque voters on Tuesday defeated a municipal ballot measure that would have banned abortions after 20 weeks of pregnancy. The referendum, believed to be the first of its kind on a municipal ballot in the United States, drew record turnout and aggressive campaigning by volunteers on both sides. The measure would have prohibited abortions after 20 weeks except when necessary to save the mother's life. Nine states have enacted similar 20-week bans through legislation, though courts have blocked such bans in Idaho, Georgia, Arizona, North Dakota, and Arkansas. Abortions after 20 weeks are rare; the Guttmacher Institute reports that 23 percent of U.S. abortion providers perform them and fewer than two percent of abortions occur after 21 weeks. The vote was seen as a test of abortion-rights messaging among Hispanic voters, who constitute nearly half of Albuquerque's population. summary: President Donald Trump fired FBI Director James B. Comey on Tuesday. In a brief letter to Comey, Trump said the firing was necessary to restore "public trust and confidence" in the FBI. Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent, said he found it "deeply troubling" that the decision came a day after former Acting Attorney General Sally Yates testified on Russia's ties to the Trump campaign and before Comey was to appear before the Senate Intelligence Committee. summary:
A Gallup poll released Tuesday showed congressional job approval at 9 percent, the lowest level since the organization began asking the question in 1974. The previous low was 10 percent, recorded twice in 2012. The survey of 1,039 national adults, conducted Thursday through Saturday, carried a margin of error of 4 percentage points.

The 9 percent figure represents a decline from October, when one account put approval at 11 percent and another at 10 percent. In September, before the government shutdown, approval stood at 19 percent. That peak followed Congress's decision not to authorize a use-of-force resolution in Syria. Approval has averaged 14 percent for the year to date, which would be the lowest annual average on record unless it rises substantially in December.

Party breakdowns in the current poll showed 8 percent of independents, 9 percent of Republicans, and 10 percent of Democrats approving. In October, Democratic approval had fallen to 5 percent from 20 percent in September, while Republican and independent approval registered in the mid-teens. summary: A federal appeals court ruled Friday that White House visitor logs for the president and most staff can be kept secret. The 3-0 decision by a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit reversed a 2011 district court ruling that all White House visitor records were subject to Freedom of Information Act disclosure requirements. The case was brought by the watchdog group Judicial Watch, which had sought all White House visitor logs from President Barack Obama's first seven months in office. Chief Judge Merrick Garland wrote for the panel that both the 1974 FOIA Amendments and the 1978 Presidential Records Act showed Congress did not want documents such as the appointment calendars of the president and his close advisers to be subject to FOIA disclosure, and that granting the request for certain visitor records would effectively disclose those calendars. The court did grant public access to some visitor logs, but not those affecting the Oval Office. The Obama administration had begun releasing visitor logs in September 2009 after media and public interest groups sought to learn who had access to the Oval Office and other West Wing areas; records from before that time had not been released. The ruling means presidents can revert to the pre-2009 policy of keeping such logs confidential. The decision would keep the visitor records confidential for up to 12 years after Obama leaves office. Judicial Watch said it was considering an appeal.

The inquiry includes potential financial entanglements between Giuliani and Ukrainian figures and counterintelligence concerns linked to those business connections. The counterintelligence concerns center on whether foreign actors tried to take advantage of Giuliani's business connections to Ukraine to reach the White House, or whether a foreign influence operation sought to exploit his business ties in Ukraine and with wealthy foreigners to make inroads with the White House. The investigation is being led by the U.S. attorney's office in the Southern District of New York. FBI counterintelligence agents have asked questions about Giuliani's ties to Lev Parnas and Igor Fruman, two associates who were arrested recently in airports and indicted on campaign finance charges. Parnas and Fruman are charged with violating campaign finance laws to give money to Republican committees, including a $325,000 contribution in 2018 to a pro-Trump super PAC called America First Action. They also helped Giuliani with efforts to investigate Democratic presidential candidate Joe Biden, although the charges appear unrelated to Giuliani's work in Ukraine. Giuliani has denied wrongdoing and said on Monday he had not been informed of any investigation, adding, "They can look at my Ukraine business all they want." Since April 2018, Giuliani has been President Trump's personal lawyer, work for which he is not paid.

summary:
On Monday during the Democratic National Convention in Philadelphia, Senator Bernie Sanders addressed delegates, urging party unity and declaring that Donald Trump must be defeated. Sanders told the audience, "We have got to defeat Donald Trump; and we have got to elect Hillary Clinton and Tim Kaine!" Some supporters booed loudly. Sanders responded, "Brothers and sisters, this is the real world that we live in. Trump is a bully and a demagogue. Trump has made bigotry and hatred the cornerstone of his campaign." He listed groups Trump had insulted: Mexicans and Latinos, Muslims, women, African Americans. Sanders said Trump does not respect the Constitution or civil liberties, calling him "a danger for the future of our country." Sanders pledged to do everything to see Trump defeated and said they would continue fighting to increase worker pay, provide universal health care, fight climate change, reform the criminal justice system, and provide a pathway to citizenship for undocumented immigrants.

Also on Monday, Republican nominee Donald Trump held a campaign town hall in Roanoke, Virginia, where he coined a new nickname for Clinton. Trump asked, "Why did Hillary get rid of her middle name?" then said, "Rotten" instead of "Rodham." "Hillary Rotten Clinton, right? Maybe that's why: It's too close," Trump said. He had previously used the nickname "Crooked Hillary."

Trump also posted on Twitter that Clinton's vice-presidential pick was "VERY disrespectful to Bernie Sanders and all of his supporters," adding that if supporters did not fight, "their blood, sweat and tears was a total waste of time." Clinton had announced her selection of Senator Tim Kaine on Friday night and appeared with him at a rally in Miami on Saturday. Kaine was widely viewed as a safe pick but drew criticism from Sanders for not being progressive enough.

On Saturday, the Democratic Rules Committee voted overwhelmingly to reduce the influence of superdelegates in the 2020 presidential election after a deal between Clinton and Sanders supporters. Reports also surfaced that Democratic National Committee Chairwoman Debbie Wasserman Schultz would not speak at the convention following the leak of internal DNC emails showing an effort to undermine Sanders's campaign.

summary:
Police in Ferguson, Missouri, used tear gas and smoke bombs Wednesday night to disperse protesters after flaming projectiles were thrown from the crowd, a St. Louis County police spokesman said. Helicopters circled overhead and smoke hung in the air. The spokesman, Brian Schellman, said he had no immediate information about the situation. Earlier Wednesday, demonstrations had been peaceful. summary:
Three police officers were killed and at least three others wounded in a shooting in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, on Sunday. Two of the dead were Baton Rouge police officers and one was an East Baton Rouge Parish sheriff's deputy. The alleged shooter was identified as Gavin Long, a black man and Marine veteran. summary:
Senator Barbara Boxer, a 74-year-old Democrat, announced last week that she will not seek re-election in 2016. Lieutenant Governor Gavin Newsom, who served eight years as mayor of San Francisco, said in a Facebook message that he will not run for the open seat. "It's always better to be candid than coy," Newsom wrote. "While I am humbled by the widespread encouragement of so many and hold in the highest esteem those who serve us in federal office, I know that my head and my heart, my young family's future, and our unfinished work all remain firmly in the state of California — not Washington, D.C."

The urgency of the needs of the people of this great state have convinced me to seriously consider looking at running for California's open Senate seat." Former Vice President Joe Biden won the Missouri Democratic primary on Tuesday evening, according to the Associated Press. Missouri was one of six states holding primaries that day, offering 68 pledged delegates. In 2016, Senator Bernie Sanders lost the Missouri primary to Hillary Clinton by less than half a percentage point, or 1,531 votes. The margin of Biden's 2020 victory in Missouri was not immediately known.

Biden was declared the winner in Missouri and Mississippi immediately after polls closed, then in Michigan — a state Sanders won in 2016 and the largest delegate prize of the night with 125 pledged delegates, with polls closing at 9:00 p.m. ET — and later in Idaho. The six states voting Tuesday — Idaho, Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, North Dakota, and Washington — offered a combined 352 delegates.

U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un held a historic summit in Singapore, the first meeting between sitting leaders of the two countries. They signed a joint statement in which the United States committed to provide unspecified security guarantees and Kim reaffirmed his commitment to the "complete denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula." The agreement contained few specifics and did not include details on how the United States would verify North Korea's nuclear disarmament. Sanders denied that Trump was making a threat to special counsel Robert Mueller when he suggested in the interview that any investigation into his family's finances would cross a red line, saying the president was "emphasizing that the special counsel should not move outside the scope of the investigation." The interview also included Trump's criticism of four other figures involved in the Russia probe, including Mueller and former FBI Director James Comey.

summary: New York State Supreme Court Justice Milton Tingling on Monday blocked Mayor Michael Bloomberg's ban on the sale of sugary drinks larger than 16 ounces from restaurants, mobile food carts and other establishments. The judge wrote that "the simple reading of the rule leads to the earlier acknowledged uneven enforcement even within a particular city block, much less the city as a whole," and that "the loopholes in this rule effectively defeat the state purpose of the rule." Tingling also wrote that the rule was an "administrative Leviathan" that would "eviscerate" the separation of powers, and that the city did not demonstrate it faced an imminent health danger from consumption of large sodas. He suggested Bloomberg overstepped his authority by bringing the rules before the Board of Health, whose members are solely appointed by the mayor, rather than the City Council. The regulations included a three-month grace period after which establishments would face fines of $200 per sale. summary:
President Barack Obama and Prime Minister David Cameron attended a NATO summit in Cardiff, Wales. The summit was originally intended to focus on Russia's military intervention in Ukraine, but efforts to assemble an international coalition against the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria (ISIS) were expected to predominate. In a joint opinion piece published in The Times of London, Obama and Cameron wrote that NATO should reject "isolationist" impulses and confront the terrorist threat posed by ISIS, stating the United States and Britain "will not be cowed by barbaric killers" and "will not waver in our determination to confront" the group.

Speaking ahead of the summit, Cameron said the UK government would not pay any ransom to ISIS militants holding a British hostage, describing it as a "desperately difficult situation" but adding that ransom money would only fuel the conflict. He referenced the killings of U.S. journalists James Foley and Steven Sotloff by the group, and noted that a British hostage had been shown in a recent video and threatened with death. Cameron said, "We don't pay ransoms to terrorists when they kidnap our citizens," and added that on other occasions payments had been made and governments had "turned a blind eye," which he called "deeply regrettable." He also said ISIS posed a direct threat to the UK and that "the world would be a safer place if we could squeeze this organisation out of existence," while ruling out cooperation with Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, whom he called "part of the problem, not part of the solution."

During the summit, Obama visited a reception hosted by Prince Charles, where the two posed for photographers and greeted a group of children. Obama, the first sitting U.S. president to visit Wales, said he was enjoying his trip and that everyone should visit the country.

summary:
Shortly before midnight on Monday, the House voted to request a conference committee with the Senate to negotiate a continuing resolution. The government shut down at midnight. Early Tuesday morning, Boehner held a brief press conference after the House vote. When a reporter asked about the 800,000 government employees facing furlough, Boehner responded, "The House has voted to keep the government open. But we also want basic fairness for all Americans under Obamacare." As the reporter attempted a follow-up, Boehner left the podium.

He said the Senate would only go to conference if the House passed that clean CR. The Senate adjourned and planned to return at 9:30 a.m. Tuesday to consider whatever the House sent over, with Reid stating the Senate would continue to table any amendments to defund or repeal the Affordable Care Act.

Collier, 26, was shot and killed on April 18 while sitting in his cruiser, allegedly by the Boston Marathon bombing suspects three days after the marathon attack. The service was open to MIT students and law enforcement officers from around the country; as many as 10,000 people were expected and thousands attended. Vice President Joe Biden and his wife Jill, Governor Deval Patrick, and Senator Elizabeth Warren were among the dignitaries present. Warren said, "We are strong. We are Collier strong. We are Boston strong," and "We will miss you, Sean." As Biden approached the podium, the crowd stood to applaud. Biden told the officers, "I am standing for you, you should not be standing for me," and added, "I know from experience that there's not much that I am able to do to fill that void." Following the capture of Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, President Obama said he was grateful for Collier's service and offered prayers to the Collier family, quoting the MIT police chief: "He was born to be a police officer." Collier's family said he died bravely in the line of duty. Before joining the MIT force, Collier worked as an information technology employee at the Somerville Police Department. Students remembered him for his outgoing and helpful personality. Student groups created memorial pages, and the MIT police department established a condolences page at officer179.mit.edu that collected over 1,100 messages in two days. The department also set up a memorial fund to create the "Collier Medal" for officers who "demonstrate the values of Officer Collier."

summary:
Republican Party rule-makers voted Friday to tie the selection of convention delegates to the results of each state's Republican primary, a change aimed at limiting the influence of insurgent candidates such as Ron Paul. The proposed change is subject to a later vote on a larger rules package. Paul won no primaries but amassed about 175 delegates partly through state party meetings and conventions that selected pro-Paul delegates. Romney allies said primary voters expect national convention delegates to be loyal to the primary winner.

In a separate credentials dispute, Paul supporters were left with only half the Maine delegates they thought they had won. Maine delegate Ashley Ryan, a 21-year-old college student who will become the state's national committeewoman, called the outcome "a huge slap in the face." Unseated Maine delegates can attend the convention with guest passes furnished by the Iowa delegation.

Paul's campaign had sought to maximize its delegate share through state party rules, including in Minnesota where Paul received a greater percentage of delegates than his vote share in non-binding caucuses.

Paul did not attack Romney as harshly as he did other Republican primary candidates. His son, Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, is scheduled to speak in primetime at the convention to help maximize libertarian enthusiasm for Romney. Some observers believed Paul's 2012 campaign laid groundwork for a future presidential run by his son.

summary: Two men, aged 18 and 20, were taken into custody early Sunday as "persons of interest" in the fatal shooting of 15-year-old Hadiya Pendleton, Chicago police said. Police spokeswoman Melissa Stratton said the two men were being questioned and no charges had been filed as of Sunday. Superintendent Garry McCarthy said he hoped murder charges would be filed Monday. Pendleton was shot and killed on January 29 in Vivian Gordon Harsh Park on the city's South Side, about a mile from President Obama's home. She was shot in the back as she and other King College Prep students took shelter from a driving rain under a canopy. Police said she was an innocent victim in a gang-related shooting. Days earlier, on January 21, Pendleton had performed at events for President Obama's inauguration with her high school band and drill team. First lady Michelle Obama attended Pendleton's funeral on Saturday, joined by White House senior adviser Valerie Jarrett and Education Secretary Arne Duncan. Civil rights leaders including Rev. Jesse Jackson had called on President Obama to attend the funeral and address gun violence in Chicago, which recorded more than 500 murders in 2012. Jackson said Pendleton's death "epitomizes this crisis" and that the president's appearance could help foster a larger conversation about gun violence in American cities.

President Obama has authorized the provision of arms to Syrian rebels fighting President Bashar al-Assad, directing the CIA to carry out the operation through a classified order, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal. The White House declined to elaborate on the order but said Obama decided to increase military support to the rebels in both scope and scale. Administration officials said on June 13 that the arms provision also requires a limited no-fly zone inside Syria, to be enforced from Jordanian territory. White House Deputy National Security Advisor Ben Rhodes said the conclusion that the Syrian regime used chemical weapons against the rebels weighed heavily in the decision, referring to chemical weapons use as a 'red line.' Jordan has offered military bases to the United States and its allies to protect a safe zone inside the kingdom. U.S. military officials estimated it would take four weeks to establish the no-fly zone. One account put the death toll in the conflict at more than 90,000, with thousands tortured in Assad's prisons.

summary: U.S. District Judge Derrick K. On Friday, a panel of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled it lacked jurisdiction to clarify the Supreme Court's decision but said Watson could interpret and enforce it. Hawaii subsequently filed a new motion asking Watson to enforce or modify the injunction he issued in March that had blocked the ban entirely.

summary:
Former President Barack Obama said Tuesday that Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden "nailed this decision" in selecting Senator Kamala Harris as his running mate. In a statement issued the same day Biden announced the pick, Obama said Harris, 55, is "more than prepared for the job" and has spent her career "defending our Constitution and defending folks who need a fair shake." Harris served as California attorney general before winning election to the Senate in 2016. If elected, she would be the first Black and South Asian American vice president and the first female vice president in U.S. history. "Michelle and I couldn't be more thrilled for Kamala, Doug, Cole and Ella," Obama said, referring to her husband, Doug Emhoff, and stepchildren. "This is a good day for our country. Now let's go win this thing." Biden and Harris were scheduled to deliver their first joint remarks Wednesday in Delaware.

Speaking Wednesday, Biden said Black and brown girls who often feel "overlooked" in their communities are now full of hope. "Today — just maybe — they are seeing themselves for the first time in a new way," he said. Biden said he chose Harris because she can govern and had a stellar record as California attorney general. Harris is the first African American woman to appear on a major party presidential ticket.

Former San Francisco Mayor Willie Brown, who served from 1996 to 2004, said Wednesday he is now pleased Harris accepted the offer after previously advising against it. Brown said he had believed Harris would be in a stronger position if appointed U.S. attorney general, and feared the vice presidency might sideline her presidential potential. "From a history standpoint, as a Black person, this is the first Black woman to rise to the level of a national ticket," Brown said, noting that only four women have previously appeared on a national ticket. Harris will become the first woman of color on a major party ticket when formally nominated at the Democratic National Convention next week.

summary:
President Donald Trump fired Christopher Krebs, director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) at the Department of Homeland Security, via tweet on Tuesday. Trump said a recent statement by Krebs about the security of the election was "highly inaccurate." Krebs had led CISA since its establishment in 2018 and was confirmed by the Senate by voice vote that year. Before the firing, Krebs and CISA had declared there was no evidence voting systems were compromised and called the 2020 election the "most secure in American history," contradicting Trump's claims of voter fraud.

On Thursday, after Trump's legal team held a lengthy press conference promoting election conspiracy theories, Krebs posted on Twitter: "That press conference was the most dangerous 1hr 45 minutes of television in American history. And possibly the craziest. If you don't know what I'm talking about, you're lucky."

Republican senators criticized the firing. Sen. Ben Sasse, a member of the Intelligence Committee, said in a statement: "Chris Krebs did a really good job — as state election officials all across the nation will tell you — and he obviously should not be fired." Sen. Rob Portman said Krebs was "very good" and "was trying to do in an unprecedented way was to connect with every state in the country, and give them what they needed to protect and have a firewall ... against cyberattacks." Sen. Comedian Stephen Colbert also commented on the firing, calling it "another example of closing the barn door after the cows voted for somebody else" and asking, "You don't fire the election security guy after we already had the secure election. How can you be this bad at criming?"

Donald Trump told the audience, "The Republican establishment, or whatever you want to call it, should embrace what's happening." Rubio's job approval among Floridians stood at 48 percent; 79 percent of likely Republican voters in Ohio approved of Kasich's performance. Among early voters in Florida, Trump held a 47 percent to 22 percent advantage over Rubio.

"I'm not really campaigning in Florida. I tried to actually call Marco last night to wish him good luck. I couldn't get through to him. But look, at the end of the day how do you tell your people that are for you to go vote for somebody else? After all, I'm not into a Stop-Trump as more as I'm Be-For-Kasich movement."  

Rubio's campaign had suggested Friday that Rubio supporters vote for Kasich in Ohio. An NBC News/Wall Street Journal/Marist poll showed Kasich leading Trump in Ohio with Ted Cruz and Rubio well behind, while Trump held a large lead over Rubio in Florida.

summary: Former Democratic presidential nominee and longtime South Dakota senator George McGovern, 90, entered hospice care in Sioux Falls earlier this week. His daughter, Ann McGovern, told the Associated Press on Monday that he was "coming to the end of his life" and had moved into Dougherty Hospice House. On Wednesday, the family issued a statement through Avera McKennan Hospital saying McGovern was "no longer responsive." A CNN report cited the same statement and added that he was on life support and suffered from a variety of ailments that had worsened over recent months due to age. McGovern was the 1972 Democratic nominee, losing to incumbent President Richard Nixon in a landslide — 49 of 50 states — on a platform that included ending the war in Vietnam. Nixon resigned less than two years later in the Watergate scandal. McGovern served in the House of Representatives from 1957 to 1961 after winning election in 1956, and in the Senate from 1963 to 1981 after winning election in 1962; he was a champion of the party's liberal wing. He lost his Senate seat in the 1980 Republican wave that accompanied Ronald Reagan's election. In later years he focused on fighting world hunger. In October 2011 he was treated for exhaustion after a lecture tour, and two months later he fell and hit his head before a scheduled C-SPAN interview. His 1972 campaign was chronicled in Timothy Crouse's "The Boys on the Bus" and Hunter S. Thompson's "Fear and Loathing on the Campaign Trail '72."

Economists had forecast a decline to 335,000. The less volatile four-week average fell 6,750 to 338,500, marking the third straight weekly decline; both figures are near pre-recession levels. summary: Secret Service Director Julia Pierson testified Tuesday before the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform about a security breach in which a man armed with a knife jumped the White House fence and entered the executive mansion. She wrote that a comprehensive discussion of Secret Service policies and procedures would require disclosures that are "at the very least law enforcement sensitive and, in some instances, classified," and that "publicly airing the very security measures employed by the Secret Service and the various challenges we confront at the White House complex will arm those who desire to cause injury — or worse — to the president and first family." She called that "beyond reckless." Committee members, including Representative Jason Chaffetz, Republican of Utah, said Monday they did not believe Pierson should be able to move the discussion behind closed doors simply to avoid embarrassing details about lapses by her agency. The following day, Representative Elijah Cummings, Democrat of Maryland and the committee's ranking member, said on MSNBC's "Morning Joe" that his confidence and trust in Pierson had eroded and that he did not feel comfortable with her in the position. As Pierson testified, White House press secretary Josh Earnest told reporters that President Obama expects the Secret Service to release the results of its investigation into the intrusion as soon as possible, saying there is legitimate public interest in how the breach occurred. summary: President Donald Trump delivered his first State of the Union address on Tuesday. According to excerpts released by the White House beforehand, Trump planned to declare a "new American moment" and offer a message of unity after his first year in office. He intended to call on Congress to pass bipartisan fixes on immigration and begin work on a large infrastructure proposal, extending "an open hand to work with members of both parties, Democrats and Republicans, to protect our citizens of every background, color and creed." He also planned a veiled criticism of former President Obama's approach: "Past experience has taught us that complacency and concessions only invite aggression and provocation. I will not repeat the mistakes of the past administrations that got us into this dangerous position." During the address, when Trump said his immigration plan ends chain migration — stating, "Under the current broken system, a single immigrant can bring in virtually unlimited numbers of distant relatives. He called for bipartisan unity on infrastructure but provided no details or road map for enacting such a plan. Trump did not mention the Russia investigation or the #MeToo movement, even as female lawmakers wore black to mark the cultural moment. Davis, who cited religious objections and said she was acting "under God's authority," had been ordered to begin issuing licenses after the Supreme Court's ruling legalizing same-sex marriage nationwide. Bunning said financial sanctions were insufficient to ensure compliance and ordered her detained until she agrees to follow the court's order. U.S. Marshals took her into custody, according to local reporter Dan Griffin of WSAZ. While Davis is jailed, the county judge's office can issue marriage licenses so that Rowan County couples may marry. Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said officials should "uphold the law." Several Republican presidential candidates also said Davis, as a public official, should issue the licenses. Breitbart News reported that Davis also claimed the authority to order her deputy clerks not to issue licenses, a claim that extends beyond her personal religious objection.

summary:
Multiple media reports said Syrian government forces used chemical weapons against rebel forces near Damascus on Wednesday, firing rockets equipped with "poisonous gas heads" in attacks that killed hundreds of people. The British government declared on Friday that Syrian government forces had used chemical weapons in Damascus. British Foreign Secretary William Hague stated the chances of a conspiracy by the opposition were "vanishingly small" and said Britain believed it was a chemical attack by the Assad regime. Hague said Britain would support a United Nations investigation into the attack sites and would push for stronger action at the UN if Syria did not grant access. He added that Security Council members had expressed support for the UN team to go there, but the team had not yet been able to do so, and the Assad regime appeared to have something to hide. Hague said the only possible explanation for casualties so intense in such a small area on this scale was a chemical attack. The governments of Russia and China had been blocking UN action over Syria this week, according to Hague.

Russia urged the government of President Bashar al-Assad on Friday to allow United Nations investigators to examine evidence of a suspected chemical weapons attack earlier in the week, joining the United States in seeking a full accounting of what happened early Wednesday in the eastern suburbs of Damascus. A Russian Foreign Ministry statement said the Russian side called on the Syrian government to cooperate with the UN chemical experts. However, Russia also accused the rebels of staging the attack to implicate Assad's government and said the opposition should guarantee safe access for the mission to the alleged site. The United States, France and other countries were pushing for an investigation into allegations that poison gas was used in the attack, which opposition forces said killed hundreds of people.

The White House had not responded to a request for comment as of the time of the reports. In June, the White House said it had determined that Assad's forces had used chemical weapons on rebel groups, prompting the Obama administration to provide military support to the opposition. Tens of thousands of people have died and millions have been displaced in the two-year-old conflict in Syria. The United States has provided more than $1 billion in humanitarian aid to the country since the crisis began.

summary: Eric Cantor, the House majority leader and Virginia Republican, lost his June 10 primary to Tea Party challenger David Brat, a college economics professor. No sitting majority leader had lost a re-election bid since the office was created in 1899. Immigration dominated the race. Brat repeatedly accused Cantor of supporting "amnesty" and wanting "open borders." Cantor opposed a comprehensive immigration overhaul but favored providing a path to legal status for young undocumented immigrants. His direct-mail pieces declared him "foursquare against amnesty," while Washington newspapers quoted him saying he was seeking a compromise with President Obama on the issue. Cantor outspent Brat by roughly $2.5 million to $200,000, much of it on negative advertisements that labeled Brat a "liberal college professor"; the ads were described as so vitriolic they lacked credibility. A subterranean Democratic effort to turn out crossover voters in the Republican primary may also have contributed to the result. After the upset, political analysts said the defeat destroyed any chance of a comprehensive immigration bill passing the House that year. National polling showed majority support for allowing undocumented immigrants to remain legally: a CBS News poll in March found 56 percent favored a path to citizenship, 12 percent favored legal residency without citizenship, and 29 percent favored deportation, with majorities across party lines supporting some form of legal status.

Former Democratic National Committee chairwoman Donna Brazile said on ABC's "This Week" on Sunday that President Donald Trump is "not prepared" for negotiations with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un. Brazile stated the president is "betting on himself," citing the absence of State Department personnel to brief him, the lack of a U.S. ambassador to South Korea, and the national security adviser focused on the issue being on paternity leave. She questioned whether Trump would understand the stakes, including technical issues such as sanctions and nuclear nonproliferation, and added that he governs "on the fly."

Brazile's comments came as lawmakers and administration officials considered a possible face-to-face meeting between Trump and Kim following a South Korean delegation's meeting with Kim last week. Kim has said he would go to the Peace House to meet South Korean President Moon Jae-in. President Trump is known as a reluctant traveler, and Kim has not left North Korea since assuming power in 2011. Some White House officials believe the meeting will not occur.

summary:
U.S. Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin said Thursday that President Donald Trump has no plans to meet with Iranian President Hassan Rouhani during the United Nations General Assembly later this month. Mnuchin stated such a meeting is "not planned at the moment," though Trump has made clear "he would sit down with Rouhani with no condition" to discuss Iran's nuclear program. Mnuchin also said the departure of former national security adviser John Bolton will not dramatically change the administration's posture on Iran, adding that he and Secretary of State Mike Pompeo "have been executing the president's maximum pressure campaign" so there is no "sea change."

On the same day, Trump told reporters he would not ask Pompeo to serve simultaneously as national security adviser and secretary of state, despite earlier discussion among White House officials about the dual role. Trump said he spoke to Pompeo about the idea and the secretary of state "liked the idea of having somebody in there with him." Trump said he now has about 15 candidates for the national security adviser post, up from a short list of five a day earlier, and expected to make a decision next week. "Everybody wants it very badly, as you can imagine," Trump said. "A lot of people want the job. It's a great job." According to several anonymous sources, the list consists largely of reliable conservatives with ties to administration stalwarts, including Vice President Mike Pence's national security adviser, retired Army General Keith Kellogg; State Department Iran envoy Brian Hook; former deputy White House national security adviser Rick Waddell; and U.S. ambassador to Germany Richard Grenell.

Two days earlier, during a press briefing with Pompeo, Mnuchin responded to CNN chief White House correspondent Jim Acosta, who asked whether the national security team was "a mess" following Bolton's departure. Mnuchin replied, "Absolutely not. That's the most ridiculous question I've ever heard of." He added, "Let me just say, the national security team, which is what you asked, consists of the national security advisor, the secretary of defense, the secretary of state, myself, the chief of staff, and many others."

summary:
Facebook Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg testified before Congress over two days this week, facing nearly 100 lawmakers and almost 600 questions about the company's handling of user data. The hearings followed revelations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly harvested data of up to 87 million Facebook users.

On Tuesday, Zuckerberg appeared before a Senate committee. Senator Orrin Hatch, Republican of Utah, asked how Facebook makes money. Zuckerberg replied, "Senator, we run ads." Senator Roger Wicker, Republican of Mississippi, asked whether Facebook tracks users' data after they log out. Senator Lindsey Graham, Republican of South Carolina, questioned whether Facebook has a monopoly and compared the service to Twitter.

Zuckerberg told the committee, "The system basically worked as it was designed," referring to the sharing of 87 million users' data with a researcher who sold it to Cambridge Analytica, a firm tied to the Trump campaign. He added, "This issue is that we designed the system in a way that wasn't good." Zuckerberg said all affected users should have been aware their data could be harvested that way and had consented to it at some point during their use of Facebook.

On Monday, before the hearings, Zuckerberg met with lawmakers he would later face, acknowledging where the company had failed and outlining steps Facebook was taking to prevent similar issues. Lawmakers continued questioning on Wednesday.

summary: Democrat Doug Jones defeated Republican Roy Moore in Alabama's U.S. Senate special election on Tuesday. The seat had been held by Republican Sen. Luther Strange. At Jones' victory party, former NBA player Charles Barkley, who had spoken at a campaign event earlier in the week urging Alabamians not to look like "idiots," told CNN's Jake Tapper the result was a wake-up call for Democrats. Barkley said the party had taken the black vote and the poor vote for granted for a long time and needed to "get off their [butt] and start making life better for black folks and people who are poor." Celebrities celebrated the victory on social media. Actress Alyssa Milano, who had canvassed for Jones, posted a tearful video thanking Alabama. Late-night host Stephen Colbert called it a "Christmas miracle," and actress Kerry Washington said voters had chosen "a more perfect union. A place where we ALL matter." Moore had faced weeks of sexual harassment and assault allegations. Regarding legislative impact, Sen. Susan Collins said Thursday there was no reason to wait for Jones to be sworn in to vote on the tax plan. Collins' spokeswoman said the Senate had always planned to pass the tax bill before the end of the year regardless of the election outcome.

Mitt Romney said in an interview that he would not support either Donald Trump or Hillary Clinton for president, but acknowledged that a Trump victory was "very possible." Romney credited Trump for connecting with voters and securing the Republican nomination, saying Trump brought a rhetoric and style perfected over his career to the political sphere. Romney added that despite thinking Trump would not be an ideal nominee, "he is. At this stage, it's rougher going, but I can't predict what's gonna happen." Romney also criticized Clinton's speaking style, saying serious women leaders do not "put their arms up in the air and make a big guffaw kind of smile" and that she appears to be acting like Bill Clinton, which "doesn't come across well."

At the Veterans of Foreign Wars convention in Charlotte, North Carolina, Republican nominee Donald Trump spoke after Clinton had addressed the same gathering on Monday. During Trump's remarks, the audience broke into sporadic chants of "lock her up." Trump referenced Clinton's appearance, saying, "And to think she was here yesterday, I guess she didn't do very well." He referred to her as "crooked Hillary Clinton" and challenged her recent statement that the VA scandal was not as widespread as reported, saying it was as if she were trying to sweep it under the rug.

The Republican National Convention in Cleveland, described by one account as "The Donald Trump National Convention," featured muddled messaging and a shared agenda centered on opposition to Clinton. Many speakers avoided discussing the candidate, and one declined to endorse him. Past presidents and many younger politicians were absent. Speakers who appeared offered pained endorsements, displayed opportunistic zeal, or worked to suppress delegate dissent.

summary:
A St. Louis County grand jury decided not to indict Ferguson police Officer Darren Wilson in the August shooting death of Michael Brown, an unarmed 18-year-old black teenager. The decision was announced Monday night by St. Louis County Prosecutor Robert P. McCulloch at a news conference. The grand jury, composed of nine whites and three blacks, had spent months examining the case. McCulloch said Wilson had faced charges ranging from first-degree murder to involuntary manslaughter, and that the jury found "no probable cause exists" to indict Wilson. The killing had set off weeks of civil unrest and a national debate over what protesters called a pattern of police brutality against young black men.

Following the announcement, hundreds gathered outside the Ferguson Police Department. Police officers in riot gear formed a line as demonstrators chanted and threw signs and other objects. "The system failed us again," one woman said. In downtown Ferguson, the sound of breaking glass could be heard as crowds ran through the streets. Peaceful protests turned violent; looters broke into stores, cars were flipped, and buildings were set on fire.

summary:

Trump's position evolved: he initially supported improved relations but would have negotiated a "better deal" than President Obama, who restored diplomatic ties in 2014. By the campaign's end, Trump promised to reverse Obama's policy, appealing to Cuban-American voters in South Florida.

President Obama offered condolences to the Castro family without praising or criticizing Castro. He said: "We know that this moment fills Cubans — in Cuba and in the United States — with powerful emotions, recalling the countless ways in which Fidel Castro altered the course of individual lives, families, and of the Cuban nation. History will record and judge the enormous impact of this singular figure on the people and world around him."

Castro's government improved conditions for the very poor, achieved health and literacy levels comparable to wealthy nations, and removed a powerful Mafia presence. It also tolerated little dissent, jailed opponents, seized private businesses and monopolized media. Opponents called him a dictator; hundreds of thousands fled, many settling in Florida and influencing U.S. policy while plotting Castro's demise without success.

Smith urged the Afghan government to sign the Bilateral Security Agreement that would allow U.S. troops to remain past 2014 and said, "The American people have paid a significant price in this conflict and it is time that we allow the Afghan people to take responsibility for their own future."

summary: Brett M. Kavanaugh was sworn in Saturday as the 114th Supreme Court justice, hours after the Senate confirmed him by a 50-48 vote. As the ceremony took place, protesters chanted outside the Supreme Court building across from the Capitol. The allegations transformed the confirmation process from a routine ideological dispute into a national debate over victims' rights, the presumption of innocence, and personal attacks on nominees. By Sunday, Kavanaugh had hired women to fill all four of his law clerk positions.

summary:
The Senate voted 54-46 on Tuesday to reject a House Republican request to name negotiators for a budget conference committee, the fourth such rejection during the standoff that has produced the first government shutdown in 17 years. The vote fell along party lines. Majority Leader Harry Reid said he would not negotiate while Republicans were blocking a straightforward spending bill to keep the government operating.

On Monday, the Senate approved without objection a House-passed bill guaranteeing pay for military personnel during the shutdown. Reid acted after Senate Republicans took to the floor demanding action on the measure, which now goes to President Obama for his signature. Earlier Monday, Democrats defeated two other House proposals that would have funded the government while altering the Affordable Care Act.

House Republicans said they would consider attaching a short-term funding extension to their next offer to the Senate. Senate Democrats responded coolly. Aides to the Democratic leadership said Monday they saw little point in legislation that would prolong the dispute, and that Reid remained committed to accepting only a budget bill without policy conditions such as a delay of the health care law. Senator Barbara Boxer of California rejected the idea of a stopgap, saying House Republicans "have to grow up and just step up to the plate." She urged Speaker John A. Boehner to resist conservative members of his party and bring the Senate budget bill to a House vote, where it would likely pass. "That's what a speaker is supposed to do," Boxer said. Lawmakers have focused increased attention on cybersecurity following allegations of Russian hacking of Democratic organizations during the 2016 U.S. presidential election and concerns about potential Russian meddling in upcoming elections in France and Germany.

summary:
Anthony Weiner, a candidate for New York City mayor and former U.S. representative for New York's 9th congressional district, acknowledged sending sexually explicit photographs to a woman, reviving a scandal that prompted his resignation from Congress in June 2011. At a press conference on Tuesday, his wife, Huma Abedin, appeared beside him and defended him. The Wall Street Journal editorial page called for Weiner to withdraw from the race, arguing he should step aside for Abedin's sake. The New York Times editorial page also urged Weiner to leave the race, writing that he should take his "marital troubles and personal compulsions out of the public eye."

Separately, Eliot Spitzer, a candidate for New York City comptroller and former governor who resigned in 2008 amid a prostitution scandal, said his wife, Silda Wall Spitzer, would not join him on the campaign trail. Spitzer told the New York Post that voters would judge him, "not who else is with me or not with me," and noted that "no other member of my family is running for office." Silda Wall Spitzer, a former corporate lawyer, now works for a private equity group focusing on clean energy investments. She stood by Spitzer during his 2008 resignation.

Edward Snowden, the former CIA employee and NSA contractor who leaked information about U.S. surveillance programs, was granted temporary asylum in Russia on Friday after spending nearly six weeks in the transit zone of Moscow's Sheremetyevo airport since arriving from Hong Kong on June 23. The asylum allows him to live and work in Russia for at least one year with some restrictions. His lawyer, Anatoly Kucherena, said Snowden is in a safe but undisclosed location and has not yet decided what he will do during his stay. Snowden's father, Lon Snowden, appeared on Russian national television on Wednesday and said he did not mind if his son remained in Russia as long as he was safe, adding that he agreed with his son's decision to stay because he believed there were no guarantees of a fair trial in the United States. The White House said it was "extremely disappointed" with the Kremlin and warned it may pull out of a planned September summit in Moscow between President Obama and President Vladimir Putin. On Friday, U.S. Ambassador Michael McFaul met with Putin aide Yuri Ushakov to discuss Snowden's "new status" along with other issues including nuclear stockpiles, missile defense, and Syria. Ushakov had previously said the Snowden case was not important enough to derail the overall U.S.-Russia relationship.

Senator Bernie Sanders criticized the ruling as "very troubling," arguing that "bosses should not be able to impose their religious beliefs on their employees" and that it undermines the government's interest in providing women access to preventive health care. The diplomatic push came a day after 16 people, including women and children, died in Gaza when a United Nations school being used as a shelter was struck; responsibility for the strike was unclear. Israeli aircraft struck 30 houses in Gaza early Friday, killing a leader of the military wing of Islamic Jihad and two of his sons.
