summary:
On the 50th anniversary of the March on Washington and Martin Luther King Jr.'s "I Have a Dream" speech, President Barack Obama, former President Bill Clinton, and members of King's family participated in commemorative events on Wednesday, August 28, 2013. King's descendants gathered for a morning interfaith service at Shiloh Baptist Church, where Dr. Alveda King, King's niece, said, "The dream is not dead. People are proving the dream is not dead. The biggest thing is love." Thousands of people traveled to the National Mall and the Lincoln Memorial for an afternoon ceremony featuring Obama's speech at the same steps where King spoke in 1963. Security was tight, with most streets around the Mall closed to vehicles, and light rain appeared to reduce early crowd sizes.

Clinton addressed the gathering, calling the 1963 march and speech "one of the most important days in American history" that "changed America," "opened minds and melted hearts ... and moved millions." He acknowledged that racial inequalities remain. According to an Associated Press account, Clinton said it was time to "stop complaining and instead get to work — for better education opportunities for all children and implementing health care for all," adding, "We must push open those stubborn gates" holding America back. Another account quoted Clinton as saying, "Martin Luther King did not live and die to hear his heirs whine about political gridlock," and suggested the remark was directed at Obama, who had frequently criticized congressional Republicans and, in a March 9 weekly address, said, "You deserve better than the same political gridlock and refusal to compromise that has too often passed for serious debate over the last few years."

summary: On Saturday evening at approximately 8:25 p.m., a vehicle traveling at a high rate of speed passed Vice President Joe Biden's Delaware residence on a public road outside the established security perimeter and fired several gunshots, according to the Secret Service. The Secret Service reported four to six shots were heard. The Bidens were not home at the time. The Washington Post reported the residence's surveillance cameras failed to capture images of the shooting or the shooter. Biden said Wednesday on NBC's "Today" that he felt "completely safe" at the home and was "not worried," adding there was "no evidence of any bullet holes anywhere" and that he thought "the security of my home is fine." It was not clear whether any shots struck the home or were aimed at it. Shortly after the shooting, police took a man into custody near the vice president's home after he allegedly resisted arrest. The man, identified as 57-year-old Rock Peters of Hockessin, was charged with reckless endangering and resisting arrest but not with the shooting. Police documents stated Peters fled from an officer near the Biden estate and scuffled with two officers. Peters alleged New Castle County police officers beat him, leaving him with a swollen nose, rib injuries, cuts on his face, and a black eye; he provided photos showing his face covered with blood and bruises. Police declined to comment on the allegation. The Secret Service said it was working with New Castle County Police to investigate and determine a motive, and whether the arrested man was connected to the shooting.

summary: First lady Melania Trump unveiled the White House holiday decorations on Monday, marking the Trump family's first Christmas in the residence. The 2017 theme, "Time-Honored Traditions," looks back at 200 years of holiday celebrations dating to the first White House Christmas party hosted by President John Adams and his wife, Abigail, in 1800. The first lady personally selected every detail of the displays, which include Christmas, Hanukkah and other seasonal decorations. More than 150 volunteers from 29 states spent the preceding week contributing a total of 1,600 hours to deck the halls, placing 1,000 feet of garland around each room's fireplace, mantels and doorways. The official White House Christmas tree is a 19-and-a-half-foot Balsam fir from Wisconsin; the residence features 53 Christmas trees in total. The White House also confirmed the display of a Nativity scene honoring the birth of Jesus Christ, marking the 50th anniversary of the scene's presence at the White House. Snopes had previously debunked rumors that the Nativity scene was not displayed during the Obama administration, citing a 2016 photo from the East Room. The first lady received the official tree on Monday accompanied by her son, Barron Trump, and shared sneak peeks of the decor on social media, writing "The decorations are up!" In a statement she said, "The president, Barron and I are very excited for our first Christmas in the White House." The first guests were children and students from Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, with whom Mrs. Trump worked on arts and craft projects. Dancers performed a number from "The Nutcracker" in the Cross Hall, a nod to the first themed White House Christmas in 1961. More than 25,000 visitors are expected for open houses and receptions through December.

The House Intelligence Committee voted unanimously Monday to release a 10-page Democratic memo countering a Republican memo released last week. The Republican memo, led by committee chairman Rep. Devin Nunes, accused the FBI and Justice Department of abusing surveillance powers to obtain a secret warrant to monitor former Trump campaign foreign policy adviser Carter Page for nearly a year. The Democratic memo alleges the GOP document used incomplete information to make misleading conclusions about the FBI's application. President Trump has until Friday to decide whether to block release of the still-classified Democratic document. White House Chief of Staff John Kelly said Tuesday that Trump has the document but has not read it, calling it "pretty lengthy," and that staff would brief him. White House spokesman Raj Shah said the president is "weighing his options" and "will respond soon" with his decision. White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said Tuesday that Trump met with Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein to discuss differences between the two memos, and that the document is undergoing "the exact same process that we did with the previous memo, in which it will go through a full and thorough legal and national security review." Trump has claimed the Republican memo "totally vindicates" him in the special counsel's investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election and possible collusion between his campaign and Moscow. The dueling memos have deepened partisan fights on the committee and become the recent focus of its probe into Russian meddling.

summary: A Greenpeace activist flew a powered paraglider over the Trump Turnberry resort in Ayrshire, Scotland, on Friday evening while President Donald Trump was staying there. The pilot carried a banner reading "Trump: Well Below Par" according to two accounts, or "TRUMP, WELL BELOW PAR #RESIST" according to a third. Greenpeace posted an image on Twitter stating they had delivered a message to Trump as he stood outside his hotel. Police Scotland Assistant Chief Constable Mark Williams confirmed a powered parachute was flown in close proximity of the Turnberry Hotel and said it is a criminal offence to fly within the airspace restriction zone. Williams stated officers were carrying out enquiries to trace the pilot and revealed the paraglider managed to escape after the incident. The U.S. Secret Service said it was working with foreign law enforcement partners investigating the unauthorized airspace incursion. Police said the pilot put himself in "grave danger" of being shot by snipers stationed around the course. The incident occurred during Trump's weekend stay at the resort with First Lady Melania Trump, ahead of his scheduled Monday travel to Russia to meet President Vladimir Putin. Large-scale protests took place in London on Friday, with organizers estimating 250,000 participants. Separately, protesters sought to fly a blimp depicting Trump as a baby over the Scottish course, though police said it would not be permitted at the resort and discussions on alternatives were ongoing. Greenpeace previously used paragliders to protest at the 2013 Formula One race in Belgium.

summary:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Tuesday directing that all executive departments and agencies of the federal government be closed on Monday, Dec. 24, 2018, and that their employees be excused from duty for Christmas Eve. The order, posted on the White House website, authorized the heads of executive departments and agencies to require certain offices or employees to remain on duty for reasons of national security, defense, or other public need. The director of the Office of Personnel Management was authorized to implement the directive.

The order followed a pattern observed in recent years when Christmas Day falls on a Tuesday. President George W. Bush issued similar orders in 2001 and 2007, and President Barack Obama did so in 2012. In 2014, Obama excused federal employees from work on Dec. 26, a Friday.

Nebraska Gov. Pete Ricketts announced that state buildings would also close on Dec. 24 and state employees would receive a day of leave, in accordance with a state law that requires Nebraska to grant the same benefit to state workers when the president gives federal employees paid time off. Exceptions were noted for law enforcement, security, military personnel, and others engaged in essential functions.

The executive order came amid ongoing budget negotiations and the prospect of a partial government shutdown. Trump had backed off a demand for $5 billion in border-wall funding on Tuesday, but Democrats and Republicans had not reached a budget agreement before a Friday deadline.

summary:
President-elect Barack Obama on Wednesday condemned the terrorist attacks in Mumbai that began that day, stating through his chief national security spokesperson Brooke Anderson that "these coordinated attacks on innocent civilians demonstrate the grave and urgent threat of terrorism" and that the United States must strengthen partnerships with India and other nations to "root out and destroy terrorist networks." The statement said Obama strongly condemned the attacks and that his thoughts and prayers were with the victims, their families, and the people of India.

On Thursday, President George W. Bush called Indian Prime Minister Manmohan Singh, according to Obama's transition office. Obama had received updates from the Bush administration's State Department as the attacks unfolded over several days.

On Friday night, Obama called Singh at approximately 10:30 p.m. Eastern time to express condolences for those killed in the Mumbai attacks and to convey that his thoughts and prayers were with the people of India and all affected, according to the transition office. The transition team also said Obama made clear during the call that there is only one U.S. president at a time.

summary: Republican Robert F. McDonnell, a former state attorney general, won the Virginia gubernatorial election on Tuesday, defeating Democratic candidate R. Creigh Deeds, an 18-year state senator from Bath County in western Virginia. The victory returned a Republican to the governor's office for the first time in eight years. With 99 percent of precincts reporting, McDonnell received 59 percent of the vote and Deeds 41 percent, though an earlier count with more than four-fifths of precincts reporting showed McDonnell at about 60 percent. McDonnell claimed victory at a Richmond hotel ballroom, telling supporters, "There's still people that need a voice, and we're going to give them that voice. This chapter is closed, but the next chapter is to be written." Deeds conceded a few miles away, saying he had called McDonnell to congratulate him and that Democrats could not give up despite the Republican sweep. The race, along with the New Jersey governor's contest, was viewed as the first referendum on President Barack Obama and the Democratic Congress before the 2010 midterm elections. A year earlier, Obama had become the first Democrat in 44 years to carry Virginia in a presidential race. Republicans cited the victory as a repudiation of the Obama administration and the national Democratic Party's agenda, especially that of departing Gov. Tim Kaine, the chairman of the Democratic National Committee. Voters expressed angst about major Obama initiatives such as health care, energy and stimulus spending, while McDonnell dominated the campaign's central issues of jobs and the economy.

summary:
A Gallup poll released Friday found that 51 percent of American adults surveyed said President Obama won the second presidential debate, held Tuesday in Hempstead, New York, while 38 percent said Mitt Romney won. The results split along party lines: 88 percent of Democrats favored Obama versus 4 percent for Romney, 78 percent of Republicans favored Romney versus 9 percent for Obama, and independents favored Obama 54 percent to 33 percent. A Gallup poll after the first debate on October 3 had shown 72 percent calling Romney the winner and 20 percent choosing Obama.

During the second debate, Obama raised Romney's videotaped remark that 47 percent of Americans are dependent on the government, making it his closing argument. Asked about public misperceptions, Romney said Obama's campaign tried to turn him into something he is not and stated, "I care about 100 percent of the American people." Obama responded that when Romney said "behind closed doors" that 47 percent considered themselves victims, "think about who he was talking about," citing the elderly receiving Social Security, veterans, students and soldiers.

Separate polling showed a national George Washington University/Politico survey of likely voters with Romney at 49 percent and Obama at 47 percent, a three-point swing from the previous week's 49-48 Obama edge, within the 3.1-point margin of error. In ten battleground states, Romney led 50 percent to 48 percent. Voters favored Obama on foreign policy 51 percent to 42 percent, while Romney led on the economy 51 percent to 45 percent and on jobs 50 percent to 46 percent. A Quinnipiac/CBS poll showed Obama's lead in Ohio narrowing from 53-43 percent in late September to 50-45 percent. An NBC/Wall Street Journal poll released Sunday showed the race tied.

summary:
On Thursday, Senate Republicans blocked a cloture vote on President Obama's nomination of former Republican Senator Chuck Hagel of Nebraska, a decorated Vietnam veteran, to be Secretary of Defense. The vote was 58 to 40, falling short of the 60 votes needed to proceed to a final confirmation vote. The tally broke down almost strictly along party lines. Democrats vowed to try again when the Senate returns from recess in 10 days. Several Republicans who voted against cloture said they would not block a final up-or-down vote.

Earlier, Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-NV) said he would not honor any requests for a "hold" on the nomination, meaning the vote would proceed to the floor. However, Hagel may still have needed 60 votes if a senator who had requested a hold objected at the time Reid attempted to move to a vote — a procedural step that is not a filibuster, since it occurs after debate has ended, but poses a similar obstacle. Ranking Member of the Senate Armed Services Committee James Inhofe (R-OK) had indicated he would request a hold based on Hagel's views on Israel, and committee member Lindsey Graham (R-SC) said he would request a hold to demand further information from the Obama administration about the September 2012 attack on the U.S. consulate in Benghazi, Libya. The committee was meeting to debate the nomination and vote on whether to recommend confirmation by the full Senate.

Speaker John Boehner (R-OH) declined to weigh in on the nomination fight, telling MSNBC's Luke Russert, "this is the House side of the Capitol. We're not involved in the Senate nomination process, so you can ask [them]." A Senate Democratic leadership aide told reporters that Senate Republicans on Thursday informed Reid they would not provide the 60 votes needed to proceed to a final vote on Hagel's nomination.

summary: About 28 to 30 Senate Democrats held an overnight session on the Senate floor Monday night into Tuesday morning to draw attention to climate change. The lawmakers, members of the Senate Climate Action Task Force, began speaking Monday evening and continued until about 9 a.m. Tuesday. Sen. Harry Reid (D-Nev.) opened the session, saying "Climate change is real. It's here," and that it was time to stop acting as if those who ignore it "have a valid point of view." Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) led the effort, which Sen. Barbara Boxer (D-Calif.) described as designed to "wake up Congress to the disturbing realities of climate change." Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) said the action aimed to send a message that "it's time for Congress to wake up and get serious" about addressing climate change, adding that the cost of inaction is too high for communities and the economy. Other participants included Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Edward Markey (both D-Mass.), Richard Blumenthal and Chris Murphy (both D-Conn.). A senator from Maine compared climate-change skeptics to appeasers who ignored the Nazi menace in the 1930s. Sen. Jeff Sessions (R-Ala.) spoke during the session to call on Democrats to present a bill, saying they lack the votes to pass one and that claims about climate change "(These false claims about climate change) become more than an exaggeration, but a deliberate misrepresentation." The Democrats acknowledged that serious climate legislation has no chance of passage in the divided Congress, where the Republican-majority House includes many members who deny the science of human-caused global warming. The Senate group is working with a parallel House caucus.

summary: Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel on Tuesday ordered a review of military hairstyle policies across all services after 16 female members of the Congressional Black Caucus criticized new Army regulations as discriminatory toward black women. The Army earlier this month issued new appearance standards that ban most twists, dreadlocks and large cornrows — styles used predominantly by African-American women with natural hair. In a letter to Hagel, the caucus members called the changes "discriminatory rules targeting soldiers who are women of color with little regard to what is needed to maintain their natural hair." Pentagon spokesman Rear Adm. John Kirby said Hagel directed the deputy secretary of defense to work with the service secretaries and military chiefs to review their respective policies over the next three months. Kirby said Hagel will make "whatever appropriate adjustments to DOD policy are necessary" after the review. A Pentagon spokesman said Hagel is "opening the aperture" beyond the Army to all services, which black servicewomen have said for decades have forced them to conform to norms based on the hair of white women. Hagel said he takes the concerns "very seriously."

summary:
Texas Gov. Rick Perry was indicted by a grand jury on Friday on charges of abusing his official powers. The indictment stemmed from Perry's threat to veto state funding for the Travis County District Attorney's office, which oversees a public corruption unit, unless District Attorney Rosemary Lehmberg resigned. Lehmberg had been arrested for drunk driving; one account said she had been convicted. She refused to resign, and Perry vetoed $7.5 million in funding.

Perry held a press conference on Saturday, calling the indictment an "abuse of power" and vowing to fight the charges. On Sunday he appeared on morning talk shows, citing support from David Axelrod, a former senior adviser to President Barack Obama. Axelrod had tweeted on Saturday: "Unless he was demonstrably trying to scrap the ethics unit for other than his stated reason, Perry indictment seems pretty sketchy." Perry quoted the tweet and said the reaction reflected that "this is way outside of the norm, this is not the way that we settle differences, political differences in this country."

Other political figures also questioned the indictment. Former Florida Gov. Jeb Bush expressed skepticism. Sen. Ted Cruz posted on Facebook that he was "proud to stand with Rick Perry" and called the indictment "highly suspect." Politico correspondent Ben White tweeted that it "seems quite perverse to indict a governor for exercising his clearly delineated constitutional authority." Other Democrats also defended Perry on Twitter.

Asked about trips to Iowa that fueled speculation about a 2016 presidential run, Perry said he was focused on the midterm elections and helping Republican Senate candidate Joni Ernst in Iowa. "I hope that I can be very helpful between now and the fourth of November so that Joni Ernst will go to the Senate," he said. "Between now and November the fourth is what I'm focused on, 2016 will take care of itself."

summary: United States Ambassador to South Korea Mark W. Lippert was attacked Thursday morning while giving a lecture in Seoul and taken to Yonsei University's Severance Hospital for treatment. South Korean police and journalists at the scene said the attacker was a knife-wielding man who stated he opposed joint U.S.-South Korean military exercises; Yonhap news agency reported the exact nature of Lippert's injuries was initially unclear, while YTN TV showed images of him bleeding from the head and wrist and said a man identified only by the surname Kim had been arrested. The State Department confirmed the attack; spokeswoman Marie Harf said Lippert's injuries were not life-threatening and that the embassy was coordinating with local law enforcement. Embassy minister-counselor for public affairs Robert W. Ogburn said Lippert was in stable condition after surgery for knife wounds to his face and left arm. Doctors at Severance Hospital said Lippert suffered a four-inch cut on the right side of his face requiring 80 stitches, as well as stab wounds to his left arm and hand that he appeared to have received while resisting the attack, and that it would take several months for him to recover full use of his injured fingers. Lippert wrote on Twitter, "Doing well & in great spirits! Will be back ASAP to advance US-ROK alliance." Lippert, 42, has served as ambassador since 2014; he previously was a foreign policy adviser to Barack Obama in the Senate, advised Obama's campaign and transition teams, served as chief of staff to Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel, and held the post of Assistant Secretary of Defense for Asian and Pacific Security Affairs. His wife gave birth in Seoul and the couple gave their son a Korean middle name.

summary: Former federal judge Stephen Larson, now in private practice, said he will file an amicus brief by early March supporting the government's effort to compel Apple to unlock an iPhone used by one of the attackers in the December 2015 San Bernardino shooting that killed 14 people. Larson said he represents victims and their families, as well as other employees affected by the attack, and is handling the matter without charge. He declined to specify the number of clients. According to one account, U.S. Attorney Eileen Decker asked Larson to represent the victims. The Justice Department and Apple both declined to comment on the planned filing. Apple chief executive Tim Cook said in a letter the previous week that the company had "worked hard to support the government's efforts to solve this horrible crime." The company initially assisted the FBI but is now contesting a court order to create new software that would bypass the phone's encryption. Cook has previously cited privacy protection and corporate values — including advocacy for gay rights and environmental initiatives — as guiding principles, telling one shareholder who questioned the return on such positions, "If you want me to do things only for R.O.I. reasons, you should get out of this stock."

summary: Senator Ted Cruz addressed the Republican National Convention in Cleveland and declined to endorse presidential nominee Donald Trump. Cruz told delegates, "To those listening, please, don't stay home in November. If you love our country, and love your children as much as I know you do, stand, and speak, and vote your conscience, vote for candidates up and down the ticket who you trust to defend our freedom and to be faithful to the Constitution." The speech drew jeers and boos from attendees. While Cruz was still onstage, Trump entered the convention floor to an enthusiastic reception; Cruz laughed awkwardly and left the stage. Afterward, Cruz's wife Heidi was escorted from the arena by security amid taunts from Trump supporters, including chants of "Goldman Sachs!" The following day, Cruz defended his refusal to endorse Trump, saying, "I am not in the habit of supporting people who attack my wife and attack my father. Neither he nor his campaign has taken back a word of what was said about my family." summary:
U.S. District Judge John Jones III ruled Tuesday that Pennsylvania's 1996 law banning recognition of same-sex marriage is unconstitutional. The decision came in a lawsuit filed by one widow, 11 same-sex couples, and one couple's teenage daughters, who argued the ban deprived them of legal and tax benefits. Following the ruling, hundreds of gay couples applied for marriage licenses in counties across the state.

On Wednesday, Governor Tom Corbett announced he would not appeal the decision. In a written statement, Corbett said he had thoroughly reviewed Judge Jones' opinion in the Whitewood case and concluded that, given the high legal threshold set by the judge, the case was extremely unlikely to succeed on appeal. He said the decision was made on the advice of his commonwealth legal team.

Corbett, a Republican who opposes same-sex marriage and has supported efforts to amend the state constitution to ban it, acknowledged that his decision went against his political beliefs and personal faith. "As a Roman Catholic, the traditional teaching of my faith has not wavered," he said. "I continue to maintain the belief that marriage is between one man and one woman. My duties as governor require that I follow the laws as interpreted by the courts and make a judgment as to the likelihood of a successful appeal."

With Corbett's decision not to appeal, same-sex marriage will remain legal in Pennsylvania without the threat of a higher court reinstating the ban. Pennsylvania becomes the 19th state to recognize same-sex marriages and was the last northeastern state to do so.

President Donald Trump on Monday told a crowd of workers in Ohio that the FBI had been "caught in the act" of spying on his campaign, referring to a House Republican memo detailing alleged surveillance abuses by the FBI and Justice Department. Press Secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said the administration was "undergoing the exact same process that we did with the previous memo, in which it will go through a full and thorough legal and national security review." The president has until the end of the week to decide whether to make the Democratic memo public. The dueling memos have become the focus of the House Intelligence Committee's probe into Russian meddling in the 2016 election, deepening partisan fights and setting up a standoff with congressional Democrats.

President Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed interest in purchasing Greenland from Denmark, according to people familiar with the deliberations who spoke to The Wall Street Journal. summary:
U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov began two days of meetings in Geneva on Thursday to negotiate a Russian proposal to inventory, isolate and eventually destroy Syria's chemical weapons stockpiles. President Barack Obama, speaking at a White House Cabinet meeting, said he was hopeful the talks could "yield a concrete result" and offer a potential path to avoid U.S. strikes against the Syrian government for a chemical attack on civilians last month that the United States blames on Syrian President Bashar Assad.

Syrian President Bashar Assad suggested Thursday that he would begin submitting data on his chemical weapons arsenal 30 days after signing an international chemical weapons ban. Kerry rejected the 30-day deadline at a news conference with Lavrov, saying, "This is not a game. It has to be real. It has to be comprehensive. It has to be verifiable. It has to be credible. It has to be timely and implemented in a timely fashion. Finally, there ought to be consequences if it doesn't take place." Kerry added, "There is nothing standard about this process," because Assad has used chemical weapons, and "The words of the Syrian regime in our judgment are simply not enough." Kerry cautioned that a U.S. military strike could occur if Assad does not agree to dismantle his chemical arsenal properly. Lavrov said the dismantling "will make unnecessary any strike against the Syrian Arab Republic."

On Saturday in Istanbul, Canadian Foreign Minister John Baird called Assad's 30-day offer "ridiculous and absurd," saying Assad should not be given extra time. Baird noted, "This is a man, who up until a week ago denied that they had any such weapons." Turkish Foreign Minister Ahmet Davutoglu, appearing with Baird, expressed skepticism that Assad was playing for time while continuing to commit atrocities.

President Barack Obama on Monday mourned what he called "yet another mass shooting" at the Washington Navy Yard in Southeast Washington, about 3 1/2 miles from the White House. Authorities reported a shooting rampage inside a building at the heavily secured installation. Obama said the victims were "courageous Americans" and "American patriots" who "know the dangers of serving abroad, but today they faced the unimaginable violence that they wouldn't have expected here at home." He called the attack a "cowardly act" and promised to make sure "whoever carried out this cowardly act is held responsible." Obama said he had been briefed by his team: "We still don't know all the facts, but we do know that several people have been shot, and some have been killed." He noted this was the second time a military installation had been targeted during his presidency, referencing the 2009 Fort Hood shootings in Texas where Army Maj. Nidal Hasan killed 13 people. Obama telephoned Navy Secretary Ray Mabus to express condolences and FBI Director James Comey to commend the agency's response. He ordered flags on federal property to be flown at half-staff through Friday, signing a proclamation that applies to all public grounds, military posts, naval vessels, and U.S. embassies and outposts overseas. Authorities gave differing accounts of the casualties and suspects. One account put the death toll at at least 12; another said 13 people were killed, including the gunman. Authorities also said shortly before Obama's speech that as many as two shooters remained on the loose and that one shooter had been killed. Another account described the attacker as a former Navy man who sprayed gunfire on office workers in the cafeteria and hallway. Obama was speaking on the fifth anniversary of the 2008 economic collapse about economic recovery progress when he addressed the shooting.

summary:
Republican Senator Mitch McConnell won a sixth term in Kentucky on Tuesday, defeating Democratic challenger Alison Lundergan Grimes. The victory positioned McConnell to become Senate majority leader if Republicans gained a net six seats to wrest control of the chamber from Democrats; thirty-six seats were contested. In South Carolina, Senators Tim Scott and Lindsey Graham also won reelection. Scott became the first African-American elected statewide in South Carolina since Reconstruction, winning the race to complete the final two years of the term of Jim DeMint, who resigned in 2012.

Less than 24 hours after the election, McConnell held a press conference at the University of Louisville. He called the Affordable Care Act a "huge legislative mistake" that is hurting states and the American people, and said, "If I had the ability, obviously I'd get rid of it." However, he signaled that with President Obama in the White House, Republicans would not be able to repeal the law wholesale. Instead, McConnell said the Republican Congress would challenge Obama's veto by targeting the least popular provisions, including a tax on medical device sales, an employer insurance mandate defining full-time work as 30 hours per week instead of 40, and the individual mandate requiring people to hold health insurance if they can afford it and do not qualify for an exemption. "I think we will be addressing that issue in a variety of different ways," he told reporters.

During the campaign, a McConnell mailer labeled "Election Violation" drew criticism. A tea party leader in the state, speaking to Louisville public radio political reporter Phillip Bailey, described it as a "deeply dishonest scare tactic" intended to discourage voters from supporting Grimes by suggesting that doing so would involve them in an illegal election scheme.

summary:
Michelle Nunn won the Democratic nomination for the U.S. Senate seat in Georgia on Tuesday, the Associated Press reported. Nunn, the daughter of former Senator Sam Nunn who held the seat for four terms, defeated three other Democrats: former state lawmaker Steen Miles, psychiatrist Branko Radulovacki, and ROTC instructor Todd Anthony Robinson. She will face the Republican nominee in the November general election to succeed retiring Republican Senator Saxby Chambliss.

The Republican primary featured seven candidates, including businessman David Perdue, Representatives Jack Kingston, Phil Gingrey, and Paul Broun, and former Secretary of State Karen Handel. The race was expected to head to a runoff on July 22. The Associated Press reported that the Republican contest remained too close to call as of Tuesday evening.

The Georgia race is among a dozen nationally watched contests as Republicans seek a Senate majority. Democrats view Georgia as a state where they could prevent Republicans from gaining the six seats needed for control. Nunn has been a formidable fundraiser. The Senate race has been expensive, with $10 million spent on television commercials through the end of last week, highlighting divisions within the Republican party. Perdue emphasized his business background, while Broun and Gingrey ran further to the right. Handel sought to capitalize on the backing of former Republican vice presidential candidate Sarah Palin, and Kingston had the support of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. The presence of three incumbent House members on the Senate ballot assured a large turnover in the state's House delegation come January.

summary: The House side of the U.S. Capitol was temporarily closed Thursday morning after a potential asbestos release during overnight abatement work. The incident began between 2:30 and 3 a.m., when workers were removing asbestos and something fell, according to one account. A hazardous-materials response team responded and collected samples to determine whether exposure occurred. The Architect of the Capitol's office said there was a potential release affecting the House side during ongoing abatement work. Engineers and certified industrial hygienists evaluated the scene and determined the building was safe to reopen, according to a release from the Architect's office, which is investigating with U.S. Capitol Police. One report said air tests came back negative. Analysts examined Kavanaugh's appellate record for clues to his potential impact. On climate change, he favored reining in the Environmental Protection Agency's efforts to cut carbon emissions, on the basis that Congress, not the courts, should set such rules. In a 2016 opinion, later overruled, he declared the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's structure "unconstitutional." On net neutrality, he argued last year that it violates internet service providers' First Amendment rights. The New York Times and Axios were reported to differ on the degree of his conservatism, but observers agreed he would be a reliable conservative vote for years to come.

summary: Federal prosecutors on Monday recommended that Roger Stone, a 67-year-old associate of President Donald Trump, serve between seven and nine years in prison after his November conviction on seven counts of obstructing Congress, lying to lawmakers and witness tampering. The charges stemmed from Stone's efforts to obtain inside information about WikiLeaks for the Trump campaign in 2016 and from former special counsel Robert Mueller's investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. In a court filing ahead of Stone's Feb. 20 sentencing before U.S. District Judge Amy Berman Jackson, an Obama appointee, the Justice Department said Stone had displayed contempt for the court and the rule of law and that sentencing guidelines called for 87 to 108 months. On Tuesday, Trump posted on Twitter that the recommendation was "very unfair" and a "miscarriage of justice," adding that "the real crimes were on the other side." Senior Justice Department officials subsequently walked back the sentencing recommendation, prompting all four federal prosecutors who tried the case to resign. Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton responded on Twitter, asking Trump whether he realized "intimidating judges is the behavior of failed-state fascists." House Speaker Nancy Pelosi accused Trump of political interference in the sentencing, said the Justice Department had "deeply damaged the rule of law" by withdrawing its recommendation, commended the prosecutors who stepped down, and called for an investigation of the department's actions. Stone was never charged with conspiring with Russia to influence the 2016 election.

President Donald Trump, in a Monday interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity, called The New York Times "a fake newspaper" and said "we don't even want that in the White House anymore. We're gonna probably terminate that and The Washington Post — they're fake." He also said the press had treated him worse than Abraham Lincoln. Another account described the cancellation as applying to White House subscriptions. In an Oval Office interview with the Times earlier this year, he said "everybody thinks The New York Times treats me terribly" and that he had not had a "good story" in the paper since becoming president. summary:
Former President Barack Obama said in a statement Tuesday that Joe Biden had "nailed" his decision to select Senator Kamala Harris as his running mate, adding that the choice underscored Biden's "own judgment and character." Obama, who has known Harris for years, said she is "more than prepared for the job" and has spent her career "defending our Constitution and defending folks who need a fair shake." He noted that Harris, 55, served as attorney general of California before her election to the Senate in 2016, and that if elected she would be the first Black and South Asian American vice president and the first female vice president in U.S. history. "Michelle and I couldn't be more thrilled for Kamala, Doug, Cole and Ella," Obama said, referring to her husband, Doug Emhoff, and stepchildren. "This is a good day for our country. Now let's go win this thing."

Susan Rice, who was reportedly on Biden's shortlist, told NBC News's Savannah Guthrie early Wednesday that Harris was a "great choice" and would "make a tremendous running mate for Joe Biden." Rice said she was "honored and humbled" to have been considered and would "do everything I possibly can to help Joe Biden become the next president of the United States and to help him succeed in governing in whatever form of fashion he wants." "I'm proud to serve him in any way he'd like," Rice added. She called Harris's status as the first woman of color on a major party ticket "so exciting" and "past time." "Black women are the backbone of the nation, not just the Democratic Party," Rice said. "I think it is energizing, it's exciting, it's historic." Rice also said she did not believe Harris was significantly to Biden's left and that the two were "very compatible" politically.

Biden said Wednesday that Black and brown girls who often feel "overlooked" in their communities are now full of hope after he tapped Harris. "Today — just maybe — they are seeing themselves for the first time in a new way," he said. Biden said he chose Harris because she can govern and had a "stellar record as attorney general of California." Biden and Harris are scheduled to deliver their first public remarks together Wednesday in Delaware.

NAACP President and CEO Benjamin Todd Jealous announced Sunday that he will step down at the end of the year. Jealous, 40, has led the organization since 2008, when he became its youngest-ever president at age 35. He submitted his resignation letter this week and will remain in the post through Dec. 31. In a written statement and an interview with USA Today, Jealous said he is leaving to spend more time with his wife and children and to teach at a university. He said he believes the organization is in a stronger position than when he took over, citing a push toward online and mobile organizing, a doubling of revenue, and growth in membership from 175,000 to 675,000 and in annual donors from 16,000 to more than 132,000. Jealous has scheduled a conference call with reporters for Monday morning to discuss the decision further. Other civil rights leaders responded with sadness and appreciation for his work stabilizing the group's finances. During his tenure, Jealous drew controversy for condemning the Tea Party movement as containing "racist elements" and for criticizing Agriculture Department official Shirley Sherrod after a misleadingly edited video surfaced; he later apologized for rushing to judgment.

summary: House Speaker Paul Ryan (R-Wis.) presided over the Capitol Christmas tree lighting ceremony on Wednesday and held a moment of silence for the victims of the mass shooting in San Bernardino, California. summary:
Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl arrived Sunday at the Landstuhl Regional Medical Center in Germany following his release on Saturday after nearly five years as a captive of the Taliban in Afghanistan. The hospital said Friday that Bergdahl remains in stable condition and is showing signs of improvement, including conversing with medical staff, becoming more engaged in his treatment plan, and resting better. While doctors say he is physically able to travel, he is not yet emotionally ready to reunite with his family. He remains without access to news media and is said to be unaware of criticism from members of Congress regarding the prisoner exchange — which involved five Taliban detainees transferred from Guantánamo Bay — and from members of his former platoon who have accused him of desertion. Bergdahl has received a letter from his sister but has not responded. He objects when staff address him as sergeant rather than private first class, the rank he held when he was captured after leaving a remote outpost in eastern Afghanistan. Medical officials are gathering details about his captivity to address medical and psychological wounds but have not yet focused on the circumstances of his departure and capture, and there is no schedule for doing so.

summary:
Former National Security Adviser Michael Flynn will invoke his Fifth Amendment protection against self-incrimination and not comply with a Senate Intelligence Committee subpoena for documents issued less than two weeks earlier as part of its investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election, the Associated Press reported. Flynn had previously sought immunity from "unfair prosecution" to cooperate. summary:
Former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Marie Yovanovitch testified before the House Intelligence Committee on Friday as part of the House Democrats' impeachment inquiry into President Donald Trump. In her opening statement, Yovanovitch said her dismissal as ambassador sent a message to "shady interests" and allowed people with corrupt intentions to take advantage of disarray in American policy in Ukraine. "If our chief representative is kneecapped, it limits our effectiveness to safeguard the vital national security interests of the United States," she said. "This is especially important now, when the international landscape is more complicated and more competitive than it has been since the dissolution of the Soviet Union. Our Ukraine policy has been thrown into disarray, and shady interests the world over have learned how little it takes to remove an American Ambassador who does not give them what they want."

As Yovanovitch testified, Trump posted criticisms of her on Twitter. He wrote that everywhere she went, things "turned bad," referencing her service in Somalia and Ukraine, and said the new Ukrainian president spoke unfavorably about her in their second phone call. Trump added, "It is a U.S. President's absolute right to appoint ambassadors."

House Intelligence Committee Chairman Adam Schiff accused Trump of witness intimidation, describing the tweet as "witness intimidation in real time by the president of the United States."

House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, in a preview clip of CBS' "Face the Nation" to air Sunday, said Trump had "made a mistake" with his Twitter attacks during the testimony. She attributed Trump's insults to "his own insecurity as an imposter" because "he knows full well that he's in that office way over his head." Pelosi said Trump knows Yovanovitch's strength and was "trying to undermine it," and added that even his most ardent supporters "have to honestly admit this is the wrong thing for the president to do." She stressed the significance of a president's words and said he "should not frivolously throw out insults."

President Barack Obama said Thursday he would like to eliminate the penny because it costs more to produce than its face value. "Any time we're spending money on something people aren't going to use, that's something that should change," he said. Asked why he had not acted, Obama replied, "I got to tell you, I don't know … It's one of those things where people get attached emotionally to the way things have been . . . The penny is something I need legislation for, and frankly given all the big issues, we're not able to get to it." He said he had asked Congress for authority to reorganize inefficient agencies but Congress had refused. The cost of producing a penny first exceeded its value in 2006 and now stands at over 2.4 cents per coin; the coin is 97.5 percent zinc and 2.5 percent copper. Changing the composition to cheaper metals is an option, though the nickel currently costs 11.18 cents to produce. Separately, Texas Republicans said Wednesday that Obama's emphasis on immigration reform in his State of the Union address had set back the effort. Rep. John Carter of Round Rock said, "He can't move the ball on immigration. … He's too divisive when it comes to Congress. If it's Obama's bill, it won't get the support it needs." Rep. Kevin Brady of The Woodlands added, "The president will invariably make it harder for both sides to come together because he sort of likes baiting Republicans on this. If he wanted to see true immigration reform, he'd lock himself in the Oval Office until Congress got it done." In a third matter, Obama warned of vulnerabilities in the air traffic control system and other networks. He touted an executive order intended to "strengthen our cyber defenses by increasing information sharing, and developing standards to protect our national security, our jobs, and our privacy," and said Congress must pass legislation to give the government greater capacity to secure networks and deter attacks.

The U.S. Capitol Police emailed all House staff cautioning lawmakers to take "reasonable and prudent precautions regarding their personal security." The email stated the suspect was in custody and that no further details on the motive or other victims were available at the time, according to Sgt. Kimberly Schneider, a Capitol Police spokeswoman.

Cantor said in his statement: "Our nation was shocked by the tragedy in Arizona earlier today. summary: Republican Rep. Jason Chaffetz of Utah, chairman of the House Oversight Committee, announced Wednesday on Instagram that he would undergo immediate foot surgery and miss three to four weeks of work, including a key vote on a spending bill to keep the government open. The surgery was to remove 14 screws and a metal plate inserted after he shattered several bones in his foot in a fall from a ladder at his home 12 years ago. "Almost 12 years ago, I shattered several bones in my foot which required 14 screws and a metal plate to repair," Chaffetz wrote. "Yes, I wish I could say I was cliff diving in Mexico but the truth is I fell off a ladder while repairing something in my garage." He said he was "sorry to miss the important work we are doing in Washington ... but medical emergencies are never convenient." A statement from University of Utah Health spokeswoman Suzanne Winchester said Chaffetz was admitted to University of Utah Hospital for surgery to resolve a serious complication from the previous injury, that the surgery was successful, and he was resting comfortably. Chaffetz, 50, announced last week he would not seek re-election in 2018. He has not announced future plans but has said he is considering private-sector jobs and is a possible candidate for Utah governor in 2020; one account said he had floated leaving Congress before the end of his term.

summary:
The Trump campaign sent a fundraising email featuring an image of a survivor of the shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, where 17 people were killed. The email, which CNN first reported, stated that "the nation has turned its attention to the senseless school shooting in Parkland, Florida" and that "President Trump is taking steps towards banning gun bump stocks and strengthening background checks for gun purchasers." It quoted Trump saying "making our schools and our children safer will be our top priority" and included a link to donate to the campaign. The same photograph had been shared on Trump's official Instagram the previous week. Trump and the first lady visited survivors in Florida on Friday, and Trump met with student survivors at the White House, where the students pushed for action to prevent further massacres.

During a listening session with students and parents affected by mass shootings, including some from Parkland, Trump proposed arming 20 percent of teaching staff at schools. He said Wednesday that a teacher adept at firearms "could very well end the attack very quickly" and suggested such teachers receive bonuses for the added responsibility. In a series of tweets Thursday, Trump denied he had ever suggested giving teachers guns, before arguing that "only the best" teachers — such as those with military experience — should be given guns. He argued a "sicko shooter" would not try to attack a school known for having armed teachers. Some teachers responded on Twitter opposing the idea.

Trump also said he would push for improvements to the federal background check system. The White House signaled support for the Fix NICS Act, a bill to address flaws in the national criminal background check database that has backing from both gun control advocates and the National Rifle Association but has not received a Senate vote.

NEA-NH President Tuttle called arming teachers "an abominable idea" and said the state's largest educators' union is convening a coalition of education associations, first responders, parent groups, and mental health professionals to offer answers to school gun violence. Lawmakers in several states, including Florida, are considering proposals to arm teachers.

summary: Mitt Romney campaigned in Ohio twelve days before the election, opening a two-day swing with a rally in Cincinnati where he framed the race as a "big choice" between his "big change" agenda and President Obama's "status quo path." Speaking for 24 minutes at a warehouse before a crowd of about 3,000, Romney used the phrase "big change" at least a half-dozen times, promising to balance the budget, restore Medicare, and turn the economy around. He cited poor-performing schools, rising debt projected to reach $20 trillion, and stubborn joblessness as evidence that "these challenges are big challenges." The Cincinnati stop was the first of three in Ohio that day, with additional events in Worthington and Defiance, followed by a rally with running mate Paul Ryan in Canton the next day. Both campaigns acknowledged the Ohio race had tightened this month, though Obama still led in most polls, in some cases within the margin of error. Separately, Romney's campaign postponed all three Sunday events in Virginia because of Hurricane Sandy, saying the move would ensure emergency resources would not be diverted; campaign offices across Virginia were collecting donations for storm relief. Romney would instead join Ryan at events in Ohio on Sunday.

summary:
Michael Brown, an unarmed 18-year-old black man, was shot and killed by a Ferguson police officer on Saturday afternoon near an apartment complex in Ferguson, Missouri, a predominantly black suburb of St. Louis. According to police, Brown pushed the officer into his car, a struggle ensued, and Brown reached for the officer's weapon before a shot was fired inside the car followed by additional shots. The St. Louis County Prosecuting Attorney's office confirmed Brown had no criminal record, with no prior misdemeanors or felonies. A preliminary autopsy performed Sunday by the St. Louis County Medical Examiner's office showed Brown died from gunshot wounds; an official autopsy was to be released later. Brown's body was turned over to his family on Wednesday. That evening, police used tear gas to disperse crowds that had gathered, and protests, some of which turned violent, continued in the area.

The hacker collective Anonymous became involved, calling the effort Operation Ferguson. Members carried out cyberattacks that crashed the city's web servers, forcing officials to communicate by text, and posted the names and address of the county police chief's family. On Thursday, Anonymous released what it said was the name of the officer involved. The St. Louis police said on Twitter that the name was incorrect and that the individual was not a police officer. The release prompted unusual dissent within Anonymous, with members accusing those who posted the information of producing faulty data and endangering one another by discussing methods openly online.

The family's attorney, Ben Crump, said funeral arrangements were on hold until a second autopsy could be performed. Crump said he was making a formal request to the Justice Department for a federal autopsy to ensure objectivity. U.S. Attorney General Eric Holder ordered a federal autopsy. Crump said the hope was that the funeral would take place by the weekend of August 23.

summary: During the third and final presidential debate on Wednesday night, Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump exchanged personal remarks on multiple occasions. Clinton asserted that at the previous debate, Trump had mocked the appearance of women who had accused him of sexual advances. Trump denied making those comments at that debate. A subsequent fact-check confirmed he did not say them at the debate itself but documented that he made such remarks in later speeches. In one speech, referring to a People magazine writer who had accused him, Trump said: "Take a look, you take a look. Look at her, look at her words. You tell me, what you think. I don't think so. I don't think so." In another, mocking Clinton's claim that he had "stalked" her onstage at the second debate, he said: "She walks in front of me, you know? And when she walked in front of me – believe me, I wasn't impressed." During the third debate, Clinton also criticized Trump for a history of misogynistic and insulting comments. Trump responded, "No one has more respect for women than I do." Later, while Clinton was answering a question — one account says it was about health care posed by Chris Wallace, another says it was about entitlement costs — Trump interjected, "Such a nasty woman." Post-debate, NBC anchor Lester Holt described the interjection as "a bizarre interjection," and anchor Savannah Guthrie said, "This is a candidate who has a deficit with women. It was so striking to see him actually go there." The fact-check also noted historical parallels: the Clintons had sought to dismiss the 1998 Monica Lewinsky allegations by mocking her appearance, and Clinton adviser James Carville had mocked accuser Paula Jones's working-class origins, saying, "Drag a hundred dollars through a trailer park and there's no telling what you'll find."

summary: Democrat Ralph Northam defeated Republican Ed Gillespie in Virginia's gubernatorial election on Tuesday, the first major loss for the GOP since Donald Trump's presidential victory. President Trump had supported Gillespie during the campaign, urging Virginians to vote for him via Twitter and a robocall in which he said Gillespie would 'help make America great again' and would 'totally turn around' what Trump called 'high crime and poor economic performance' in the state. After the race was called, Trump tweeted: 'Ed Gillespie worked hard but did not embrace me or what I stand for. Don't forget, Republicans won 4 out of 4 House seats, and with the economy doing record numbers, we will continue to win, even bigger than before!' Prince William County Board of Supervisors Chairman Corey Stewart, who nearly defeated Gillespie in the GOP primary running a Trump-inspired campaign, said Gillespie had rejected Trump, distanced himself from him, would not campaign with him, and would not retweet Trump's endorsement. Former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Steele criticized Trump for blaming Gillespie. Gillespie appeared hesitant to link himself with the White House; Politico reported campaign officials were concerned Trump's historically low approval numbers would mobilize Democrats if the president was more involved. This marked the second time in recent months Trump backed a losing candidate, following Alabama Senator Luther Strange's primary defeat.

President Donald Trump announced on Thursday that he would replace national security adviser H.R. McMaster with John Bolton, a former U.S. ambassador to the United Nations. Bolton will become Trump's third national security adviser, following Michael Flynn and McMaster. Trump wrote on Twitter that McMaster had done "an outstanding job & will always remain my friend." The White House said Bolton would assume the role on April 9. McMaster, a three-star Army general, had been appointed in 2017 after Flynn's dismissal. The change follows Trump's dismissal of Secretary of State Rex Tillerson last week and his replacement with CIA Director Mike Pompeo. The appointments of Bolton and Pompeo, both viewed as hard-liners on Iran and North Korea, were described by some observers as signaling a more confrontational foreign policy approach. Former NATO Supreme Allied Commander James Stavridis predicted that Bolton would advise Trump to take a hard-line position in upcoming talks with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, including an uncompromising demand that Pyongyang abandon its nuclear program entirely, and that tensions would increase. McMaster's departure had been anticipated for weeks amid reports of a strained relationship with the president. It also came after a White House leak revealed Trump had been advised in briefing documents not to congratulate Russian President Vladimir Putin on his re-election victory, but did so anyway.

summary: Indiana Governor Mike Pence, the Republican vice presidential nominee, made a series of public statements in early October 2016 addressing his running mate Donald Trump. On Thursday, October 6, Pence appeared on CNN's "New Day" and told Chris Cuomo that Trump's proposed Muslim ban was "not Donald Trump's position now," saying he and Trump "have been very, very clear about the issue of suspending immigration from countries that have been compromised by terrorism." Pence had called Trump's December 2015 proposal for a "total and complete shutdown of Muslims entering the United States" "offensive and unconstitutional," but by July said the refined policy to suspend immigration from "terror states" was the "right call." On Friday, October 7, after a 2005 video surfaced in which Trump made lewd comments about women, Pence released a statement saying: "As a husband and father, I was offended by the words and actions described by Donald Trump in the eleven-year-old video released yesterday. I do not condone his remarks and cannot defend them." He added he was "grateful that he has expressed remorse and apologized to the American people" and that "We pray for his family and look forward to the opportunity he has to show what is in his heart when he goes before the nation tomorrow night." Pence also declined to fill in for Trump at a Saturday campaign event in Wisconsin. On Sunday, October 9, after the second presidential debate, Pence tweeted: "Congrats to my running mate @realDonaldTrump on a big debate win! Proud to stand with you as we #MAGA." The Drudge Report debate poll showed Trump leading 90-10 twenty-five minutes after the debate. Trump campaign manager Kellyanne Conway also expressed enthusiasm about Trump's debate performance.

summary:
House Speaker John Boehner and President Barack Obama met at the White House on Sunday to discuss the fiscal cliff, a combination of tax increases and spending cuts scheduled to take effect in January unless Congress reaches a deficit-reduction agreement. According to aides to both leaders, the meeting produced a joint statement. The session followed a telephone conversation between the two men on Wednesday and discussions between their aides on Thursday. A White House aide said Obama also spoke with Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid and House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi on Friday. Boehner had said on Friday that there was "no progress" in the negotiations.

On the House floor, Boehner said the talks remained stalled because the White House had not presented a concrete plan. He stated, "The longer the White House slow-walks this process the closer our economy gets to the fiscal cliff." He described the Sunday meeting as "nice" but said it did not break the stalemate. Republicans have offered $800 billion in additional revenue from eliminating tax loopholes and deductions for high earners; Obama rejected that proposal and has insisted that negotiations cannot advance until Republicans agree to raise tax rates on the wealthy.

In prepared remarks to reporters, Boehner said the White House is resistant to cutting spending, which Republicans identify as the source of the deficit, and that Obama seeks far more in tax increases than in spending reductions. Pelosi, speaking after Boehner's floor remarks, said Obama deserves credit for spending cuts Congress enacted this year and for Medicare reductions in the health-care law. She said the objective now is to secure more revenue from tax increases on the wealthy and that Boehner will have to accept that, adding, "We've committed to the cuts, we've acted upon the entitlements."

summary: The White House announced on Sunday that President Obama will meet Ukrainian Prime Minister Arseniy Yatsenyuk at the White House on Wednesday. The White House said the meeting will focus on finding a peaceful resolution to Russia's ongoing military intervention in Crimea that would respect Ukrainian sovereignty and territorial integrity, and will also discuss international support for Ukraine's economic challenges and the importance of uniting the country ahead of May presidential elections. A referendum on whether Crimea should secede from Ukraine and join Russia is scheduled for next week. Russian troops are on the ground in Crimea; Russian President Vladimir Putin has denied responsibility for the standoff, arguing the troops are not official members of the Russian military. The United States and European officials have responded by issuing economic sanctions against Russia. Yatsenyuk became prime minister after former President Viktor Yanukovych left office following prolonged protests in Kiev and elsewhere. In Kiev on Sunday, tens of thousands rallied in Independence Square to mark the 200th anniversary of the birth of poet Taras Shevchenko; the gathering also served as a memorial for the more than 80 people who died there. Yatsenyuk told the crowd, "Our fathers and grandfathers have spilled their blood for this land... We won't budge a single centimeter from Ukrainian land. Let Russia and its president know this." One account reported that rival rallies turned violent in Crimea on Sunday.

summary:
Ben Carson met with Donald Trump at the Mar-a-Lago resort in Palm Beach, Florida, on Thursday morning for a breakfast meeting that lasted more than an hour. Carson, who had spoken by phone with Ted Cruz, Marco Rubio and John Kasich over the previous week, said none of the three had stood out and he was still unsure whether to endorse any candidate. Trump secured Carson's endorsement during the meeting, which took place in an ornate corner of the resort where original owner Marjorie Merriweather Post once took breakfast.

That evening, the 12th Republican debate of the campaign season was held at the University of Miami at 8:30 p.m. ET. The debate, hosted by CNN, Salem Media Group, The Washington Times and the Republican National Committee, featured Trump, Cruz, Rubio and John Kasich. Jake Tapper moderated, with Dana Bash, Hugh Hewitt and Stephen Dinan as questioners. It was broadcast live on CNN and streamed online without login requirements.

On Friday morning, Trump told reporters the party had held enough debates and said he was unaware of a scheduled March 21 debate in Salt Lake City, indicating he would not attend. He praised the Miami debate as more genteel than earlier encounters in which he faced attacks from Rubio and Cruz, saying it would be nice to finish with that one. The Republican field could shrink after the March 15 primaries in Florida and Ohio, though Cruz in particular was said to be eager for a one-on-one debate with Trump.

summary: The Senate Judiciary Committee on Thursday unanimously approved President Trump's nomination of Christopher Wray to serve as FBI director, sending the nomination to the full Senate for a confirmation vote. Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, an Iowa Republican, said the unanimous support was a strong indication of faith in Wray's abilities. Trump announced Wray's selection last month after firing FBI Director James Comey in May amid tensions over the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. During his confirmation hearing last week, Wray testified that he would conduct the job "without regard to any partisan political influence," adding, "I believe to my core that there's only one right way to do this job. And that is with strict independence. By the book. Playing it straight. Faithful to the Constitution." The committee vote followed a 50-minute interview Trump gave to The New York Times on Wednesday, dominated by the Russia investigation. In the interview, Trump criticized five key figures in the probe, including Attorney General Jeff Sessions and Special Counsel Robert S. Mueller, who was appointed after Sessions recused himself in March and Comey was fired in May. Democrats on the committee, who had sharply criticized Trump's dismissal of Comey, were largely supportive of Wray. Senator Dianne Feinstein quoted the Times article during the meeting, relaying Trump's description of a conversation with Comey about former national security adviser Michael Flynn: "He said I said 'hope' — 'I hope you can treat Flynn good' or something like that. I didn't say anything," Trump told the Times. "Even if I did, that's not — other people go a step further. I could have ended that whole thing just by saying — they say it can't be obstruction because you can say: It's ended. It's over. Period." Feinstein said she was "hopeful" Wray would be willing to push back against Trump, adding, "We need leaders with steel spines, not weak knees."

On Wednesday, a shooting occurred at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida. Law enforcement responded to reports of an active shooter at 5901 Pine Island Road. The Broward County Sheriff's Office advised the public to avoid the area and said it was working a developing incident. Coral Springs police told teachers and students to remain barricaded until reached by officers. Accounts differed on casualties: the sheriff's office was cited as saying there were multiple injuries; one report said several people were injured; a later account said 17 people were killed. One report identified the suspected shooter as a former student who was taken into custody. The incident was described as the 18th school shooting of 2018 by one tally, which also noted at least 11 shootings on school property since January 1 and roughly the 50th of the academic year. Researchers and gun control advocates said school shootings had occurred at a rate of about one a week since 2013. A former senior FBI official, Katherine W. Schweit, said, "We have absolutely become numb to these kinds of shootings, and I think that will continue." A vigil followed the shooting, where attendees chanted "no more guns." U.S. Representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz urged political engagement, saying, "We must hold other people's elected officials accountable. We must make sure that they hear us... We will help lead you to help other communities elect people who will do the right thing, who will make sure no one's families ever have to go through this again." Former Representative Gabrielle Giffords called on Congress to pass gun control legislation, adding, "if Congress doesn't act, American voters must." Earlier, on Tuesday, a shooting in Benton, Kentucky, left two 15-year-old students dead and 18 injured, described as the worst so far in 2018.

summary: First lady Melania Trump issued her first public statement Wednesday since undergoing an embolization procedure Monday at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center to treat a benign kidney condition. In a Twitter post, she wrote: "A sincere thank you to Walter Reed Medical Unit and to all who have send good wishes and prayers! I am feeling great and look forward to getting back home at the White House soon." The first lady's communications director, Stephanie Grisham, said Monday the procedure was successful with no complications and that Trump would likely remain at the hospital for the rest of the week. President Donald Trump visited his wife at the Maryland hospital for the third consecutive day Wednesday, arriving by helicopter shortly after 4:30 p.m. and staying nearly two hours, according to White House pool reports. He had also visited on Monday and Tuesday. On Tuesday, the president told reporters at the Capitol that the first lady was "doing really, really well." On Monday he tweeted: "Successful procedure, she is in good spirits. Thank you to all of the well-wishers!" During a Capitol visit Wednesday, the president joked that the first lady should be the one visiting him in the hospital, not the other way around.

President Donald Trump held an indoor campaign rally at a manufacturing facility in Henderson, Nevada. The Trump campaign promoted the event with a statement saying: "If you can join tens of thousands of people protesting in the streets, gamble in a casino, or burn down small businesses in riots, you can gather peacefully under the 1st Amendment to hear from the President of the United States." Former White House press secretary Ari Fleischer criticized the decision as "irresponsible" and a "bad idea." Other journalists and political pundits from left and right also criticized the event. Nevada Gov. Steve Sisolak said: "Tonight, President Donald Trump is taking reckless and selfish actions that are putting countless lives in danger here in Nevada. The President appears to have forgotten that this country is still in the middle of a global pandemic." Reports indicated masks were worn by "some" or "very few" attendees, who also appeared not to practice social distancing. Trump told a Las Vegas Review-Journal reporter: "I'm on a stage and it's very far away. And so I'm not at all concerned." One attendee said: "if I catch Covid, that's the consequences of my actions, so I'm willing to take that risk and have a good time today." During the rally, a protester briefly interrupted Trump, who asked: "Get him out of here, would you?" The crowd chanted "U.S.A.!" and then "All lives matter!" as the president looked on. He did not acknowledge the chant, which soon returned to "U.S.A." before he continued speaking. Trump also attacked Gov. Sisolak at length in his Review-Journal interview regarding rally locations. Former Republican presidential candidate Herman Cain died just over a month after attending Trump's previous indoor rally in Tulsa, where a surge in COVID-19 cases was reported three weeks later. Nevada had an 8.5% positive test rate at the time.

summary:
President Barack Obama released his fiscal 2014 budget proposal on Wednesday, a $3.77 trillion plan the White House said would shrink federal deficits and expand the economy. The administration said the budget would replace $1.2 trillion in automatic spending cuts known as the sequester with $1.8 trillion in deficit-reduction measures over ten years. The plan included reductions in Social Security and Medicare spending, achieved partly through adopting the chained Consumer Price Index, which would also affect veterans' disability benefits. It proposed tax increases primarily on high-income earners and a 94-cent-per-pack increase in the cigarette tax to fund expanded preschool programs. The budget also called for $50 billion in public works spending.

The White House said every new initiative was fully paid for and would not add "a single dime to the deficit." A House and Senate Republican Budget Committee analysis disputed this, finding the plan achieved $119 billion in net deficit reduction rather than $1.8 trillion. The GOP analysis projected the budget would generate $8.2 trillion in new debt, raising total U.S. debt to $25.4 trillion over the decade, an increase of $60,980 per household. Republicans said the proposal would raise taxes by $1.1 trillion on top of existing increases from the Affordable Care Act and prior legislation. Speaker John Boehner said the budget resembled Obama's previous two proposals, both unanimously rejected by the Senate, and argued the president had not addressed spending growth. One account reported the deficit-reduction package included $580 billion in revenue increases; the Republican analysis cited a higher tax figure. summary:

His supporters held demonstrations from Atlanta to Philadelphia and outside the Michigan Capitol in Lansing, where the mood was described as grim, and outside the elections department in North Las Vegas, where an armed supporter raised a fist as Trump flags flew. summary: McDonald's Corporation announced on June 9 the hiring of Robert Gibbs as executive vice president and global chief communications officer and Silvia Lagnado as executive vice president and global chief marketing officer. Gibbs served as White House press secretary during President Barack Obama's first term, as communications director during Obama's Senate tenure and 2008 campaign, and as an adviser to the 2012 re-election campaign; he left the White House in 2011 and co-founded The Incite Agency, a strategic communications advisory firm, in 2013. summary:
President Donald Trump on Wednesday tweeted a warning to Russia that U.S. missiles "will be coming" to Syria, writing: "Get ready Russia, because they will be coming, nice and new and 'smart!' You shouldn't be partners with a Gas Killing Animal who kills his people and enjoys it!" The tweet followed new reports of a chemical weapons attack by Syrian President Bashar Assad's government. Russia vowed to shoot down any missiles fired at Syria.

The Wednesday tweet drew criticism that Trump had telegraphed a military strike to the Russian-backed Assad regime, undercutting his stated practice of not announcing military decisions in advance — a practice he had frequently criticized former President Barack Obama for not following.

On Thursday morning, Trump rejected that criticism in a tweet: "Never said when an attack on Syria would take place. Could be very soon or not so soon at all! In any event, the United States, under my Administration, has done a great job of ridding the region of ISIS. Where is our 'Thank you America?'"

Also on Wednesday, comedian Trevor Noah, host of "The Daily Show," criticized the president's choice of words in the missile threat. Noah said Trump sounded more like a matchmaker than a world leader, likening the tweet to a blind-date offer: "It's like he's saying to the Russians, 'I know you don't like blind dates but these missiles they're really nice, really smart. Just come, no pressure. It's just a launch.'"

Last spring, Trump ordered missile strikes against Syria after photographs surfaced showing children killed or severely injured by gas agents. The Assad regime and Russia have denied any use of chemical weapons.

summary: President Obama's re-election campaign raised $114 million in August, narrowly exceeding the $111 million reported by Mitt Romney's campaign and ending a three-month streak in which the Republican nominee had outpaced the incumbent. In July, Romney collected $101 million to Obama's $75 million; in June, $106 million to $71 million; in May, $77 million to $60 million. The August total marked the first time in the 2012 cycle that Obama and the Democrats surpassed $100 million in a single month. The Obama campaign said it received contributions from 1.1 million new donors in August and that 98 percent of its donations were for $250 or less; the Romney campaign said 94 percent of its donations were at that level. Romney's campaign reported $168.5 million cash on hand; Obama's did not release an on-hand figure. The Romney campaign issued a memo on Monday describing any post-convention polling gain for Obama as a "sugar high" that would not last. A CNN/ORC International poll conducted after the conventions showed Obama leading 52 percent to 46 percent, within the survey's margin of sampling error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. Both campaigns said readings immediately after the conventions can be ephemeral and that the race was likely to remain competitive through Election Day.

summary: British Prime Minister David Cameron recalled Parliament to debate military options against Syria and said the country was considering a proportionate response to a chemical weapons attack he described as absolutely abhorrent. Cameron's spokesman said British armed forces were making contingency plans, that a military response was on the table but not yet committed, and that any response would be taken under a strict international framework.
