Parliament was set to vote on whether Britain would wait for United Nations inspectors to rule before taking military action; the inspectors were supposed to wrap up their investigation and leave Syria by Saturday. President Obama said the White House believed Assad was responsible for attacking rebel forces and civilians in the Damascus area with poison gas, and that the United States did not believe the opposition possessed chemical weapons of that sort. summary:
President Donald Trump spoke by telephone with South Korean President Moon Jae-in on Wednesday, and the White House said Trump expressed openness to talks between the United States and North Korea "at the appropriate time, under the right circumstances" while both leaders stressed the importance of continuing the maximum pressure campaign against North Korea. The call followed the first high-level talks between the two Koreas in two years, in which North Korea agreed to send a delegation to the Olympic Games and both sides agreed to hold talks on reducing border tensions. Moon said he was open to meeting Kim Jong Un to resolve the nuclear standoff but that the success of such a summit must be guaranteed beforehand.

On Saturday at Camp David in Thurmont, Maryland, Trump told reporters he would be open to speaking with Kim Jong Un, though not without preconditions. "Sure. I always believe in talking," Trump said. "If something can happen and something can come out of those talks, that would be a great thing for all of humanity." He added that Kim "knows I'm not messing around" and reiterated that the U.S. stance against North Korea's nuclear ambitions is "very firm." Trump had previously dismissed the notion that the nuclear standoff could be resolved through direct talks, even as top Cabinet officials stressed the need for diplomacy.

Also on Saturday at Camp David, Trump met with Republican House and Senate leaders, top White House aides, and select Cabinet members to discuss the 2018 agenda, describing the sessions as "perhaps transformative in certain ways." He told reporters he was done campaigning for insurgents challenging incumbent Republicans in primaries, saying after a stinging loss in Alabama — where he had supported Roy Moore after the primary, and Moore's defeat handed Democrats a Senate seat — "I don't see that happening." Trump said he planned a robust midterm campaign schedule supporting incumbents and "anybody else that has my kind of thinking."

summary: The House Oversight and Government Reform Committee announced Friday that a forthcoming report by the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration will detail what the committee called "excessive spending" by the Internal Revenue Service on conferences. The committee scheduled a hearing for Thursday to examine the audit. The same inspector general previously confirmed accusations that the IRS tax-exempt unit had unfairly targeted certain groups seeking tax-exempt status. Committee Chairman Rep. Darrell Issa (R-CA) stated that the American people expect tax dollars to be used responsibly, "not for financing lavish hotel suites and entertainment for government employees," and said the committee would investigate "abuses of public trust and an IRS culture that shuns accountability." The hearing will focus on a 2010 IRS conference. Acting IRS Commissioner Danny Werfel described that conference as "an unfortunate vestige from a prior era," acknowledged there were legitimate reasons for it, but said "many of the expenses associated with it were inappropriate and should not have occurred," adding that cutting such excesses has been a priority. The House Ways and Means Committee also planned an IRS hearing for Tuesday. The White House said President Barack Obama is concerned about excessive spending by the IRS and other agencies on conferences and travel. White House spokesman Jay Carney said Obama has taken action to reduce spending and installed new IRS leadership after the agency acknowledged unfairly targeting conservative groups. An inspector general's report set for release Tuesday is expected to state the IRS spent about $50 million on at least 220 conferences for employees between 2010 and 2012. Eastwood spoke before Mitt Romney's formal acceptance speech, following an introduction by Senator Marco Rubio, and criticized Obama for failing to deliver on promises. President Obama responded on Friday when his campaign tweeted a photograph of him sitting in a chair marked "the president" with the caption "This seat's taken." In an interview with USA Today released Sunday, Obama called himself a "huge Clint Eastwood fan" and described the Academy Award winner as "a great actor, and an even better director." Asked whether he was offended by the performance, Obama said, "if you're easily offended, you should probably choose another profession." Ann Romney appeared on several network programs Friday morning, including CBS News, ABC's "Good Morning America," and NBC's "Today" show. She said she wished more people had seen a biographical video about her husband that aired earlier, telling CBS, "Yes, I do wish more people had seen those touching moments." Of Eastwood, she said, "He's a unique guy and he did a unique thing last night … I didn't know it was coming." She added that she doubted anyone could have planned what Eastwood would do on stage and said, "We were just thrilled, frankly I was thrilled, for his support."

President Obama traveled to Boston on Thursday, three days after twin bombings near the finish line of the Boston Marathon, to deliver remarks at an interfaith memorial service at the Cathedral of the Holy Cross. First Lady Michelle Obama also attended. The White House announced the visit Wednesday. Massachusetts Gov. Deval Patrick invited former Gov. Mitt Romney, who was joined by former governors Michael Dukakis and William Weld. The bombings on Monday killed three people, including an 8-year-old boy, and wounded more than 170. Hours after the explosions Obama vowed that those responsible would be brought to justice. In remarks on Tuesday he called the bombings an act of terrorism but said investigators did not yet know who carried them out, adding that the American people refuse to be terrorized. The Thursday service opened with Obama greeting the city and quoting scripture: "Run with endurance the race that is set before us." He described the morning of the race, the crowds, and the city's character. The trip marked the fourth time Obama had traveled to a city reeling from mass violence; the previous visit was to Newtown, Connecticut, after the school shooting in December.

summary: Vice President Joe Biden spoke Tuesday at a Democratic National Committee reception for Jewish American Heritage Month in Washington. Biden said Jewish culture and Jewish values "are such an essential part of who we are," and added, "Jewish heritage has shaped who we are – all of us, us, me – as much or more than any other factor in the last 223 years. And that's a fact." He credited Jewish leaders in media and entertainment with influencing American attitudes toward gay marriage, citing the sitcom "Will and Grace" and social media. "I bet you 85 percent of those changes, whether it's in Hollywood or social media are a consequence of Jewish leaders in the industry," he said. "The influence is immense, the influence is immense. And, I might add, it is all to the good." Biden also praised Jewish contributions to science, immigration reform, the civil-rights movement, the arts, the law and feminism, saying, "I think you vastly underestimate the impact you've had on the development of this nation. We're a great country because of the contributions and most importantly because of Jewish heritage and the values you brought." New York Magazine's Jonathan Chait described the praise as so profuse that white supremacists were citing the speech as evidence of a secret Jewish conspiracy.

Sanders named former CIA Director John Brennan and former FBI Director James Comey among those under review, and former Director of National Intelligence James Clapper said he was also among the officials named. China declared a new air defense identification zone over the East China Sea last week, requiring all aircraft entering the zone to notify Chinese authorities beforehand and warning of unspecified defensive measures against non-compliance. The zone covers the Diaoyutai and Senkaku islands, a frequent flashpoint between China and U.S. allies in the Pacific, and had previously been considered international airspace. The United States said it would not honor the zone and rejected China's unilateral declaration. The Pentagon vowed not to comply with the restrictions, saying the zone would inflame regional tensions, and U.S. military aircraft, including bombers, flew into the zone without notification. China scrambled fighter jets to enforce the zone, according to one account. At the same time, the State Department advised U.S. commercial air carriers to comply with China's notification requirements; spokeswoman Jen Psaki said the U.S. remains deeply concerned about the declared zone but issued the guidance to civilian airlines. Administration officials said the decision was made in part because of concern about an unintended confrontation. The guidance could be interpreted in the region as a concession. The United States has been conducting intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance operations and large-scale training missions with allies in the area, and since August 2013 has flown unmanned surveillance missions over the island chains under a defense security agreement with Japan agreed to by then-Defense Secretary Leon Panetta and Japanese Defense Minister Satoshi Morimoto.

President Donald Trump delivered his first Oval Office address Tuesday night, arguing that a security and humanitarian crisis at the U.S.-Mexico border required Congress to approve his immigration proposal, including funding for a border barrier. He called the situation a "crisis of the heart and the crisis of the soul." Major television networks — ABC, CBS, NBC, CNN, Fox broadcasting, Fox News Channel, Fox Business Network and MSNBC — aired both the address and the Democratic response. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer delivered the rebuttal, standing side by side. They said the partial government shutdown must end before border funding talks continue and accused Trump of spreading misinformation. Social media reaction focused on the serious tone of their remarks, with many users comparing the pair to disappointed parents, the American Gothic painting, a law-firm commercial or a hostage video. The following day, Pelosi and Schumer held a media availability with furloughed federal workers to discuss the shutdown's effects. A nationwide Reuters/Ipsos poll released Tuesday found Americans increasingly blaming Trump for the shutdown, which had closed about a quarter of the federal government and left about 800,000 federal workers without paychecks. The shutdown entered its third week.

summary:
President Barack Obama said wildfires in the western United States are worsening in large part due to climate change, citing a consistent escalation in the severity and length of the wildfire season driven by higher temperatures and diminished water resources. summary:
Edward Snowden, a former National Security Agency contractor and Booz Allen Hamilton employee, was charged this month with three counts of espionage and theft of government property for leaking classified information to The Guardian and The Washington Post revealing NSA surveillance of millions of domestic phone calls and major websites. He faces up to 30 years in prison.

U.S. officials requested his extradition from Hong Kong. National Security Adviser Tom Donilon said Hong Kong had been "a historically good partner of the United States in law enforcement matters, and we expect them to comply with the treaty in this case." Hong Kong denied the request, telling the U.S. Department of Justice it did not fulfill legal requirements and questioning U.S. spying on Hong Kong citizens. White House press secretary Jay Carney said: "We are just not buying that this was a technical decision by a Hong Kong immigration official."

The United States also asked Russia to expel Snowden. National Security Council spokesperson Caitlin Hayden said the U.S. expects "the Russian government to look at all options available to expel Mr. Snowden back to the US to face justice for the crimes with which he is charged." State Department spokesperson Jen Psaki said persons wanted on felony charges "should not be allowed to proceed in any further international travel, other than is necessary to return him to the United States."

According to people familiar with the situation, the Chinese government made the final decision to allow Snowden to leave Hong Kong on Sunday, a move Beijing believed resolved a diplomatic problem while gaining a publicity windfall. Hong Kong authorities have insisted their judicial process remained independent, but observers said foreign policy is the domain of the Chinese government. Analysts said Snowden's departure addressed two Chinese concerns: avoiding a long legal wrangle that could ensnare U.S.-China relations, and a Chinese public that widely regards Snowden as a hero. The extradition battle could take months or years, and Snowden can seek to avoid it by claiming political persecution and requesting asylum.

summary:
Libyan Prime Minister Ali Zeidan was kidnapped from a Tripoli hotel where he lives under tight security, held for six hours, and freed after a small gunfight, Reuters reported Thursday. Rebel gunmen said they took Zeidan in retaliation for a U.S. raid over the weekend that captured Abu Anas al-Libi, a top terror suspect wanted for his role in the 1998 U.S. Embassy bombings in Kenya and Tanzania. The rebels acted after Secretary of State John Kerry said the Libyan government had a role in helping the United States capture al-Libi.

Al-Libi was captured Saturday in Libya and is being held on a U.S. Navy ship under the laws of war, two law enforcement officials said. He has not been read his Miranda rights. A team of U.S. investigators from the military, intelligence agencies and the Justice Department has been deployed to question him. It was unclear when he would be brought to the United States to face charges. A federal judge ruled in 2010 that the government could prosecute a terror suspect in New York despite holding him for five years in custody because the government has the authority to do so during wartime.

At a Wednesday press conference, President Barack Obama said al-Libi had been indicted by a federal court and needed to "be brought to justice." "We know that Mr. al-Libi planned and helped execute plots that killed hundreds of people, a whole lot of Americans," Obama said. "And we have strong evidence of that. And he will be brought to justice." Some civil rights groups have questioned the seizure and interrogation of al-Libi.

Republican Sens. Lindsey Graham, Kelly Ayotte and Saxby Chambliss said al-Libi should be sent to Guantanamo Bay, arguing intelligence officials need far more than a couple of months at sea to sufficiently question him. Graham accused Obama of making a political choice not to use Guantanamo, a prison the president has vowed to close. Democratic Rep. Adam Schiff backed civilian prosecution.

November 22, 2013 marked the 50th anniversary of the assassination of President John F. Kennedy. President Barack Obama ordered flags at the Capitol and all government buildings lowered to half-staff for the day. In a presidential proclamation released Thursday, Obama said the anniversary is a day to honor Kennedy's memory and "celebrate his enduring imprint on American history," adding that Kennedy's vision for the United States and the world lives "in the generations he inspired." Earlier in the week, Obama visited Kennedy's grave at Arlington National Cemetery. On Friday, the president was scheduled to meet with representatives of the Peace Corps, which Kennedy established. Live ceremonies at Dealey Plaza in Dallas began at 12:30 p.m. Eastern time.

Members of Congress reflected on Kennedy's legacy and their recollections of the day of the assassination. Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid posted a photograph of a 1961 letter he received from Kennedy thanking campaign supporters. Several lawmakers said they were in school when they heard the news. Senator Jay Rockefeller, who was working at the State Department in 1963, told The Hill he was in a taxi when he learned of the shooting; the driver pulled over and they listened to the radio together. House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi shared a link to the commencement address Kennedy delivered at Trinity College, her alma mater, in 1958. Pelosi graduated in 1962. In that speech, Kennedy spoke of the public's "disdain" for politics and urged graduates: "I would urge therefore that each of you, regardless of your chosen occupation, consider entering the field of politics at some stage in your career."

summary:
Russia carried out its first airstrikes in Syria on Wednesday, with the Russian defense ministry reporting 20 strikes. summary:
British Prime Minister David Cameron recalled Parliament on Tuesday to debate a military response to a chemical weapons attack in the Damascus suburbs the previous week. His spokesman said armed forces were making contingency plans for a proportionate response under a strict international framework and that Cameron would consult world leaders to coordinate any action. The defeat meant the United States would proceed without its closest security and intelligence ally; some observers noted France might provide European military and political cover for any U.S.-led action.

summary: President Trump reportedly attempted to fire Special Counsel Robert Mueller in December after news reports that Mueller had subpoenaed Deutsche Bank for records related to Trump's finances. Separately, FBI agents raided the office and hotel room of Michael Cohen, Trump's personal attorney, pursuant to a search warrant obtained by federal prosecutors in Manhattan based partly on a referral from Mueller. The Washington Post reported Cohen is under investigation for possible bank fraud, wire fraud, and campaign finance violations. Trump reacted strongly, telling reporters the raid was "a real disgrace," "an attack on our country," and "an attack on what we all stand for." summary:
President Donald Trump met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Singapore on Tuesday for the first face-to-face meeting between a sitting U.S. president and a North Korean premier. During a press conference afterward that lasted more than an hour before his departure on Air Force One, Trump said he had shown Kim a video depicting a potential economic future for North Korea if it denuclearized and opened to the world. "That was a version of what could happen and take place," Trump said. He also said he had pointed out North Korea's "great beaches" as locations for condos and hotels. "You could have the best hotels in the world," Trump said. "Think of it from the real estate perspective."

Trump announced he would suspend joint military exercises with South Korea, removing a sticking point for Pyongyang, which has called the drills a pretext for a strike on the North. He said he expects Kim to work "very quickly" to dismantle the nuclear arsenal and described a "special bond" between the two leaders. "I think our whole relationship with North Korea and the Korean peninsula is going to be a very different situation than it has in the past," Trump said. "We've developed a very special bond."

Trump said he trusts Kim Jong Un. "I may be wrong, I mean I may stand before you in six months and say, 'Hey I was wrong,'" he said, adding, "I don't know that I'll ever admit that, but I'll find some kind of an excuse."

The timing of a formal order to cease the exercises was unclear. A spokesman for U.S. Forces Korea said directions to halt the drills had not been received. "In coordination with our ROK partners, we will continue with our current military posture until we receive updated guidance from the Department of Defense (DoD) and/or Indo-Pacific Command (INDOPACOM)," the spokesman said, according to South Korea's Yonhap News Agency. South Korea said it would seek the "precise meaning" of Trump's plan.

summary:
The United Nations Security Council on Friday adopted a resolution demanding an end to Israeli settlement building in occupied territories. The measure passed 14 to 0, with the United States abstaining. Ambassador Samantha Power raised her hand as the lone abstention, and applause broke out in the council chambers. The United States had the power to veto the resolution but declined to do so despite pressure from President-elect Donald Trump, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and U.S. lawmakers. The Obama administration's abstention broke a longstanding U.S. policy of shielding Israel from United Nations action describing the settlements as illegal. The administration's decision reflected accumulated frustration over Israeli settlements, though the resolution is not expected to have practical impact on the ground.

Trump, in a statement Thursday, said: "As the United States has long maintained, peace between the Israelis and the Palestinians will only come through direct negotiations between the parties, and not through the imposition of terms by the United Nations." He added: "This puts Israel in a very poor negotiating position and is extremely unfair to all Israelis." About an hour after the vote, Trump tweeted a warning that "things will be different" soon. Power said: "One cannot simultaneously champion expanding Israeli settlements and champion a viable two-state solution that would end the conflict. One has to make a choice between settlements and separation."

Israel's ambassador, Danny Danon, denounced the measure and told council members: "Would you ban the French from building in Paris?" Unnamed Israeli officials said Saturday evening that the U.S. failure to veto was the "last sting of President Obama" that exposed his "true face," adding: "Now it's easier to understand what we dealt with the past eight years." Netanyahu thanked Trump for his promise of support at the international body after he takes office.

summary: President Donald Trump held a post-midterm-election news conference at the White House on Wednesday. During the session, Trump called on CNN correspondent Jim Acosta, who questioned the president's use of the word "invasion" to describe a Central American migrant caravan. After a back-and-forth, Trump said, "Honestly, I think you should let me run the country, you run CNN, and if you did it well, your ratings would be much better. Okay, that's enough." Acosta attempted to ask another question, and a White House aide tried to take the microphone from his hand. Acosta said, "Pardon me, ma'am," and retained the microphone to ask about the Russia investigation. Trump then said: "I will tell you what, CNN should be ashamed of itself having you working for them--you are a rude, terrible person, you shouldn't be working for CNN. You're a very rude person, the way you treat Sarah Huckabee is horrible, and the way you treat other people are horrible, you shouldn't treat people that way." Trump moved to another reporter, but Acosta stood and asked another question. Trump said, "Okay, just sit down, please. When you report fake news, which CNN does, a lot, you are the enemy of the people." During the same conference, Trump told other journalists to sit down and accused a PBS reporter of posing a racist question when she asked about white nationalists. He blamed the press for divisiveness in politics. CNN responded that Trump's attacks on the press had gone too far, stating that while the president does not respect a free press, he has a constitutional responsibility to protect it. Also on Wednesday, the Trump administration revoked Acosta's White House press credentials. The revocation contradicted a statement Trump made in June 2016, when he was the presumptive Republican nominee. In a telephone interview with CNN at the time, Trump said he would not ban reporters from White House briefings if he became president. "It's a different thing," Trump said then. "In my case, I'm a person running for office. I rent these large arenas [...] so I have an option. When I'm representing the United States, I wouldn't do that. But I would let people know if somebody's untruthful."

President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un began their second nuclear summit in Hanoi, Vietnam, on Wednesday with a roughly 20-minute one-on-one meeting attended only by interpreters, followed by a dinner at the Metropole Hotel. Trump described their relationship as a "very special relationship" and said he hoped "a lot of things are going be to solved." Kim, according to a translator, said they exchanged "very interesting dialogue," to which Trump replied, "Boy if you could have heard that dialogue, what you would pay for that dialogue." Trump appeared jovial at the dinner, joking with reporters. The leaders were expected to hold more substantive talks on Thursday. Separately, former NBA player Dennis Rodman shared a letter he wrote to Trump ahead of the summit, calling himself Trump's "Ambassador of Goodwill to North Korea" and predicting Trump was "on the cusp of a big, beautiful deal" that would make him "the front runner for a Nobel Peace Prize without question." Eric Trump appeared to appreciate Rodman's letter.

summary:
The federal government shut down on Oct. 1 after Congress failed to pass a spending bill. Approximately 800,000 workers were furloughed and numerous government services closed. The impasse centered on Republican demands to include restrictions on the Affordable Care Act, which became law in 2010 and was upheld by the Supreme Court in June 2012, in the continuing resolution.

He also told reporters that the debate had shifted beyond defunding the health law to a matter of Republican "dignity" and leverage in upcoming debt-ceiling negotiations.

President Barack Obama and Senate Democrats criticized Stutzman's remarks on Thursday. Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-Nev.) said, "If I disrespected Marlin Stutzman, I'm sorry," and Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) offered to engage in a "group hug" with the congressman. Sen. On Thursday, Stutzman released a statement walking back his comments: "Yesterday, I carelessly misrepresented the ongoing budget debate and Speaker Boehner's work on behalf of the American people. Despite my remarks, it's clear that the American people want both parties to come to the table to reopen the government, tackle this nation's debt crisis, and stop Obamacare's pain."

Democrats sought a vote on a "clean" continuing resolution to fund the government while budget negotiations continued. Most if not all Democrats supported the measure, and enough Republicans had publicly signaled support to pass it, but the House Republican leadership did not allow the vote.

summary:
Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif and U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry offered conflicting accounts of why nuclear talks in Geneva stalled over the weekend of Thursday 6 p.m. to Saturday 5:45 p.m., with the next round of P5+1 negotiations slated to reconvene Nov. 20.

Zarif blamed Western powers on Tuesday, responding to Kerry's Monday remarks in Abu Dhabi. "Mr. secretary, was it Iran that gutted over half of U.S. draft Thursday night? And publicly commented against it Friday morning?" Zarif tweeted. "No amount of spinning can change what happened within P5+1 in Geneva from 6 P.M. Thursday to 5:45 P.M. Saturday. But it can further erode confidence," he continued. "We are committed to constructive engagement. Interaction on equal footing key to achieve shared objectives."

Mohammad Ali Shabani, a political analyst with close ties to Zarif, said: "It's the United States which should get their partners on board, not Iran." He added: "From the information that is available, what was on the table was an American proposal. It was France that ripped into it, not Iran." Analysts said the message was tailored to a domestic audience and that Zarif had little choice but to take this line.

Kerry gave a different version. "[We were] unified on Saturday when we presented a proposal to the Iranians, and the French signed off on it, we signed off on it, and everybody agreed it was a fair proposal. There was unity, but Iran couldn't take it at that particular moment, they weren't able to accept that particular thing," he said. Iran reportedly rejected the deal because it excluded language that would give Iran the green light to enrich.

On Friday, Kerry, EU foreign policy chief Catherine Ashton, and Zarif met for five hours. A senior U.S. official said Kerry and Ashton were to meet separately at the luxury Geneva hotel where they were both staying on Saturday morning before inviting Zarif to join them; there was no immediate indication of how long the three-way meeting would last. The negotiations appeared to have made some progress in a major diplomatic push despite fierce opposition from Israel and uncertainty in Congress. The talks aim to offer Iran sanctions relief in exchange for proving its atomic ambitions are peaceful.

summary: President Donald Trump held a joint press conference with King Abdullah II of Jordan at the White House on Wednesday. The press conference took place in the Rose Garden. Earlier in the day, the two leaders held an expanded bilateral meeting, and a working luncheon was scheduled afterward. Also on Wednesday, first lady Melania Trump and Queen Rania of Jordan visited Excel Academy, an all-girls public charter school in Washington, accompanied by Education Secretary Betsy DeVos. At the press conference, Trump addressed a reported chemical weapons attack in Syria that had occurred the previous day. He said the attack on children had a "big impact" on him, calling it a "horrible, horrible thing" that "doesn't get any worse than that." Trump stated that his attitude toward Syria and President Bashar al-Assad "has changed," and that the attack "crosses many, many lines, beyond a red line — many, many lines." He criticized the Obama administration for declaring a red line on chemical weapons use in Syria and then backing down. However, Trump said he would not signal any plans for U.S. action: "I'm not saying I'm doing anything one way or the other, but I'm certainly not going to be telling you." He did not offer details on any policy shift. The day's agenda also included meetings to discuss brokering a peace agreement between Israel and the Palestinians.

summary: White House Chief Strategist Stephen K. Bannon departed the White House on Friday after what was described as a turbulent seven-month tenure. White House Press Secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said in a statement that Chief of Staff John Kelly and Bannon had mutually agreed that Friday would be Bannon's last day, adding, "We are grateful for his service and wish him the best." The departure came amid criticism of President Trump for saying that "both sides" were to blame for deadly violence in Charlottesville, Virginia, the previous weekend, where a counterprotester was killed during a rally in which white supremacists used Tiki torches; at least one torch brand disavowed the use. Critics accused the president of channeling Bannon when he equated white supremacists and neo-Nazis with left-wing protesters. Bannon, who helped Trump win the 2016 election by embracing shared nationalist impulses, had been featured on a February Time magazine cover titled "The Great Manipulator." Following the announcement, Axios reported that Bannon visited New York for a five-hour meeting with billionaire Bob Mercer as he "prepares for war," with the two planning to be a "well-funded force on the outside." Friends of Bannon said he "felt liberated since it became clear he was being pushed out" and could return to Breitbart News, where he was once executive chairman, to operate what he reportedly calls a "killing machine." The exit was the latest in a series of high-profile West Wing shake-ups.

President Donald Trump met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and afterward stated the U.S. relationship with Russia had changed, saying he had no reason to believe Russia hacked the 2016 election and appearing to accept Putin's denial over the conclusions of U.S. intelligence agencies. Homeland Security Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen, speaking at the Aspen Security Forum in Colorado on Thursday, said she had not seen evidence that Russian interference in election infrastructure was intended to favor a particular party, while adding she still stands behind the intelligence community's assessment that Russia meddled in the election and that its influence operations aimed to cause chaos on both sides. Republican senators pushed back against Trump's rhetoric. Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman Richard Burr said Putin ordered an influence campaign aimed at the 2016 elections to undermine faith in the democratic process, that Russia conducted a coordinated cyberattack on state election systems and hacked critical infrastructure, and that any statement by Putin contradicting these facts is a lie. Burr said he believes U.S. intelligence officials and that members of Congress believe Russia attempted to meddle but was unsuccessful in changing the outcome. He said the president is conflating meddling with collusion allegations, for which there does not appear to be evidence. Senator John Cornyn said the 12 Russians indicted by special counsel Robert Mueller should be extradited to the U.S., though he acknowledged that would be wishful thinking.

summary: Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney declared Jerusalem the capital of Israel during a visit to the city on Sunday, saying he would seek to move the U.S. embassy there from Tel Aviv if the Israeli government assented. "A nation has the capacity to choose its own capital city, and Jerusalem is Israel's capital," Romney said in an interview on CNN conducted in Jerusalem. "I think it's long been the policy to ultimately have our embassy in the nation's capital of Jerusalem." Romney delivered a speech in Jerusalem and gave several televised interviews during a trip aimed at emphasizing ties to Israel and boosting support among Jewish Americans and supporters of Israel. In his speech he referred to Jerusalem as the capital of the Jewish state and called Israel "the startup nation." He said both countries believe in democracy, the rule of law and opposition to Iran becoming a nuclear power, and that the United States must be "unapologetic ambassadors" to advance shared values. Jerusalem is claimed by both Israelis and Palestinians. Recent U.S. presidential administrations have avoided the question and maintained the embassy in Tel Aviv despite a 1995 law declaring Jerusalem the capital. House Majority Leader Eric Cantor said in a statement: "For thousands of years, Jerusalem has been the eternal capital of the Jewish people, but this administration refuses to say if Jerusalem is the true capital. At a moment when Israel is facing so many perils, the United States should be standing by our ally, not quibbling or quarreling about its capital city." The trip came one day after President Barack Obama signed legislation Friday to expand military and civilian cooperation with Israel. The bill reiterated U.S. support for a negotiated two-state solution. Romney's campaign said the candidate was happy steps were taken to enhance security cooperation but that the bill "does nothing" to address whether Obama recognizes Jerusalem as the capital of Israel. Romney's overseas trip included stops in Britain and Poland.

summary: During the first presidential debate in Denver, Republican nominee Mitt Romney referred to the Affordable Health Care for America Act as "ObamaCare," adding, "I apologize, Mr. President. On ABC's This Week, senior adviser David Plouffe said, "We still believe this will be a close race -- there's no doubt it will tighten," noting Obama must perform well in three upcoming debates. Former Pennsylvania governor Ed Rendell attributed Obama's rise to Romney's mistakes and warned against over-confidence. Asked about spending in Arizona, Axelrod said, "We are always looking for opportunities."

summary: The Rev. Al Sharpton announced Tuesday that he would lead a national "Justice for Trayvon" day of rallies and vigils in 100 cities on Saturday to press for federal civil rights charges against George Zimmerman. Zimmerman, a neighborhood watch volunteer, was acquitted Saturday by a six-member jury of second-degree murder and manslaughter charges in the February 2012 shooting death of 17-year-old Trayvon Martin in Sanford, Florida. Zimmerman said he fired in self-defense. The Justice Department said Sunday it was restarting its investigation into the shooting to consider possible hate crime charges. The federal inquiry had begun shortly after the shooting but was delayed during the state criminal trial. Civil rights leaders had called on the department to re-examine the case and said they remained convinced the shooting had a racial element. Martin was black. Protests and rallies occurred across the country following the verdict, including gatherings on Sunday that drew from a few dozen to more than a thousand people. Demonstrators voiced support for Martin's family and called the verdict a miscarriage of justice. The NAACP and protesters are calling for federal civil rights charges. Sharpton, speaking outside the Justice Department with several ministers, said the events would show "we are not having a two- or three-day anger fit. This is a social movement for justice." He acknowledged possible legal hurdles but cited "a blatant civil rights question of does Trayvon Martin and the Trayvon Martins of this country have the civil right to go home." Saturday's rallies and vigils are planned for noon in front of federal court buildings in cities including Los Angeles, Chicago, Philadelphia, and New York. A conference is scheduled for next week in Miami to develop a plan addressing Florida's "stand-your-ground" law, which gives people wide latitude to use deadly force if they fear death or bodily harm.

summary: Rep. Chris Gibson (R-N.Y.) signed the Americans for Tax Reform "Taxpayer Protection Pledge" in 2010 as a candidate for New York's 20th Congressional District. After redistricting, he represents the 19th Congressional District. Gibson argues the pledge no longer binds him because it was made to the taxpayers of a specific numbered district. His office stated he does not plan to re-sign it for the 19th District, explaining "the pledge is to your constituents of a numbered district." John Fund wrote that the loophole fails because half of Gibson's new constituents were in his old district and the pledge extends to all Americans. Grover Norquist, president of Americans for Tax Reform, told Fund that "one would hope Representative Gibson would treat his constituents with more respect than he is showing." Norquist also told CNN that lawmakers understand the pledge binds them for their entire congressional tenure, not merely a two-year term, and that candidates re-sign only when seeking a different office. Gibson maintains he can "consider all comprehensive packages brought forward as a result of bipartisan negotiations" without technically violating the pledge. Separately, Rep. Peter King (R-N.Y.) made a similar argument on NBC's "Meet the Press," saying a pledge signed years earlier applies only to that Congress, analogizing to a 1941 declaration of war against Japan. Norquist rejected King's reasoning as well. Gibson represents his former district during the lame-duck session.

summary:
President Barack Obama and first lady Michelle Obama met for coffee Monday morning with House Speaker John Boehner, House Majority Leader Eric Cantor and Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell, along with their wives, ahead of the presidential inauguration. Cantor and Boehner spokesman Brendan Buck tweeted about the meeting, and McConnell's office confirmed his attendance.

Later, during the inaugural luncheon, Boehner was seated to Michelle Obama's left. President Obama leaned behind his wife to speak with Boehner, who tapped the first lady's arm. Boehner appeared to crack a joke; the president laughed, while Michelle Obama glanced up, looked down, shook her head and rolled her eyes. The moment was interrupted when Sen. Chuck Schumer led a round of applause for the chef and caterer.

President Obama subsequently made brief remarks, saying: "Michelle and the speaker of the House came to a meeting of the minds that I may be delaying the proceedings too much. And so I'm just going to be extraordinarily brief and say thank you."

Obama and Boehner had been at odds for months over budget issues; after the latest deal to avert the fiscal crisis, Boehner said he would no longer negotiate with the president one-on-one.

Attorney General Eric Holder sent two letters to Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) and testified at a hearing during the week of March 4, 2013, as the Senate considered the nomination of John Brennan to be CIA director. On Tuesday, March 5, Holder wrote to Paul that it was possible, "I suppose," to imagine an "extraordinary circumstance in which it would be necessary and appropriate" under U.S. law for the president to authorize the military to "use lethal force" within the United States. The same day, the Justice Department turned over documents outlining the legal rationale for targeting Americans overseas involved in terror-related activities. On Wednesday, March 6, Paul conducted a nearly 13-hour filibuster, saying he would end it and allow a vote on Brennan if Holder would state specifically that drone attacks would not be carried out on U.S. citizens in America. Also Wednesday, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) questioned Holder at a hearing, repeatedly asking whether the Constitution allows a drone to kill a U.S. citizen on U.S. soil who is not posing an "imminent and immediate threat of death or bodily harm." Holder initially qualified his answers, saying he did not think such force was "appropriate," and at one point said, "Let me be clear. I've not been clear." Cruz pressed him, and Holder conceded it would be unconstitutional. On Thursday, March 7, Holder sent a second, two-sentence letter to Paul. Sen. Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.) called on Republicans to allow a procedural vote on the Brennan nomination as soon as possible. The Senate resumed work at 2 p.m.; Paul had not yet spoken on the floor about the new letter.

summary: The Obama re-election campaign announced the appointment of Katherine Archuleta as political director, with one account placing the announcement Thursday and another Friday. Archuleta, who currently serves as chief of staff to Labor Secretary Hilda Solis, becomes the first Latina to hold the position on a major presidential campaign, according to campaign sources cited by multiple outlets. A Denver native, Archuleta previously served as chief of staff to former Transportation Secretary Federico Pena and as senior adviser for policy and initiatives to Denver Mayor John Hickenlooper, helping coordinate the 2008 Democratic National Convention in Denver. She also served as executive director of the National Hispanic Cultural Center Foundation and has nearly 18 years of government experience. In her new role, she will be responsible for political outreach with an emphasis on Hispanic community outreach, as well as communication with elected officials and groups. The appointment comes as President Obama prepares to visit Puerto Rico to court Latino voters; the Hispanic population grew 43 percent between 2000 and 2010, according to census data. Archuleta is expected to start within days at the Chicago-based campaign headquarters, joining a team that includes campaign manager Jim Messina, who stepped down as deputy White House chief of staff earlier this year, and chief strategist David Axelrod, who left his post as White House senior adviser. During the 2008 campaign, Patrick Gaspard and Matthew Nugen served as national political directors. Campaign spokesman Ben LaBolt confirmed the hiring.

summary: A CNN/ORC poll released Monday showed support for the Affordable Care Act at 35 percent, down from 40 percent in late November and 41 percent in October, marking a record low in the survey's trend. Opposition stood at 62 percent, up from 58 percent in November and 56 percent in October. The poll was conducted December 16 through 19 among more than 1,000 adults by landline and cellphone, with a margin of error of 8.5 percentage points or less. Monday was the final day to enroll for coverage effective January 1. Forty-two percent of respondents said the law would hurt their family, while 16 percent said it would improve their lives; the latter figure was described as essentially unchanged from earlier in the year. Fifteen percent of all respondents opposed the law because they believe it is not liberal enough, meaning half the public either supports the law or opposes it from the left. Forty-three percent disapprove from the right, according to a breakdown of the 62 percent who disapprove. Sixty-one percent said they believed they could keep the same doctor, while 63 percent expected their health care costs to rise under the law. The CNN poll contrasted with a Washington Post-ABC News poll conducted last week that showed support rebounding slightly to 46 percent as problems with the HealthCare.gov website decreased. The Obama administration last week announced another change exempting people with canceled plans from some of the law's requirements.

summary: CVS Caremark, the largest U.S. drugstore chain by overall sales, announced Wednesday that it would stop selling cigarettes and other tobacco products at its 7,600 pharmacies effective October 1. The company estimated the decision would reduce annual revenue by about $2 billion, a fraction of its $123 billion in sales for 2012. Chief executive Larry J. Merlo said the chain employs about 26,000 pharmacists and nurse practitioners who help patients manage chronic conditions such as high cholesterol, high blood pressure and heart disease, all linked to smoking. "We came to the decision that cigarettes and providing health care just don't go together in the same setting," Merlo said. In a separate statement he added, "Ending the sale of cigarettes and tobacco products at CVS/pharmacy is the right thing for us to do for our customers and our company to help people on their path to better health. Put simply, the sale of tobacco products is inconsistent with our purpose." President Obama praised the move, saying CVS "sets a powerful example" and that the decision would advance his administration's efforts to reduce tobacco-related deaths, cancer and heart disease, lower health care costs, and ultimately save lives. First lady Michelle Obama wrote on Twitter, "Now we can all breathe a little easier, and our families can live healthier."

summary:
Former President Bill Clinton will campaign for Kentucky Secretary of State Alison Lundergan Grimes on February 25 in Louisville, Grimes told the Louisville Courier-Journal on Friday. Grimes is challenging Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell in a race that has drawn significant national attention and funding. "We are very excited to have President Clinton coming into town to make his first campaign stop of this election cycle," Grimes said. She also said Clinton called her and said he wanted to make the race his top priority, and that his decision to make Kentucky his first midterm stop "speaks volumes about the momentum behind my candidacy and our campaign."

The Clintons' relationship with Grimes's father, Jerry Lundergan, spans decades. Lundergan, a former Kentucky Democratic Party chairman, led Bill Clinton's presidential campaigns in the state and served as Kentucky chairman of Hillary Clinton's 2008 presidential campaign. His company catered Chelsea Clinton's wedding. Bill Clinton carried Kentucky twice, the last Democrat to do so, and recorded a video for Grimes's campaign kickoff last summer.

Polling data presents a competitive picture. A Bluegrass Poll released Thursday showed Grimes leading McConnell by four percentage points and leading McConnell's Republican primary challenger Matt Bevin by five points, with McConnell's approval rating in the state having declined. The Fix rated McConnell's seat as the seventh most likely to flip party control. Both candidates have been raising substantial sums. Democrats view Clinton as a valuable surrogate in Republican-leaning states where President Obama's approval ratings are low.

summary:
President Barack Obama hosted French President François Hollande for a state visit Tuesday, the first state dinner of Obama's second term. The day began with a formal welcome at the White House followed by a joint news conference at midday. At the news conference, Obama said there is no country with which the United States has "a no-spy agreement," adding that the U.S. endeavors to protect privacy rights as it collects foreign intelligence. He said the United States and its allies remain concerned about specific potential terrorist networks and will maintain a robust intelligence-gathering effort while respecting privacy. The remarks came after revelations that the U.S. had spied on allied leaders, drawing severe criticism from Europe.

Monday, the two presidents informally opened the visit with a trip to Thomas Jefferson's home at Monticello, Virginia. Tuesday's schedule also included Obama meetings with senior advisers and Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel.

The state dinner Tuesday night accommodated some 350 guests in a tent on the South Lawn. The menu blended American ingredients with French influence: quail eggs from Pennsylvania, American Osetra caviar from Illinois, 12 kinds of potatoes, a winter garden salad of petite mixed radishes, merlot lettuce and baby carrots inspired by the first lady's kitchen garden, and a main course of dry-aged rib eye from a Colorado family farm topped with Vermont blue cheese. Purple irises decorated the setting and Grammy-winning artist Mary J. Blige performed.

Hollande attended without a partner following his recent split from Valerie Trierweiler. White House social secretary Jeremy Bernard told reporters Monday he did not yet know who would sit beside Obama in the seat Trierweiler would have occupied.

summary:
The Dalai Lama delivered the opening prayer on the Senate floor Thursday morning. Approximately a dozen senators were present, according to multiple accounts. Senate Chaplain Barry Black usually opens the session, but guest chaplains occasionally appear.

Sen. Patrick Leahy (D-Vt.) introduced the Dalai Lama to Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii), the chamber's only Buddhist, and Sen. Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.), who touched foreheads with him before he began. The Dalai Lama asked senators to forgive his "broken English," saying some pronunciation may not be right, and then offered what he called his "favorite prayer," which he prays daily for inner strength: "As long as space remains and as long as sentient beings remain, until then may I too remain and help dispel the misery of the world." He also said that if one speaks or acts with a pure mind, happiness will follow.

Afterward, Leahy and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-Nev.) thanked him. Reid said: "I know I speak for the entire Senate family when I express our gratitude for the prayer to open the Senate and his words of encouragement and his blessing. His Holiness often says he's only a simple monk, born to a farming family in northeastern Tibet, but to millions of people in Tibet and across the globe, he is much more. He is a source of hope and inspiration in a world that can sometimes seem very dark." Reid also said: "Spreading a message of peace, he motivates countless people to practice compassion among each other."

The Dalai Lama has been in the United States for several weeks and met with President Obama last month. He planned to meet Thursday with Reid and Minority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.). China condemned the visit with Obama and said it would severely harm U.S.-China relations; the White House downplayed the warning and expressed concern about tensions and human rights issues in Tibetan areas. The Dalai Lama is a Nobel laureate who relinquished his political role as leader of the Tibetan government-in-exile in 2011.

summary:
Edward Snowden, the former National Security Agency contractor who leaked details of U.S. telephone and Internet surveillance programs, received temporary asylum in Russia on August 1 after spending more than five weeks in a Moscow airport following his arrival from Hong Kong. His current whereabouts in Russia are not public. The United States has charged Snowden in federal court in Alexandria, Virginia, with violations of the Espionage Act and seeks his extradition, which Russia has refused.

Snowden's father, Lon Snowden, has obtained a Russian visa to visit his son, according to multiple reports. Lon Snowden and family attorney Bruce Fein have not disclosed when they will travel to Moscow. Lon Snowden has said he wants his son to return to the United States eventually but believes a fair trial is unlikely given public statements by government officials labeling Edward Snowden a traitor. Lon Snowden and Fein appeared on ABC's "This Week" on Sunday.

Russian lawyer Anatoly Kucherena, who has been the primary source of information about Snowden in Russia, told Russian news agencies on Thursday that Edward Snowden and his father had communicated directly over the Internet for the first time since Snowden fled the United States. Kucherena said this contact occurred against legal advice and urged them to avoid further communication, even via encrypted messages, until they meet in person. Kucherena had previously served as the sole intermediary for contact between father and son. According to an Interfax report on Wednesday citing a source familiar with the situation, the visit will be kept confidential and details will be released only after the meeting occurs at a secret location. Kucherena's office said he would be on holiday for the remainder of August.

summary:
A senior Obama administration official said Sunday there was "very little doubt" that Syrian President Bashar al-Assad's military forces had used chemical weapons against civilians last week, and that a Syrian promise to allow United Nations inspectors access to the site was "too late to be credible." President Donald Trump, speaking from his Mar-a-Lago resort in Palm Beach, Florida, where he spent the weekend, said he had discussed the North Korean missile launches in meetings and described Kim Jong Un as "acting very, very badly," according to a White House pool report. Other congressional Democrats also called for Mueller's public testimony.

summary:
Tuesday's midterm elections gave Republicans control of the Senate and expanded their majority in the House. On Wednesday, President Obama held a press conference and spoke by phone with Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell and House Speaker John Boehner.

At the press conference, Obama said it was "good news" that both chambers are now controlled by Republicans because McConnell and Boehner "can come together and decide what their agenda is" and "have sufficient majorities to make real progress." He said he would "certainly be going to be spending a lot more time with them now because that's the only way that we're going to be able to get some stuff done." The president announced he will host McConnell, Boehner and other congressional leaders at the White House on Friday.

McConnell, in line to become majority leader, said voters expect newly empowered Republicans and the Democratic White House to find common ground for fast action. He cited trade agreements and rewriting the tax code as specific areas for agreement. McConnell said he does not expect Obama to agree with everything the Republican-led Senate initiates and expects some Republican ideas will draw a veto.

On the Affordable Care Act, Republican leadership aides in the Senate and House said a few more repeal votes are likely because many new Republican lawmakers campaigned on dismantling the law. Obama said he would oppose changes that "undermine the structure of the law" or "take away health care from the 10 million people who now have it and the millions more who are eligible to get it," but would be "open and receptive" if Republicans proposed "responsible changes to the Affordable Care Act to make it work better."

President Barack Obama delivered his State of the Union address on Tuesday night. Near the end of the speech, Obama said, "I have no more campaigns to run." Some Republicans in the audience applauded. Obama smiled and added, "I know, because I won both of them." His party had lost the midterm elections two months earlier, giving Republicans control of both houses of Congress for the first time during his presidency. Obama made no reference to the midterm results, offered no concessions about his leadership, and proposed no compromises. He laid out an expansive and expensive legislative agenda. Economic indicators were rising and his poll numbers had rebounded slightly.

As Obama was leaving the House chamber, 2012 Republican presidential nominee Mitt Romney posted a statement on Facebook. Romney called the speech "disappointing" and a partisan diatribe. He said Obama was "more interested in politics than in leadership" and "more intent on winning elections than on winning progress." Romney said Obama ignored the fact that voters had elected a Congress favoring smaller government and lower taxes. Romney specifically criticized Obama's tax proposal as a "maze of new taxes and complexities" and called for lower rates and a simpler tax code. Romney was reportedly considering another presidential bid.

On Friday in San Diego, Romney debuted a new theme focused on income inequality. He said, "Under President Obama the rich have gotten richer, income inequality has gotten worse and there are more people in poverty in America than ever before." The remarks were seen as an effort to address his personal wealth and past comments about the 47 percent of Americans who pay no income taxes. A poll of Iowa Republicans taken the previous week showed Romney leading the field of potential GOP contenders with 21 percent support. Obama has called income inequality "the defining challenge of our time." Obama's pollster, Joel Benenson, told reporters last year he thought "the attention on inequality is a bit overhyped."

summary:
The military trial of U.S. Army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan began Tuesday at Fort Hood, Texas, under heavy security. Hasan, a psychiatrist, is charged with killing 13 people and wounding 32 others in a November 2009 shooting rampage at the base. Nearly four years after the attack, Hasan entered the courtroom in a wheelchair, paralyzed from the waist down after being shot by an officer during the rampage. He is acting as his own attorney before a jury of senior Army officers.

In an opening statement lasting little more than a minute, Hasan said quietly, "the evidence will clearly show that I am the shooter." He added that there was "death and destruction on both sides," but that the prosecution's evidence would show only one side. He said the evidence would show he fought on the "wrong side," then switched sides, and stated, "We the mujahedeen are imperfect Muslims" trying to establish a perfect religion. "I apologize for any mistakes I've made in this endeavor," he said, without elaborating.

Hasan does not deny carrying out the attack, which he has described as a defense of Islam and, according to one account, a defense of Taliban leadership. Under military law, he is forbidden to plead guilty because he faces a possible death sentence; the last execution in the U.S. military justice system was in 1961.

The government classifies the shooting as "workplace violence," a designation that prevents victims from receiving Purple Heart medals. The Pentagon has stated that defense counsel will argue Hasan cannot receive a fair trial because a branch of government has indirectly declared him a terrorist.

summary: Congress approved and President Obama signed legislation Thursday morning that reopened the federal government and restored the Treasury's borrowing authority, ending a 16-day partial shutdown. The Senate had negotiated a deal Wednesday to fund the government through December 15 and suspend the $16.7 trillion debt ceiling until early February, with Treasury "extraordinary measures" potentially extending that deadline to May or June. The House voted first on the Senate agreement Wednesday, a procedural move that allowed faster passage. Speaker John Boehner relied on Democratic votes to pass the measure after a large number of Republicans opposed it, violating the informal "Hastert Rule" requiring majority Republican support for legislation brought to the floor. The bill's "default prevention" section established a mechanism allowing the president to increase the debt limit unilaterally unless Congress passed a joint resolution of disapproval by a two-thirds supermajority in both chambers, enough to override a presidential veto. On Wednesday, before the final vote, Obama met with Vice President Biden, Treasury Secretary Jack Lew, and Secretary of State John Kerry as the Thursday default deadline approached.

summary:
The White House announced Tuesday that Hope Hicks would serve as communications director on a permanent basis. Hicks, 28, had been interim communications director since mid-August, following the departure of Anthony Scaramucci, whose tenure lasted 10 days. White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders confirmed the appointment Tuesday, and a White House spokesperson told CNN the same day. According to the White House, the move had been expected for several weeks.

Hicks is a longtime aide to President Donald Trump. She was one of the first staffers to join his 2016 campaign and served as its lead spokeswoman. Her relationship with Trump began while she worked at Hiltzik Strategies, a New York public relations firm founded by Matthew Hiltzik, a longtime Hillary Clinton supporter. She left the firm to work for the Trump Organization on projects including Ivanka Trump's fashion line. At the White House, her previous role was strategic communications director. She is considered one of Trump's most valued advisers and one of the few aides to avoid the infighting that has largely defined the presidency. Hicks has not moved into the office designated for the communications director, opting to remain at her desk just outside the Oval Office.

Hicks is the third White House communications director in the administration's nearly eight months. The position has been difficult to fill: Jason Miller declined the job in December citing family reasons; Mike Dubke, the first full-time communications director, resigned in May; Sean Spicer, the former press secretary who filled in as communications director when the role was open, resigned in July; and Scaramucci was removed after less than two weeks over harsh language he used about two then White House advisers.

The White House also announced three other communications team appointments Tuesday: Mercedes Schlapp, a former Fox News contributor, and Raj Shah and Steven Cheung, who already held positions on the team.

summary: President Barack Obama signed an executive order on Wednesday tightening sanctions on North Korea, the White House announced. The order implemented a United Nations Security Council resolution adopted two weeks earlier in response to North Korea's nuclear test in January and a long-range missile launch in February. Warmbier had been detained for attempting to steal a political propaganda poster from his hotel in Pyongyang and had tearfully apologized. Separately, North Korean leader Kim Jong-un ordered preparations for further weapons tests, according to state media and South Korean reports. The official Korean Central News Agency said Kim ordered a test to estimate the heat stability of a rocket warhead tip. South Korea's Yonhap News Agency reported Kim also declared a nuclear warhead explosion test and test-fires of ballistic rockets capable of carrying nuclear warheads would be conducted "in a short time." summary: The Federal Reserve raised short-term interest rates on Wednesday for the first time since the financial crisis, increasing the target federal funds rate to a range of 0.25 percent to 0.5 percent. The move, widely anticipated, marked the first rate increase in nearly a decade. Fed officials described the decision as a vote of confidence in the U.S. economy and emphasized that future increases would be gradual, contingent on continued economic growth. Officials projected short-term rates would rise by about one percentage point per year over the next three years. Chair Janet Yellen said at a post-meeting news conference, "The economic recovery has clearly come a long way, although it is not complete." On Thursday, the first day of the new target, the effective federal funds rate traded at 0.37 percent, near the middle of the target range, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Stock market movements were relatively mild through Thursday, as were changes in the dollar and commodities. Mortgage and other loan rates, as well as savings and investment yields, were expected to remain low for years. Historical data cited by Robert Johnson, president of the American College of Financial Services, showed the S&P 500 delivered an average 5.9 percent annualized return during periods when the Fed was raising rates between 1966 and 2013, though with inflation averaging 5.1 percent the real return was 0.8 percent. By contrast, during periods when the Fed was lowering rates, stocks gained 10.6 percent annualized with inflation averaging 4.2 percent.

summary: Jury selection resumed Monday in the federal death-penalty trial of Dylann Roof, 22, who is charged with hate crimes, obstruction of religion and other counts in the June 2015 shooting deaths of nine African American parishioners at Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Charleston, South Carolina. The selection process had been halted on November 7 after Roof's lawyers questioned his ability to understand the case against him. U.S. District Judge Richard Gergel ruled on Friday that Roof is competent to stand trial, clearing the way for the process to restart. On Monday, 516 potential jurors were to report to the courthouse for individual questioning by the judge; once 70 qualified jurors are identified, attorneys may use peremptory strikes to reduce the pool. The same judge also ruled on Monday that Roof may represent himself in the proceedings, which are expected to last several months; if survivors testify, Roof could question them directly. Roof has pleaded not guilty to the federal charges, which include the murder of nine people and the attempted murder of three. Prosecutors have said Roof was indoctrinated by white supremacist ideology online and carried out the attack as an act of racial hatred. Roof was previously found competent to stand trial in state court, where he faces a separate death-penalty trial on nine counts of murder. Testimony from the federal competency hearing has been sealed, and questions about what prompted the hearing remain unanswered.

summary: President Trump said Tuesday at his golf club in Bedminster, New Jersey, "North Korea best not make any more threats to the United States. They will be met with fire and fury like the world has never seen." He added of Kim Jong-un, "He has been very threatening beyond a normal state, and as I said, they will be met with fire and fury, and frankly power the likes of which this world has never seen before." Administration officials said a pre-emptive military strike, while a last resort, is among options made available to the president. Trump's comments followed North Korean ballistic missile tests and reports that North Korea can now fit a miniaturized nuclear device on a missile. In response, North Korea threatened to launch medium-range missiles into waters around the U.S. territory of Guam. On Thursday, Trump said his warnings "may not be tough enough." Former Vice President Al Gore told Newsweek on Friday that Trump "inherited this crisis" and "can't be blamed for all of this," noting the previous three presidents were unable to find an adequate solution. Gore also called Trump's "intemperate comments on North Korea really unwise" and said he hoped Trump would listen to his secretary of defense and national security adviser, "both of whom are immensely respected," adding, "I hope their cooler heads will prevail."

summary:
Former FBI Director James Comey's memos documenting his interactions with President Donald Trump became the subject of multiple developments in early 2018. Senator Charles E. Grassley revealed that Comey authored seven memos about his conversations with Trump before his firing in May 2017, and that the government had deemed four of those seven to contain classified information. Comey had provided at least four memos to a law professor friend. Grassley said that, by that math, at least one of the leaked memos must have contained classified information. Attorney Ty Clevenger, who filed a grievance against Comey, wrote to the New York lawyers' disciplinary committee that if Comey leaked classified information it could violate New York bar rules prohibiting a lawyer from engaging in "illegal conduct that adversely reflects on the lawyer's honesty, trustworthiness or fitness as a lawyer." Clevenger wrote that a deliberate leak would be "analogous to willful breach of client confidentiality." Clevenger said he was also pursuing bar complaints against former Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton and her top lawyers over their handling of Clinton's emails.

Separately, a newspaper reported that Special Counsel Robert Mueller had been able to substantiate claims made by Comey in the memos describing his conversations with Trump. Those memos describe multiple interactions, including one in which Trump asked Comey to end the FBI's investigation into former national security adviser Michael Flynn. Comey had testified before the Senate Intelligence Committee that Trump asked him to end the Flynn investigation and that the president demanded his "loyalty" during an "uneasy" conversation. Trump denied both that he asked for loyalty and that he asked Comey to drop the Flynn investigation. The New York Times reported that Trump called Comey a "nut job" while meeting with Russian officials in the Oval Office the day after the firing, and said, "I faced great pressure because of Russia... That's taken off," apparently referring to the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election. Flynn later pleaded guilty to lying to the FBI about contacts with Russian officials.

Comey, who was working on a book titled "A Higher Loyalty: Truth, Lies, and Leadership" due out in the spring, tweeted on Sunday that he hoped the new year would bring "more ethical leadership focused on the truth and lasting values," in what appeared to be a reference to Trump.

summary: Senator Rand Paul (R-Ky.) said he would oppose a bipartisan budget agreement announced Tuesday that would replace $63 billion in sequestration cuts over two years and set discretionary spending at just over $1 trillion for each of the next two fiscal years. Ryan defended the agreement as the best Republicans could obtain, and House Republican leaders endorsed it. Senator Marco Rubio (R-Fla.) also opposed the deal. Paul, a freshman senator and potential 2016 presidential contender along with Ryan and Rubio, had previously opposed the fiscal-cliff agreement and the bill that reopened the government in October. summary:
Federal and state authorities executed two federal search warrants at the Statehouse office and home of Rhode Island House Speaker Gordon Fox on Friday. The U.S. attorney's office confirmed that the FBI, IRS, state police, and the U.S. attorney's office were engaged in a law enforcement action. Three state police officers stood outside Fox's closed office door, and authorities were seen carrying an evidence bag and empty cardboard boxes. Officials did not disclose the subject or target of the investigation, and a spokesman for the U.S. attorney's office declined to say whether the warrants were connected to Fox. Fox's spokesman, Larry Berman, said state police had asked everyone to leave the office.

On Saturday, Fox, a Providence Democrat, announced in a written statement that he was resigning as speaker and would not seek re-election. He said he did not want the raids to distract his colleagues from addressing the state's challenges and that he wanted to focus on his family and the investigation.

On Monday, Fox's chief of staff, Frank Anzeveno Jr., announced his resignation. Anzeveno, a former state representative who also served as chief of staff to Fox's predecessor, Bill Murphy, said he had known "for a while" that Fox would not run again and had planned to leave at the end of the General Assembly session in June. He said recent events accelerated his departure. Anzeveno also disclosed that Fox had decided not to run before the raids but did not want to announce the decision so that the focus would remain on issues before the House. Fox had said publicly as recently as December that he planned to run for re-election in the fall and seek another term as speaker in 2015.

summary:
The Senate will begin Donald Trump's impeachment trial next week, halting most other business. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell had not shared the text of trial procedures with Senate Democrats as of Thursday afternoon. McConnell has a plan, supported by senators such as Susan Collins, to postpone votes on witnesses and documents until after the House presents its case and the president's lawyers offer a rebuttal. Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Lindsey Graham said on "Fox News Sunday" that immediate dismissal of the articles of impeachment is "dead for practical purposes." Graham said many senators who expect to acquit the president still believe the Senate needs to hear the House's case and the president's answer. He said there are not enough votes to dismiss the case early. Graham also said that if the Senate calls one witness, it will call all witnesses, and that he wants the trial to conclude as quickly as possible so voters can choose the next president.

The Martin Luther King Jr. holiday weekend will be busy for prosecution and defense teams preparing for the trial. Committee hearings will not take place during the trial.

summary: Former Treasury Secretary Lawrence H. Summers withdrew from consideration to succeed Ben S. Bernanke as chairman of the Federal Reserve, prompting a rise in U.S. stock markets and leaving Janet L. Yellen, the Fed's vice chairwoman since 2010, as the leading candidate for the nomination. According to one account, Summers withdrew on Sunday, bowing to opposition from at least five Senate Democrats; another report noted the withdrawal coincided with a market rally Monday morning, when the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 165 points, or more than 1 percent, in the first hour of trading and the Nasdaq also advanced sharply. Summers had been viewed as likely to curtail the Fed's stimulus program more aggressively than other contenders. President Barack Obama had been expected to announce his choice as early as September. Throughout the summer, White House aides signaled Obama preferred Summers, his former chief economic adviser, though the White House denied a Nikkei report that a decision had been finalized. White House spokeswoman Amy Brundage dismissed the Japanese newspaper's account that the administration was "in the final stages" or "set to" nominate Summers. A potential Summers nomination faced bipartisan resistance: liberal lawmakers favored Yellen, and Senator John Cornyn (R-Texas) said he would vote against Summers. After Summers's departure, officials close to the White House said Yellen became the front-runner by elimination. Some of Summers's supporters, including several of Obama's closest advisers, had privately raised concerns that Yellen's central role in crafting current Fed policy might limit her willingness to change course, and that institutions benefit from fresh leadership. Yellen had told friends in recent weeks she did not expect to be nominated; if selected, she would be the first woman to hold the post. Bernanke's term expires at the end of the year.

summary:
The Federal Reserve concluded a two-day policy meeting on Wednesday and announced it would continue its stimulus program unchanged. The central bank said it would keep purchasing $85 billion per month in Treasury and mortgage-backed securities and maintain its benchmark short-term interest rate near zero. The bond purchases are intended to keep borrowing costs low to encourage hiring and investment. The Fed stated the economy is growing only moderately and still needs support. It said it would hold the short-term rate at its record low at least as long as the unemployment rate remains above 6.5 percent and the inflation outlook stays mild. The Fed noted that budget policies in Washington have restrained growth. 

Regarding the 16-day partial government shutdown that occurred since the September meeting, one account said the Fed stated it would "await more evidence" that the economy was improving before reducing stimulus and referenced the shutdown and near breach of the borrowing limit as factors that had shaken the economy. Another account said the Fed made no mention of the 16-day shutdown in its statement. The Fed also no longer expressed concerns about higher mortgage rates, a concern it had flagged in September.

The announcement was widely expected by investors. In September, the Fed had voted not to begin tapering its bond-buying program, a decision described by some as a "relatively close call." Since then, the shutdown delayed the release of key economic data and dented consumer confidence, and incoming readings on employment and housing have been soft. Economists said tapering remains off the table for now. Michael Hanson, U.S. economist for Bank of America Merrill Lynch, said the vote not to taper would likely not be as close this time. Steven Ricchiuto, U.S. chief economist at Mizuho Securities USA, said the timing of tapering is still open to debate, with some expecting a December start and others pointing to 2014. Investors will scrutinize the post-meeting statement, though Hanson noted the most interesting aspects of the discussion will not be revealed until the minutes are released in mid-November.
