summary:
The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans ruled Thursday that Texas may enforce provisions of House Bill 2 requiring abortion clinics to meet the same building, equipment and staffing standards as ambulatory surgical centers. The three-judge panel stayed a lower court order that had blocked the requirements, saying the state had a good chance of prevailing on appeal. In August, a lower court judge had ruled the restrictions created an "impermissible obstacle" for women seeking abortions.

The ruling took immediate effect. According to the Center for Reproductive Rights, 13 clinics closed overnight, leaving eight abortion clinics operating in the state, all in major metropolitan areas. Texas has 5.4 million women of reproductive age, the second-highest number in the country.

The law, passed in July 2013 after a marathon filibuster by Democratic state Senator Wendy Davis, also bans abortion after 20 weeks and requires doctors who provide abortions to have admitting privileges at local hospitals; the appeals court has previously upheld that portion. Major medical associations opposed the ambulatory-surgical-center standards as medically unnecessary and dangerous, while the state argued they improved patient care. Providers said the standards were unnecessary and costly.

Nancy Northup, president and chief executive of the Center for Reproductive Rights, said the ruling "has gutted Texas women's constitutional rights and access to critical reproductive health care, and stands to make safe, legal abortion essentially disappear overnight." Davis is now running for governor.

summary: President Barack Obama will appear on a special episode of NBC's "Running Wild with Bear Grylls" during a three-day trip to Alaska aimed at promoting climate change action, NBC and the White House announced Monday. We have been able to work with the Secret Service to find a couple of interesting things for the president to participate in." Earnest called the appearance "an admittedly unorthodox but legitimately interesting way for the president to reach an audience that obviously cares about conservation." The show, in its second season, features Grylls in one-on-one adventures with celebrities who are tested on their survival skills and pushed "to their mental and physical limits," according to NBC. Previous participants have included Kate Winslet, Drew Brees, Kate Hudson, and Channing Tatum. Grylls previously starred in the Discovery Channel series "Man vs. Wild." The White House said it plans to devote all of the resources of its social media operation to maximize the impact of the trip.

summary:
President Barack Obama addressed the National Governors Association at a White House dinner Sunday night, joking about the emerging conflict with Senate Republicans over a Supreme Court nomination to replace Justice Antonin Scalia, who died Saturday. "Tonight, I plan to fulfill my duty and give you an indisputably qualified set of remarks," Obama said. "I trust that you'll give them a fair hearing." Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and other Republicans have vowed to block any Obama nominee, arguing the next president should fill the vacancy. Obama maintains the Senate has a constitutional duty to give his nominee a fair hearing and expects to announce a selection within weeks. He also quipped: "This is my final governor's dinner — at least, my final one as president. I'm just kidding. I wanted to see how Michelle would react."

On Wednesday, California Attorney General Kamala Harris, a reported contender, said she was not interested. "I'm not putting my name out there, I'm running for United States Senate," Harris said while campaigning for the state's open Senate seat. "Let's put that out there right now. Clinton's communications director, Jennifer Palmieri, wrote on Twitter: "We are not responding to Trump. But everyone who understands the humiliation this degrading language inflicts on all women should," adding the hashtag #ImWithHer. The Clinton campaign mobilized a network of female supporters to denounce Trump as "sexist" and a practitioner of "pathetic, frat-boy politics." On Tuesday, Clinton held a rally in Keota, Iowa, where a 10-year-old girl who said she had asthma asked how to deal with bullies. Clinton replied that she had had "terrible things" said about her and added that the country "shouldn't let anybody bully his way into the presidency." She also said: "We are not treating each other with the respect and the care that we should show toward each other... stand up to bullies wherever they are." Trump tweeted in response: "The Hillary Clinton staged event yesterday was pathetic. Be careful Hillary as you play the war on women or women being degraded card." Clinton accused Trump of "bigotry," "bluster," and "bullying." Trump later said on Twitter that "schlonged" is a common political phrase.

CNN held a town hall event Monday evening from 8 p.m. to 11 p.m. ET, hosted by Anderson Cooper and Wolf Blitzer. Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, Ohio Governor John Kasich, Texas Senator Ted Cruz, and Donald Trump appeared in person at the CNN Election Center in Washington; Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders was interviewed remotely from the campaign trail.

On CNN's "The Final 5 Candidates" broadcast, Cruz said he would move the U.S. embassy in Israel to Jerusalem and asserted that both Trump and Clinton would not keep their promises to do so. Cruz stated that Trump and Clinton had each promised the move at AIPAC earlier that day, but added, "Everyone watching them knows, if they get into the White House, they will exercise the waiver, and they won't move it to Jerusalem." He contrasted himself: "When I say I'm going to do something, I do it."

In a separate interview with Wolf Blitzer broadcast Monday evening on CNN, Cruz said Trump's campaign is "built on a lie" and described Trump's pattern when scared: "he begins lashing out, he begins attacking, he begins insulting, he begins yelling, often he begins cursing." Cruz argued Trump is "enmeshed in the corruption of Washington" despite being viewed as an outsider. He called Trump's and Clinton's remarks on Israel "empty campaign rhetoric," including Trump's promise to move the embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. Cruz said he had "zero interest whatsoever" in being Trump's running mate, predicting a Trump nomination would be a "disaster" and lead to defeat by Clinton. Cruz also defended Frank Gaffney, his newly named foreign policy adviser who has questioned President Obama's birthplace, calling Gaffney "someone I respect" and a "serious thinker."

summary: Corey Lewandowski, campaign manager for Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump, was charged with misdemeanor battery Tuesday by police in Jupiter, Florida, for an incident on March 8 in which he allegedly grabbed reporter Michelle Fields by the arm as she attempted to ask Trump a question during a press conference. Lewandowski turned himself in and was released. Police released security-camera footage that they said showed Lewandowski roughly pulling Fields out of the way. The Trump campaign had previously denied that Lewandowski touched Fields and attacked her credibility. A campaign spokeswoman said Tuesday the campaign "wholeheartedly supports" Lewandowski. Trump posted on Twitter that the video showed "nothing" and suggested Fields had changed her account after learning of the recording. Fields responded on Twitter that her story had not changed and told Trump to "stop lying." The incident drew criticism from Democratic operative Jesse Fallon, who said a candidate must take responsibility for staff conduct, and from Correct the Record founder David Brock, who urged Trump to fire Lewandowski. John Weaver, a strategist for Republican rival John Kasich, said Lewandowski would have been fired long ago if he worked for Kasich.

summary:
On the opening day of the Democratic National Convention in Philadelphia, supporters of Bernie Sanders heckled from the convention floor, marched in the streets, and protested outside the arena. Jody Feldman, a delegate from California, said, "I'm booing now, and I'm going to boo for four more days." Supporters shouted "Bernie for president!" and "We are so disappointed!" During Sanders's prime-time endorsement of Hillary Clinton, the reaction was lukewarm and recalcitrant. As delegates entered the convention hall Monday night, protesters yelled, "Hell no, D.N.C.! We won't vote for Hillary!" and "Lock her up!" from the streets. The Wall Street Journal reported that the day before the convention, protesters chanted "lock her up" and some wore "Hillary for Prison" T-shirts during a march in Philadelphia. The chants reflected concerns about party unity, exacerbated by the release of DNC emails showing party officials discussing ways to undermine Sanders's primary challenge. Clinton had been cleared of wrongdoing by the Justice Department in the investigation of her private email server use, though FBI Director James Comey criticized her "extreme carelessness" in handling sensitive information.

On Thursday night, during Clinton's acceptance speech, she reached out to Sanders and his supporters. She acknowledged that his campaign "inspired millions of Americans, particularly the young people who threw their hearts and souls into our primary." Sanders delegates had protested all week with various degrees of success, and some threatened to storm out of her speech. Sanders, sitting in the audience, smiled when Clinton mentioned him. Clinton said, "You've put economic and social justice issues front and center, where they belong. And to all of your supporters here and around the country: I want you to know, I've heard you. Your cause is our cause." She highlighted a progressive platform including making college "tuition-free for the middle class and debt-free for all." Her speech was interrupted multiple times by chants from the crowd, though cheers for Clinton often drowned out the hecklers.

summary: After the July 2018 Helsinki summit, which drew criticism for President Trump's refusal to publicly confront Russian President Vladimir Putin over election interference, the two governments exchanged proposals for a follow-up meeting. Trump initially invited Putin to Washington in the fall. The White House said Trump was "open" to visiting Moscow, and Putin said he was "ready to come to Washington" if conditions were right. National Security Adviser John Bolton said Trump believed the next meeting should occur in 2019, after the special counsel probe into Russian election interference — which Bolton called "the Russia witch hunt" — concluded. The White House then backed away from the fall plan, saying the Kremlin had not immediately accepted its invitation. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Russia agreed another meeting should occur but had not formally accepted the fall invitation. Ushakov said it would be wise to "let the dust settle" and discuss matters "in a business-like way. But not now." Trump and Press Secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders had said the previous week that preparations were underway for a Washington meeting that fall. Ushakov also noted other opportunities, including the November G20 summit in Argentina, which both leaders were slated to attend. Meanwhile, a poll conducted during the Helsinki period showed Trump's approval at a new high, with 88 percent support among Republicans — the strongest within-party backing since George W. Bush after September 11. The same poll found 51 percent of voters disapproved of the U.S.-Russia relationship, 45 percent said Trump was "too friendly" with Putin, and 65 percent believed Russia interfered in the 2016 election, up 8 points from June 2017. Trump had waffled on whether he accepted that conclusion.

summary: On Sunday, President Donald Trump posted a series of tweets directed at unnamed progressive congresswomen "who originally came from countries whose governments are a complete and total catastrophe," saying they should "go back and help fix the totally broken and crime infested places from which they came." The remarks were widely understood to refer to four Democratic representatives — Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts, and Rashida Tlaib of Michigan — all women of color. Nearly every candidate for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination criticized the tweets. Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi repeated her accusation that Trump wanted to "make America white again." Ocasio-Cortez said the president used the "language of white supremacists." On Monday, Trump denied he was being racist and expressed no remorse when informed that white nationalist groups found common cause with his message. He added that the members of Congress "hate our country," harbor hatred of Jews and love for terrorist groups, and are "free to leave" the United States if they choose.

summary:
The first 2020 presidential debate between President Donald Trump and former Vice President Joe Biden took place Tuesday at 9:00 p.m. ET at Case Western Reserve University and the Cleveland Clinic in Cleveland, Ohio. The 90-minute event was moderated by Fox News anchor Chris Wallace. Topics announced in advance included each candidate's record, the coronavirus pandemic, the economy, alleged racial injustice, protests, and violence, and the integrity of the 2020 elections. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the audience was limited and the candidates were spaced apart on stage. Wallace said beforehand he would try to be "as invisible as possible" and likely would not fact-check the candidates.

According to Wallace, speaking after the debate to Fox News colleague Bill Hemmer, the Trump family did not arrive until Tuesday afternoon — between 3:00 and 5:00 p.m. — leaving insufficient time for the president to be tested for the virus on site and receive a result before the 9:00 p.m. start. Wallace said the arrangement operated on an "honor system" for people entering the hall from both campaigns. Hemmer noted the Cleveland Clinic stated the candidates themselves had been tested and tested negative by their respective campaigns, not by the clinic.

The Trump campaign later said President Trump was taken to Walter Reed National Military Medical Center early Friday evening "out of an abundance of caution."

Ahead of the debate, the Trump campaign claimed the Biden campaign had agreed days earlier to a pre-debate inspection for electronic earpieces but then abruptly reversed course and declined. Trump campaign communications director Tim Murtaugh said in a statement: "Joe Biden's handlers several days ago agreed to a pre-debate inspection for electronic earpieces but today abruptly reversed themselves and declined."

Subsequent debates were scheduled: Vice President Mike Pence and Senator Kamala Harris on October 7, and Trump and Biden again on October 15 and 22.

summary: National Security Adviser Michael Flynn appeared at the White House daily press briefing Wednesday and declared that the United States was "officially putting Iran on notice" following a recent Iranian ballistic missile test and other actions the administration described as provocative. Flynn read a statement condemning "such actions by Iran that undermine security, prosperity and stability throughout and beyond the Middle East, and place American lives at risk." He did not specify what measures the United States might take in response. Flynn characterized the Trump administration as changing course after what he called "weak and ineffective" policies toward Iran, which he said had emboldened what he described as the world's largest state sponsor of terrorism. The statement was also noted as critical of the Obama administration. The missile test, conducted Tuesday, was said to violate a United Nations Security Council resolution restricting Iran's ballistic missile program, a charge Iran denies. Other administration officials indicated the White House was considering sanctions and other measures. Separately, Houthi militants backed by Iran were reported to have attacked a Saudi naval vessel Monday, killing two Saudi crew members. The same day, President Trump tweeted that Iran was "taking over" Iraq, though it was not immediately clear what the tweet referenced; Iran has participated in military operations against the Islamic State in Iraq since 2014. As a candidate, Trump had criticized the 2015 international agreement to curb Iran's nuclear program and vowed to abandon it.

summary: President Trump gave an interview to Fox News host Bill O'Reilly that aired Sunday before the Super Bowl, with excerpts released Saturday. In the interview, O'Reilly called Russian President Vladimir Putin "a killer." According to one account, Trump responded: "There are a lot of killers. Got a lot of killers. What, do you think our country's so innocent?" Another account quoted Trump as saying: "There are a lot of killers. Trump said he respected Putin as a leader of his country and believed it was better to get along with Russia than not, though he did not know if they would get along. He also said Russian assistance in fighting radical Islamic terrorism would be valuable. The interview occurred amid scrutiny of Trump's relationship with Russia and Putin following intelligence assessments that Russia interfered in the 2016 presidential election by hacking emails of the Democratic National Committee and advisers to Hillary Clinton. Excerpts drew condemnation from some conservatives, including the Wall Street Journal's deputy editorial page editor, who tweeted that Trump put the U.S. on moral par with Putin's Russia and had slandered his country. On Tuesday, Trump wrote on Twitter: "I don't know Putin, have no deals in Russia, and the haters are going crazy – yet Obama can make a deal with Iran, #1 in terror, no problem!" Separately, a phone call between Trump and Putin added to concerns about Trump's preparation for discussions with foreign leaders. During the campaign, Trump had mentioned the START treaty, getting its name wrong, and claimed it stopped the United States from updating its nuclear arsenal while Russia built more warheads. The treaty remains in effect unless violated.

summary: U.S. Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin dismissed climate activist Greta Thunberg's call for divestment from fossil fuels during a press briefing at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, saying the 17-year-old should study economics in college before offering economic advice. (I don't have a degree in economics either) We need to drastically reduce our use of fossil fuels. Keep up the fight @gretathunberg." The post was deleted approximately 30 minutes later. Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman also criticized Mnuchin, tweeting: "It's the people insisting that protecting the planet is incompatible with growth who don't know economics."

summary:
In 2010, while working for a National Security Agency contractor, Edward J. Snowden completed a course that trains security professionals to think like hackers and understand their techniques, earning a "certified ethical hacker" certification, according to a résumé he later prepared. Security experts said the certification would have given him some of the skills needed to rummage undetected through NSA computer systems and gather the highly classified surveillance documents he leaked in June 2013.

Sen. Charles Schumer (D-N.Y.) warned the Ecuadorian government against granting asylum to Snowden, stating that trade preferences, including over 85,000 business visas issued annually to Ecuadorians, would be in jeopardy if Ecuador allowed Snowden to avoid extradition on charges of espionage and theft of government property.

Snowden's father, Lonnie Snowden, proposed a deal to Attorney General Eric Holder in a letter, saying his son would likely return to the United States if promised he could remain free prior to trial, not be subjected to a gag order, and be tried in a venue of his choosing. Lonnie Snowden also proposed that if those terms were violated, the government should agree to dismiss charges. He said he had not spoken to his son since April 2013.

As of late June 2013, Edward Snowden was believed to be in the international terminal of Moscow's Sheremetyevo Airport, where he arrived after fleeing Hong Kong, and had reportedly requested asylum in Ecuador. The Justice Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment. President Barack Obama said he would not engage in "wheeling and dealing and trading and a whole host of other issues, simply to get a guy extradited so he can face the justice system here in the United States."

summary: Arizona Governor Jan Brewer vetoed Senate Bill 1062 on Wednesday evening. The legislation would have allowed businesses to refuse service to individuals on religious freedom grounds, effectively permitting discrimination against same-sex couples. The bill reached Brewer's desk on Monday, starting a five-day period for her to sign or veto it before it would become law automatically on Saturday. While the measure was pending, Brewer said she would "do the right thing for the state of Arizona" and would read the bill and be briefed on it before deciding. Arizona's two Republican U.S. senators, John McCain and Jeff Flake, publicly urged a veto. The conservative Center for Arizona Policy supported the bill as protection against activist federal courts, while the Arizona Chamber of Commerce and Industry sought a veto. Brewer was in Washington attending the National Governors Association meeting during the deliberation period. Following the veto, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton praised the decision at the University of Miami, saying Brewer was "recognizing that inclusive leadership is really what the 21st century is all about." The ACLU of Arizona executive director Alessandra Soler said, "Discrimination has no place in Arizona, or anywhere else," and expressed gratitude that the governor stopped the law from taking effect.

summary:
Senate Minority Leader Harry Reid, 75, underwent follow-up surgery on his right eye Wednesday at George Washington University Hospital. The surgery was described by his spokeswoman as "a necessary step to assist in recovering full vision in his right eye." Reid was released Wednesday evening and has been resting at his Washington residence. Doctors will continue to monitor his eye and hope to have a clearer prognosis for his vision in the coming days.

Reid injured his right eye on Jan. 1 when an exercise band he was using snapped, causing him to tumble headfirst into a set of cabinets at his Nevada home. He suffered broken ribs and shattered bones around the eye. During initial surgery on Jan. 26, the shattered bones were repaired and excessive blood was drained from the area. At that time, Reid said the prognosis for regaining full sight was uncertain.

Reid is expected to miss the remainder of this week in the Senate. Lawmakers are on recess next week, and he is expected to return to work after the recess. Reid is up for re-election in 2016.

On Monday, Reid was at the Capitol and told reporters he thinks President Obama will formally submit a request Wednesday for an authorization for use of military force against the Islamic State. Republicans have been making an effort to recruit a high-profile challenger for his re-election bid.

summary: Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney announced Wisconsin Representative Paul Ryan as his vice presidential running mate on Saturday morning in Norfolk, Virginia. The announcement took place at the Nauticus Museum at 8:45 a.m. ET, according to the Romney campaign, which also said Romney would launch a four-day bus tour through swing states. During the introduction, Romney misspoke, referring to Ryan as "the next president of the United States." Romney corrected the mistake, putting his arm around Ryan and clarifying that Ryan was the vice presidential nominee. Romney said he makes a mistake every once in a while but did not make a mistake with his selection of Ryan. It was the pair's first joint appearance as the Republican ticket. Several other politicians who had been considered for the position offered congratulations. Ohio Senator Rob Portman, described as a close second choice, said in a statement Saturday morning that Romney had made a great choice and called Ryan one of his best friends in Congress and a former colleague on the House Ways and Means Committee. Former Minnesota Governor Tim Pawlenty said Ryan's addition would help Republicans win Wisconsin and called him a respected leader and bold thinker. Florida Senator Marco Rubio, who would have been the first Hispanic on a major-party presidential ticket, wrote on Twitter that Romney had made a great choice. New Hampshire Senator Kelly Ayotte also tweeted, calling it a "fantastic VP choice" and saying the ticket would get the fiscal house in order. Portman and Rubio were both notified on Friday that they would not be selected. Ryan, a seven-term congressman, had been the focus of recent speculation, particularly among conservative commentators who cited his authorship of a House-backed budget plan seeking to curb entitlement spending and convert Medicaid into a voucher-like system.

summary:
South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley said she does not consider previous time in elected office a prerequisite for replacing Sen. Jim DeMint, who announced he would leave the Senate in the new year to become president of the Heritage Foundation. "It is not about time in office, which I think is the wrong way of looking at government," Haley told local reporters. "It's the effect and the result they can show in office."

CNN reported that Haley had narrowed her choice to five candidates: Rep. Tim Scott, Rep. Trey Gowdy, former state Attorney General Henry McMaster, former South Carolina first lady Jenny Sanford, and Catherine Templeton, who heads the state Department of Health and Environmental Control. Scott, the first black Republican elected to statewide office in South Carolina since Reconstruction, was described as DeMint's favored selection. Haley disputed the CNN report, telling the Charleston Post and Courier that only her husband knows the names on her actual list.

Sanford, the ex-wife of former Gov. Mark Sanford, has not held elected office but was involved in her husband's campaigns and policy-making before his extramarital affair and their divorce. She was an early supporter of Haley, who called her a "confidante." Sanford told the Columbia Free-Times she would consider serving and would be "honored" to receive the appointment. Templeton is a conservative attorney chosen by Haley to lead the environmental agency.

Mark Sanford has said he could run for the seat in 2014. A poll showed Jenny Sanford with a 44 percent approval rating and Mark Sanford with 30 percent; voters' first choice for the appointment was comedian Stephen Colbert, with Jenny Sanford second. Whoever Haley appoints will stand for election in 2014 and could face a primary challenge. The FBI began investigating Weiner after a 15-year-old girl shared with the Daily Mail text messages she said she received from him. Weiner released a statement saying he had provided the Daily Mail with information showing he had likely been the subject of a hoax, adding, "I have no one to blame but me for putting myself in this position. I am sorry." Abedin announced on August 29 that she would separate from her husband, saying, "After long and painful consideration and work on my marriage, I have made the decision to separate from my husband. Anthony and I remain devoted to doing what is best for our son, who is the light of our life. During this difficult time, I ask for respect for our privacy." The Washington Post reported Abedin told people she did not know how her emails ended up on Weiner's computer and said she did not regularly use it. Her lawyers did not search Weiner's computer when she agreed to hand over emails to the State Department because she did not believe any of her emails would be on it. FBI Director James Comey sent a letter Friday revealing a review of newly discovered emails related to the previously closed investigation into Clinton's private server. Divorce lawyers and data analysts said less public versions of such data spills occur frequently in separations. John Slowiaczek, president-elect of the American Academy of Matrimonial Lawyers, said, "The problem is, once they've already engaged in bad behavior, it's out there. You can't recapture it, you can't bury it."

summary:
President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un were in Singapore on Monday preparing for a summit scheduled to begin at 9 a.m. Tuesday, the first meeting between a sitting U.S. president and a North Korean leader. According to a U.S. official who spoke on condition of anonymity, the leaders plan to shake hands and then meet one on one with only translators present for up to two hours before admitting their advisers. Trump departed the Group of Seven summit in Canada on Saturday morning ahead of schedule to travel to Singapore. Kim Jong Un was expected to arrive on Sunday, according to Reuters, and his close aide Kim Chang Son was already in Singapore to prepare. At a news conference Saturday, Trump said he would know within the "first minute" of meeting Kim whether the North Korean leader was serious about abandoning his nuclear program. The U.S. hopes the summit will start negotiations to eliminate North Korea's rapidly advancing nuclear weapons program.

Former NBA player Dennis Rodman arrived in Singapore around midnight Monday wearing a T-shirt promoting PotCoin, a cryptocurrency company that has sponsored his previous travel to North Korea. Rodman told reporters at Changi Airport he came "to see what's going on" and hoped "that things turn out to be well for everyone in the world." He said he thought Kim had "bigger things to worry about than seeing me right now," though he noted past meetings with Kim had been surprises. White House officials said Rodman would play no official role in the diplomatic negotiations, and Trump said last week that Rodman had not been invited to the summit. Rodman is one of the few Westerners to have met Kim during visits to Pyongyang.

President Barack Obama altered his campaign schedule beginning Sunday as Hurricane Sandy approached the Eastern seaboard. Obama flew to Orlando, Florida, on Sunday evening and had planned to appear Monday with former President Bill Clinton at three rallies: at Central Florida University in Orlando; in Youngstown, Ohio; and in northern Virginia. The White House announced changes as the storm was forecast to make landfall along the Eastern seaboard later Monday. White House spokesman Jay Carney said "the president continues to be regularly updated on the storm."

Accounts differ on the Orlando event: one report said Obama cancelled the Orlando appearance and returned to Washington; another said the two presidents would still appear together Monday morning in Orlando before Obama returned to Washington and Clinton continued to Ohio joined by Vice President Joe Biden. The Virginia event was cancelled. Obama also cancelled a planned Tuesday trip to Green Bay, Wisconsin, and the White House announced Tuesday morning that Wednesday campaign events in Ohio were cancelled so Obama could remain in Washington to "ensure that all available federal resources continue to be provided to support ongoing state and local recovery efforts." The president had not campaigned since Saturday in New Hampshire. The Tuesday and Wednesday schedule remained uncertain. The Obama campaign said it would withhold fundraising e-mails starting Tuesday in Virginia, Pennsylvania, North Carolina, New Jersey, and Washington, D.C. Republican nominee Mitt Romney also cancelled campaign events Monday night and Tuesday; his campaign added an event in Kettering, Ohio, near Dayton, to draw attention to the storm.

summary: President Barack Obama and Iranian President Hassan Rouhani are both scheduled to address the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, prompting widespread speculation about a possible encounter between the two leaders. The White House said Monday that no meeting with Rouhani appears on Obama's schedule, but Press Secretary Jay Carney added that a meeting is generally possible and that "the extended hand has been there from the moment the president was sworn into office." Carney also said the administration has noticed "a significant change in language and tone from the new Iranian government when compared to its predecessor" and called the shift "rather dramatic." The two leaders could cross paths at the U.N.'s annual luncheon. If a formal meeting occurs, it would be the first between a U.S. president and an Iranian head of state since Jimmy Carter met Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi in Tehran on New Year's Eve 1977. Secretary of State John Kerry is expected to meet his Iranian counterpart on Thursday, which would mark the highest-level contact between the two countries since diplomatic relations were severed in 1980. Senators from both parties warned Obama that engagement could be a diplomatic trap allowing Iran to buy time for a nuclear weapons program. Former New York City mayor Rudy Giuliani said preconditions should include a nuclear inventory, international inspectors, the release of political prisoners, and an airlift for an estimated 3,000 dissidents. Obama's Tuesday speech is expected to address Iran's nuclear program, the Syrian civil war, and the Middle East peace process.

summary:
The FBI opened a civil rights investigation Monday into the death of 18-year-old Michael Brown, who was fatally shot by a Ferguson police officer on Saturday. Cheryl Mimura, a spokeswoman for the FBI's St. Louis field office, said the agency is investigating possible civil rights violations and is monitoring the case while working with St. Louis County police. Mimura noted the FBI would investigate such a shooting regardless of public attention.

According to Ferguson police, Brown was shot after an officer encountered him and another man on the street. Police said one of the men pushed the officer into his squad car, physically assaulted him in the vehicle, and struggled with the officer over the officer's weapon, with at least one shot fired inside the car. The struggle then spilled onto the street, where Brown was shot multiple times. Witnesses have said the officer fired on Brown as he tried to run away.

A candlelight vigil for Brown was held Sunday, and tensions erupted later that night. Nearly three dozen people were arrested after a crowd looted and burned stores, vandalized vehicles, and taunted officers.

Ferguson Police Chief Thomas Jackson said the department planned to release the officer's name on Friday morning. On Thursday, the hacker collective Anonymous released what it said was the officer's name as part of what it called Operation Ferguson. The group also urged citizens to confront police, caused the city's web servers to crash, and posted the names and address of the county police chief's family. St. Louis police said on Twitter that the name released by Anonymous was wrong and that the man identified was not a police officer. Within Anonymous, members accused those who posted the information of producing faulty details and endangering one another.

summary:
Two plainclothes New York City police officers were shot Monday night while responding to a reported grocery store robbery in the Bronx. The shooting occurred around 10:30 p.m. near East 184th Street in the Tremont section. The officers, identified as Andrew Dossi, 30, and Aliro Pellerano, 38, were coming off their shift when they and three other plainclothes officers responded to the call. According to police, the officers approached suspects at a Chinese restaurant, where the shooter opened fire from inside and police returned fire. Dossi was shot in the lower back and arm; Pellerano was shot in the chest and arm. Early Tuesday, police described Dossi's condition as critical but stable and Pellerano's as stable, though another account said both officers were in critical but stable condition. Mayor Bill de Blasio visited the hospital and said the officers went "above and beyond the call to protect their fellow New Yorkers."

By Tuesday, police had arrested two people in connection with the shooting. One suspect was captured about 12 hours after the shooting. A second person arrived at a hospital with a gunshot wound — described in one account as an arm wound and in another as a wound to the back — and doctors notified police. Charges were pending. Earlier, around 4:45 a.m. Tuesday, police released video of the person they said fired at the officers. Police Commissioner William J. Bratton said at a news conference at St. Barnabas Hospital that the department was searching for two suspects.

The shooting came about two weeks after two officers were fatally shot while sitting in their patrol car in Brooklyn, an event that had raised tensions between the police and Mayor de Blasio. Police unions had said the mayor stoked anti-police sentiment by supporting protests against the police killings of unarmed black men in New York and Missouri. The incident also occurred on the same day the city announced record low crime levels.

summary:
President-elect Donald Trump promised on Twitter Friday that he would soon make key administration staffing decisions, writing, "Will soon be making some very important decisions on the people who will be running our government!" A busy day was planned in New York. The transition press pool received little guidance on Trump's movements; a pool report issued Friday morning said reporters had gotten no assurance there would not be movements and that the only notable development was the Trump Tower marquee being temporarily papered over for window cleaning. During the campaign, Trump repeatedly left the traveling press behind and mocked reporters for asking if he would wait before starting rallies. Spokeswoman Hope Hicks said, "We fully expect to operate a traditional pool and look forward to implementing our plans in the near future. We appreciate your patience as we navigate the transition process."

In his victory speech early Wednesday, Trump cited infrastructure as a top priority, saying, "We are going to fix our inner cities and rebuild our highways, bridges, tunnels, airports, schools, hospitals. We're going to rebuild our infrastructure, which will become, by the way, second to none." On Election Day, voters in Los Angeles, Seattle and Atlanta were poised to approve billions of dollars in spending on buses, rail lines and other public transportation projects, reflecting broader support for local infrastructure ballot measures.

During the campaign, Senator Bernie Sanders, stumping for Hillary Clinton in September, said of Trump, "The truth is, if you look at Donald Trump's record, what you find is this guy is a pathological liar." Sanders added, "I'm not talking about a little lie there, or stretching the truth here. I am talking about him coming up with things in his head that do not exist. There are psychological definitions there." Sanders also said, "It is trying to divide this country up. It is telling us that we are supposed to hate Muslims, we are supposed to hate Mexicans, if we are men we are supposed to hate women, we are supposed to hate anyone who is different than we are." Shortly before the election, Sanders tweeted, "I hope we defeat Donald Trump and we defeat him badly."

summary: The Clinton campaign announced Saturday it would participate in vote recounts in Wisconsin, Pennsylvania and Michigan if they proceed, despite stating it does not expect the effort to change the outcome. Campaign general counsel Marc Elias wrote in a Medium post that the campaign's analysts had not found evidence of sabotage or "any actionable evidence of hacking or outside attempts to alter the voting technology." Elias said the campaign did not plan to initiate recounts on its own but believed it had "an obligation to the more than 64 million Americans who cast ballots for Hillary Clinton to participate in ongoing proceedings to ensure that an accurate vote count will be reported." He added he did not expect recounts to erase what he said was a roughly 107,000 combined vote margin separating the candidates in the three battleground states. The Obama administration said it was "confident in the overall integrity of electoral infrastructure" and that the elections were "free and fair from a cybersecurity perspective." In a separate statement, Elias said the campaign took concerns "extremely seriously" and noted the election cycle was "unique in the degree of foreign interference witnessed throughout the campaign," citing the U.S. government's conclusion that Russian state actors were behind hacks of the Democratic National Committee and Clinton campaign officials' email accounts, and a Washington Post report that the Russian government was behind much of the "fake news" propaganda circulating online in the closing weeks. Elias said the campaign had "quietly taken a number of steps in the last two weeks to rule in or out any possibility of outside interference in the vote tally in these critical battleground states." Donald Trump was due to be sworn in as president in January.

President-elect Donald Trump spoke by telephone with Taiwan President Tsai Ing-wen, the first such contact between a U.S. president or president-elect and a Taiwanese leader since the United States severed diplomatic relations with Taiwan in 1979 and recognized Beijing as the government of China under the "one China" policy. In a Dec. 11 interview with Fox News Sunday, Trump said he fully understood the policy but did not know why the United States had to be bound by it unless a deal could be made with China involving trade and other issues. "I don't want China dictating to me and this was a call put into me," Trump said. "It was a very nice call. Short. And why should some other nation be able to say I can't take a call?" He also criticized China over its currency policies, actions in the South China Sea, and handling of North Korea. China reacted sharply. The state-run Global Times wrote in an editorial that Trump was "ignorant as a child" in diplomacy and that China needed to "launch a resolute struggle with him" so he would understand that China and the rest of the world "are not to be bullied." Fox News reported that China flew a nuclear-capable bomber over the South China Sea following the call. An Fengshan, spokesman for China's Taiwan Affairs Office, said any breach of the one-China principle would "seriously affect peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait" and undermine relations between Beijing and Washington.

summary:
Former Sen. Barbara Boxer (D-CA) said Thursday on MSNBC's "Live" that Republicans in the Senate were handling Professor Christine Blasey Ford's accusation against Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh "worse than" they handled Anita Hill's accusations against Clarence Thomas in 1991. Boxer said Hill "got no justice" and that Thomas "is still sitting on that bench with a cloud over his head and he votes against women's rights time after time." She said Republicans "have learned nothing in 27 years." Boxer noted that four of ten Democratic members of the Senate Judiciary Committee are women, while zero of eleven Republican members are women. She said Senators Orrin Hatch and Chuck Grassley, who were on the committee during the Hill hearings and called for an FBI investigation then, "are walking away from their own precedents on the committee."

Rep. Kevin Cramer (R-ND), the Republican Senate nominee in North Dakota, said Friday in a radio interview on KNOX that giving credence to Ford's allegation is "absurd." He described Ford's claim as "even more absurd" than Hill's because Kavanaugh and Ford were teenagers at the time and because it was "an attempt or something that never went anywhere." Cramer said, "These are teenagers who evidently were drunk according to her own, her own statements. They were drunk when it evidently happened... even by her own accusation."

Anita Hill was a professor at the University of Oklahoma College of Law in 1991 when she accused Thomas, who was confirmed as a justice. Christine Blasey Ford is a clinical psychology professor at Palo Alto University. Ford has accused Kavanaugh, whose confirmation hearing is continuing with the prospect of Ford testifying.

President Donald Trump hosted the 2018 college football national champion Clemson Tigers at the White House on Monday, January 14, 2019. The event was scheduled for 6:30 p.m. ET in the East Room. Trump announced the visit on January 11, stating he looked forward to hosting the team from South Carolina. On the morning of the event, Trump told reporters the team would be served "McDonald's, Wendy's, and Burger King, with some pizza," and guessed it would be their favorite food. One account included Domino's pizza among the offerings. The White House said Trump paid for the food himself because much of the residence staff was furloughed during the partial government shutdown. Clemson had defeated the Alabama Crimson Tide for the championship. Star quarterback Trevor Lawrence favors Chick-fil-A, according to one report. The fast-food menu drew varied reaction on Twitter, including comparisons to previous administrations and references to Wendy's social-media presence. Separately, Ayesha Curry, a bestselling cookbook author and wife of Golden State Warriors guard Stephen Curry, invited the Clemson team to a "real feast and celebration" after the White House visit. The invitation followed a Twitter user's joke referencing Stephen Curry's September 2017 statement that he did not want to visit the White House after the Warriors' NBA championship because he did not "stand for what our president has said, and the things he hasn't said at the right time." Trump subsequently said the Warriors' invitation had been withdrawn.

summary:
BuzzFeed News published a report on Friday alleging that President Trump directed his former personal attorney Michael Cohen to lie to Congress about a proposed Trump Tower project in Moscow. The report, attributed to two law enforcement officials, also stated that Trump had hoped to travel to Russia during the 2016 presidential campaign to meet with President Vladimir Putin. Late Friday, the office of Special Counsel Robert Mueller issued a rare public statement disputing the article. Peter Carr, a spokesman for Mueller, said: "BuzzFeed's description of specific statements to the Special Counsel's Office, and characterization of documents and testimony obtained by this office, regarding Michael Cohen's congressional testimony are not accurate." Anthony Cormier, who co-authored the BuzzFeed report, told CNN he had not personally reviewed the evidence but said the story was "100 percent accurate" based on information provided to the special counsel.

On Friday, Trump posted on Twitter quoting a Fox News commentator and wrote that Cohen was "lying to reduce his jail time!" Cohen was sentenced to three years in prison in December after pleading guilty to lying to Congress and campaign finance violations related to hush-money payments. Trump also tweeted "Watch father-in-law!" Deputy Press Secretary Hogan Gidley called the report "absolutely ridiculous" and said it did not warrant a presidential response, according to CBS correspondent Mark Knoller.

On Saturday, Trump spoke to reporters as he left the White House for Dover Air Force Base to attend the return of four Americans killed in Syria. He called the BuzzFeed story "phony" and said mainstream media coverage of it was "disgraceful" and a "disgrace to journalism," adding: "It hurts me to say it but mainstream media has truly lost its credibility. This is a very bad thing for our country."

summary:
The House Judiciary Committee advanced two articles of impeachment against President Trump on Friday, charging abuse of power in his dealings with Ukraine and obstruction of Congress. The full House of Representatives was scheduled to vote on the articles on Wednesday, December 18, with impeachment expected to pass the Democratic-held chamber. If the House votes to impeach, the process moves to the Republican-led Senate for a trial, where a two-thirds majority — including at least 20 Republicans — would be required for removal. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell told Fox News he expects Trump to be acquitted, saying there is "zero chance" the president is removed from office.

On Tuesday night, designated "Impeachment Eve," MoveOn reported more than 600 rallies across all 50 states, with hundreds of thousands of participants in locations ranging from suburban areas to small towns.

A Gallup poll conducted December 2 through 15 and released Wednesday showed Trump's job approval rating at 45 percent, up six percentage points since the House opened the impeachment inquiry in the fall. The same poll found 46 percent of Americans support impeachment and removal, down six points from the first reading after Speaker Nancy Pelosi announced the inquiry, while 51 percent oppose impeachment and removal, up five points over the same period. Real Clear Politics tracked eight major polls on the question; only two showed a bare majority of 50 percent supporting impeachment. Tom Bevan, founder of the news organization, said "support for impeachment is officially underwater."

summary: Deputy National Security Adviser Tony Blinken said Friday on NPR's "Morning Edition" that President Obama has the authority to take limited military action in Syria without congressional approval, but "it's neither his desire nor intention to use that authority absent Congress backing him." The same day, the White House announced that Obama canceled a trip to California scheduled for Monday and Tuesday to remain in Washington and lobby members of Congress on a resolution authorizing force. The trip had included a fundraiser and a speech to the AFL-CIO. The schedule change was announced from St. Petersburg, Russia, where Obama was attending the G-20 summit. A Senate panel has approved an authorization resolution, but a significant number of senators remain unconvinced and opposition is growing in the House. On CBS's "Face the Nation," House Intelligence Committee Chairman Mike Rogers (R-MI) said Congress would not authorize a strike if the vote were held today, adding that the administration lost support over the past week. Rogers criticized the White House for not having strong relationships with Congress, said the process "should have started two years ago," and called the administration's explanation of the national interest "awful." He agreed with host Bob Schieffer that authorization would fail today. Rogers said Obama needed to be empowered for a negotiated settlement but the country lacks credibility to tell Syrian rebels to pause fighting. He described the administration's congressional strategy as "mystifying," noting Obama did not call Congress back into session after announcing Saturday that he would seek authorization.

summary:
U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry on Monday said in London that Syrian President Bashar Assad could end the crisis by turning over all his chemical weapons to international control. State Department spokeswoman Marie Harf said the same day that Kerry was not putting forth a formal proposal and that the United States would consider the idea floated by the foreign ministers of Russia and Syria with "serious skepticism" because it might be a stalling tactic. Harf said Syria had consistently refused to destroy its chemical weapons in the past.

On Tuesday, Kerry told the House Armed Services Committee that the United States was still awaiting a proposal from the Russians about how Syria could agree to give up its chemical weapons, but would not wait long. He said any proposal must not be used as a delaying tactic and must be verifiable, real, and include tangible conditions for Assad to forfeit his chemical weapons. Kerry was testifying to persuade committee members to back President Obama's request for authorization of military action against Syria, a strike that could be avoided if Syria gave up its weapons.

On Thursday, Kerry and his team began two days of meetings with Russian counterparts in Geneva. At a news conference with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, Kerry rejected Assad's suggestion that he begin submitting data on his chemical weapons arsenal 30 days after signing an international chemical weapons ban. Kerry said Assad had cited a 30-day lead time as standard, but responded, "There is nothing standard about this process," because Assad had used chemical weapons. "The words of the Syrian regime in our judgment are simply not enough," Kerry said. He listed requirements: the process had to be real, comprehensive, verifiable, credible, timely, and implemented in a timely fashion, with consequences if it did not take place. Kerry cautioned that a U.S. military strike could occur if Assad did not agree to dismantle his chemical arsenal properly. Lavrov said the dismantling "will make unnecessary any strike against the Syrian Arab Republic."

The U.S. State Department issued a fact sheet on Wednesday rebutting what it called "10 False Claims About Ukraine" made by Russian President Vladimir Putin during a news conference the previous day. The department's statement rejected Putin's assertions that Ukraine's new government is illegitimate, that its parliament is under the influence of extremists or terrorists, that Russian forces were acting to protect Russian military assets, that there have been attacks on churches, that a humanitarian crisis is prompting Ukrainian refugees to seek Russian asylum, and that ethnic Russians were targeted for violence requiring rescue. The fact sheet stated there were "absolutely no evidence of a humanitarian crisis" and "no credible reports of any ethnic Russians being under threat" outside Russian state media. The department characterized Putin's narrative as "startling Russian fiction," invoking Fyodor Dostoyevsky's formula "two plus two equals five." Separately, commentary has attributed responsibility for the Russian intervention to the Obama administration's "reset" policy, spearheaded by then-Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, which was mistakenly translated into Russian as "overcharge." That commentary also cited Russian moves to support Bashar al-Assad in Syria, build nuclear facilities in Iran, and invade Crimea as consequences of perceived U.S. weakness, and noted that media outlets and intelligence services had not predicted an invasion.

On February 14, 2018, a shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida killed 17 people and injured 14 others. The accused shooter was identified as 19-year-old Nikolas Cruz, a former student who had been expelled for disciplinary reasons. Cruz allegedly used an AR-15 rifle purchased legally from a dealer in Coral Springs roughly a year earlier.

In the week following the shooting, several developments occurred. On February 20, police were called to Oberlin High School in Louisiana after a student commented that a square root symbol "looked like a gun." The Allen Parish Sheriff's Office searched the student's home and found no guns or evidence of access to guns, and no evidence of intent to commit harm. The sheriff's office stated the student used "extremely poor judgment" but there was no evidence to support criminal charges.

Broward County Sheriff Scott Israel defended his office's response to the Parkland shooting amid questions about whether deputies hung back instead of pursuing the gunman. Israel said that to his knowledge, deputies followed protocol and did not wait for specialized teams before entering the school, but that details remained unclear and were being examined.

Students rallied outside the U.S. Capitol on Wednesday calling for gun control legislation. The protest was one of several student demonstrations, including a walkout at a Florida high school where students marched to Stoneman Douglas. A national school walkout was planned for March 14, and a "March for Our Lives" was expected on March 24 in cities across the country.

U.S. Senator John McCain underwent surgery at the Mayo Clinic in Phoenix on Sunday to treat an intestinal infection related to diverticulitis and was in stable condition on Monday, his office said in a statement. The 81-year-old Arizona Republican was diagnosed with brain cancer in July 2017 and received chemotherapy and radiation treatment. In December he was treated at a military hospital outside Washington for side effects of cancer therapy. Since then he has been participating in physical therapy at his home in Cornville, Arizona, near Sedona, as he recovers from the side effects of cancer treatment. McCain had previously said he planned to return to Washington in January but remained at home. His office said he has remained engaged in his work as chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee and has had frequent visits from family, friends, staff and Senate colleagues. His wife Cindy McCain posted on Twitter: "My husband @SenJohnMcCain is doing well after his surgery," adding that he was looking forward to getting back home. McCain, the 2008 Republican presidential nominee who lost to Barack Obama, is serving his sixth Senate term. On Friday, before the surgery, McCain applauded President Donald Trump's decision to launch airstrikes on Syria; he has been a vocal proponent of U.S. military engagement in Syria for years and visited anti-Assad rebels in 2013.

The special election for Ohio's 12th Congressional District remained too close to call after counting concluded Tuesday night. Republican Troy Balderson led Democrat Danny O'Connor by a narrow margin. Democratic National Committee Chairman Tom Perez said the closeness of the contest in a district President Trump won by double digits in 2016 and Republicans have held since 1983 signaled Democratic competitiveness nationwide, noting more than 60 Republican-held districts are rated more competitive for Democrats than OH-12.

The dedication ceremony for the George W. Bush Presidential Center took place Thursday in Dallas before a crowd of 10,000. All five living presidents attended — Barack Obama, Bill Clinton, Jimmy Carter, George H.W. Bush, and the honoree, George W. Bush — along with their wives. Former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, former British Prime Minister Tony Blair, and children of former presidents were also present. A military guard carried a line of flags off the stage as the ceremony concluded.

Bush, known for punctuality, began his remarks a few minutes early. He opened with humor, joking there was a time he would not be found in a library, much less found one. Citing Alexander Hamilton's concern that former presidents would wander like "discontented ghosts," he said, "actually, I think we seem pretty happy." His tone grew more serious: "In the end, leaders are defined by the convictions that they hold." His chief conviction, he said: "The United States of America must strive to expand the reach of freedom." He noted his joy that his father was able to attend: "41, it is awesome that you are here today." Tears filled his eyes as he called the presidency "the honor of a lifetime" and said, "Whatever challenges come before us, I will always believe our nation's best days lie ahead." Through tears he added a "God bless," then smiled, winked, and waved.

Obama, who had previously characterized Bush's policies as having "wiped away a budget surplus" and "crashed the economy," praised his predecessor's service at the ceremony, observing the tradition that sitting presidents set aside partisan differences to honor the shared experience of the office.

summary:
Former National Security Agency contractor Edward Snowden, who leaked details of classified surveillance programs, remained in the transit zone of Moscow's Sheremetyevo Airport this week after fleeing Hong Kong over the weekend. Sen. Tom Coburn, Republican of Oklahoma, appeared Tuesday on MSNBC's "Morning Joe" and said the inability to secure Snowden's return demonstrated failed foreign policy by the Obama administration, adding that China and Russia were benefiting from the situation.

The organization declined to discuss his plans, citing security concerns, and on Monday denied reports that Snowden was being debriefed by Russian intelligence.

Lonnie Snowden, the father of Edward Snowden, sent a letter to Attorney General Eric Holder proposing terms under which his son would return to the United States. He said Edward Snowden would likely come back if assured he could remain free before trial, not be subject to a gag order, and be tried in a venue of his choosing. Lonnie Snowden also proposed that charges be dismissed if those terms were violated. He said he had not spoken to his son since April and expressed concern about the people surrounding him.

President Barack Obama said Thursday he would not engage in "wheeling and dealing and trading and a whole host of other issues, simply to get a guy extradited so he can face the justice system here in the United States." The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Edward Snowden has reportedly requested asylum in Ecuador.

summary:
The death of former White House press secretary James S. Brady has been ruled a homicide by a medical examiner in Northern Virginia, where Brady died at age 73. The ruling comes 33 years after Brady was shot in the head during John Hinckley Jr.'s March 1981 assassination attempt on President Ronald Reagan. Hinckley emptied a six-shot .22-caliber revolver, striking Brady and leaving him partially paralyzed; Brady never regained normal use of his limbs and underwent hours of surgery and further operations over the years.

Brady died earlier this week — one account said Monday, another said Tuesday — from what his family described as a series of health issues. The Virginia medical examiner attributed the death to the 1981 bullet wound. The medical examiner's office would not comment on the cause and manner of death, though a spokeswoman confirmed an autopsy was completed.

The District of Columbia Metropolitan Police were notified of the homicide ruling Friday and are investigating. Hinckley, now 59, was found not guilty by reason of insanity in 1982 and has been confined to St. Elizabeths Hospital in Washington, receiving psychiatric treatment. summary: The Senate confirmed Mari Carmen Aponte as U.S. ambassador to El Salvador on Thursday. The vote to end debate was 62 to 37, with nine Republicans joining all Democrats and independents. Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau released a statement on Saturday expressing sorrow over the death of Cuban leader Fidel Castro, who died Friday according to an announcement by his brother Raul on Cuban state television. In the statement, Trudeau described Castro as "a larger than life leader who served his people for almost half a century" and "a legendary revolutionary and orator" who "made significant improvements to the education and healthcare of his island nation." Trudeau noted that his father, former Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau, "was very proud to call him a friend" and that he himself had met Castro at his father's funeral. Trudeau acknowledged Castro as "a controversial figure" but said "both Mr. Castro's supporters and detractors recognized his tremendous dedication and love for the Cuban people who had a deep and lasting affection for 'el Comandante.'" He added: "We join the people of Cuba today in mourning the loss of this remarkable leader."

The statement drew immediate criticism. Republican U.S. Senators Marco Rubio of Florida and Ted Cruz of Texas, both Cuban-Americans, denounced Trudeau's remarks. Rubio called the statement "shameful" according to one account, while another reported he called it "shameful and embarrassing." Cruz called it "disgraceful." Cruz, who was born in Canada to a father who fled Cuba after participating in the early days of the revolution, issued further comments on Cuba and Castro. Canadian politicians also criticized the statement. President Barack Obama offered condolences to Cubans without directly praising Castro. President-elect Donald Trump stated: "Though the tragedies, deaths and pain caused by Fidel Castro cannot be erased, our administration will do all it can to ensure the Cuban people can finally begin their journey toward prosperity and liberty."

Castro had attended Pierre Trudeau's funeral in Montreal in 2000. A spokeswoman for Trudeau, Andree-Lyne Halle, confirmed Monday that the prime minister would not travel to Havana for Castro's funeral. Governor General David Johnston, Queen Elizabeth II's representative as Canada's head of state, will attend in his place.

summary: Former President Donald Trump delivered his first major post-presidency address as the final scheduled speaker at the Conservative Political Action Conference in Orlando, Florida, on Sunday. He took the stage at 5 p.m. ET, more than an hour behind schedule, and was greeted by a cheering crowd. "Do you miss me yet?" he asked as attendees responded enthusiastically. During the speech, Trump attacked the Biden administration, the media, and immigrants, echoing themes from his 2016 campaign announcement. He criticized Biden's reversal of several Trump-era policies, including the end of the transgender military ban, rejoining the Paris climate agreement, and reversing a visa ban on legal immigration. Trump repeated numerous false claims about voter fraud and the 2020 election results, alluding to his belief that the election was stolen. "Who knows, who knows, I may even decide to beat them for a third time," he said with a grin, referencing a potential 2024 run. Trump dismissed reports that he would start a third party, calling them "fake news." "I am not starting a new party. That was fake news," he said. "Wouldn't that be brilliant? Let's start a new party and divide our vote," he added sarcastically. The Wall Street Journal had reported in January that Trump was discussing the possibility, citing people familiar with the matter. Trump reaffirmed his movement would remain in the Republican Party: "We have the Republican party. It's going to unite and be stronger than ever before." Regarding media coverage, Fox News aired the speech live. CNN continued its coronavirus pandemic coverage, while MSNBC continued its "PoliticsNation" program but aired a short clip. An MSNBC spokesperson declined to comment on the decision not to air the speech, and CNN did not respond to a request for comment. CNN's Brianna Keilar later said Trump's address was packed with "false narratives and talking points" pushed by Fox News hosts, contributors, and guests.

summary: After the first presidential debate in Denver on Oct. 3, 2012, national and state polls showed gains for Republican nominee Mitt Romney against President Barack Obama. The shift was consistent with the largest debate-induced swings in past presidential campaigns; in seven of the last nine debate series the challenger gained more than the incumbent. Obama acknowledged on the Tom Joyner radio show Wednesday that he had been "too polite" in the first debate, and his supporters were calling for a more aggressive performance at the next debate, scheduled for Tuesday at Hofstra University in New York. summary: At the 2015 MTV Video Music Awards on Sunday, rapper Kanye West, 38, announced he would run for president in 2020. Accepting the Video Vanguard Award, West said, "I'm not a politician, bro," and told the crowd, "I have decided in 2020 to run for president." During the speech he also said he had "rolled up a little something to knock the edge off," and added, "I'm confident. I believe in myself. We the millennials, bro. This is a new mentality. We're not going to control our kids with brands. We're not going to teach low self-esteem and hate to our kids. We're going to teach our kids that they can be something ... to believe in themselves." He declared, "It ain't about me, It's about ideas, bro!" Host Miley Cyrus reacted by saying, "Trump, you had my vote. But now, Kanye West for president!" In an interview with Rolling Stone published Wednesday, Donald Trump said he was watching the broadcast and commented, "I hope to run against him someday." Trump said he doesn't "quite get" comparisons between himself and West, adding, "He's actually a different kind of person than people think. He's a nice guy," and noted West's "extremely positive" past comments about him. On Monday, the Democratic Party posted on Twitter that it would welcome West's candidacy and shared GIFs mocking Republican candidates Chris Christie, Marco Rubio, and Scott Walker on immigration. White House Press Secretary Josh Earnest, traveling to Alaska on Air Force One, told the Associated Press he was looking "forward to seeing what slogan he [Kanye] chooses to embroider on his campaign hat."

President-elect Donald Trump selected Steven Mnuchin, 53, as his nominee for Treasury secretary, according to reports Tuesday. Mnuchin, a Yale graduate, spent 17 years at Goldman Sachs before leaving in 2002 to found the hedge fund Dune Capital Management. He also invested in the entertainment industry and housing. Mnuchin served as national finance chairman for Trump's presidential campaign and was at Trump Tower Tuesday meeting with the transition team. The same day, Trump met with Goldman Sachs president and chief operating officer Gary Cohn as he continued vetting Cabinet candidates, and held a private dinner with Mitt Romney as his inner circle debated the secretary of State selection. Transition spokesman Jason Miller said Trump was "taking people who've been successful in all different walks of life" and had "fantastic relationships with a number of industry titans." Democratic National Committee spokesman Adam Hodge criticized the selection as a betrayal of Trump's "drain the swamp" pledge, calling Mnuchin a "billionaire hedge fund manager and Goldman Sachs alumnus who preyed on homeowners struggling during the recession." During the campaign, Trump had run an ad portraying the Goldman Sachs chief executive as the personification of a global elite that had "robbed our working class." As Treasury secretary, Mnuchin would oversee proposed tax cuts, an infrastructure spending plan, and sanctions against nations including Cuba and Iran.

President Donald Trump's nominee for secretary of the Navy, Philip Bilden, withdrew from consideration on Sunday, citing privacy concerns and the difficulty of separating himself from his business interests to meet federal ethics requirements. In a letter, Bilden wrote that he "fully support[s] the president's agenda" but determined he "will not be able to satisfy the Office of Government Ethics requirements without undue disruption and materially adverse divestment of my family's private financial interests." Bilden, a businessman and former military intelligence officer in the Army Reserve, recently retired after 25 years from the global private equity management firm HarbourVest Partners LLC. His vast financial holdings, many earned in Hong Kong, would have made it difficult to survive scrutiny by the Office of Government Ethics, according to USNI News. Defense Secretary James Mattis confirmed the withdrawal in a statement, saying Bilden's decision was a "personal decision driven by privacy concerns and significant challenges he faced in separating himself from his business interests." Mattis said he would make a recommendation to Trump for a new nominee in the coming days. The withdrawal follows a similar decision weeks earlier by Vincent Viola, Trump's pick for secretary of the Army, who also cited an inability to disentangle himself from his business interests. Eight days before Bilden's withdrawal, White House Press Secretary Sean Spicer had condemned reports that Bilden would withdraw, tweeting that he was "100% committed" to the job.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Wednesday urged the United States to begin direct talks with North Korea to resolve the nuclear crisis, saying: "We should talk to parties whose behavior we want to change, whose behavior we want to influence." That account said China and Japan supported the resolution. Other accounts described the resolution as still under negotiation earlier in the week.

summary:
Following the massacre of nine people at a black church in Charleston, South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley on Monday called for the removal of the Confederate battle flag from the Statehouse grounds in Columbia and pledged to order legislators back for a special session if they did not act on the issue themselves. The flag had flown on the grounds since a 2000 bipartisan compromise moved it from atop the Capitol dome to a Confederate monument; for 15 years lawmakers had declined to revisit the matter, calling the compromise settled. Removing the flag requires a two-thirds majority in the legislature.

On Tuesday, Republican Lt. Gov. Henry McMaster, who chaired the state Republican Party when the 2000 compromise was reached and who had said during his failed 2010 gubernatorial bid that he considered the issue resolved, posted on his official Facebook page that "the time has come to consider an appropriate location for the Confederate flag."

South Carolina newspapers treated Haley's announcement as major news. The Post and Courier in Charleston ran a front-page editorial calling for the flag to come down. The Herald-Journal of Spartanburg led with an image of Haley's news conference and also prominently featured a lawmaker who likened removal efforts to a "Stalinist purge." Other state papers, including The Island Packet of Bluffton and The State in Columbia, led with flag images and lawmaker responses.

Elsewhere in the region, coverage varied. The Brunswick News in Georgia led with local weather. In Alabama, some newspapers examined how the South Carolina debate might affect their state. In Mississippi, where the Confederate emblem is part of the state flag, the Republican leader of the state assembly said it was time to change the flag. The largest metropolitan newspapers in the South led with the story.

summary:
Billionaire investor George Soros contributed $6 million in mid-December 2015 to Priorities USA Action, a super PAC supporting Hillary Clinton's presidential campaign, according to Federal Election Commission disclosures filed Sunday. The donation brought Soros's total contributions to pro-Clinton super PACs during the 2015 period to $8 million, according to one account, which included a $1 million gift earlier in the year to the same committee and a separate $1 million contribution to American Bridge 21st Century. Another report placed his total super PAC giving for the 2016 election cycle at more than $8 million, exceeding his combined contributions to such groups during the entire 2012 and 2014 cycles. A third account stated Soros had given $7 million to Priorities USA Action specifically in the current cycle.

Priorities USA Action reported raising $41 million on Clinton's behalf in 2015, with $25.3 million collected in the final six months; Soros's December contribution represented nearly one-quarter of that half-year total. Other major donors to the committee in 2015 included media executive Haim Saban and his wife Cheryl, who gave $5 million combined; philanthropist Laure Woods, who contributed $2.3 million; and investor Donald Sussman, who gave $2.5 million. Together, those four donors accounted for two-fifths of the super PAC's 2015 fundraising.

Soros, chairman of Soros Fund Management, has a history of substantial political giving. In 2004, he contributed $18.5 million to outside groups working to elect Democrats and defeat President George W. Bush. He supported John Kerry's presidential bid that year and backed Barack Obama's campaigns in 2008 and 2012, giving $1 million to Priorities USA in 2012 when it supported Obama's re-election.

According to an email from Neera Tanden, president of the Center for American Progress, a former campaign aide relayed to Clinton that Soros appreciated her willingness to meet with him on policy matters. Tanden wrote that Soros said he had been impressed by his ability to reach Clinton directly and noted he had never met with President Obama, though Tanden added she thought he had.

summary: Democrat Phil Murphy won the New Jersey gubernatorial election on Tuesday, defeating Republican Lieutenant Governor Kim Guadagno by approximately 13 percentage points, according to exit polls. The margin roughly matched Hillary Clinton's 14-point victory in the state over President Trump in 2016. Guadagno, who was endorsed by former Governor Christine Todd Whitman at a campaign event in Mount Holly during the final push, faced headwinds from both Trump's unpopularity in the state and outgoing Governor Chris Christie's historically low approval ratings, which stood at 22 percent in exit polls. Public opinion polls had shown Murphy with a consistent double-digit lead throughout the general election campaign. Murphy campaigned on liberal issues without pivoting toward the center, while Guadagno focused heavily on lowering the state's high property taxes before veering right in the final month to rally conservative voters, seizing on Murphy's openness to making New Jersey a "sanctuary state." The strategy did not appear to resonate with the state's predominantly Democratic electorate. Observers noted that Democrats were unlikely to view the New Jersey result as evidence of a building wave for the 2018 midterms, though Murphy's victory helped Democrats begin to reduce the Republican majority in governors' mansions nationwide.
