summary: The U.S. House of Representatives voted 405-11 on Tuesday to adopt a nonbinding resolution formally recognizing the 1915 killing of an estimated 1.5 million Armenians by the Ottoman Empire as genocide. The measure also rejects efforts to associate the U.S. government with denial of the Armenian genocide or any other genocide. Historians estimate up to 1.5 million Armenians were killed around World War I, and many scholars regard it as the 20th century's first genocide. Turkey disputes the genocide designation, saying the death toll has been inflated and that those killed were victims of a civil war. The vote followed Turkey's military incursion into northern Syria against Kurdish forces. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi said, "Recent attacks by the Turkish military against the Kurdish people are a stark reminder of the danger in our own time." Turkey's foreign minister responded on Twitter: "This shameful decision of those exploiting history in politics is null & void for our Government & people." At a U.S. Helsinki Commission hearing Thursday, Rep. Steve Cohen (D-Tenn.) said he had always opposed the resolution but voted for it because "Turkey doesn't seem to respect the United States at all." Cohen cited a 2017 incident in which Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's bodyguards assaulted protesters in Washington, D.C., and the recent Syrian incursion, adding, "I can just say this that the mood of the Congress has changed as well. There were never 218 votes for the Armenian resolution" before this year. Gonul Tol, director of the Center for Turkish Studies at the Middle East Institute, testified that "a genocide resolution should be about genocide. It should not be weaponized and politicized." Former U.N. Ambassador Samantha Power wrote in a New York Times op-ed that the vote is "a reminder of how important truth-telling is to American foreign policy, and how ultimately self-defeating it is for the United States to bend to autocratic pressure tactics, whether from Turkey or anywhere else."

summary:
On Friday, women's rights advocates and members of the Connecticut General Assembly joined Democratic gubernatorial candidate Ned Lamont and his running mate Susan Bysiewicz in calling for an FBI investigation into Brett Kavanaugh's nomination to the U.S. Supreme Court. Lamont said the nomination threatened women's health in Connecticut and demanded a public statement from Republican candidate Bob Stefanowski, who had declined to offer an opinion on the issue during a televised debate earlier in the week. "Rights are going to be jeopardized if Kavanaugh is approved for the Supreme Court," Lamont said, speaking shortly before the Republican majority on the Senate Judiciary Committee voted to advance the nomination.

Also on Friday, Senate Judiciary Committee member Jeff Flake (R-AZ) stated that the floor vote on Kavanaugh should be delayed for up to one week to allow an FBI investigation into the allegations against the nominee. Flake said he would vote to advance the nomination to the floor with the understanding that such an investigation would occur. "I think it would be proper to delay the floor vote for up to, but not more than, one week, in order to let the FBI continue — to do an investigation, limited in time and scope to the current allegations that are there, and limited in time to no more than one week," Flake said. He added that he would only be comfortable moving forward with Kavanaugh on the floor if there is further FBI investigation.

Obama said that ten days earlier, men, women, and children were massacred in Syria in the worst chemical weapons attack of the 21st century. summary: Freedom Industries, the company whose tank ruptured on Jan. 9 and released 7,500 gallons of chemicals into the Elk River, leaving 300,000 West Virginia residents without clean water, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection. summary: Hillary Clinton stepped down as Secretary of State on Friday, handing over the department to former Senator John Kerry. During her four-year term beginning in 2009, Clinton traveled 956,733 miles to 112 countries, making more than 100 trips abroad and becoming the most traveled Secretary of State in the department's history, surpassing the record set by Madeleine Albright, who took 96 trips from 1997 to 2001. A poll commissioned by The Hill found that 43 percent of voters view Clinton more favorably following her tenure. She has not disclosed future plans, though speculation persists about a potential 2016 presidential candidacy, which she has not ruled out. On her final day, in an interview with The Associated Press, Clinton said critics of the administration's handling of the September attacks in Benghazi, Libya, that killed four Americans including Ambassador J. Christopher Stevens are not living in an "evidence-based world" and that their inability to "accept the facts" is unfortunate for the nation. An independent panel had previously denounced the State Department for failures related to Benghazi and assigned blame to four agency officials; Clinton was not personally faulted in the report, though she later accepted responsibility during congressional testimony.

The Pentagon announced Thursday that two B-2 stealth bombers completed a training mission to South Korea in a show of military force amid rising tensions with North Korea. The White House said the United States is prepared to defend South Korea and respond to any military threat, and urged Pyongyang to restrain its "bellicose rhetoric" after the regime threatened Washington with "miserable destruction." House Republican lawmakers pressed for tougher sanctions targeting banks that continue to do business with North Korea in efforts to block the regime from profiting from drug trafficking and missile sales.

North Korea views the joint military drills as part of a U.S. plot to invade and objects particularly to U.S. nuclear activities in the region. summary:
Director of National Intelligence James Clapper testified before the Senate Intelligence Committee on Wednesday, calling on former NSA systems analyst Edward Snowden to return the remaining secret documents he took. Clapper said Snowden's disclosures of National Security Agency surveillance programs had caused "profound damage" by revealing methods to terrorists, who he said are changing how they communicate to avoid detection. Snowden's revelations showed the NSA sweeps up millions of Americans' phone and Internet records, prompting an outcry that led President Barack Obama to ask agencies and Congress to consider reforms.

Earlier this month, Obama delivered a speech outlining intelligence reforms, including new limits on the NSA's ability to collect and search data about nearly all Americans' phone calls. He directed Clapper and Attorney General Eric H. Holder Jr. to develop additional reforms.

The administration subsequently announced new declassification rules permitting Internet companies — including Google, Microsoft, Yahoo, and Facebook — to disclose aggregate data about the number of government demands for customer information. The companies dropped their lawsuits before the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court. The rules do not allow disclosure of what information is collected or the volume of data. A provision bars start-up companies from revealing information about government requests for two years. Holder and Clapper said in a joint statement that the disclosure of aggregate data addresses an important area of concern to communications providers and the public.

On Monday, a group of lawmakers wrote to Obama demanding Clapper's removal as Director of National Intelligence, stating his continued role is incompatible with restoring trust and ensuring transparency. The legislators noted that Clapper denied under oath early last year that the NSA spied on millions of Americans, later saying he had tried to give the "least untruthful" answer without revealing classified information. They said asking Clapper to report on needed reforms is not a credible solution.

The lawmakers also cited documents released by Snowden showing the NSA intentionally attempted to undermine private companies' encryption methods, a practice Obama did not mention in his speech. They criticized the omission and advocated for higher standards for the use of National Security Letters, which compel individuals and businesses to turn over information to the government.

summary: Congress passed a $16.3 billion bill to address long wait times for veterans' health care at Department of Veterans Affairs facilities. summary:
President Obama announced on Saturday that he would seek congressional authorization before launching a military strike against the Syrian government in retaliation for a chemical weapons attack. The decision came as American destroyers armed with Tomahawk missiles waited in the Mediterranean Sea. In a hurriedly organized Rose Garden appearance, Obama said he was prepared to give the order but was mindful of his role as president of "the world's oldest constitutional democracy." The move followed a week of diplomatic isolation: the United Nations Security Council had not authorized force, the British parliament had voted against military action, and nearly every NATO member declined to participate. France was the only major ally to express support for a potential strike.

The Syrian opposition coalition, based in Istanbul, issued a statement Sunday urging Congress to approve the strike, warning that failure to respond would encourage dictators in Iran, North Korea, and elsewhere. The opposition also called for increased arms shipments to rebel forces.

summary:
U.S. Rep. James Lankford won the Republican nomination for Oklahoma's open U.S. Senate seat Tuesday, capturing more than 50 percent of the vote in a seven-candidate primary and avoiding an August runoff. The 46-year-old two-term congressman from Edmond, a Baptist minister and junior member of House leadership, will face the Democratic nominee and an independent in November. The seat opened because Sen. Tom Coburn decided to forego the final two years of his term amid a recurrence of cancer. Oklahoma has not sent a Democrat to the Senate in three decades.

Lankford faced a fierce challenge from former Oklahoma House Speaker T.W. Shannon, who was backed by national Tea Party groups and had endorsements from Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas and former Alaska Gov. Sarah Palin, as well as hundreds of thousands of dollars in spending from the Senate Conservatives Fund. Shannon, who is of Native American heritage, would have been the Senate's second African-American Republican in the current session. Shannon had been closing on Lankford's early lead, but the Mississippi Senate runoff drew money and attention from national conservatives that could have otherwise been targeted at the Oklahoma race, and Shannon struggled to maintain momentum without more outside money.

Lankford received a boost from Coburn, who stopped short of endorsing him but attacked outside groups running ads against Lankford and complimented the congressman's integrity in remarks Lankford used heavily in his final ad push. The state's other senator, James Inhofe, also easily won his GOP primary Tuesday.

After the votes were counted, The Associated Press quoted Lankford as saying: "We have said all along — the other six folks in this race are not our opponent." He also pledged to work with Democrats if he won in November. "I have not written off our nation," he said. "We have been through difficult times before. We can resolve this."

In the race for Lankford's House seat, former Oklahoma state Sen. Steve Russell and state Corporation Commissioner Patrice Douglas advanced to a runoff.

Donald Trump spent Friday and Saturday campaigning in Iowa ahead of the Feb. 1 caucuses. On Friday night, he stayed at the Holiday Inn Express in Sioux Center, Iowa, his first overnight stay in an early-voting state during the campaign. Speaking to reporters, Trump said of the hotel: "Good mattress, staff was great, good mattress, good everything. It's different and it's certainly not Mar-a-Lago, but it's very nice. I actually enjoyed it. It was good, it was clean." On Saturday, Trump held a rally in Sioux Center. There he declared, "I could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody and I wouldn't lose any voters, okay? It's, like, incredible," and illustrated the statement by pointing his finger like a gun and cocking his thumb. The audience laughed. That evening, Trump stayed at the Royal Amsterdam Hotel in Pella, Iowa, a Dutch-style hotel, where he dined on steak and potatoes in the hotel restaurant.

summary: President Obama on Wednesday formally nominated Sharon Block and Richard Griffin Jr. to the National Labor Relations Board, re-submitting the two positions after a federal appeals court ruled their January 2012 recess appointments unconstitutional. Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau made his first official visit to Washington in 19 years this week, meeting with President Obama at the White House. The remark referenced Donald Trump's questions about Cruz's eligibility. Obama also praised Trudeau's "positive and optimistic vision" and drew parallels between Trudeau's rise and his own.

summary: President Donald Trump on Monday ordered the expulsion of 60 Russian diplomats from the United States and the closure of the Russian consulate in Seattle in response to a nerve agent attack earlier this month in Salisbury, United Kingdom, that targeted former Russian spy Sergei Skripal and his daughter. White House Press Secretary Sarah Sanders will attend the Winter Olympics closing ceremony in Pyeongchang, South Korea, as part of the U.S. delegation, a White House official confirmed. Pence's appearance at the opening ceremony drew criticism from U.S. athletes including skier Gus Kenworthy and figure skater Adam Rippon, who both cited the vice president's record on LGBTQ issues. Ivanka Trump's planned attendance at the closing ceremony has also drawn criticism on social media.

summary:
House Speaker Paul Ryan will lead a bipartisan congressional delegation to Puerto Rico on Friday to survey damage from Hurricanes Irma and Maria. The delegation includes House Appropriations Committee Chairman Rodney Frelinghuysen of New Jersey, the committee's top Democrat Nita Lowey of New York, Puerto Rico's Resident Commissioner Jenniffer González-Colón, and House Republican Conference Chair Cathy McMorris Rodgers. The visit follows a meeting last week between Ryan and González-Colón in the speaker's office.

The House is expected to vote this week on a disaster relief package of at least $29 billion, the second installment of federal aid for areas affected by Hurricanes Maria, Irma, and Harvey in Puerto Rico, Texas, Florida, and the U.S. Virgin Islands, as well as wildfire recovery. The Trump administration requested $29 billion last week, including $12.8 billion for the Federal Emergency Management Agency's disaster relief fund, $16 billion for debt relief for the federal flood insurance program, and $576.5 million for wildfire recovery. Puerto Rico Governor Ricardo Rosselló has asked Congress for an additional $4.6 billion in federal grant and loan programs. Another aid package is likely before the end of the year.

Most of Puerto Rico remains without power, and many residents lack adequate food and water supplies. During the visit, Ryan and the delegation plan to meet with local officials and emergency personnel and hold a news conference. Ryan previously visited Texas and Florida after Hurricanes Harvey and Irma.

New York Governor Andrew Cuomo is planning a trade mission to Cuba, according to reports from The Wall Street Journal and a statement from his spokeswoman Melissa DeRosa on Saturday. The trip would follow the Obama administration's announcement of relaxed trade and travel restrictions and steps toward normalizing relations with Cuba after roughly 50 years. The Wall Street Journal reported Saturday that Cuomo would announce the mission in his Wednesday state-of-the-state address, citing a person familiar with the matter. DeRosa said details would be announced later and did not specify a travel date, adding the trip would be part of a "Global NY" initiative. Cuomo, who recently began his second term as the state's Democratic governor, has previously announced plans for trade missions to Israel, China, Mexico and elsewhere during the term; one account said he is planning five trade missions with Cuba as the first.

The Obama administration's new rules, described as adopted on Friday or earlier this month, allow travelers who fit into one of a dozen categories — including government work, humanitarian work, research and education — to travel to Cuba without applying for a license beforehand. One account said Cuomo's visit would be the first by a major U.S. public official to the communist nation since the changes; another said it would be the first by a high-profile U.S. official since the accord was announced.

On Saturday, a congressional Democratic delegation led by Sen. Patrick Leahy of Vermont began a three-day visit to Cuba to discuss expectations for normalization. Traveling with Leahy were Sens. Dick Durbin of Illinois, Debbie Stabenow of Michigan and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, and Reps. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland and Peter Welch of Vermont. Leahy said in a statement the lawmakers want to explore opportunities for greater cooperation and encourage Cuban officials to address issues of concern to Americans and their representatives in Congress. Many congressional Republicans have been cool to the administration's effort.

summary: Fifteen Republican senators sent a letter to the White House on Thursday urging President Barack Obama to withdraw the nomination of former Senator Chuck Hagel (R-Neb.) for Secretary of Defense. It claimed that historically no Secretary of Defense nominee has been confirmed with more than 11 opposing votes and asserted that a nominee would require 89 votes for confirmation. The letter followed an announcement by Senator Richard Shelby (R-Ala.) that he would vote for Hagel, making him the third Republican senator to do so. Senators John McCain (R-Ariz.) and Kelly Ayotte (R-N.H.), both of whom opposed Hagel, did not sign the letter; McCain was not involved in drafting it. Separately, Senators Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) had sought additional information — Cruz on Hagel's finances and Graham on the September 11, 2012, attack on the U.S. mission in Benghazi, Libya. Despite the letter, Republicans signaled increased willingness to allow a full Senate vote on the nomination after the Presidents Day recess. Under Senate rules, presidential nominations require 50 votes for confirmation, and a filibuster of a Defense secretary nominee would be unprecedented.

summary:
The House of Representatives rejected its version of the farm bill on Thursday, a measure that would have cut the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program by more than $20 billion. The vote came as the Senate advanced a comprehensive immigration overhaul and, separately, had already passed its own farm bill with bipartisan support. The Senate farm bill reduces food stamp spending by $4 billion and cuts overall spending by $24 billion, with backing from more than 10 Republicans. The current farm bill expires in September.

Senator Michael Bennet of Colorado urged the House to take up the Senate farm bill, saying farmers and ranchers "are left to scratch their head once again about why Congress can't get their work done." Representative Trey Gowdy, Republican of South Carolina, who voted against the House farm bill, said, "If you think this is hard, try getting 218 on a path to legal status."

Meanwhile, the House Judiciary Committee voted 20 to 15 on Tuesday to approve an enforcement-focused immigration bill. The legislation would make unlawful presence in the United States a federal crime rather than a civil offense and would authorize state and local officials to enforce federal immigration law. Republicans said the bill is needed to ensure enforcement; Democrats called it dangerous and disappointing, particularly as the Senate considers a bill that includes a pathway to citizenship. Protesters in the hearing room chanted "Shame, shame!"

summary: President Barack Obama stopped by a private White House meeting Monday with celebrities including singer Jennifer Hudson and actors Amy Poehler, Michael Cera and Kal Penn. Representatives for Oprah Winfrey, Alicia Keys and Bon Jovi also attended, along with officials from the Internet video sites YouTube and Funny or Die. The White House said the artists had expressed interest in helping spread the word about the health insurance marketplaces opening Oct. 1 under the health care law signed in 2010. The White House also said Obama told the artists they could help reach young uninsured Americans who will be vital to the law's success. The Associated Press reported that insurers need healthy young customers to help offset the costs of older, sicker consumers. Aides discussed the rollout of the exchanges at the meeting. YouTube and Funny or Die are working on promotions featuring comedians.

A Gallup poll released February 24 found that 53 percent of Americans believe leaders of other countries do not respect President Obama, while 41 percent believe they do. It was the first time in annual world affairs polling that a majority said Obama is not respected. In 2009, 67 percent said he was respected; in 2013, 51 percent said so. Among Democrats, 69 percent said Obama is respected and 28 percent said he is not; among independents, 49 percent said he is respected and 57 percent said he is not; among Republicans, 21 percent said he is respected and 77 percent said he is not. Gallup said the decline may be tied to specific international matters from the past year, including the revelation that the U.S. was listening in on foreign leaders' phone calls, the situation in Syria, increased tensions with Russia, and an uneasy relationship between Obama and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Foreign policy had been a strong suit for Obama, with the winding down of wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and the killing of Osama bin Laden. Over the past year, Obama's decision to seek authorization for force in Syria after setting a "red line" on chemical weapons went over poorly, and Congress appeared set to deny the request. More recently, the administration warned of "consequences" for the Ukrainian government if it cracked down too far on anti-government protesters. In 2007, only 21 percent of Americans thought world leaders respected President George W. Bush.

Last month, Senate Republicans blocked a vote on Cordray, a former Ohio attorney general. Democrats and the White House have rejected changes to the bureau's design. The decision to bypass the Senate is expected to intensify partisan tensions ahead of the November elections.

summary:
Senator Claire McCaskill, Democrat of Missouri, appeared at the Christ the King United Church of Christ on Old Halls Ferry Road in Ferguson to meet with members of the St. Louis Metropolitan Clergy Coalition and other civic and faith leaders. Afterward she told reporters, "The police response has been part of the problem." In a separate statement on Thursday, McCaskill said, "This kind of response by the police has become the problem instead of the solution," adding that while she respects law enforcement's work, her constituents are allowed peaceful protests and police need to respect and protect that right. McCaskill was in Ferguson Thursday speaking with constituents and was scheduled to speak with Attorney General Eric Holder later that day. On Friday, McCaskill wrote about developments including the naming of the officer who shot Michael Brown.

Ferguson Police Chief Thomas Jackson identified the officer as Darren Wilson, a six-year veteran, at a Friday press conference. Jackson said the initial contact between Wilson and Brown was not related to a robbery that occurred minutes earlier, stating the robbery "had nothing to do with the stop." Police released surveillance video of the alleged robbery. The Washington Post reported that Jackson appeared to contradict himself at other times and did say the robbery was a factor.

Representative Lacy Clay, Democrat of Missouri, whose district includes Ferguson, praised residents who guarded stores from looting. Clay condemned the release of the robbery video, telling protesters through a bullhorn, "They have attempted to taint the investigation... They are trying to influence a jury pool by the stunt they pulled today," according to the Associated Press.

Looting and clashes with police broke a relative peace late Friday night and early Saturday. The Justice Department said the FBI had conducted interviews with witnesses as part of its investigation into Brown's death.

In recent days, police used tear gas and rubber bullets against protesters who said they were assembled peacefully. Two reporters were arrested Wednesday night after saying they were doing their jobs, and video shown on MSNBC showed police dismantling an Al Jazeera crew's TV equipment after driving them away with tear gas.

summary: Bernie Sanders conceded defeat in the Missouri Democratic primary on Thursday, telling the Associated Press he would not seek a recount despite trailing Hillary Clinton by less than half of one percent of the total vote. According to the AP, unofficial results showed Clinton leading 49.61 percent to 49.37 percent. Sanders said a recount would probably not affect the number of delegates awarded and he would "prefer to save the taxpayers of Missouri more money." Under Missouri law, a candidate may request a recount when the margin is less than 0.5 percentage points. The AP reported that each candidate had won 32 delegates based on Tuesday's vote, with Clinton receiving an additional two delegates for winning the statewide vote. A CNN report, citing Sanders spokesman Michael Briggs, said the senator would not request a recount to "save the taxpayers of Missouri some money" and put the final delegate split at 36-35. Clinton's Missouri victory completed a clean sweep of all five contests held Tuesday — Missouri, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio, and Illinois. Pre-election polling released Monday by the Democratic-leaning firm Public Policy Polling had shown Sanders with a one-point lead in Missouri, 47 percent to 46 percent, while Clinton led in Ohio by five points and in Illinois by three points. The same polling showed Clinton with larger advantages in Florida (57 percent to 32 percent) and North Carolina (56 percent to 37 percent). The next Democratic contests were scheduled for Arizona, Idaho, and Utah.

summary: A fire that destroyed the Victoria Islamic Center in Victoria, Texas, on Jan. 28 has been ruled arson, with no evidence of a hate crime, federal and state investigators said. Victoria Fire Chief Taner Drake said investigators are working to follow tips that could lead to an arrest. A GoFundMe page set up to raise donations for rebuilding had collected more than $1.1 million as of Wednesday, surpassing its $850,000 goal, with more than 23,000 donations. summary: President Barack Obama delivered his second inaugural address on Monday, offering what one account described as less detail on specific plans for the next four years but more of his political philosophy. In the speech, Obama devoted a single word — "deficit" — to the issue that had brought Washington to the brink of fiscal crises repeatedly during his first term. He conceded that "outworn programs are inadequate to the needs of our time" and called for training more math and science teachers, building roads, and funding more research labs, though he did not explain how such spending would be reconciled with demands to stabilize the national debt. The address argued for a progressive view of government founded on history and the conviction that American prosperity and the preservation of freedom depend on collective action, and it was characterized as Obama's most eloquent description of the common heritage embodied in the phrase "we the people." Almost immediately after the address concluded, an email from "Barack" arrived in supporters' inboxes thanking them — "Thank you for making this possible. It's an honor to be your president. Now it's time to finish what we started — let's get going." The message promoted Organizing for Action, an advocacy group formed from the former campaign organization Obama for America, and included a link to a video featuring Michelle Obama describing the group's purpose. The organization, which had been tapped to build support for the health care law in 2009-2010, is designed to fight for the president's second-term agenda by supporting the legislative agenda voters endorsed, training grassroots organizers, and organizing around local issues. According to USA TODAY's Fredreka Schouten, Organizing for Action may run issue-focused advertising but cannot run ads calling for the election or defeat of specific candidates. In the coming days, political combat was expected to continue over the debt ceiling, gun control, national security, and tax policies affecting income inequality.

He referenced the diary of Thomas Thistlewood, a British landowner who documented cruel treatment of slaves. Bashir apologized on air during the next broadcast. Critics, including Bill O'Reilly and Howard Kurtz at Fox News, called for MSNBC to discipline him. Bashir did not appear on his show after November 22. On Monday, the network told Politico he was on vacation, not suspended, and did not say when he would return. In a statement released Wednesday, Bashir said he had asked for additional time off around Thanksgiving, which led to further reflection and a meeting with MSNBC President Phil Griffin. After that meeting, he tendered his resignation, saying he hoped his colleagues would "be allowed to focus on the issues that matter without the distraction of myself, or my ill-judged comments." Griffin issued a statement accepting the resignation, thanking Bashir for "three great years with MSNBC" and calling him "a good man and respected colleague."

summary:
President Barack Obama held a year-end news conference at the White House on Friday afternoon before departing for a 16-day holiday vacation in Hawaii with his family. At the conference, which lasted about an hour, Obama addressed the troubled rollout of the Affordable Care Act, calling it his biggest mistake of the year, defended National Security Agency data-gathering programs, and pledged not to negotiate with Republicans over raising the debt limit. He also acknowledged that major legislative priorities including gun legislation and immigration reform had failed to advance in Congress. The president's job approval and personal favorability ratings had fallen to around the lowest point of his presidency at the end of his fifth year in office. This was the first time his vacation departure had not been delayed by legislative action in Washington.

The Obama family — the president, first lady Michelle Obama, her mother, and daughters Malia and Sasha — left Washington Friday evening and arrived in Honolulu early Saturday morning. It was the fifth consecutive year they spent the holidays in Hawaii, Obama's childhood home. The White House said no public events were scheduled through Sunday, Jan. 5. Obama planned to review a 300-page report outlining recommendations to reform the NSA and other surveillance programs, with an announcement on which proposals he supports expected in January.

During the vacation, the family stayed at a rented home on Oahu. On Saturday, Obama golfed with White House aides at the Marine Corps course at Kaneohe Bay. On Sunday, the family attended a college basketball game between the University of Akron and Oregon State at the University of Hawaii; the Oregon State team is coached by Michelle Obama's brother, Craig Robinson. After the game, they dined at Morimoto Waikiki, a restaurant run by chef Masaharu Morimoto, known for the "Iron Chef" television series. The family returned to Washington on Jan. 5.

summary:
On September 19, Omar Gonzalez jumped the White House fence while carrying a knife and entered the executive mansion. Accounts differ on how far he penetrated the building. One account stated he reached the front doors of the North Portico. Another, citing the Washington Post, reported he overpowered a guard at the entrance, ran through much of the first floor, passed through the East Room, and was moving toward the Green Room before being apprehended. Alarm buttons known as "crash boxes" had reportedly been muted because they were considered noisy and malfunctioned at irregular intervals.

The incident prompted congressional scrutiny. Representative Michael McCaul, chair of the House Committee on Homeland Security, wrote to Secret Service Director Julia Pierson expressing concern about the breach and about what he described as a lack of communication between state officials and the Secret Service regarding potential threats to the president and his family. McCaul requested answers by October 10 to a list of questions, including the process for receiving threat information from local law enforcement and policies for the use of deadly force at the White House complex. He also asked what Congress could do to strengthen the Secret Service's protective mission.

The House Oversight and Government Reform Committee held a hearing at which Pierson testified. She said the Secret Service had shown restraint by not shooting Gonzalez and acknowledged that security had not been properly executed on the day of the breach. She said she was conducting a review. Representative Stephen Lynch, a Democrat on the committee, said he had low confidence in Pierson and wished she would protect the White House as vigorously as she was defending her reputation.

Separately, it was reported that in July, police had arrested Gonzalez for reckless driving and found several assault rifles and a map of Washington, D.C., with a marking around the White House in his vehicle.

summary: South Korea announced Wednesday that unspecified components of the U.S. Terminal High-Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system had been installed at a site in the country's southeast, according to a South Korean statement and Yonhap News Agency. Yonhap reported the components included two or three launchers, intercept missiles, and a radar. About 8,000 police officers were mobilized and the main road to the site was blocked earlier Wednesday. The announcement came a day after North Korea conducted live-fire artillery drills Tuesday, the 85th anniversary of the founding of the Korean People's Army. On Thursday, South Korean Defense Ministry spokesman Moon Sang-gyun said the THAAD system would soon go into "actual operation" and that the positioning of some equipment gave South Korea and the U.S. the capability to cope with North Korea's missile provocations. The U.S. had deployed THAAD in early March after North Korea fired four missiles into the Sea of Japan. China and Russia view the system's radar as a security threat; Beijing has vigorously opposed the deployment. On Saturday, North Korea launched a ballistic missile around 5:30 a.m. local time from near Pukchang Airfield in central North Korea, according to U.S. and South Korean military officials. U.S. Pacific Command said the missile did not leave North Korean territory, while South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said the test "failed." The missile was believed to be a mobile-launched, short- to medium-range missile, similar to one launched earlier in the month that blew up almost immediately. The launch came amid heightened tensions, with the Trump administration urging China to take a more proactive role in restraining North Korea's nuclear ambitions.

White House Chief Strategist Steve Bannon departed his position on Friday, according to a White House statement and multiple reports. Press Secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said in a statement that Chief of Staff John Kelly and Bannon "mutually agreed today would be Steve's last day" and that the administration was "grateful for his service and wish him the best." Bannon, the former executive chairman of Breitbart News, had helped President Trump win the 2016 election. His exit followed a turbulent seven-month tenure and came as the president faced criticism for saying "both sides" were to blame for deadly violence in Charlottesville, Virginia, the previous weekend. Critics accused Trump of channeling Bannon when he equated white supremacists and neo-Nazis with left-wing protesters. The New York Times, citing two administration officials, reported that Trump had told senior aides he decided to remove Bannon and that the president and senior officials were debating when and how to dismiss him; as of Friday morning the two men were still discussing Bannon's future, the officials said. A person close to Bannon insisted the parting was Bannon's idea and that he had submitted his resignation to the president on August 7, to be announced at the start of the week, but the announcement was delayed in the wake of the Charlottesville unrest. Bannon's influence had been highlighted by a February Time magazine cover labeling him "The Great Manipulator." His departure was the latest in a series of high-profile West Wing shake-ups.

summary: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), a candidate for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination, appeared at a rally in Georgia on Thursday and on CBS's "Face the Nation" on Sunday. I will not compromise on women's reproductive freedom." Gillibrand called for the protections of Roe v. Wade to be written into federal law, saying "Federal law should supersede harmful state laws that take away women's reproductive freedom," and advocated repeal of the Hyde Amendment, which bars federal funds for health coverage that includes abortion. She also pledged to nominate only Supreme Court justices who would vote to uphold Roe v. Wade. Sen. Elizabeth Warren has called for similar changes to federal law. On "Face the Nation," Gillibrand said the anti-abortion laws in multiple states resulted from President Donald Trump starting "a war" on women: "This is nothing short of all-out assault on women's reproductive freedoms. She added, "President Trump has started a war on America's women if it's a fight he wants to have it's a fight he's going to have, and he's going to lose." summary:

Campaign representatives met with Post executive editor Marcus Brauchli to raise their concerns. Post spokesperson Kris Coratti said, "We are very confident in our reporting." The Romney campaign also posted a document it called the "real facts" of the story on its website. The Post reported that the Romney campaign did not comment for the original article.

A lower court had ruled the delay was negligent and awarded the families $4 million each, later reduced to $100,000. summary:
President Barack Obama and first lady Michelle Obama traveled to Boston on Thursday for an interfaith memorial service at the Cathedral of the Holy Cross, three days after the Boston Marathon bombing that killed three people and injured more than 170. The service began at 11 a.m. A White House statement said the president would dedicate his remarks "to those who were gravely wounded or killed in Monday's bombing near the finish line of the Boston Marathon."

In his address, Obama opened with "Hello, Boston!" and quoted scripture: "run with endurance the race that is set before us." He described the scene on Monday morning: the sun rising over the Statehouse dome, spring blooming in the Common and Public Garden, fans heading to Fenway Park, runners setting out from Hopkinton on the 26.2-mile course, and hundreds of thousands of Bostonians lining the streets to cheer them on. "It was a beautiful day to be in Boston," he said, "a day that explains why a poet once wrote that this town is not just a capital, not just a place. Boston, he said, 'is the perfect state of grace.'"

The visit followed a day of political frustration for the president. On Wednesday, Senate Republicans blocked several of his gun-control proposals. Obama called it "a pretty shameful day for Washington" and vowed to continue pressing the issue through executive action and in the 2014 congressional elections. After the memorial service, he hosted a White House reception for Greek Independence Day.

British Prime Minister David Cameron on Tuesday recalled Parliament to debate military options against Syria, stating the country was considering a "proportionate response" to the "absolutely abhorrent" chemical weapons attack. According to Reuters, Cameron's spokesman said British armed forces were "making contingency plans" while a military response remained on the table but uncommitted, and any action would "be taken under a strict international framework" with Cameron consulting world leaders for coordination. The statement followed remarks by U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry that suggested the United States was preparing military intervention against Syrian President Bashar Assad's regime.

On Thursday, Cameron announced Britain would release intelligence on the reported chemical weapon assault. Parliament then voted on a motion to authorize military action in principle; the motion failed 285 to 272. Cameron said he would not override Parliament and assured Labour leader Ed Miliband: "I can give that assurance. I strongly believe in the need for a tough response to the use of chemical weapons, but I also believe in respecting the will of this House of Commons."

U.S. President Barack Obama said the White House believed Assad was responsible for a poison gas attack on rebel forces and civilians in the Damascus area. Assad denied responsibility and blamed rebel forces for killing hundreds of civilians. United Nations weapon inspectors were expected to conclude their investigation and depart Syria by Saturday.

summary: President Donald Trump nominated federal appeals court judge Neil Gorsuch to fill the Supreme Court seat left vacant by the death of Justice Antonin Scalia. Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office during a meeting with conservative activists, Trump said that if Democrats attempted to filibuster the nomination, Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell should invoke the "nuclear option" — a rules change allowing confirmation by a simple 51-vote majority rather than the current 60-vote threshold. "If we end up with that gridlock I would say, 'If you can, Mitch, go nuclear,'" Trump said. "Because that would be an absolute shame if a man of this quality was put up to that neglect. I would say it's up to Mitch, but I would say, 'Go for it.'" Asked directly whether he would pursue that course, McConnell declined to answer but said, "We're going to get the judge confirmed." Vice President Mike Pence told PBS's "NewsHour" that he was hopeful Republicans would not need to use the nuclear option, adding that the administration was committed to supporting Gorsuch's nomination. Republicans hold 52 Senate seats, meaning at least eight Democrats would need to support Gorsuch to break a filibuster. Several Senate Democrats announced opposition to the nomination following Trump's announcement. Trump praised Gorsuch as "a terrific person," "a spectacular man," and "perfect in just about every way." Pence described Gorsuch as "a first-class intellect, a fourth-generation Coloradan, and someone who in a fair and impartial way is going to uphold the Constitution and apply the law as written." The nuclear option was previously invoked in 2013 by then-Majority Leader Harry Reid for lower-court nominations.

summary: President Donald Trump announced Wednesday that the United States would recognize Jerusalem as the capital of Israel and move its embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, though he set no timetable for the relocation. Trump described the decision as a recognition of reality and a long-overdue step to advance the peace process, arguing that past administrations' approaches had not worked. Former President Jimmy Carter said in a statement that the fundamental shift in decades-old U.S. policy exacerbates tensions throughout the Arab and Muslim world and that any change to the status of Jerusalem without Palestinian consent jeopardizes any prospect for peace. Carter expressed hope that protests would remain nonviolent. Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas planned to travel to Jordan on Thursday to meet King Abdullah II, seen as Abbas's closest Arab ally, to coordinate a response. Both Israelis and Palestinians claim Jerusalem as their political capital and as a sacred religious site. Israel controls the entirety of the city. The city's status has been disputed since the 1948 Arab-Israeli War; before that, the United Nations designated Jerusalem as a special international zone. Israel seized the western half in 1948 and the eastern half in the 1967 war. Most foresee a peace deal that would give western Jerusalem to Israel and eastern Jerusalem to a future Palestinian state.

Billionaire Democratic donor and environmentalist Tom Steyer on Friday told San Francisco news outlet KQED that he had purchased 535 copies of Michael Wolff's book "Fire and Fury: Inside the Trump White House" — one for every member of Congress — and planned to have citizen volunteers deliver them to each congressional office. On Monday, Steyer announced at a press conference in Washington, D.C., at an office space overlooking the Capitol that he would not run for political office in 2018. "I'm not going to run for office in 2018, that's not where I can make the biggest difference," he said. "I'm willing to do whatever it takes to help save our country. And I believe the most important task for me, the task which I feel called to do, is organizing and mobilizing America's voters." Steyer said he would channel at least $30 million toward his advocacy group, NextGen America, to build a voter mobilization effort targeting millennial turnout across 10 states, focusing on 24 Republican-held districts and swing seats Democrats are defending. Democrats need to flip at least 24 seats to win back the House majority. His decision not to run leaves state Sen. Kevin de León as Sen. Dianne Feinstein's only serious Democratic primary challenger in California and keeps the state's gubernatorial primary field unchanged. Steyer spent more than $91 million during the 2016 campaign, including donations to candidates, super PACs, and NextGen America.

First Lady Melania Trump attended President Donald Trump's first State of the Union address at the Capitol on Tuesday but arrived separately, traveling with guests she had invited rather than with the president. Her spokeswoman, Stephanie Grisham, said the travel plans were "honoring her guests for the true heroes they are," and that the first lady held a White House reception and photo opportunity for the guests and their families before accompanying them to the Capitol, where she and Karen Pence hosted a meet-and-greet before the speech.

The separate arrival followed a week in which the first lady canceled a planned trip to Switzerland with the president, made an unannounced visit to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, and traveled to Mar-a-Lago in Florida, where she spent part of the time at the spa, according to aides and reports. Aides said she was focusing on her role and her family.

The independent travel and low public profile came after The Wall Street Journal reported earlier in January that adult-film actress Stormy Daniels had been paid $130,000 shortly before the 2016 election to keep quiet about an affair she said she had with Donald Trump a decade earlier, when the Trumps were newlyweds and shortly after the birth of their son, Barron. Two people close to the couple said the report blindsided the first lady and left her furious with her husband.

As the president's motorcade traveled from the White House to the Capitol on Tuesday night, a few dozen protesters gathered along the route, chanting "Hey hey, ho, ho, Donald Trump must go" and holding signs including one that read "F—K Trump." A heavy Capitol Police presence kept the demonstrators off the street, and the crowd dispersed after the motorcade passed.

summary:
Senator Carl Levin, a Democrat who has represented Michigan since 1979 and is the state's longest-serving senator, announced Thursday that he will retire rather than seek re-election in 2014. The 78-year-old Levin said in a statement: "This decision was extremely difficult, because I love representing the people of Michigan in the U.S. Senate and fighting for the things that I believe are important to them." He added that he and his wife decided he could best serve by concentrating on legislative issues over the next two years "without the distraction of campaigning for re-election."

Levin is the sixth senator and fourth Democrat to announce retirement ahead of the 2014 elections, joining Democrats Jay Rockefeller of West Virginia, Tom Harkin of Iowa and Frank Lautenberg of New Jersey and Republicans Saxby Chambliss of Georgia and Mike Johanns of Nebraska. Democrats will defend 21 Senate seats next year compared with 14 for Republicans.

The open seat shifts attention to Michigan, where Republicans have won four statewide offices including the governorship but have not captured a Senate seat in nearly 20 years. National Republican Senatorial Committee communications director Brad Dayspring said Levin's decision "knocks a Democratic Senate already on defense far back on their heels and offers us a real pickup opportunity." Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee chairman Michael Bennet said he is confident the party will hold the seat: "We fully expect to keep Michigan blue."

Possible Democratic candidates include Representative Gary Peters, former Representative Mark Schauer and state Senate Minority Leader Gretchen Whitmer. Representative Mike Rogers, chairman of the House Intelligence Committee, is giving "serious consideration" to the race, according to the Detroit Free Press. Republican Representative Candice Miller has said she will not run.

summary:
The Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the 2009 Nobel Peace Prize to President Barack Obama on Friday, October 9, less than a year into his presidency. Nominations for the prize had closed two weeks after his inauguration. The committee cited Obama's efforts to strengthen international diplomacy and cooperation between peoples, referencing criteria that include fraternity between nations, abolition or reduction of standing armies, and promotion of peace congresses.

summary: Sen. Marco Rubio (R-Fla.) will deliver the Republican Party's response to President Obama's State of the Union address. The decision was announced Wednesday. House Speaker John Boehner's office issued a statement praising Rubio as "one of our party's most dynamic and inspiring leaders" whose "family's story is a testament to the promise and greatness of America." Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell said Rubio "embodies the optimism that lies at the heart of the Republican vision for America." Rubio's office released a bilingual statement in which he said, "I'm honored to have this opportunity to discuss how limited government and free enterprise have helped make my family's dreams come true in America." The address will be delivered in both English and Spanish. Rubio plans to tape a Spanish version for networks including Telemundo and Univision. In past years, separate lawmakers have delivered the English and Spanish responses. Rubio follows former Indiana Gov. Mitch Daniels, who gave the 2012 response, and previous responders Louisiana Gov. Bobby Jindal in 2009, Virginia Gov. Bob McDonnell in 2010, and Rep. Paul Ryan in 2011. Rubio, in his third Senate year, is mentioned as a likely 2016 presidential contender. The selection draws attention to his prominent role in a bipartisan group of senators calling for a pathway to citizenship for the nation's 11 million illegal immigrants, an issue that has divided the GOP. The same week, Rubio used Twitter to downplay a Time Magazine cover labeling him "The Republican Savior" and "the great Hispanic hope of the Republican Party."

summary:
A Bloomberg National Poll conducted June 6-9 found President Obama's favorability rating at 44 percent, the lowest of his presidency in that survey, with 52 percent viewing him unfavorably. His job approval rating stood at 43 percent, the lowest since the 2013 health care rollout problems. Pollster J. Ann Selzer said Obama's likeability had previously stayed ahead of perceptions of job performance but "it appears he is no longer likeable enough." The poll cited Veterans Affairs management and the exchange of five Guantanamo Bay detainees for Sergeant Bowe Bergdahl as recent issues affecting ratings.

A USA Today/Pew Research Center poll found 68 percent of veterans said Obama made the wrong decision in the Bergdahl swap, while 16 percent supported it. Among the general public, 43 percent said the decision was wrong and 34 percent said it was right. Six percent of veterans said they sympathized with Bergdahl after his platoon members accused him of desertion.

A CBS News poll released Tuesday found 56 percent of Americans said the United States paid too high a price for Bergdahl's release, rising to 65 percent among veterans. Forty-five percent disapproved of the deal and 37 percent approved. The poll showed a partisan divide, with most Republicans disapproving and a majority of Democrats approving. The CBS poll noted the USA Today/Pew survey showed 43 percent disapproval and 34 percent approval.

summary:
Thomas Eric Duncan, the first person diagnosed with Ebola on United States soil, is in critical condition at a Texas hospital, officials said Saturday. The hospital stated: "Mr. Duncan is in critical condition," after previously describing him as seriously ill. Duncan flew from Roberts International Airport in Monrovia on September 19, landing at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, and did not display symptoms until after arriving in Dallas.

Binyah Kesselly, chairman of the Liberia Airport Authority, said Thursday that Duncan lied on an airport screening questionnaire, answering "no" when asked whether he had had contact with any person who might have been stricken with Ebola in the past 21 days. "He lied on his form," Kesselly said. "If he had answered truthfully, he would have been sent to secondary screening immediately and not allowed to leave." Kesselly said Duncan would be prosecuted upon his return. Dr. Thomas R. Frieden, director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, declined to answer when asked about Kesselly's report but suggested that people often do not understand their level of exposure to infectious diseases.

Representative Kenny Marchant, a Texas Republican whose district includes Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, wrote to House Speaker John Boehner and to Representative Michael McCaul, chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, urging a travel ban from Liberia. "We must act swiftly to reduce any further spread of this disease in the United States," Marchant wrote. "Prohibiting travel to the United States for individuals traveling from or through Liberia would greatly reduce this risk to the public." He also wrote: "I would appreciate the House Homeland Security Committee reviewing the most effective measures at implementing a travel ban from Liberia and ensuring the safety of the American public from this deadly virus." Liberia is one of three main West African countries struggling to control the outbreak, along with Sierra Leone and Guinea; Marchant did not call for a ban on the other two.

Republican presidential candidate Ron Paul, a Texas congressman, criticized the Obama administration for the killing of U.S.-born al Qaeda operative Anwar al-Awlaki. Al-Awlaki was killed Friday in a U.S. drone or air strike; U.S. and Yemeni officials said the strike targeted his convoy in Yemen. Paul described the killing as an "assassination" and said America's leaders must think hard about "assassinating American citizens without charges."

Speaking Friday at Saint Anselm College in New Hampshire, Paul warned against casually accepting such violence against U.S. citizens, even those with strong ties to terrorism. He said al-Awlaki was never tried or charged, and "no one knows if he killed anybody," though he might have been associated with Umar Farouk Abdulmutallab, the "underwear bomber."

At a University of New Hampshire town hall on Monday, Paul said an "impeachment process would be possible" for President Obama over the strike. He added, "You could do more investigating into this. I put responsibility on the president. This is obviously a major step in the wrong direction." Paul said calling for impeachment was typical for him: "I just said almost every president I've known I'd probably have to vote for impeachment, because there's very little respect for the Constitution -- and certainly there's no respect for the Constitution for assassinating American citizens." Paul had previously called Obama's authorization of military action in Libya without congressional approval an "impeachable offense."

summary: Republicans in the North Carolina General Assembly convened a surprise special session Wednesday and introduced legislation to reduce the authority of incoming Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper, who takes office in January. The measures would end the governor's control over election boards, require state Senate approval of cabinet appointments, remove the governor's power to appoint University of North Carolina trustees, and convert hundreds of managerial positions in state agencies from at-will to civil-service protections. Republicans hold veto-proof majorities in both chambers. Outgoing Republican Gov. Pat McCrory conceded the race last week after a nearly monthlong challenge. On Friday, McCrory signed a bill curtailing the governor's power to appoint members to state boards, including the Board of Elections. Cooper threatened to sue, calling the measures "more ominous" than any "partisan power grab." Democratic National Committee chair candidate Tom Perez condemned the legislation, likening it to practices in "autocracies like Russia" and noting reports that the Trump transition team said McCrory would "definitely" receive an administration position. Separately, McCrory delivered his statutorily required budget recommendations to Cooper on Tuesday, proposing raising average teacher pay to $55,000 by 2018, a $1 billion transportation bond, $40 million over two years for mental-health initiatives, and nearly $700 million for state reserves.

He said he was pressing on "because the vacuum was so huge" between him and the other candidates, adding, "We cannot be a normal party... summary: On April 24, 2012, Armenian Remembrance Day, President Barack Obama commemorated the 1915 massacre of Armenians in the waning days of the Ottoman Empire, describing it as "one of the worst atrocities of the 20th century." Turkish leaders reject the term, saying the figures are inflated and that there were deaths on both sides as the empire collapsed. As a presidential candidate on October 2, 2008, Obama wrote that "the Armenian Genocide" was "a widely documented fact" and "undeniable," and pledged: "As President I will recognize the Armenian Genocide." In his 2012 statement, Obama said, "I have consistently stated my own view of what happened in 1915. My view of the history has not changed. A full, frank, and just acknowledgment of the facts is in all of our interests." The Armenian National Committee of America chairman called the 2008 pledge a "stark lie." Turkey is a NATO ally.

summary:
North Korea on Monday threatened to launch nuclear strikes against the United States and South Korea as the two allies began their annual joint military exercises. The threat was carried in a statement by the National Defense Commission and published by the official Korean Central News Agency, which said "the army and people of the (North) will take military counteraction for preemptive attack so that they may deal merciless deadly blows at the enemies" and that "if we push the buttons to annihilate the enemies even right now, all bases of provocations will be reduced to seas in flames and ashes in a moment." The statement accused the United States and South Korea of working "with bloodshot eyes to infringe upon the dignity, sovereignty and vital rights" of North Korea. South Korean Defense Ministry spokesman Moon Sang Gyun said that if North Korea launches a provocation, the South's military will respond "sternly and mercilessly."

The drills, which start Monday and run through the end of April, involve 17,000 American and 300,000 South Korean troops, with thousands of American Marines having arrived in South Korea in the past week. The exercises test the allies' ability to respond to North Korean attacks on the Korean Peninsula. North Korea characterizes the drills as rehearsals for an invasion, while Washington and Seoul describe them as annual defensive springtime war games.

Tensions have risen following North Korea's fourth nuclear test in January, in which it claimed to have tested a hydrogen bomb, and a long-range rocket launch over Japanese airspace on February 7 that was widely condemned as a banned missile test. The United Nations Security Council responded with its toughest sanctions in decades. Last week, hours after the sanctions were approved, North Korea fired several short-range projectiles into the sea. The Korean Central News Agency also reported that leader Kim Jong Un ordered nuclear weapons to be readied for use. North Korea has made similar threats during previous exercises, but this year tensions are described as higher because of the recent nuclear test and ensuing international condemnations. South Korea has taken a harder than usual line toward the North.

summary: Khizr Khan, a Muslim immigrant and father of U.S. Army Captain Humayun Khan, who was killed in Iraq in 2004, spoke at the Democratic National Convention on Thursday, July 28. Holding a pocket-sized Constitution, Khan asked Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump whether he had read the document and offered to lend him his copy. Khan also said Trump had sacrificed nothing for his country. Trump responded in an ABC "This Week" interview aired Sunday, July 31, questioning why Khan's wife, Ghazala Khan, did not speak at the convention: "She probably — maybe she wasn't allowed to have anything to say. You tell me." Ghazala Khan wrote in a Washington Post op-ed published Sunday that she remained silent because she was too emotional: "Walking onto the convention stage, with a huge picture of my son behind me, I could hardly control myself. What mother could?" On CNN's "State of the Union" the same day, Khizr Khan said the world had seen "the blackness of his character, of his soul" and called Trump "totally incapable of empathy" and "a black soul" unfit for leadership. The Council on American-Islamic Relations called on Trump to apologize for remarks disparaging Ghazala Khan and for repeated use of anti-Muslim stereotypes, and launched a social media campaign for Monday, August 1, from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. using the hashtag #CanYouHearUsNow, urging Muslim women to tweet about who they are and how they speak out. The ACLU began distributing free pocket Constitutions with the coupon code POCKETRIGHTS, one per person through the election.

President Trump signed an executive order banning entry for 90 days from Iraq, Iran, Syria, Yemen, Libya, Sudan and Somalia, halting the U.S. refugee resettlement program for 120 days and indefinitely suspending Syrian refugee resettlement. Weekend protests erupted at U.S. airports. Uber faced criticism after continuing service at New York airports during the protests, which some interpreted as seeking to profit. At a regularly scheduled all-hands meeting Tuesday at Uber's San Francisco headquarters, employees questioned Chief Executive Travis Kalanick about his membership on Trump's economic advisory council, asking what would prompt him to resign. On Friday, U.S. District Judge James Robart in Seattle issued a nationwide hold on the order effective immediately. The State Department had provisionally revoked up to 60,000 visas on Friday to comply with the order; on Saturday it reversed the revocation, stating that people covered by the order holding a valid visa may now travel, though the reversal reportedly does not apply to those who physically had their visas revoked at airports. Washington Attorney General Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, filed the lawsuit three days after the order was signed, joined by Minnesota. Kalanick resigned from the advisory council on Thursday. On Friday night he tweeted that Uber's head of litigation was buying airline tickets for stranded drivers. Trump tweeted Saturday that the ruling was "ridiculous and will be overturned!".

summary: French President François Hollande visited Washington for a state visit including a joint press conference with President Barack Obama and a state dinner on Tuesday. summary: Anti-government protesters clashed with police in Kiev's Independence Square on Tuesday as demonstrations that began in late November continued. The protests started after President Viktor Yanukovych rejected a European Union trade agreement in favor of a $15 billion bailout from Russia. By Tuesday, protesters were using rocks, bats and fire bombs against police, who responded with stun grenades and water cannons. Burning barricades sent flames into the night sky. At least 18 people died in Tuesday's clashes, according to one account, and hundreds were injured. Other reports gave higher figures: Reuters put the toll at 50, while CNN reported more than 100 killed as of Thursday morning. An earlier figure cited 25 deaths on Tuesday alone. Yanukovych announced a truce Wednesday night, though one account placed the announcement early Thursday; the truce collapsed as protesters viewed it as a stunt. The White House said it was "outraged by images of Ukrainian security forces firing automatic weapons on their own people," and spokesman Jay Carney called on Yanukovych to immediately withdraw security forces from downtown Kiev and respect the right of peaceful protest, while also urging protesters to express themselves peacefully. The U.S. State Department issued a travel alert for Ukraine and imposed visa bans on 20 Ukrainian officials. The demonstrations had most recently focused on whether Yanukovych would honor demands for constitutional reforms limiting presidential powers.

summary: Mexico's attorney general, Jesus Murillo Karam, said Tuesday the government would appeal the court ruling that freed Rafael Caro Quintero, a former leader of the Guadalajara Cartel who was serving a 40-year sentence for the 1985 abduction, torture and killing of U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration agent Enrique "Kiki" Camarena and Mexican pilot Alfredo Zavala. Caro Quintero, 60, left prison on Friday after 28 years, with 12 years remaining on his sentence. The release followed a court decision on August 7. One account said a judge in the western state of Jalisco ordered his release on a technicality; another said an appeals court overturned the sentence on procedural grounds; a third said a Mexican court ruled he had been improperly tried in federal court for a state offense. The U.S. National Security Council said Sunday it was "deeply concerned" by the release. NSC spokeswoman Caitlin Hayden said in a statement that the United States is working with Mexican authorities to see those responsible for Camarena's murder face justice in the United States. Mexican Foreign Minister Jose Antonio Meade said the dispute would not affect relations with Washington because both governments opposed the court ruling, which he said should be "revised." Murillo Karam declined to say whether the government knew Caro Quintero's current whereabouts. U.S. officials expressed concern that a second person convicted in the Camarena case might also be freed; one report attributed this to defense lawyers, another to U.S. officials, and a third said an accomplice was believed to be facing early release. A Republican lawmaker said the release raised serious questions about the Mexican justice system as it implements judicial reforms. The House Appropriations Committee last month approved $148 million to combat organized crime and drug trafficking in Mexico; the spending bill awaits House action after recess.

summary: Rep. Trey Radel (R-Fla.), 37, plans to return to the House of Representatives next week when the chamber reconvenes after a two-week break. In the spirit of Christmas, thank you for this gift to serve you." He also wrote that his "passion remains undaunted" and that he stands ready to serve the entire community. Members of both parties, according to one account, and Florida Republican officials including the state party chairman, according to others, have called on Radel to resign. He has said he has no plans to do so. Politico reported his expected return Tuesday; Radel represents a heavily Republican district and could face a primary challenge next year.

The remarks came days after Ryan told CNN he was "just not ready" to endorse Trump, who had become the presumptive Republican nominee after rivals Ted Cruz and John Kasich suspended their campaigns. Ryan and Trump met Thursday at Republican National Committee headquarters in Washington, a session that drew intense media attention with all three major cable networks streaming live coverage. Following the meeting, Ryan did not endorse Trump. On Friday, Trump told NBC's "Today" program he was "a little bit surprised, but not that surprised, frankly" by the lack of an endorsement. "No, I think it's a process," Trump said. "We did, as you know ... get endorsed by many, many people, and they're pouring in now. Many senators and many congressmen -- we got many endorsements yesterday." Trump added, "And I think that will come, and if it doesn't come, I'll go my separate way." Ryan issued a statement saying he was encouraged by the meeting. Trump separately told Fox News' "Fox and Friends" the meeting was positive: "We had a great meeting. I thought it was a really good meeting, and I think over a short period of time, things will come together."

summary: A split has emerged inside the Bernie Sanders campaign over whether the senator should end his candidacy after the June 7 primaries in California, New Jersey and four other states and unite behind Democratic front-runner Hillary Clinton, or continue to the July Democratic National Convention and attempt to win the nomination. One faction, composed of longtime loyalists who guided Sanders's political career in Vermont and Congress, is reluctant to concede a race that has exceeded expectations. Another faction, with ties to broader party interests focused on defeating Republican presumptive nominee Donald Trump and winning congressional seats, favors unification. Sanders has signaled he intends to continue past Tuesday, but the internal debate indicates his next move is not settled. Democratic officials, fundraisers and operatives have grown impatient, urging Sanders to exit the race and begin party unity efforts. New York hedge-fund manager Orin Kramer, who has raised funds for both President Barack Obama and Clinton, said: "I would hope people would understand what a Trump presidency would mean and act accordingly—and 'accordingly' means quickly." Clinton campaign chairman John Podesta said on "Fox News Sunday" that the campaign expects to secure the delegates needed on Tuesday night for Clinton to become the first woman nominee on a major-party ticket in the United States. Podesta said Clinton will have the necessary delegates regardless of Sanders's decision about staying in the race until the convention. He said the Clinton campaign will make every effort to reach out to Sanders supporters and expressed hope that Sanders would join the effort, noting Sanders's stated commitment to work "seven days a week to stop Donald Trump." Podesta dismissed polls showing a tightening general-election race, attributing the shift to Trump's consolidation of Republican voters.

summary:
During a bilateral press conference with Finnish President Sauli Niinistö on Monday, President Trump mistakenly confused two Finnish journalists sitting side by side. When Niinistö called on Maria Annala, Trump asked, "Again? You're going to give her -- the same one?" referring to Paula Vilén, who had asked a question earlier. Niinistö replied, "No, she's not the same lady. They are sitting side by side." Annala responded, "We have a lot of blonde women in Finland." Afterward, PBS NewsHour's Lisa Desjardins spoke with the two journalists; Vilén described the exchange as a "lifetime event."

At the same press conference, Trump defended his Friday night pardon of former Maricopa County Sheriff Joe Arpaio, which was announced as Hurricane Harvey, a Category 4 storm, approached Texas. Asked about the timing, Trump said, "I assumed the ratings would be far higher." He praised Arpaio, who had been convicted of criminal contempt after accusations of racial profiling and who operated a "Tent City" jail, saying, "He's done a great job for the people of Arizona. He's strong on borders and strong on illegal immigration. He is loved in Arizona, and I thought he was treated unbelievably unfairly." Trump also claimed "a lot of people think it was the right thing to do," despite criticism from House Speaker Paul Ryan and Senator John McCain, among others. Trump also criticized leakers in reference to Chelsea Manning's case.

On CNN's "Situation Room," political correspondent Dana Bash called Trump's ratings remark "abhorrent," saying she did not believe it was tongue-in-cheek and noting Trump's background in reality television and focus on ratings.

summary: President Donald Trump formally endorsed Republican Senate candidate Roy Moore in a telephone call on Monday, prompting the Republican National Committee to restore its financial support for the Alabama nominee. The RNC had severed fundraising ties with Moore three weeks earlier following allegations that he had molested two teenagers when he was in his 30s. Trump posted on Twitter that Republicans needed Moore's vote "on stopping crime, illegal immigration, Border Wall, Military, Pro Life, V.A., Judges 2nd Amendment and more," and later spoke with Moore by phone. White House spokesman Raj Shah described the call as "positive." Moore thanked Trump on Twitter, saying he looked "forward to fighting alongside the President to #MAGA." The RNC's reversal came at Trump's direct urging, according to one account, and hours after Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell said Alabama voters should "make the call" on whether to send Moore to the Senate. Former Republican presidential nominee Mitt Romney criticized the endorsement on Twitter; Moore responded that Romney "doesn't care about the truth anymore." The special election against Democratic nominee Doug Jones was scheduled for the following week. On Wednesday, Senator Ben Sasse told reporters the RNC's decision "doesn't make any sense" if the committee believed the women who had accused Moore.

CIA Director Mike Pompeo met secretly with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Pyongyang over Easter weekend, April 1-2, 2018, for more than an hour. President Donald Trump later said the two "got along" and described it as a "great meeting," adding that Pompeo had not been initially scheduled to meet Kim face-to-face. The White House released photographs of the meeting on Thursday, April 26, the same day the Senate confirmed Pompeo as secretary of state. White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders posted the images on Twitter, writing that Pompeo would "do an excellent job helping @POTUS lead our efforts to denuclearize the Korean Peninsula."

In a broadcast interview on Sunday, Pompeo said the United States had an "obligation" to pursue a diplomatic solution and that a "real opportunity" for progress existed. He said he and Kim held in-depth talks about what a "complete, verifiable, irreversible mechanism" for denuclearization might look like.

On Friday, April 27, South Korean President Moon Jae-in met Kim at the border in the first visit by a North Korean leader to the South since the 1953 armistice. The two leaders agreed to pursue a permanent peace treaty and the complete denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula. The White House welcomed the summit, with Sanders saying the United States was "hopeful that talks will achieve progress toward a future of peace and prosperity" and appreciated close coordination with Seoul.

Trump and Kim are expected to hold their own summit in late May or early June, though the date and location have not been finalized.

summary: U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un held a summit in Singapore on Tuesday. During the meetings Trump showed Kim the presidential limousine, known as "The Beast," and played a short video on an iPad that depicted a denuclearized North Korea under the theme "two men, two leaders, one destiny." After the summit Trump told Fox News the meeting had been "really fantastic" and "better than anybody could have expected." He described Kim as "a very smart guy" and "a great negotiator" and said "I think we understand each other." Asked about North Korea's human rights record, Trump said "a lot of other people (have) done some really bad things" and cited other nations where "a lotta bad things were done." The U.S. State Department estimates Kim's regime holds between 80,000 and 120,000 political prisoners in forced labor camps, and Kim is suspected of ordering the assassination of his half-brother at a Malaysian airport in 2017. Critics said the summit legitimized Kim and produced more headlines than substantive progress. In the same interview Trump called Chinese President Xi Jinping "an incredible guy" and noted Xi is "essentially president for life. That's pretty good."

summary: Former President George H.W. Bush, 93, attended a monthly pancake breakfast at American Legion Post 159 in Kennebunkport, Maine, on Saturday during Memorial Day weekend. He posted on Twitter that he was "delighted to join the veterans, including my dear friend Gen. Brent Scowcroft" at the event. Hours after the breakfast on Sunday, Bush experienced low blood pressure and fatigue and was taken to Southern Maine Health Care hospital in Biddeford. His spokesman, Jim McGrath, said Bush was "awake and alert, and not in any discomfort" and would remain under observation for several days. In a Wednesday tweet, McGrath added that Bush was talkative and in good spirits but that treatments to address his blood pressure were expected to take several more days. Bush had arrived in Maine on May 20 after being treated for a blood infection at Houston Methodist Hospital, where he was admitted April 22 — the day after the funeral for his wife, Barbara Bush, who died April 17 in Houston — and discharged May 5. The 41st president, who turns 94 on June 12, has spent part of every summer in Kennebunkport since childhood except during his World War II service as a naval aviator.
