summary: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) deleted a tweet on Thursday after mistakenly identifying fellow Democrat Rep. John Yarmuth (D-Ky.) as a Republican. The Republican Party of Kentucky had posted a photo of Yarmuth, chairman of the House Budget Committee and a member of Congress since 2007, posing with a cardboard cutout of Ocasio-Cortez, commenting that it "looks like" she is "calling the shots" for the state's Democrats. Ocasio-Cortez shared the tweet and wrote, "GOP: Let's pose our older male members next to cardboard cutouts of young female legislators." Twitter users quickly noted that Yarmuth is a Democrat. Ocasio-Cortez deleted the tweet within minutes and did not offer an explanation. Her office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Yarmuth responded on Twitter, saying he took the photo because he "wanted everyone to know" he welcomes Ocasio-Cortez in Kentucky, adding that he welcomes her "regardless of what old white male Republicans think." He also noted he was previously a Republican before switching parties 35 years ago. The National Republican Congressional Committee criticized the error, noting Ocasio-Cortez is a co-sponsor of one of Yarmuth's bills, and tweeted, "Maybe if @AOC spent more time interacting with lawmakers and less time making coloring books, she'd recognize the other socialist Democrats in her caucus." Some conservatives highlighted the mistake, while other social media users compared it to President Donald Trump's frequent false statements. The incident followed a previous instance last month in which Ocasio-Cortez conflated the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. She has said on Yahoo's "Skullduggery" podcast that she writes her own tweets. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) recently remarked that a "glass of water" with a "D next to its name" could have won Ocasio-Cortez's district.

summary: Army Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl was freed in exchange for five Taliban detainees held at Guantanamo Bay. President Obama said he made "no apologies" for the swap and would do it again. The deal drew immediate political reaction. Senate Intelligence Committee Chair Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.) and ranking member Saxby Chambliss said Congress was not given the 30-day notification required by law. House Intelligence Committee Chair Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) and Rep. Tom Cole (R-Okla.) were scheduled to discuss the criticism on ABC's "This Week." CBS's "Face the Nation" also booked Feinstein, Chambliss, and journalist David Rohde, who was held by the Taliban in 2008. CNN's "State of the Union" planned interviews with Secretary of State John Kerry and Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.); Kerry was expected to address whether Bergdahl was being "swiftboated" by conservatives, and McCain to weigh in on whether the swap endangered Americans. Fox News Sunday scheduled former Attorney General Michael Mukasey, who called the deal a "ghastly transaction," and former Army Vice Chief of Staff Gen. Jack Keane. NBC's "Meet the Press" was pre-empted by French Open coverage. Radio producer Matt Binder documented social media posts showing conservatives who had long urged leaders to "leave no man behind" and bring Bergdahl home at any cost reversing their position after the swap. The Huffington Post reported that Republican lawmakers critical of the Taliban release had previously pressed the administration to secure Bergdahl's return. A letter to the editor criticized the swap as a "big mistake" and the Rose Garden appearance with Bergdahl's parents as a "photo-op flop," expressing disillusionment with Obama.

summary: New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie's supporters are in the early stages of forming a leadership political action committee that would allow him to travel, hire staff and lay groundwork for a possible 2016 presidential campaign, several sources told CNN on Tuesday. The committee is expected to be formed soon, possibly before the end of the month, one supporter said. Former Republican Governors Association executive director Phil Cox is involved in the effort; Christie chaired the RGA during the 2014 election cycle. The New York Times first reported the move toward forming the PAC. The PAC would not begin operating before Christie's scheduled attendance at the Jan. 21 swearing-in of Maryland Gov.-elect Larry Hogan, one of several Republican governors elected in 2014 under Christie's RGA chairmanship, according to the Times. Former Florida Gov. Jeb Bush established his own leadership PAC last week as he explores a possible bid, and former Massachusetts Gov. Mitt Romney, the 2012 Republican nominee, recently told donors he is considering another run. Christie was in Iowa on Friday as he weighs a presidential run, attending the inauguration of Iowa Gov. Terry Branstad in Des Moines. The appearance was part of a tour of swearing-in ceremonies for Republican governors he helped elect as RGA chair. Christie told reporters he would hold private meetings in the city before returning to New Jersey later in the day. He repeated that he feels no pressure to decide quickly. "We're not voting in Iowa here for nearly 13 months. So let's everybody take a deep breath," Christie said. "I don't know about you, but I don't feel the need to rush something as serious as deciding if you want to run for the president of the United States." Christie has made numerous visits to the leadoff caucus state and is scheduled to return next week for a conservative summit. Iowa Republican Party Chairman Jeff Kaufmann met with Christie Friday and described a "free-flowing conversation." "He has a very big personality, a very straightforward guy. summary:
Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia died Saturday at a resort in Texas, immediately elevating the question of his successor to the center of the presidential campaign. Prominent Republicans called for the next president to make the nomination, while President Obama said he would nominate a replacement despite objections.

At Saturday night's Republican presidential debate, former Florida Gov. Jeb Bush said Republicans need to "fight and fight and fight" to get conservatives nominated and confirmed to the Supreme Court. Describing himself as an "Article Two guy" who believes in a strong executive branch, Bush said President Obama should nominate a "consensus" replacement — a "lover of liberty" who "believes in limited government" in Scalia's tradition.

On Sunday, appearing on CNN's "State of the Union," Bush was asked about his father's and brother's Supreme Court appointees. He called President George H.W. Bush's 1990 appointment of David Souter "unfortunate," saying Souter "wandered off into the liberal camp for sure." Conservatives have long criticized the appointment; Souter's 2009 retirement allowed Obama to appoint Sonia Sotomayor. Bush defended his brother's choice of Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr., saying he was disappointed in the Affordable Care Act ruling but that Roberts "made some really good rulings beyond that."

Bush said the lesson from the Souter experience is to pick someone with "a proven, longstanding record, a history that you can point to" — "the Scalia approach." He added, "He was very consistent on his interpretation and his rulings. And that's what we need." Like other Republican candidates, Bush said he supports a Senate delay of confirmation until a new president takes office next year, and he hopes to be that president.

Hillary Clinton campaign chairman John Podesta's verified Twitter account was hacked Wednesday night. A tweet reading "I've switched teams. Vote Trump 2016. Hi pol" was posted to the account, though sources differ on the exact wording. The tweet was quickly deleted. Clinton spokesman Nick Merrill confirmed the account had been hacked and said the campaign had informed Twitter and was working to secure it. Podesta said on Tuesday that the FBI had contacted him over the weekend regarding what he described as a "victim of a criminal hack" and that he was working with them. "It doesn't feel great," Podesta said. "But I am kind of zen about it at this stage, personally."

The hack occurred amid the ongoing release of Podesta's emails by WikiLeaks, which began publishing more than 5,000 of his messages in recent days. The emails have been embarrassing for the Clinton campaign, revealing internal deliberations and some off-color comments. Podesta has accused Russian intelligence agencies of being behind the email leak and suggested the Trump campaign may be involved. Following the latest email release, which included Podesta's Apple ID and password, several of his accounts were reportedly compromised. The "Hi pol" in the hacker's tweet appeared to reference 4chan's "politically incorrect" board. Social media users criticized Podesta's security practices, urging the use of two-factor authentication and stronger passwords.

summary:
A gunman opened fire Wednesday morning at a Republican congressional baseball practice in Alexandria, Virginia, wounding five people, among them House Majority Whip Steve Scalise of Louisiana. Scalise remained in critical condition Wednesday night. Rep. Bill Johnson, Republican of Ohio, who was at the practice, said the members had been "sitting ducks" and called it an "act of God" that the shooter's aim was thrown off; he added that many lawmakers jumped into the first-base dugout and the gunman then worked his way around behind the fence. President Trump delivered a statement from the Diplomatic Room of the White House urging Americans to come together, saying that despite differences, those who serve in the capital do so because they love the country, and that the nation is strongest when unified.

In the wake of the shooting, the House Natural Resources Federal Lands Subcommittee canceled a hearing scheduled for Wednesday morning on the Sportsmen's Heritage and Recreational Enhancement Act, an 18-provision bill covering guns, hunting and outdoor recreation sponsored by Rep. Jeff Duncan, Republican of South Carolina, who was at the practice. Subcommittee spokeswoman Molly Block confirmed the cancellation. The Senate Appropriations Committee also postponed a hearing with the Senate Sergeant at Arms and Capitol Police Chief Matthew Verderosa. Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Rep. John Conyers of Michigan postponed a news conference planned to discuss a lawsuit against President Trump. Other Capitol events proceeded, including separate hearings at which Secretary of State Rex Tillerson and Defense Secretary Jim Mattis testified. Audio of the shooting recorded from nearby by Tryshah Taylor shortly after the incident began was obtained by The Hill.

summary: The United States on Saturday ordered all non-essential employees of its mission to Somalia to leave Mogadishu, citing specific threat information against U.S. personnel at Mogadishu International Airport. The State Department said the security situation in Somalia remains extremely unstable and the threat to U.S. citizens critical. The U.S. Mission to Somalia has been based in neighboring Kenya since the closure of the U.S. embassy in 1991; the first U.S. ambassador to Somalia in a quarter-century told Radio Muqdisho in June that offices for a permanent diplomatic presence were expected to open in Mogadishu late this year. Several countries maintain embassies at the heavily fortified airport. The order followed U.S. military strikes on Friday against Islamic State group-allied fighters in the northern Puntland region, described as the first such strikes in Somalia; the military said several terrorists were killed. Last month, a truck bombing in Mogadishu killed more than 350 people according to Somali officials, making it the deadliest attack in the country's modern history; the State Department confirmed at least 300 dead and said two U.S. citizens were among the victims. The attack has been blamed on the al-Qaida-linked extremist group al-Shabab. Somali intelligence officials said the bomb was intended for the airport but detonated in a crowded street after soldiers opened fire and flattened a tire. ISIS-linked fighters in Somalia are reported to have switched allegiance from al-Shabab in recent years.

summary:
President-elect Donald Trump on Thursday posted on Twitter that "The United States must greatly strengthen and expand its nuclear capability until such time as the world comes to its senses regarding nukes." The tweet came hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin said he wanted to strengthen Russia's own nuclear capabilities in the coming year. At a news conference Friday, Putin said Russia and the United States need to discuss ways to "normalize our relations" and downplayed suggestions of a new nuclear arms race, calling Trump's Twitter comments "nothing new." 

Newly appointed White House Press Secretary Sean Spicer told CNN that Trump's message was directed at Russia and any other country considering increasing nuclear stockpiles. "The bottom line is this, the president is going to put our nation's security and safety first ... he's not going to be a passive president," Spicer said. "He's going to be active and make sure that our safety is number one." In a telephone conversation with MSNBC "Morning Joe" co-host Mika Brzezinski, Trump said, "Let it be an arms race. We will outmatch them at every pass and outlast them all," according to Brzezinski.

China's Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Hua Chunying said Friday that Beijing is "paying close attention" to what nuclear weapons policy Trump's administration will follow. Hua said countries with the largest nuclear arsenals should bear special responsibility for disarmament and take the lead in "drastically and tangibly cutting the number of nuclear weapons." China advocates a ban on and destruction of nuclear weapons, Hua said. The United States and Russia hold the vast majority of the world's nuclear weapons, with more than 7,000 warheads each, while China has an estimated 260, according to the Arms Control Association. New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie raised nearly $6.2 million for his re-election campaign through May 3, according to his campaign. The Republican governor has 14,260 donors from all 50 states and the District of Columbia, with 85 percent of contributions coming from New Jersey. Campaign chairman William Palatucci called the haul "an unprecedented show of support" and "widespread enthusiasm" for Christie. The campaign reported over $3.4 million cash on hand after spending $1.2 million last week on its first television advertisement in the New York City and Philadelphia markets. Christie's Democratic opponent, state Sen. Barbara Buono, has raised $738,000 and qualified for $1.02 million in public matching funds, according to The Star-Ledger. A Quinnipiac University poll showed Christie leading Buono by 32 points. The governor attended a Silicon Valley fundraiser hosted by Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg in February. The finance report will be filed Monday with the state Election Law Enforcement Commission.

On Friday, while speaking to a group of schoolchildren in Trenton, Christie killed a spider that crawled on his desk near his phone. He told the students that one fun part of being governor is being allowed to kill bugs on your desk without getting into trouble. Christie tweeted that he had "saved a few school children from a spider." People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals President Ingrid Newkirk said Christie probably killed it without thinking, adding that "some people put the spider outside, but spiders are often scary" and that can prevent people from pondering their worth.

NBC announced Tuesday that Christie will guest-host an hour of the "Today" show on May 24, broadcasting from the Jersey shore as part of the program's "Great American Adventure" road trip. The location has not been finalized. The road trip involves the show's anchors traveling to five U.S. destinations in a single week. Christie has emphasized the Jersey shore's importance as a tourist destination since Superstorm Sandy. Former Alaska Gov. Sarah Palin and former first lady Laura Bush have previously co-hosted an hour of the morning show. A spokesman confirmed Tuesday that Christie underwent weight loss surgery in February. Christie is running for a second term in November.

summary:
President Donald Trump and House Speaker Nancy Pelosi exchanged letters and public statements on Thursday as the partial government shutdown continued. On Wednesday, Pelosi sent Trump a letter suggesting they reschedule his State of the Union address, slated for January 29, unless the government re-opened that week; she proposed delivering the address in writing as an alternative. Trump responded Thursday with a letter informing Pelosi that a congressional delegation trip she had planned to Brussels, Egypt, and Afghanistan "has been postponed" while the shutdown continues.

Earlier Thursday, Pelosi held a press conference at 10:45 a.m. Eastern, blaming Trump for what she called the "TrumpShutdown" and reiterating that she would not agree to funding for a border wall even after the government reopens. "I'm not for a wall," she told reporters.

Trump spoke at the Pentagon later Thursday on missile defense, urging Democrats to circumvent Pelosi and negotiate directly with him on border security. "While many Democrats in the House and Senate would like to make a deal, Speaker Pelosi will not let them negotiate. The party has been hijacked by the open-borders fringe," he said. He added that he hoped Democratic lawmakers would "step forward to do what's right for our country."

Trump said he had tried to hold two meetings at the White House with Democrats this week. One drew no Democratic attendees; a second with the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus included some Democrats, who agreed to meet but stated in a statement that negotiations could not occur until the government is fully opened.

summary: Israel agreed to a 12-hour halt in its military offensive in Gaza starting Saturday morning, according to an early Saturday announcement by the Israeli military. Israeli media reported that Hamas also agreed to the initial lull. The military said efforts to locate and destroy Hamas tunnels would continue during the pause, that Gaza civilians who had been asked to evacuate should not return, and that it would respond if its forces or Israeli civilians came under fire. The decision came hours after Israel's security cabinet rejected a proposal by U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry for a seven-day cease-fire and further talks, according to a minister who attended the meeting. A senior Israeli official later said the cabinet had "expressed its position in principle on some initial draft proposals that were not formally presented" and that Israel would continue working with Kerry. Later on Saturday, Israel proposed a four-hour extension of the truce. Hamas official Sami Abu Zuhri rejected the extension, sending a text message stating: "No agreement to extending the calm for an additional four hours." Hamas fired five rockets at Israel late Saturday. Israel's Cabinet then extended the humanitarian cease-fire for 24 hours but said it would respond to any attacks from Gaza. In Paris, Kerry and European foreign ministers from the United States, Britain, Germany, Italy, Turkey and Qatar gathered to discuss how to build on the 12-hour lull and transform it into a sustainable truce. French Foreign Minister Laurent Fabius said: "All of us call on the parties to extend the humanitarian ceasefire that is currently under way." The Palestinian health ministry reported the death toll from 19 days of fighting had topped 1,000, many of them civilians, as officials recovered bodies in devastated neighborhoods. Forty-two Israelis have reportedly been killed. The temporary truce allowed residents to return home, gather supplies and witness the destruction. In the West Bank, at least six Palestinians were killed during clashes with Israeli forces.

summary: Former FBI Director James B. Comey testified before the Senate Intelligence Committee on Thursday. During the hearing Comey said he had used a friend to leak a memo he wrote documenting an exchange with President Trump. He also described a January 27 dinner at the White House that he learned would be "just the two of us," for which he broke a date with his wife, and said the arrangement made him "uneasy." President Trump responded on Friday in a tweet: "Despite so many false statements and lies, total and complete vindication…and WOW, Comey is a leaker!" Trump's personal lawyer, Marc Kasowitz, said at a press conference after the hearing that it would be left to the "appropriate authorities" whether to investigate the leaks Comey described along with other leaks from the White House. A columnist wrote that Comey's account of his interactions with Trump resembled the experience of a woman harassed by a powerful, predatory boss. Across the country, bars and other venues held watch parties for the testimony. In Washington, D.C., people began lining up Wednesday night for public seating; Shaw's Tavern served Russian vodka, "covfefe coffee" and an "FBI breakfast" of French toast, bacon and ice cream. Watch parties were also reported in Houston at Axelrad Beer Garden, on the West Coast including a yoga viewing event in Los Angeles, in Sacramento, and by the Dallas Democratic Party, which played bingo during the hearing.

summary: Julian Assange, founder of WikiLeaks, was arrested Thursday in London after Ecuador allowed British officers into its embassy, where he had lived since 2012. U.S. authorities charged him with conspiracy to commit computer intrusion related to the release of classified information provided by Chelsea Manning, carrying up to five years in prison. The Swedish prosecutor's office said it received a request from an accuser's lawyer to reopen a rape investigation dropped in 2017; deputy chief prosecutor Eva-Marie Persson said prosecutors would determine how to proceed with no set time frame. More than 70 British legislators signed a letter urging Home Secretary Sajid Javid to prioritize extradition to Sweden if that country requests it. President Donald Trump told reporters he knew "nothing about WikiLeaks" and "it's not my thing," despite having said "I love WikiLeaks" during the 2016 campaign and displaying a poster about Hillary Clinton's emails in his debate war room. Then-Attorney General Jeff Sessions had said in April 2017 that arresting Assange was a Justice Department priority. Assange denied wrongdoing.

summary:
Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), 86, the oldest Republican senator, said Monday he will not attend the 2020 Republican National Convention because of the coronavirus pandemic. "I'm not going to go. And I'm not going to go because of the virus situation," Grassley told Iowa reporters on a conference call, according to the Des Moines Register. He had attended every Republican convention since his election to the Senate in 1980, making this the first he would miss in 40 years.

The convention was initially scheduled for Aug. 24-27 at the Spectrum Center in Charlotte, North Carolina. Republicans moved the majority of events, including President Trump's nomination acceptance speech, to Jacksonville, Florida, after a dispute with North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper and Charlotte Mayor Vi Lyles over social-distancing requirements and mask mandates. Trump said the move "looked good" when agreed upon weeks earlier, but acknowledged cases were now "spiking up a little bit" in Florida. "It really depends on the timing. Look, we're very flexible, we could do a lot of things," he said.

Florida has seen record numbers of positive COVID-19 tests in recent weeks, and Jacksonville has mandated masks indoors and in public places. Several other Republican officials have said they have not decided whether to attend. The United States death toll from the virus has exceeded 130,000. A scaled-back Democratic National Convention is scheduled for Aug. 17-20 in Milwaukee.

summary: Twitter permanently suspended the account of former Ku Klux Klan leader David Duke on Friday for repeated violations of its rules on hateful conduct, the company said. A Twitter spokesperson confirmed the suspension, stating the account was "permanently suspended for repeated violations of the Twitter Rules on hateful conduct." The company did not specify which posts triggered the ban. Twitter's hateful conduct policy prohibits promoting violence or threatening attacks against people based on religious affiliation, race, and ethnic origin. The action aligns with recently updated guidance on harmful links, which previously covered malware and terrorist websites and was expanded this week to include "hateful conduct and violence," according to a spokesperson. Under the new rules, Twitter may suspend accounts dedicated to sharing hateful content or that attempt to circumvent blocks on links to such material. Duke led the KKK from 1974 to 1978 and had maintained an active Twitter account since 2009. His YouTube channel was suspended late last month. A Twitter spokesperson had said last month, before the removal, that Duke had not been banned because he was not currently a KKK member and had publicly distanced himself from the organization. The KKK, founded during Reconstruction after the Civil War, is the oldest white supremacist group in the United States and has expressed anti-Black, anti-semitic, anti-immigrant, and anti-gay views. Twitter has faced increasing pressure to address hateful content and misinformation, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic.

summary:
President Barack Obama was inaugurated for a second term. In his inaugural address, he devoted a single word — "deficit" — to the fiscal issue that had repeatedly brought Washington to the brink of crisis during his first term. He acknowledged that "outworn programs are inadequate to the needs of our time" and called for training more math and science teachers, building roads, and funding more research labs, without specifying how such spending would be reconciled with debt stabilization.

The ceremony included Kelly Clarkson singing "My Country 'Tis of Thee," Reverend Luis León delivering the benediction, and Beyoncé performing the national anthem. Former vice-presidential nominee Paul Ryan attended. After the address, Obama signed documents formalizing his inauguration and transmitted to the Senate his nominations of Chuck Hagel, Jack Lew, John Kerry, and John Brennan for cabinet and national security positions, saying he expected the Senate to confirm them "with great dispatch."

Shortly after the speech, the campaign sent an email from "Barack" to supporters thanking them and promoting Organizing for Action, the advocacy group formed from the former Obama for America campaign organization. The email included a link to a video featuring Michelle Obama describing the group's purpose. Organizing for Action was designed to support the legislative agenda, train grassroots organizers, and organize around local issues. According to USA TODAY's Fredreka Schouten, the group can run issue-focused advertising but cannot run ads explicitly calling for the election or defeat of specific candidates.

summary: The Virginia Supreme Court on Thursday reversed a 2012 jury verdict that had found the state negligent in the deaths of two students killed during the April 16, 2007, shootings at Virginia Tech. The justices ruled that the university had no duty to warn students of potential acts by the gunman, Seung-Hui Cho, who shot two students in a dormitory shortly after 7 a.m. before killing 30 more people in Norris Hall and then himself, for a total of 32 students and faculty members killed. The lawsuit was brought by the families of Julia Pryde and Erin Peterson, who had refused a state settlement offer in 2008 and sought $10 million in damages, asserting that the university delayed a campuswide alert that might have saved lives. According to the court ruling, campus authorities delayed the alert for about two hours to notify the victims' families and investigate further; the alert went out minutes before Cho continued his rampage. A Montgomery County jury in March 2012 had ruled the state was negligent and awarded each family $4 million, but a judge reduced the awards to the state cap of $100,000 each. The Supreme Court disagreed with the negligence finding. "Based on the limited information" the school had, the ruling stated, "it cannot be said that it was known or reasonably foreseeable that students in Norris Hall would fall victim to criminal harm." Attorney General Ken Cuccinelli's spokesman, Brian Gottstein, said the ruling supports the contention that "Cho was the lone person responsible for this tragedy" and that neither Tech nor state officials were negligent. Robert T. Hall, a lawyer for the families, said the ruling "was very much a surprise" and asked, "If you have a duty to protect, a duty to keep safe, a duty to ensure safety, how do you do that if you don't warn them there is a gunman on the loose?"

summary: President Donald Trump on Friday tweeted that changes are coming to the H-1B visa program that would bring "simplicity and certainty" to holders' stay, including "a potential path to citizenship," and said the administration wants "to encourage talented and highly skilled people to pursue career options in the U.S." The H-1B program allows U.S. companies to hire foreign workers in specialized occupations, particularly in technology and science, and is capped by law at 85,000 visas per year, with demand exceeding supply so that visas are awarded by lottery. The administration revised the application process in 2018 to favor applicants with advanced degrees. Trump had said in 2018 that his administration planned to overhaul the program but did not offer specifics on Friday. The tweet came as a partial government shutdown entered its fourth week amid an impasse over Trump's demand for $5.7 billion to fund a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border, a central 2016 campaign promise. Trump had repeatedly said Mexico would pay for the wall but backtracked from that position on Thursday and was said to be considering using emergency disaster funds instead. Separately, during a Thursday visit to the U.S.-Mexico border, Trump argued for wall funding by stating that wheels are older than walls, saying "a wheel works and a wall works," a claim that drew responses on Twitter.

summary: Julian Assange, founder of WikiLeaks, was arrested Thursday at the Ecuadorian embassy in London, where he had lived since 2012. British police took him into custody after a judge found him guilty of breaching bail conditions related to a Swedish rape investigation that had been suspended two years earlier; he was also arrested on a U.S. extradition warrant. The U.S. Justice Department charged Assange with conspiracy to "knowingly access a computer, without authorization and exceeding authorized access" to obtain classified information that "could be used to the injury of the United States," alleging he assisted Chelsea Manning in 2010 in determining a password stored on a Pentagon computer. The American Civil Liberties Union condemned the arrest, with Ben Wizner, director of its Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project, stating that any prosecution for WikiLeaks' publishing operations would be "unprecedented and unconstitutional" and would set a dangerous precedent for journalists. Edward Snowden also condemned the arrest as a "dark moment for press freedom." More than 70 British legislators signed a letter Friday urging Home Secretary Sajid Javid to ensure Assange faces Swedish justice if prosecutors there reopen the sexual misconduct allegation. President Donald Trump told reporters he knew "nothing about WikiLeaks," despite having said "I love WikiLeaks" during his campaign and, according to Bloomberg, displaying a poster of Assange in his debate war room reading "Dear Hillary, I miss reading your classified emails." Then-Attorney General Jeff Sessions had said in April 2017 that Assange's arrest would become a Justice Department priority. Assange has denied wrongdoing.

summary: A federal judge on Monday temporarily blocked North Dakota's new law banning abortions once a fetal heartbeat is detected, which can occur as early as six weeks into pregnancy. U.S. District Judge Daniel Hovland in Bismarck issued a preliminary injunction preventing the law from taking effect on Aug. 1 while courts consider its merits. Hovland wrote that the law is "clearly invalid and unconstitutional" and "in direct contradiction to a litany of United States Supreme Court cases addressing restraints on abortion," citing Roe v. Wade (1973) and subsequent precedent. In his order, Hovland also wrote that "the State has extended an invitation to an expensive court battle over a law restricting abortions that is a blatant violation of the constitutional guarantees afforded to all women." The lawsuit was filed by the Center for Reproductive Rights on behalf of North Dakota's only abortion clinic. The law had passed the Republican-controlled legislature and was signed by Gov. Jack Dalrymple earlier this year. Legal experts said the law would not survive because it challenges the Supreme Court's viability standard, which permits abortion until a fetus can survive outside the womb, typically around 24 weeks. Center for Reproductive Rights legal program director Bebe Anderson said: "The nation's most extreme abortion ban has been blocked, and the message to hostile politicians could not be clearer: The rights of women guaranteed under the U.S. Constitution and protected by 40 years of Supreme Court precedent cannot be legislated away."

summary: Mitt Romney won the Conservative Political Action Conference presidential straw poll with 38 percent of the vote, according to results released Saturday. Rick Santorum placed second with 31 percent, followed by Newt Gingrich at 15 percent and Ron Paul at 12 percent. The poll, conducted by Fabrizio McLaughlin and sponsored by The Washington Times, drew 3,408 respondents and was held online for the first time, producing the second-highest turnout in the conference's history. Paul had won the straw poll in the previous two years, according to one account, while another noted his 2011 victory. Romney had encouraged students to attend the conference, and 44 percent of them participated in the poll. The three candidates addressed the conference on Friday, one report said, while the straw poll results were announced on Saturday. Separately, polling in Michigan showed Santorum gaining ground in a state considered favorable to Romney, whose father served as governor there. Both the Romney campaign and its super PAC planned heavy spending in Michigan to counter Santorum's momentum. A Santorum victory in Michigan would give him a 4-0 record in Midwestern states and weaken Romney's standing ahead of Super Tuesday. Arizona, which votes the same day, was seen as more favorable to Santorum demographically, but his limited funds forced a strategic focus on Michigan.

summary:
South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley is considering a short list of five candidates to replace U.S. Sen. Jim DeMint, who announced he would resign in January to lead the Heritage Foundation. According to a CNN report citing a Republican close to Haley, the list includes U.S. Rep. Tim Scott, U.S. Rep. Trey Gowdy, former state Attorney General Henry McMaster, Department of Health and Environmental Control director Catherine Templeton, and former South Carolina first lady Jenny Sanford. The Republican close to Haley said all five expressed interest when contacted by Haley's office. Sanford, whose ex-husband Mark Sanford served as governor from 2003 to 2011 before leaving the state without notifying staff to visit his girlfriend in Argentina, told the Associated Press she had spoken with one of Haley's representatives and said, "If asked, I'd seriously consider accepting the offer." Scott, who is African American, has been frequently mentioned in news reports as a leading candidate. The appointee would serve until a 2014 special election for the remaining two years of DeMint's term.

Haley told South Carolina reporters Wednesday that her selection criteria emphasize results over tenure. "It is not about time in office, which I think is the wrong way of looking at government," she said. "It's the effect and the result they can show in office." She noted that two potential appointees — Sanford and Templeton — have no experience in elected office, adding that she herself had no political history when elected to the state House in 2004 and came from the business world, like Sanford. Haley also said, "We are never going to find someone as conservative and staunch as Jim DeMint... What I think we will find is someone who understands the state of South Carolina and the crisis we're going through."

A poll found South Carolina voters' first choice for the appointment was comedian Stephen Colbert, with Sanford second. Sanford has a 44 percent approval rating; Mark Sanford has a 30 percent approval rating. Mark Sanford has said he could run for the seat in 2014, potentially setting up a Republican primary contest between the former spouses.

summary:
The Congressional Budget Office reported Tuesday that raising the federal minimum wage to $10.10 an hour by 2016 would reduce total employment by about 500,000 workers, or 0.3 percent, with estimated losses ranging from zero to one million, while lifting 900,000 workers out of poverty. summary:

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit in Richmond heard the first appellate arguments on the constitutionality of the 2010 Affordable Care Act on Tuesday. A three-judge panel — all appointed by Democratic presidents — presided over the consolidated hearing combining two cases: one brought by Liberty University and another by the federal government after a lower court ruled against it in a suit filed by Virginia Attorney General Ken Cuccinelli. The panel comprised senior judge Diana Gribbon Motz, appointed by President Bill Clinton in 1994, and Obama appointees Andre Davis and James Wynn. The full 14-member court is evenly divided between Democratic and Republican appointees; the odds of randomly drawing three Democratic appointees were roughly 10 to 1. Court observer Brad Joondeph wrote on the ACA litigation blog that the panel composition "could not have turned out much better" for the administration.

summary:
Alan Krueger, chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers, announced Tuesday that he will return to Princeton University as Bendheim professor of Economics and Public Affairs in time for the fall term. In a statement, Krueger said he is grateful to President Obama "for the chance to do what I could to help the nation recover from the worst economic crisis since the Great Depression." Krueger, a labor economist who previously served as assistant secretary for economic policy at the Treasury Department and joined the White House staff in 2011, has been the public face of the administration for the monthly jobs report. His departure was expected because of the prospect he might lose tenure at Princeton.

Jason Furman, principal deputy director of the National Economic Council, is expected to be nominated as Krueger's successor. President Obama intends to nominate Furman, according to a person familiar with the decision who spoke on condition of anonymity because the nomination has not been announced. Furman, who holds a doctorate in economics from Harvard, served as an economist in the Clinton administration, worked at the World Bank, and advised several Democrats including John Kerry during his presidential campaign. Before joining the Obama campaign, he worked at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities and the Hamilton Project, a research group developed by former Treasury Secretary Robert E. Rubin. Furman's research has focused on fiscal and tax policy, Social Security and monetary policy. The Council of Economic Advisers is one of two conduits of economic advice to the president; the other is the National Economic Council. If confirmed by the Senate, Furman would replace Krueger. The nomination might signal a more powerful role for the council, which in recent years has been less central than the National Economic Council and the Treasury Department.

Obama praised Krueger's stewardship, saying, "He understands who we're fighting for — middle-class families and anyone working to climb into the middle class. Alan was the driving force behind many of the economic policies that I have proposed that will grow our economy and create middle-class jobs."

After Thursday night's Republican debate in Houston, Texas Senator Ted Cruz told CNN's Jake Tapper that he and Florida Senator Marco Rubio are friends and that both would make a better candidate and a better president than Donald Trump. During the debate, both Cruz and Rubio directed their attacks at Trump, who entered the contest after consecutive victories in New Hampshire, South Carolina and Nevada. The debate preceded Super Tuesday, when a dozen states will vote. Cruz, who won the Iowa caucuses earlier in February, is seeking to stop Trump in his home state of Texas, which votes on Tuesday. Cruz said he is the only candidate who has beaten Trump and is positioned to do so again on Super Tuesday, noting that he leads in Texas polling while Rubio trails Trump in Florida. Cruz also criticized Rubio for not attacking Trump sooner, saying he was glad Rubio finally took on Trump during the debate but that it should have happened earlier and that other candidates had been afraid to challenge Trump. Cruz said the debate provided clarity and argued that Trump would likely lose to Democratic front-runner Hillary Clinton in a general election, which he called a very bad outcome for the country. The debate also featured Trump defending Planned Parenthood, discussing a hand-raising pledge on the nominee, commenting on the size of his hands, and disavowing the Ku Klux Klan; Governor John Kasich said he would win Ohio; and Rubio stated that "the climate is always changing."

summary:
The House of Representatives voted Wednesday to impeach President Donald Trump for incitement of insurrection, exactly one week after a mob attacked the Capitol while lawmakers were convening to approve President-elect Joe Biden's Electoral College victory. The vote was 232-197 on a single article. Ten Republicans joined Democrats, making Trump the first president in U.S. history to be impeached twice and marking the most bipartisan presidential impeachment in modern times. Four Republicans did not vote: Representatives Kay Granger of Texas, Andy Harris of Maryland, Gregory Murphy of North Carolina, and Daniel Webster of Florida. The previous impeachment saw every House Republican vote against both articles.

Representative Liz Cheney of Wyoming, the No. 3 House Republican, announced the day before that she would vote to impeach, calling it a "vote of conscience." She wrote: "None of this would have happened without the President. The President could have immediately and forcefully intervened to stop the violence. He did not. There has never been a greater betrayal by a President of the United States of his office and his oath to the Constitution."

The House must vote to send the article of impeachment to trigger a Senate trial. The Senate is not expected to convene a trial before January 19. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell supports the impeachment proceedings and is "done" and "furious" with Trump, according to sources familiar with his thinking who spoke to Fox News.

Nebraska Governor Pete Ricketts, a Republican and Trump supporter, criticized the impeachment, saying it "serves no good purpose" and will further divide the nation. He said the president's time in office is nearly over after his November loss to Biden and added: "We ought to focus on healing, bringing Democrats and Republicans together and focusing on a smooth transition."

Initial jobless claims have remained below 375,000 for most of the year, a level economists associate with steady hiring. The housing market continued to recover, with builder confidence, sales, and prices increasing, though the sector still faces low inventory and tight credit conditions. summary: Ukrainian police announced Thursday they had opened an investigation into whether former U.S. Ambassador Marie Yovanovitch was under illegal surveillance before her recall. The announcement followed the release two days earlier by Democratic lawmakers of documents showing Lev Parnas, an associate of President Donald Trump's personal lawyer Rudy Giuliani, communicating about Yovanovitch's removal. The materials included messages from a Connecticut Republican congressional candidate who claimed to have Yovanovitch under surveillance and suggested he could arrange for her to be harmed. The Ukrainian Interior Ministry, which runs the police forces, said in a statement that Ukraine's position is not to interfere in the domestic affairs of the United States, but that it cannot ignore such illegal activities on its territory. The statement added that the published messages contain facts of possible violations of Ukrainian law and the Vienna Convention on diplomatic relations. It also acknowledged the messages might have been just bravado and fake conversation between two U.S. citizens. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo had not commented on the possible threats to one of his department's officials. Ukraine also said it would investigate Russia's alleged hacking of Burisma, the gas company frequently mentioned in the impeachment inquiry. The investigation comes as the Senate prepares to begin an impeachment trial of President Trump on Tuesday. Giuliani, a key figure in the alleged pressure campaign to get Kyiv to investigate former Vice President Joe Biden, said he would love to be a witness at the trial and asserted he has facts, witnesses, documents and recordings that are being suppressed to protect Biden. The Government Accountability Office said Thursday that the administration's freezing of nearly $400 million in military aid to Ukraine broke the law. No evidence has emerged that Biden acted improperly regarding Ukraine. The Senate is widely expected to acquit Trump along mostly party lines.

summary: Multiple polls released in early October 2012 showed a tight presidential race between President Barack Obama and Republican challenger Mitt Romney. An American Research Poll released October 9 found Obama at 47 percent and Romney at 48 percent among likely voters in Ohio, where both candidates were campaigning that day for the state's 18 electoral votes. National Gallup tracking among registered voters conducted October 4 through 6, in the three days following the first presidential debate on October 3, showed the candidates tied at 47 percent each. That represented a shift from the three days before the debate, September 30 through October 2, when Obama led 50 percent to 45 percent. Gallup's seven-day rolling average as of Saturday interviewing gave Obama a 3-point lead, 49 percent to 46 percent. Gallup also reported its first likely-voter estimate, based on interviews conducted October 2 through 8, showing Romney ahead 49 percent to 47 percent. The same survey found Obama leading among registered voters 49 percent to 46 percent. Both figures were within the margin of error, and Gallup said neither provided a statistically significant lead. The five-point swing toward Romney when moving from registered to likely voters indicated a turnout advantage for Romney, according to the pollster. In debate-reaction findings, two-thirds of Americans surveyed by Gallup in the two days after the debate said they watched it. Seventy-two percent said Romney won, compared with 20 percent for Obama. Among Democrats, 49 percent said Romney won versus 39 percent for Obama; among independents, 70 percent favored Romney and 19 percent Obama. Gallup described Romney's 52-point margin as the largest in a debate-reaction poll it has measured, exceeding Bill Clinton's 42-point margin over George H.W. Bush in a 1992 town-hall debate. Gallup's analysis suggested Romney's initial post-debate gains among registered voters might be short-lived, but that his turnout advantage meant Obama would need a strong lead among all registered voters to be assured of winning the popular vote. The pollster concluded that if the election were held at that time, the race would be too close to call.
